cards.topic: Calls and puts
cards.question: What is a call option and what is a put option?
cards.answer: A **call** gives the holder the **right, but not the obligation, to buy** an underlying asset at a fixed price (the **strike** $K$) on or before a given date (the **expiry** $T$). A **put** gives the right to **sell** at the strike. The buyer pays an upfront **premium** to the seller (the **writer**) for this right. At expiry a call pays $\max(S_T-K,0)$ and a put pays $\max(K-S_T,0)$. So a long call is a bullish bet with limited downside (the premium), and a long put is a bearish bet or insurance against a fall. The seller receives the premium and takes the opposite, potentially large, risk.

follow_ups.q: Who has the obligation in an option?
follow_ups.a: The seller (writer). If the buyer exercises, the call seller must deliver the underlying at $K$ and the put seller must buy it at $K$. The buyer only has a right.

follow_ups.q: Why would anyone sell an option if the loss can be unlimited?
follow_ups.a: To earn the premium. Implied vol tends to be above realised vol on average (the variance risk premium), so systematic sellers, hedged or partly covered, make money on average in exchange for tail risk. Covered call selling is a classic yield-enhancement strategy.

follow_ups.q: What is cash vs physical settlement?
follow_ups.a: Physical: shares actually change hands at the strike. Cash: only the payoff amount is paid. Index options are cash-settled because you cannot deliver an index easily.

cards.topic: Payoff vs P&L
cards.question: What is the difference between an option's payoff and its P&L? Draw the P&L of a long call, short call, long put and short put.
cards.answer: The **payoff** is what the option pays at expiry, e.g. $\max(S_T-K,0)$ for a call. The **P&L** (profit and loss) nets off the premium: for the buyer, P&L $=$ payoff $-$ premium (ideally the premium compounded to expiry). A long call's P&L is $-c$ below the strike, then rises one-for-one, crossing zero at the breakeven $K+c$. A short call is the mirror image: $+c$ capped gain, unlimited loss above $K+c$. A long put loses $p$ above $K$ and gains as the stock falls, with breakeven $K-p$ and a maximum gain of $K-p$. A short put earns $p$ at most and loses down to $-(K-p)$ if the stock goes to zero. Before expiry, P&L is mark-to-market: today's option value minus what you paid.

follow_ups.q: What is the maximum loss of a short put?
follow_ups.a: Strike minus premium, reached if the stock goes to zero. It is large but bounded, unlike a short call whose loss is unbounded.

follow_ups.q: Can you lose money on a long call that expires in the money?
follow_ups.a: Yes, if the stock ends between $K$ and $K+c$: the payoff is positive but smaller than the premium. And before expiry, MtM can fall even if spot rises, e.g. if implied vol drops.

follow_ups.q: What does the P&L curve look like one month before expiry?
follow_ups.a: A smooth convex curve above the expiry hockey stick for a long option, the gap being time value. It converges to the hockey stick as expiry approaches.

cards.topic: Intrinsic and time value
cards.question: What are intrinsic value and time value of an option?
cards.answer: An option's price splits into **intrinsic value** plus **time value**. Intrinsic value is what you would get by exercising right now: $\max(S-K,0)$ for a call, $\max(K-S,0)$ for a put (some desks measure it against the forward instead of spot). Time value is everything else: the extra you pay for the chance that the option becomes more valuable before expiry. Time value comes from **volatility** and **time remaining** (plus a carry component from rates and dividends). It is largest for at-the-money options, where uncertainty about finishing in or out of the money is maximal, and it decays to zero at expiry - that decay is **theta**.

follow_ups.q: Where is time value highest?
follow_ups.a: At the money (more precisely near the forward). That is where uncertainty about the final exercise decision is greatest, and it is also where gamma and vega peak.

follow_ups.q: Can an option trade below intrinsic value?
follow_ups.a: An American option cannot (you would exercise immediately and pocket the difference). A European deep ITM put can trade below $K-S$ because the $K$ is received only at expiry, so it is worth about $Ke^{-rT}-S$.

follow_ups.q: How does time value evolve as expiry approaches?
follow_ups.a: It shrinks to zero; for ATM options roughly proportional to $\sqrt{T}$, so the decay accelerates in the last weeks.

cards.topic: Moneyness
cards.question: What do ITM, ATM and OTM mean? What is 'ATM forward' versus 'ATM spot'?
cards.answer: **Moneyness** says where the strike sits relative to the underlying. A call is **in-the-money** (ITM) if $S>K$, **at-the-money** (ATM) if $S\approx K$, **out-of-the-money** (OTM) if $S<K$; for puts it is the reverse. **ATM spot** means $K=S_0$; **ATM forward** (ATMF) means $K=F_0=S_0e^{(r-q)T}$, which is what traders usually mean because at that strike call and put have the same price (by put-call parity). Desks also measure moneyness by **delta**: a "25-delta put" is an OTM put with delta $-0.25$, the standard in FX quoting. Moneyness matters because Greeks and implied vol depend on it: gamma, vega and time value peak around ATM, and the vol smile is a function of moneyness.

follow_ups.q: What is a 25-delta put?
follow_ups.a: An OTM put whose strike is chosen so its delta is $-0.25$. Delta-based strikes are the standard in FX vol quoting (25-delta risk reversals and butterflies).

follow_ups.q: At which strike is a call worth the same as a put?
follow_ups.a: At the forward, $K=F_0$, by put-call parity.

follow_ups.q: Is an ATM spot call on a non-dividend stock worth more or less than the ATM spot put?
follow_ups.a: More, when $r>0$: the forward is above spot, so the call is effectively ITM relative to the forward.

cards.topic: American vs European options
cards.question: What is the difference between a European, an American and a Bermudan option? Which is worth more?
cards.answer: A **European** option can only be exercised at expiry; an **American** option can be exercised at any time up to expiry; a **Bermudan** can be exercised on a set of discrete dates (common in callable bonds and swaptions). Since the American gives strictly more rights, $V_{Am} \ge V_{Berm} \ge V_{Eu}$. The extra value is the **early-exercise premium**. For a call on a non-dividend-paying stock that premium is zero - you should never exercise early - so American and European calls are worth the same. For puts, and for calls on dividend-paying stocks, early exercise can be optimal, so American is worth strictly more. Single-stock listed options are typically American; index options (e.g. SPX, Euro Stoxx 50) are European and cash-settled. The names are just conventions, not geography.

follow_ups.q: Why is an American call on a non-dividend stock never exercised early?
follow_ups.a: Exercising gives $S-K$ now, but the call is always worth at least $S-Ke^{-rT} > S-K$. You would throw away time value and the interest on $K$. Selling the call (or shorting stock against it) always beats exercising.

follow_ups.q: How do you price an American option?
follow_ups.a: Binomial/trinomial trees with a max(exercise, continuation) check at each node, finite-difference PDE solvers with an obstacle constraint, or Longstaff-Schwartz regression Monte Carlo for multi-asset cases.

follow_ups.q: Where do you see Bermudan options?
follow_ups.a: Bermudan swaptions and callable bonds in rates; callable features and autocallables with discrete observation dates in equity structured products.

cards.topic: Forwards vs options
cards.question: What is the difference between a forward and an option? Why does a forward cost nothing to enter while an option has a premium?
cards.answer: A **forward** is an **obligation** to buy or sell at a fixed price $F$ at date $T$; its payoff $S_T-F$ is **linear** and can be negative. An **option** is a **right**; its payoff $(S_T-K)^+$ is **non-linear** (convex) and never negative. Because the forward price is set so that the contract is worth zero at inception, there is no upfront payment: gains and losses are symmetric. An option has a one-sided payoff, so the buyer must pay a **premium** for the protection against the bad side. Hedging-wise, a forward locks in a price (removes both downside and upside), whereas an option buys protection while **keeping the upside**. A long call minus a long put at the same strike equals a long forward - which is put-call parity.

follow_ups.q: How is a forward price determined?
follow_ups.a: By cost of carry: $F_0=S_0e^{(r-q)T}$ for a stock/index; for FX $F_0=S_0e^{(r_d-r_f)T}$. Otherwise you could buy spot, finance it and sell forward (or the reverse) for riskless profit.

follow_ups.q: Why might a corporate prefer an option to a forward?
follow_ups.a: When the exposure is uncertain (e.g. a tender they may not win) or when they want protection while keeping upside if the market moves in their favour. They pay a premium for that flexibility.

follow_ups.q: What is the delta and gamma of a forward?
follow_ups.a: Delta is $e^{-q(T-t)}$ in spot terms (about 1), gamma is zero: a forward is linear. That is why options, not forwards, are used to trade volatility.

cards.topic: Put-call parity
cards.question: What is put-call parity and why must it hold?
cards.answer: For European options with the same strike $K$ and expiry $T$: $C - P = S_0e^{-qT} - Ke^{-rT}$, or equivalently $C - P = e^{-rT}(F_0-K)$. It holds because both sides are the same payoff: a long call plus a short put pays $(S_T-K)^+ - (K-S_T)^+ = S_T - K$ in every state of the world, which is exactly a forward bought at $K$. Two portfolios with identical payoffs must have the same price today, otherwise you buy the cheap one, sell the expensive one and lock in a riskless profit. It is **model-free**: no assumption on volatility or the distribution of returns, only no-arbitrage, borrowing at $r$ and known dividends. Consequences: a call and a put at the same strike have the same gamma and vega, and at $K = F$ they cost the same.

follow_ups.q: Does put-call parity depend on Black-Scholes?
follow_ups.a: No. It is purely a static replication/no-arbitrage argument. It holds whatever the volatility or distribution, as long as you can borrow/lend at $r$ and dividends are known.

follow_ups.q: Why must a call and a put with the same strike have the same implied vol?
follow_ups.a: Because parity fixes $C-P$ independently of vol. If they had different implied vols, plugging them into Black-Scholes would violate parity, which is an arbitrage.

follow_ups.q: How does parity work for American options?
follow_ups.a: It becomes bounds: $S_0 - K \le C - P \le S_0 - Ke^{-rT}$ for a non-dividend stock, because the American put can be exercised early.

cards.topic: Put-call parity arbitrage
cards.question: Stock at 100, 1-year call and put both struck at 100. Rates are 5%, no dividends. The call trades at 12 and the put at 5. Is there an arbitrage? How do you trade it?
cards.answer: Parity requires $C - P = S - Ke^{-rT} = 100 - 95.12 = 4.88$. The market has $C - P = 7$, so the **call is rich relative to the put** by 2.12. Sell the expensive side, buy the cheap side: **sell the call, buy the put, buy the stock, and borrow 95.12** (the PV of the strike). Today's cash flow: $+12 - 5 - 100 + 95.12 = +2.12$. At expiry, the stock plus the long put minus the short call is worth exactly 100 whatever happens (if $S_T>100$ the call is exercised and you deliver the stock for 100; if $S_T<100$ you exercise the put and sell at 100), which repays the loan of $95.12e^{0.05}=100$. So you lock in 2.12 today with no risk. This long stock + long put + short call package is called a **conversion**; the opposite is a **reversal**.

follow_ups.q: What is a conversion vs a reversal?
follow_ups.a: Conversion: long stock, long put, short call - a synthetic riskless bond. Reversal: short stock, short put, long call - synthetic riskless borrowing. Market makers use them to exploit or hedge parity deviations.

follow_ups.q: Why might an apparent parity violation not be an arbitrage?
follow_ups.a: Hard-to-borrow stock (shorting cost), unexpected dividends, American early exercise risk, bid-ask spreads and funding costs. The residual is often the implied borrow/repo rate.

follow_ups.q: How can you extract the market's dividend expectation from options?
follow_ups.a: From parity: $S_0e^{-qT} = C - P + Ke^{-rT}$, so the implied forward/dividends are backed out from call and put prices at the same strike. Desks do this to build implied dividend curves.

cards.topic: Option price bounds
cards.question: What are the no-arbitrage bounds on the price of a European call and put?
cards.answer: For a European call on a non-dividend stock: $\max(S_0 - Ke^{-rT}, 0) \le C \le S_0$. The upper bound: a call can never be worth more than the stock itself, since the stock pays $S_T \ge (S_T-K)^+$. The lower bound: the call pays at least what a forward struck at $K$ pays, and a forward is worth $S_0-Ke^{-rT}$; and the call is never negative. For a European put: $\max(Ke^{-rT}-S_0, 0) \le P \le Ke^{-rT}$ - it can never pay more than $K$ at expiry. American versions: $C_{Am} \ge S_0-K$ and $P_{Am} \ge K-S_0$ (you can exercise immediately), and $P_{Am} \le K$. Also: call prices must decrease and be convex in strike, and increase with maturity for American options.

follow_ups.q: Why must call prices be convex in strike?
follow_ups.a: Because a butterfly (long $K-h$, short 2 at $K$, long $K+h$) has a non-negative payoff, so its price must be $\ge 0$; that is exactly the discrete convexity condition. Its limit gives the risk-neutral density.

follow_ups.q: What is the maximum value of a call spread 100/110?
follow_ups.a: Its payoff is at most 10, so its price is at most $10e^{-rT}$. It must also be non-negative.

follow_ups.q: Can a European call with longer maturity be worth less than a shorter one?
follow_ups.a: For a non-dividend stock, no (in practice). With large discrete dividends, a longer European call can be cheaper because the stock drops at the ex-date. For American calls, longer maturity is always worth at least as much.

cards.topic: Synthetic positions
cards.question: How do you build a synthetic long stock, a synthetic put and a synthetic call?
cards.answer: All synthetics come from put-call parity, $C - P = S - Ke^{-rT}$ (no dividends). **Synthetic long stock / forward**: long call + short put at the same strike (plus lending $Ke^{-rT}$ to get the stock itself). **Synthetic long put**: long call + short stock + lend $Ke^{-rT}$, i.e. $P = C - S + Ke^{-rT}$. **Synthetic long call**: long put + long stock - borrow $Ke^{-rT}$, i.e. $C = P + S - Ke^{-rT}$. So a **protective put** (stock + put) is economically a call plus cash, and a **covered call** (stock - call) is economically a short put plus cash. Traders use synthetics when one instrument is cheaper, more liquid, or easier to trade (e.g. shorting a hard-to-borrow stock synthetically via options).

follow_ups.q: Why is a covered call economically similar to a short put?
follow_ups.a: By parity, stock minus call equals bond minus put. Both have capped upside (the premium/strike) and full downside exposure. Covered call writers are effectively short a put.

follow_ups.q: How would you short a stock that is hard to borrow?
follow_ups.a: Synthetically: buy a put and sell a call at the same strike. The option prices then embed the borrow cost, so the synthetic is not free - parity with the borrow rate tells you the implied cost.

follow_ups.q: What are the Greeks of a synthetic forward?
follow_ups.a: Delta about 1 (exactly $e^{-qT}$ for the forward-equivalent), gamma zero, vega zero, because call and put gamma and vega at the same strike cancel.

cards.topic: Option pricing drivers
cards.question: What are the factors that determine an option's price, and how does each affect a call and a put?
cards.answer: Six inputs (Black-Scholes world): **spot $S$**, **strike $K$**, **time to expiry $T$**, **volatility $\sigma$**, **interest rate $r$**, and **dividends / yield $q$**. Rising spot increases the call and decreases the put (delta). A higher strike decreases the call and increases the put. Higher **volatility increases both** calls and puts (positive vega), because options have convex payoffs. Longer maturity usually increases both (more time for moves), with exceptions for deep ITM European puts or high dividends. Higher rates increase calls and decrease puts, because they raise the forward and lower the PV of the strike. Higher dividends decrease calls and increase puts, because they lower the forward. The only input you cannot observe is volatility, so the market quotes options by their implied volatility.

follow_ups.q: Which input is not directly observable?
follow_ups.a: Volatility. Everything else is observable (spot, strike, time, rates, dividend forecasts are at least tradable). Hence options are quoted in implied vol, and the vol surface is the key market object.

follow_ups.q: Why doesn't the expected return of the stock matter?
follow_ups.a: Because the option can be replicated by delta-hedging with the stock and cash; the replicating portfolio's cost does not depend on the drift. Equivalently, we price under the risk-neutral measure where the drift is $r-q$.

follow_ups.q: Can a longer-dated option be worth less?
follow_ups.a: For European options, yes in some cases: deep ITM puts with high rates, or calls on stocks with large dividends before the longer expiry. American options are always worth at least the shorter one.

cards.topic: Volatility up: option value
cards.question: What happens to the price of a call and of a put when volatility goes up? Why?
cards.answer: **Both increase.** An option's payoff is convex: if the stock moves a lot in your favour you gain a lot, but if it moves a lot against you, your loss is capped at the premium. Higher volatility spreads out the distribution of the final price, increasing the probability of big favourable moves without increasing your maximum loss, so the expected payoff rises for calls **and** puts. Formally, by Jensen's inequality, spreading a distribution raises the expectation of a convex function. The sensitivity is **vega**, which is the same for a call and a put with the same strike and maturity (put-call parity), is largest near the money and grows with $\sqrt{T}$. So a long option position is **long volatility**, and an option seller is short volatility.

follow_ups.q: Is vega the same for a call and a put?
follow_ups.a: Yes, at the same strike and maturity: $C - P$ depends only on $S$, $K$, $r$, $q$, $T$, not on $\sigma$, so $\partial C/\partial\sigma = \partial P/\partial\sigma$.

follow_ups.q: Where is vega largest, and how does it scale with maturity?
follow_ups.a: Near the money (ATM forward), and it grows like $\sqrt T$: long-dated options carry much more vega; short-dated ones carry more gamma.

follow_ups.q: If you are short options, what vol scenario hurts you?
follow_ups.a: Implied vol rising (MtM loss via vega) and realised vol being higher than the implied you sold (gamma losses while hedging).

cards.topic: Interest rates and dividends effect
cards.question: Why does a higher interest rate increase the value of a call and decrease the value of a put? And what do dividends do?
cards.answer: Two equivalent explanations. **Via the forward**: the option really depends on the forward price $F = Se^{(r-q)T}$. Higher rates raise the forward (holding stock is more expensive to finance), which pushes calls up and puts down. **Via replication**: a call is like buying the stock later: you keep your cash invested until you pay $K$, so the PV of $K$ falls when rates rise, which helps the call; a put holder receives $K$ later, whose PV falls, which hurts the put. **Dividends** work the opposite way: the stock price drops by the dividend on the ex-date and option holders do not get the dividend, so higher dividends lower the forward, reduce calls and increase puts. For equity index options, dividend expectations are a major pricing input and a traded risk in their own right.

follow_ups.q: For which options is rho most important?
follow_ups.a: Long-dated options (rho scales with $T$), options on rates, and FX options where the domestic and foreign rate differential drives the forward.

follow_ups.q: Why do banks care so much about dividend risk?
follow_ups.a: Structured products (autocallables) leave equity derivatives desks structurally long dividends; if companies cut dividends (as in 2020) the desks lose. They hedge with dividend futures/swaps.

follow_ups.q: What happens to a stock price on the ex-dividend date and to an option on it?
follow_ups.a: The stock drops by roughly the dividend. The option price does not jump, because the dividend was already anticipated in the forward; only an unexpected dividend change moves option prices.

cards.topic: Black-Scholes assumptions
cards.question: What are the assumptions of the Black-Scholes-Merton model, and which ones fail in practice?
cards.answer: Black-Scholes assumes: (1) the underlying follows a **geometric Brownian motion** with **constant volatility** $\sigma$ (so log-returns are normal, prices lognormal, paths continuous); (2) a **constant, known risk-free rate** at which you can borrow and lend without limit; (3) known dividends (or none); (4) **frictionless markets**: no transaction costs, no taxes, continuous trading, short-selling allowed, assets perfectly divisible; (5) **no arbitrage**; (6) European exercise. The ones that fail most visibly: **volatility is not constant** (it is stochastic and depends on strike - the smile), **returns have fat tails and jumps** (crashes, earnings gaps), and **hedging is discrete and costly**. Yet the model is used everywhere as a **quoting language**: traders plug in an implied vol per strike and maturity, which absorbs the model's flaws.

follow_ups.q: Why is Black-Scholes still used if its assumptions are wrong?
follow_ups.a: It is a quoting convention: one number (implied vol) per option, comparable across strikes and maturities. The smile absorbs the model's flaws, and the BS Greeks are a robust first-order risk language.

follow_ups.q: Which assumption is most important for the replication argument?
follow_ups.a: Continuous paths with known (constant or deterministic) volatility and continuous costless trading. With jumps or unknown vol, the option cannot be perfectly replicated by stock and cash.

follow_ups.q: What models relax constant volatility?
follow_ups.a: Local volatility (Dupire): vol is a deterministic function $\sigma(S,t)$ fitted to the surface. Stochastic volatility (Heston, SABR): vol follows its own random process. Jump-diffusion (Merton): adds jumps to fit short-dated skew.

cards.topic: Black-Scholes formula
cards.question: Write down the Black-Scholes formula for a European call and a put and explain each term.
cards.answer: For a stock with spot $S$, dividend yield $q$, rate $r$, vol $\sigma$, strike $K$, maturity $T$: $C = Se^{-qT}N(d_1) - Ke^{-rT}N(d_2)$ and $P = Ke^{-rT}N(-d_2) - Se^{-qT}N(-d_1)$, with $d_1 = \frac{\ln(S/K) + (r-q+\frac12\sigma^2)T}{\sigma\sqrt T}$ and $d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt T$. $N$ is the standard normal CDF. Reading the call: it is the value of **receiving the stock** if it finishes above $K$, $Se^{-qT}N(d_1)$, minus the value of **paying the strike** if it finishes above $K$, $Ke^{-rT}N(d_2)$. $N(d_2)$ is the **risk-neutral probability** that the call ends in the money; $N(d_1)$ is the call's **delta** (with $q=0$). In forward form: $C = e^{-rT}[F N(d_1) - K N(d_2)]$ with $F = Se^{(r-q)T}$.

follow_ups.q: What does $\sigma\sqrt T$ represent?
follow_ups.a: The standard deviation of the log-return between now and expiry. It is the natural unit for moneyness and time value; ATM option prices are roughly $0.4\sigma\sqrt T$ times spot.

follow_ups.q: What is the call worth when vol goes to zero?
follow_ups.a: $e^{-rT}\max(F-K, 0)$: the discounted intrinsic value against the forward, since the future is deterministic.

follow_ups.q: What is the call worth when vol goes to infinity?
follow_ups.a: It tends to $Se^{-qT}$, the stock itself: $d_1\to+\infty$ and $d_2\to-\infty$, so $N(d_1)\to1$, $N(d_2)\to0$.

cards.topic: N(d1) and N(d2) intuition
cards.question: What is the intuition behind N(d1) and N(d2) in Black-Scholes? Is delta the probability of exercise?
cards.answer: $N(d_2)$ is the **risk-neutral probability that the call expires in the money**, $\mathbb Q(S_T>K)$; $e^{-rT}N(d_2)$ is the price of a digital paying 1 if $S_T>K$. $N(d_1)$ (times $e^{-qT}$) is the call's **delta**, the number of shares in the replicating portfolio. It is also a probability of exercise, but under the **stock measure** (using the stock as the unit of account), which weights up-states more, so $N(d_1) > N(d_2)$. Therefore **delta is not exactly the probability of exercise**: it overstates it, by more when $\sigma\sqrt T$ is large. For short-dated or low-vol options the two are close, which is why traders use delta as a quick proxy ("a 25-delta call has roughly a 25% chance of finishing in the money"). And neither is a real-world probability: both use the risk-neutral drift, not the expected return.

follow_ups.q: Why is an ATM call's risk-neutral probability of exercise below 50% when rates are zero?
follow_ups.a: Under GBM the median of $S_T$ is $S_0e^{-\frac12\sigma^2T}$, below the mean $S_0$ because the lognormal is right-skewed. So $S_T > S_0$ happens with probability $N(-\frac12\sigma\sqrt T) < 0.5$.

follow_ups.q: What is the price of a digital call in Black-Scholes?
follow_ups.a: $e^{-rT}N(d_2)$ per unit payout. In the presence of skew you must add a correction: digital $= -\partial C/\partial K$ including the smile slope.

follow_ups.q: Is $N(d_2)$ the real probability the option ends ITM?
follow_ups.a: No, it is risk-neutral: it uses drift $r-q$ instead of the true expected return. It is the market price of the digital, which embeds risk premia.

cards.topic: Risk-neutral pricing
cards.question: What is risk-neutral pricing? Why doesn't the expected return of the stock appear in the Black-Scholes formula?
cards.answer: Because an option can be **replicated** by a dynamic portfolio of the stock and cash, its price must equal the cost of that portfolio - otherwise there is arbitrage. The replication cost depends on how much the stock *fluctuates* (volatility), not on where it is *expected* to go (drift): whatever the drift, the hedge adjusts, and the stock's risk premium is already embedded in today's spot price. Mathematically, this means we can price **as if** investors were risk-neutral: assume every asset grows at the risk-free rate, compute the expected payoff under that "risk-neutral measure" $\mathbb Q$, and discount at $r$. It is a **computational device**, not a belief that people are risk-neutral. Two investors who disagree on the stock's expected return will still agree on the option price, as long as they agree on volatility.

follow_ups.q: Two stocks with the same volatility, one expected to return 5% and the other 20%. Which call is worth more?
follow_ups.a: The same (same spot, strike, rates, dividends, vol). The option is priced by replication with the stock; the expected return is already embedded in the spot price.

follow_ups.q: What is the market price of risk?
follow_ups.a: $(\mu - r)/\sigma$, the excess return per unit of risk. Girsanov's theorem removes it when moving from the real-world to the risk-neutral measure; volatility is unchanged.

follow_ups.q: When is the risk-neutral measure not unique?
follow_ups.a: In incomplete markets (jumps, stochastic vol, unhedgeable risks). Then there are many $\mathbb Q$ consistent with no arbitrage, and the market picks one via traded option prices (calibration).

cards.topic: Black-Scholes PDE derivation
cards.question: Derive the Black-Scholes PDE using a delta-hedging argument.
cards.answer: Take an option $V(S,t)$ on a stock following $dS = \mu S\,dt + \sigma S\,dW$. Build the portfolio $\Pi = V - \Delta S$: long the option, short $\Delta$ shares. By Itô, $dV = V_t\,dt + V_S\,dS + \frac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS}\,dt$. Choosing $\Delta = V_S$ cancels the $dS$ term, so $d\Pi = (V_t + \frac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS})\,dt$ - **riskless**. No arbitrage says a riskless portfolio must earn the risk-free rate: $d\Pi = r\Pi\,dt = r(V - SV_S)\,dt$. Equating gives the **Black-Scholes PDE**: $V_t + \frac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS} + rSV_S - rV = 0$ (replace $rSV_S$ by $(r-q)SV_S$ with dividends). $\mu$ has vanished. In Greek language: $\Theta + \frac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma + rS\Delta - rV = 0$, which is the **gamma-theta trade-off**.

follow_ups.q: Why does the drift $\mu$ disappear?
follow_ups.a: Because the $dS$ term (which carries $\mu$) is fully hedged away by the short $\Delta$ shares. Only the $\frac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma$ term, which depends on the size of moves, survives.

follow_ups.q: What does the PDE say in trading terms?
follow_ups.a: With $r=0$: $\Theta = -\frac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma$. A delta-hedged long option pays theta each day and earns gamma P&L from moves; if realised vol equals implied vol, they cancel on average.

follow_ups.q: How do you solve the PDE numerically?
follow_ups.a: Finite differences (explicit, implicit, Crank-Nicolson) on a grid in $S$ and $t$, marching backward from the payoff. American options add the constraint $V \ge$ payoff at each step.

cards.topic: ATM option price mental approximation
cards.question: Without a calculator: what is the price of a 1-year at-the-money call on a stock at 100 with 20% volatility? And a 3-month one?
cards.answer: Use the ATM approximation $C \approx P \approx 0.4\,\sigma\sqrt T\,S$ (for an ATM-forward option, with small rates). One year, 20% vol: $0.4\times0.20\times1\times100 = 8$. The exact Black-Scholes value with zero rates is 7.97. Three months: $\sqrt{0.25} = 0.5$, so $0.4\times0.2\times0.5\times100 = 4$. The **straddle** (call + put) is twice that: about $0.8\,\sigma\sqrt T\,S$, which is also roughly the **expected absolute move** of the stock by expiry, since $\mathbb E|Z| = \sqrt{2/\pi} \approx 0.8$. The 0.4 comes from $1/\sqrt{2\pi} \approx 0.399$. With positive rates and no dividends, an ATM-spot call is worth a bit more (e.g. 10.45 at 5% rates) and the put a bit less.

follow_ups.q: Where does the 0.4 come from?
follow_ups.a: From $1/\sqrt{2\pi}\approx0.399$, the standard normal density at 0: the ATM call is about the expected positive part of a normal move of size $\sigma\sqrt T$.

follow_ups.q: What is the breakeven move of a 1-month ATM straddle at 25% vol?
follow_ups.a: Straddle $\approx 0.8\times0.25\times\sqrt{1/12}\approx 0.8\times0.25\times0.289 \approx 5.8\%$ of spot. The stock must move about 5.8% either way by expiry.

follow_ups.q: How much is a 1-year ATM call worth if vol doubles from 20% to 40%?
follow_ups.a: About double: 8 to 16 (exactly 7.97 to 15.85). ATM option prices are nearly linear in vol.

cards.topic: One-step binomial tree
cards.question: A stock is at 100 and in one year will be either 120 or 80. Rates are zero. What is the price of a call struck at 100? Show two methods.
cards.answer: **Replication**: find $\Delta$ shares and cash $B$ matching the call in both states. Up: $120\Delta + B = 20$; down: $80\Delta + B = 0$. So $\Delta = \frac{20-0}{120-80} = 0.5$ and $B = -40$ (borrow 40). Cost today: $0.5\times100 - 40 = 10$. **Risk-neutral**: find $p$ such that the stock is fairly priced: $100 = 120p + 80(1-p)$, so $p = 0.5$. Call $= 0.5\times20 + 0.5\times0 = 10$. Both give **10**, and the real-world probability of going up never matters. With a rate, discount and use $p = \frac{(1+r)S - D}{U-D}$; e.g. with 5% rates $p=0.625$ and the call is $0.625\times20/1.05 = 11.90$. The put, by parity, is $10 - 100 + 100 = 10$ at zero rates.

follow_ups.q: What if the real-world probability of an up move is 90%?
follow_ups.a: The price is still 10. The call can be replicated with 0.5 shares and a 40 loan whatever the probabilities; the stock's price of 100 already reflects the market's views and risk aversion.

follow_ups.q: What would violate no-arbitrage in this tree?
follow_ups.a: If $(1+r)S_0$ were outside $[S_d, S_u]$: e.g. with a 25% rate, cash beats the stock in both states - short stock, lend the proceeds, riskless profit. Equivalently $p$ would not be in $(0,1)$.

follow_ups.q: How do you extend this to many steps?
follow_ups.a: Build a recombining tree with $u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}$, $d = 1/u$, compute payoffs at maturity and roll back with risk-neutral expectations. As steps go to infinity it converges to Black-Scholes.

cards.topic: Multi-step binomial trees and American options
cards.question: How do you price an American put with a binomial tree? Walk through a two-step example.
cards.answer: Build a recombining tree: each step the stock goes up by $u$ or down by $d$ (Cox-Ross-Rubinstein: $u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}$, $d=1/u$), with risk-neutral probability $p = \frac{e^{r\Delta t}-d}{u-d}$. At maturity, compute payoffs. Then roll back: at each node the **continuation value** is the discounted risk-neutral expectation of the two child nodes; for an American option, the node value is $\max(\text{exercise value}, \text{continuation value})$. Example: $S=100$, $u=1.1$, $d=0.9$, gross rate 1.02 per step, $K=100$: $p = 0.6$. At the down node (90), continuation is 8.04 but exercise gives 10, so you **exercise early**. The European put is worth 3.38, the American 4.15; the 0.77 difference is the early-exercise premium.

follow_ups.q: How do you get delta and gamma from a tree?
follow_ups.a: Delta from the first-step nodes: $(V_u - V_d)/(S_u - S_d)$. Gamma from the change in delta across the second-step nodes divided by the spot difference. Theta from comparing nodes with the same spot two steps apart.

follow_ups.q: Why use a tree rather than Monte Carlo for an American option?
follow_ups.a: Backward induction naturally gives the continuation value at each node. Monte Carlo goes forward in time and needs regression tricks (Longstaff-Schwartz) to estimate continuation values.

follow_ups.q: Would you ever exercise the American call in this tree early?
follow_ups.a: No: with no dividends the continuation value (12.35 at the up node) always exceeds intrinsic (10). Early exercise of a call on a non-dividend stock is never optimal.

cards.topic: Black's model
cards.question: What is Black's model (Black-76) and when is it used?
cards.answer: Black's model prices European options on a **forward or futures price** $F$ rather than on spot: $C = e^{-rT}[F N(d_1) - K N(d_2)]$, $P = e^{-rT}[K N(-d_2) - F N(-d_1)]$, with $d_{1,2} = \frac{\ln(F/K) \pm \frac12\sigma^2T}{\sigma\sqrt T}$. It is Black-Scholes where the underlying has no drift under the pricing measure (a forward costs nothing to hold, so no carry term). It is the market standard for **options on futures** (commodities like Brent, gold; bond futures; index futures), for **interest-rate caps/floors** (each caplet is a call on a forward rate) and **swaptions** (options on a forward swap rate). It is convenient because you do not need to model dividends, storage costs or convenience yields separately: all carry is inside the observed forward.

follow_ups.q: How is a caplet priced with Black's model?
follow_ups.a: As a call on the forward rate: notional times accrual fraction times $P(0,T_{pay})[F N(d_1) - K N(d_2)]$, with $F$ the forward rate for the period and $\sigma$ the caplet Black vol.

follow_ups.q: Why do rates desks often quote normal (Bachelier) vol?
follow_ups.a: Because rates can be negative or near zero, where lognormal dynamics break down; normal vol (in basis points per year) is stable across rate levels and handles negative rates.

follow_ups.q: Is Black's model consistent with Black-Scholes?
follow_ups.a: Yes: substituting $F = Se^{(r-q)T}$ gives exactly the BS formula. Black just takes the forward as the primitive.

cards.topic: Currency options
cards.question: How do you price an FX option? What is special about currency options?
cards.answer: FX options are priced with **Garman-Kohlhagen**, i.e. Black-Scholes where the **foreign interest rate plays the role of the dividend yield**: $C = S e^{-r_f T}N(d_1) - K e^{-r_d T}N(d_2)$, $d_1 = \frac{\ln(S/K) + (r_d - r_f + \frac12\sigma^2)T}{\sigma\sqrt T}$, with $S$ quoted as domestic per foreign (e.g. EURUSD = USD per EUR: EUR is foreign, USD domestic). The logic: holding foreign currency earns the foreign rate, just like a stock pays dividends. Special features: (1) **symmetry**: a EUR call/USD put is the same contract as a USD put/EUR call - every FX option is a call on one currency and a put on the other; (2) the market quotes **implied vols by delta** (ATM, 25-delta risk reversals and butterflies), not by strike; (3) premium and delta conventions differ by pair (premium-adjusted delta when premium is paid in foreign currency); (4) the forward is driven by the **interest-rate differential**.

follow_ups.q: What does a negative EURUSD 25-delta risk reversal mean?
follow_ups.a: EUR puts (USD calls) are more expensive in vol than EUR calls: the market pays a premium for protection against EUR depreciation vs USD.

follow_ups.q: Why is a EUR call the same as a USD put?
follow_ups.a: The right to buy EUR N at strike K (paying N*K USD) is exactly the right to sell N*K USD for N EUR. It is one contract seen from two currencies.

follow_ups.q: Which rate plays the role of the dividend yield?
follow_ups.a: The foreign (base currency) rate $r_f$: holding the foreign currency earns $r_f$, just as holding a stock earns its dividends.

cards.topic: Index options
cards.question: What is specific about options on an equity index (like the Euro Stoxx 50 or S&P 500) compared with single-stock options?
cards.answer: Index options are usually **European** and **cash-settled** (you cannot deliver 50 stocks easily), whereas single-stock listed options are usually American and physically settled. They are priced with Black-Scholes/Black using the index forward, where the **dividend yield** of the index matters a lot. Index implied vol is typically **lower** than the average single-stock vol because of diversification: index variance depends on the **correlation** between constituents, which is the basis of **dispersion trading**. Index skew is **steeper** than single-stock skew because in a crash correlations jump to one and everything falls together, and because investors massively buy index puts to hedge portfolios. They are the main tool for macro hedging and the building block of most retail structured products in Europe (autocallables on Euro Stoxx 50 or CAC 40). The VIX is computed from S&P 500 index options.

follow_ups.q: Why is index implied vol lower than single-stock vols?
follow_ups.a: Diversification: index variance depends on correlations; with correlations below 1, idiosyncratic moves partially cancel.

follow_ups.q: What is a dispersion trade?
follow_ups.a: Short index vol, long single-stock vol (usually via variance swaps or straddles). It profits if realised correlation is lower than implied - essentially short correlation.

follow_ups.q: Why is index skew steeper than single-stock skew?
follow_ups.a: Crash risk: correlations spike in selloffs, and investors structurally buy index puts to hedge portfolios, pushing up downside implied vols. Single stocks have more idiosyncratic, two-sided risk (e.g. takeover upside).

cards.topic: Why options are quoted in vol
cards.question: Why do traders quote options in implied volatility rather than in price?
cards.answer: Because implied vol is the only **unobservable** input in Black-Scholes and it strips out everything mechanical. An option's price depends on spot, strike, maturity, rates and dividends, so prices of different options are not comparable: 3 EUR for one option may be cheap and 1 EUR for another expensive. Implied vol normalises all that: one number that says how "expensive" optionality is, comparable across strikes, maturities and even underlyings. It is also **more stable**: when spot moves, option prices change constantly, but the implied vol quote stays roughly the same, so a market maker's quote does not go stale every tick. Traders then express views and risk in vol terms (vega, vol points), and the conversion to price is done with the agreed model (Black-Scholes/Black). A quote like "the 3-month 90% put is 24 vol, 23.5 / 24.5" is standard.

follow_ups.q: How do you compute implied vol from a price?
follow_ups.a: Numerically invert BS, e.g. Newton-Raphson using vega as the derivative, or bisection. The solution is unique since price is increasing in vol.

follow_ups.q: What is a delta exchange?
follow_ups.a: When trading an option quoted in vol, the counterparties also exchange the delta hedge in the underlying at a reference spot, so the trade is delta-neutral and the vol quote stays valid if spot moves.

follow_ups.q: Is implied vol a forecast of future volatility?
follow_ups.a: Partly. It reflects expected vol plus a risk premium and supply/demand (e.g. hedgers buying puts). On average implied vol has exceeded subsequent realised vol for equity indices.

cards.topic: Numerical methods: trees, PDE, Monte Carlo
cards.question: When would you price an option with a tree, a PDE solver or Monte Carlo?
cards.answer: Use **closed forms** (Black-Scholes, Black) whenever they exist: vanillas, digitals, simple barriers. **Trees** (binomial/trinomial) are intuitive and good for **American or Bermudan options on one underlying**, because backward induction handles early exercise naturally. **PDE / finite differences** do the same job more accurately and faster for low-dimensional problems (one or two state variables): American options, barriers, local-vol models; they give Greeks cheaply off the grid. **Monte Carlo** is the tool for **path-dependent and multi-asset** payoffs - Asians, worst-of autocallables on several indices, baskets - because its cost grows only linearly with the number of underlyings (no curse of dimensionality). Its drawbacks: slow convergence ($1/\sqrt N$), noisy Greeks, and early exercise needs regression (Longstaff-Schwartz). Structured product desks price most autocallables by Monte Carlo under local or stochastic vol.

follow_ups.q: How does Monte Carlo error scale?
follow_ups.a: As $1/\sqrt N$: to divide the error by 10 you need 100 times more paths. Variance reduction (antithetics, control variates, Sobol sequences) improves the constant or the rate.

follow_ups.q: How do you handle early exercise in Monte Carlo?
follow_ups.a: Longstaff-Schwartz: at each exercise date, regress realised discounted continuation cash flows on functions of the state (e.g. polynomials of spot) to estimate the continuation value, and exercise where intrinsic exceeds it.

follow_ups.q: How do you simulate correlated underlyings?
follow_ups.a: Generate independent normals and multiply by the Cholesky factor of the correlation matrix, then use them in each asset's lognormal step.

cards.topic: Greeks overview
cards.question: What are the Greeks? Give each one's definition and what it tells a trader.
cards.answer: The Greeks are the **sensitivities of an option's value to its inputs**; a trader's book is managed through them. **Delta** $\partial V/\partial S$: exposure to the underlying's direction, and the hedge ratio. **Gamma** $\partial^2V/\partial S^2$: how fast delta changes, i.e. convexity; long options are long gamma and profit from large moves. **Vega** $\partial V/\partial\sigma$: exposure to implied volatility. **Theta** $\partial V/\partial t$: time decay, the daily cost of holding optionality (negative for long options). **Rho** $\partial V/\partial r$: sensitivity to interest rates, mainly relevant for long-dated options. Second-order cross Greeks such as **vanna** (delta vs vol) and **volga** (vega vs vol) matter for smile risk. A desk's risk report aggregates these across all positions; the trader decides which to hedge (delta nearly always, often vega and gamma by maturity bucket).

follow_ups.q: Which Greeks are the same for a call and a put with the same strike and maturity?
follow_ups.a: Gamma and vega (and hence volga/vanna). Their difference is a forward, which has delta about 1 and no gamma or vega.

follow_ups.q: What is a P&L explain?
follow_ups.a: The daily decomposition of the book's P&L into delta, gamma, vega, theta, rho and residual contributions, e.g. $\Delta\,dS + \frac12\Gamma dS^2 + \mathcal V d\sigma + \Theta dt$. A large unexplained residual signals a model or booking problem.

follow_ups.q: What are second-order Greeks traders watch?
follow_ups.a: Vanna ($\partial\Delta/\partial\sigma$), volga ($\partial\mathcal V/\partial\sigma$), charm ($\partial\Delta/\partial t$), and for exotics cross-gamma and correlation sensitivity.

cards.topic: Delta
cards.question: What is delta? What values can it take for calls and puts, and how can you interpret it?
cards.answer: Delta is the sensitivity of the option price to the underlying: $\Delta = \partial V/\partial S$. For a long call it is between 0 and 1 (deep OTM near 0, ATM around 0.5, deep ITM near 1); for a long put between $-1$ and 0; and by parity $\Delta_C - \Delta_P = 1$ (times $e^{-qT}$). Three interpretations: (1) **P&L sensitivity**: a delta of 0.6 means the option gains about 0.6 for a 1-point rise in spot; (2) **hedge ratio**: to be neutral you short 0.6 shares per call - that is the replicating portfolio; (3) a rough **probability of expiring in the money** (a proxy, strictly $N(d_2)$ is the risk-neutral probability). Desks talk in **cash delta** ($\Delta\times S\times$ quantity), the equivalent stock position in currency. Delta is not constant: it moves with spot (gamma), vol (vanna) and time (charm).

follow_ups.q: How does call delta change as expiry approaches?
follow_ups.a: It converges to 1 if ITM and 0 if OTM. For options near the strike, delta swings violently between the two - gamma becomes very large.

follow_ups.q: What happens to the delta of an OTM call when vol rises?
follow_ups.a: It increases: higher vol makes it more likely to end ITM, pulling deltas toward the middle. Conversely an ITM call's delta falls. This cross-sensitivity is vanna.

follow_ups.q: What is the delta of a put-call pair (long call, short put, same strike)?
follow_ups.a: $\Delta_C - \Delta_P = e^{-qT}\approx 1$: it is a synthetic forward.

cards.topic: Delta of an ATM call
cards.question: What is the delta of an at-the-money call? Is it exactly 0.5?
cards.answer: Roughly 0.5, but in Black-Scholes it is **slightly above 0.5** for an ATM-spot call. With zero rates and dividends, $\Delta = N(d_1)$ with $d_1 = \frac12\sigma\sqrt T > 0$, so $\Delta = N(\frac12\sigma\sqrt T)$: for 1 year at 20% vol, $N(0.1) = 0.54$. Two effects push it above one half: the **lognormal drift/convexity term** $+\frac12\sigma^2$ in $d_1$ (the call's upside is unbounded while the downside of the stock is bounded at zero), and **positive rates** (the forward is above spot, so an ATM-spot call is actually ITM relative to the forward: 0.64 at 5% rates). Dividends pull it down. The ATM put delta is $\Delta_C - 1 \approx -0.46$. For short-dated options it is very close to 0.5 (0.51 for 1 month at 20%). In practice the skew also shifts it: with a negative skew, the smile-adjusted delta of a call is usually a bit lower than the BS delta.

follow_ups.q: What is the delta of an ATM put?
follow_ups.a: Call delta minus $e^{-qT}$: about $-0.46$ for a 1-year 20%-vol option with zero rates.

follow_ups.q: What is the delta of an ATM straddle?
follow_ups.a: Call delta plus put delta, about $2N(d_1)-1 \approx 0.08$ for 1y 20% vol: slightly positive. The strike that makes it exactly zero (DNS) is slightly above the forward, $K = Fe^{\frac12\sigma^2T}$.

follow_ups.q: How does the ATM delta change if vol goes up?
follow_ups.a: It rises (further above 0.5) since $d_1 = \frac12\sigma\sqrt T$ increases with vol at zero rates.

cards.topic: Gamma
cards.question: What is gamma, where is it highest, and why does a trader care?
cards.answer: Gamma is the rate of change of delta with the underlying: $\Gamma = \partial^2V/\partial S^2 = \partial\Delta/\partial S$. It measures **convexity**. Long options (calls or puts) have positive gamma; short options negative. It is **highest ATM and near expiry**: a short-dated ATM option's delta swings between 0 and 1 on small moves. Traders care because gamma determines how much **re-hedging** is needed and the P&L from moves: a delta-hedged long-gamma position makes money on big moves either way, about $\frac12\Gamma(\Delta S)^2$, because it buys low and sells high when re-hedging; a short-gamma position loses on big moves and must buy high/sell low. That gain is paid for by **theta**. So gamma is the trader's exposure to **realised volatility**, whereas vega is exposure to **implied** volatility.

follow_ups.q: You are long gamma and delta-neutral. The market drops 3%. What do you do?
follow_ups.a: Your delta has become negative (you are short), so you buy the underlying to re-hedge - buying after a fall. You made money on the move ($\approx\frac12\Gamma dS^2$), and re-hedging locks it in.

follow_ups.q: Why does gamma of an ATM option explode near expiry?
follow_ups.a: Delta must go from about 0 to about 1 over a shrinking range of spot around the strike; the slope of delta ($\Gamma\propto 1/(S\sigma\sqrt T)$) therefore blows up. OTM and ITM gammas go to zero.

follow_ups.q: What is the difference between gamma and vega exposure?
follow_ups.a: Gamma is exposure to realised vol (P&L from actual moves when delta hedging); vega is exposure to implied vol (MtM change when the market's vol quote moves).

cards.topic: Theta
cards.question: What is theta? Why does an ATM option decay faster close to expiry? Can theta be positive?
cards.answer: Theta is the change in option value as time passes, all else equal: $\Theta = \partial V/\partial t$, usually quoted per day. Long options generally have **negative theta** (they lose time value every day); short options earn it. ATM time value is about $0.4\sigma\sqrt T S$, a **square-root function of time**, so the decay per day $\propto 1/\sqrt T$ accelerates as expiry nears: a 1-month ATM option loses about 3.5 times more per day than a 1-year one. OTM options' time value decays earlier and then flattens. Theta **can be positive**: a deep ITM European put (you would like to receive $K$ now; as time passes, the discounting on $K$ shrinks and its value rises toward intrinsic), and similarly for deep ITM European calls on high-dividend or high-foreign-rate underlyings. Most importantly, theta is the **price of gamma**: $\Theta \approx -\frac12\Gamma\sigma^2S^2$ for a delta-hedged option at zero rates.

follow_ups.q: Why does a 1-month option decay faster per day than a 1-year option?
follow_ups.a: Time value scales like $\sqrt T$; its derivative $\propto 1/\sqrt T$ is larger for small $T$. A 1-month ATM option loses about $\sqrt{12}\approx3.5$ times more per day.

follow_ups.q: Do OTM options decay the same way as ATM ones?
follow_ups.a: No. Far OTM options lose most of their value earlier (their time value in % terms collapses as the chance of reaching the strike vanishes), then theta flattens near zero close to expiry. ATM theta keeps accelerating until the end.

follow_ups.q: If you sell options to collect theta, what risk do you take?
follow_ups.a: Short gamma (losses on large realised moves) and short vega (losses if implied vol rises). Theta is compensation for those risks, not free money.

cards.topic: Gamma vs theta trade-off
cards.question: Explain the relationship between gamma and theta. If you are long gamma, what do you need for your position to make money?
cards.answer: For a delta-hedged option, gamma and theta are two sides of the same coin. The Black-Scholes PDE gives, with zero rates, $\Theta = -\frac12\Gamma\sigma^2S^2$: every day, a long-gamma position pays theta and in exchange earns $\frac12\Gamma(\Delta S)^2$ from the moves via re-hedging. These balance exactly when the realised squared move equals the one implied by the vol you paid: $(\Delta S/S)^2 = \sigma_{impl}^2\,\Delta t$. So a **long gamma position makes money if realised volatility exceeds the implied volatility** at which it was bought; a short gamma position makes money if realised is below implied. Daily breakeven: the stock needs to move about $\sigma/\sqrt{252} \approx \sigma/16$ per day - at 20% vol, about 1.25%. Big moves in either direction help the long gamma side; quiet markets help the short gamma side.

follow_ups.q: You bought options at 20% implied vol and realised vol turns out to be 15%. What happened to your delta-hedged P&L?
follow_ups.a: You lost: gamma gains were smaller than the theta you paid. Roughly the loss is proportional to $\sigma_{impl}^2 - \sigma_{real}^2$, weighted by your gamma along the path.

follow_ups.q: Why can a trader who is 'right on vol' still lose money gamma trading?
follow_ups.a: Because P&L is gamma-weighted: if the big moves happen when the option is far from the strike (low gamma) and the market is quiet when gamma is high, the P&L can be negative even if average realised vol exceeded implied. Discrete hedging noise also matters.

follow_ups.q: What is the rule of 16?
follow_ups.a: $\sqrt{252}\approx 16$: annual vol divided by 16 gives the typical daily move. 16% vol means about 1% per day.

cards.topic: Vega
cards.question: What is vega? How does it vary with strike and maturity?
cards.answer: Vega is the sensitivity of the option price to **implied volatility**: $\mathcal V = \partial V/\partial\sigma$, usually quoted per 1 vol point. It is the same for a call and a put with the same strike and expiry, positive for long options. It is **largest near the money** (ATM forward) and **grows with maturity** like $\sqrt T$: long-dated options carry a lot of vega and little gamma, while short-dated options carry little vega and a lot of gamma. ATM, $\mathcal V \approx 0.4\,S\sqrt T$ per unit of vol, i.e. about $0.4\sqrt T$% of spot per vol point. Traders manage vega **by maturity bucket** because implied vols of different expiries do not move in parallel: short-dated vols move much more than long-dated ones. Vega exposure is also often expressed in "vega-notional" for variance swaps.

follow_ups.q: Why do desks bucket vega by maturity?
follow_ups.a: Short-dated vols are much more volatile than long-dated ones and they do not move together, so a total vega number hides risk. Being long 1-month vega and short 2-year vega is not flat.

follow_ups.q: What is the relationship between vega and gamma in Black-Scholes?
follow_ups.a: $\mathcal V = \Gamma\sigma S^2 T$: for the same option, vega equals gamma times $\sigma S^2 T$. Long gamma always means long vega, but the ratio depends strongly on maturity.

follow_ups.q: In relative terms, which option is more sensitive to vol: ATM or OTM?
follow_ups.a: OTM. Absolute vega peaks ATM, but as a percentage of premium OTM options are much more sensitive to vol.

cards.topic: Vanna and volga
cards.question: What are vanna and volga, and why do they matter?
cards.answer: They are second-order volatility Greeks. **Vanna** $= \partial^2V/\partial S\,\partial\sigma = \partial\Delta/\partial\sigma = \partial\mathcal V/\partial S$: how delta changes when vol moves, or how vega changes when spot moves. It is positive for OTM calls and negative for OTM puts (for long positions), and near zero ATM. **Volga** (vomma) $= \partial^2V/\partial\sigma^2 = \partial\mathcal V/\partial\sigma$: the convexity of the option in vol. It is near zero ATM (ATM prices are almost linear in vol) and positive for OTM options in the wings. They matter because vol is not constant: when spot moves, implied vol moves too (skew), so vanna creates P&L; and when vol itself is volatile, long volga earns money like gamma does in spot. The market **smile** can be seen as the price of vanna and volga: the **risk reversal** is mostly a vanna trade and the **butterfly** a volga trade - the idea behind the "vanna-volga" pricing method used for FX exotics.

follow_ups.q: Where is volga largest?
follow_ups.a: In the wings: moderately OTM options (around 10-25 delta). ATM options have near-zero volga because their price is nearly linear in vol.

follow_ups.q: How does vanna create P&L on an equity book?
follow_ups.a: Spot and vol move together (spot down, vol up). Vanna times $dS\,d\sigma$ is then non-zero: e.g. a long OTM put position (negative vanna) with $dS<0$, $d\sigma>0$ earns positive vanna P&L.

follow_ups.q: What is the vanna-volga method?
follow_ups.a: A practical FX exotic pricing method: BS price plus the market cost of the vanna and volga, estimated using 25-delta risk reversals and butterflies, weighted by the exotic's own vanna/volga.

cards.topic: Greeks signs of long and short options
cards.question: Give the sign of delta, gamma, vega and theta for a long call, short call, long put and short put. What about a long straddle?
cards.answer:
| Position | Delta | Gamma | Vega | Theta |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Long call | + | + | + | - |
| Short call | - | - | - | + |
| Long put | - | + | + | - |
| Short put | + | - | - | + |
| Long straddle | ~0 | + | + | - |

The rule: **buying any option makes you long gamma and long vega and short theta**; selling any option makes you short gamma, short vega, long theta. Only the **delta sign** depends on call vs put. A long ATM straddle is roughly delta-neutral and long gamma/vega: a pure volatility position. (Theta can be positive in edge cases such as deep ITM European puts.)

follow_ups.q: Is a short put bullish or bearish?
follow_ups.a: Bullish: positive delta. You profit if the stock stays above the strike. It is also short vol (short gamma and vega).

follow_ups.q: How can you be long vega but short gamma?
follow_ups.a: Calendar spread: sell a short-dated option (lots of gamma, little vega) and buy a long-dated one (lots of vega, little gamma).

follow_ups.q: What position is long gamma and short vega?
follow_ups.a: The reverse calendar: buy short-dated options, sell long-dated ones.

cards.topic: Greeks vs time and moneyness
cards.question: How do gamma, vega and theta of an ATM option change as expiry approaches? And for an OTM option?
cards.answer: For an **ATM** option, as $T\to0$: **gamma explodes** ($\propto 1/\sqrt T$), **theta explodes** in magnitude ($\propto 1/\sqrt T$), and **vega shrinks** to zero ($\propto\sqrt T$). The option becomes a short-dated bet on realised moves: huge gamma, small vega. For an **OTM** (or ITM) option, gamma, vega and theta all **go to zero** near expiry, because the option is almost certainly worthless (or almost certainly exercised) and small moves no longer change that. Across strikes, all three Greeks form a bell shape centred near the forward; for long maturities the bell is wide and flat, for short maturities it is narrow and spiky. Practical consequences: short-dated ATM options create **pin risk** and hedging headaches at expiry; long-dated books are dominated by vega.

follow_ups.q: What is pin risk?
follow_ups.a: At expiry with spot very close to a strike, the option writer does not know if it will be exercised, and delta flips between 0 and 1: hedging becomes a gamble. Large open interest at a strike can even 'pin' the stock near it through dealer hedging flows.

follow_ups.q: Why does an OTM option's gamma go to zero near expiry?
follow_ups.a: The strike becomes many standard deviations away ($\sigma\sqrt T$ small), so the option is almost surely worthless and small moves do not change its delta.

follow_ups.q: Which is more exposed to a vol spike: a 1-week or a 1-year ATM option?
follow_ups.a: In price terms the 1-year (vega 0.40 vs 0.055 per point). But short-dated implied vols move much more, so in practice the gap is smaller.

cards.topic: Delta hedging
cards.question: What is delta hedging? How does a market maker who sold a call to a client hedge it?
cards.answer: Delta hedging means offsetting an option's directional exposure with the underlying so that the combined position does not gain or lose on small spot moves. A market maker who **sells a call** with delta 0.6 on 100,000 shares is short 60,000 shares' worth of delta, so they **buy 60,000 shares**. As spot and time change, delta changes (gamma), so the hedge must be **rebalanced**: if the stock rises, the call's delta increases, they buy more shares (at higher prices); if it falls, they sell shares (at lower prices). Because the dealer is short gamma, re-hedging makes them buy high and sell low; that systematic loss is what the option premium's time value pays for. If realised volatility turns out equal to the implied vol they sold at, hedging costs exactly offset the premium (in theory); below it they make money, above it they lose. Rebalancing frequency is a trade-off between hedging error and transaction costs.

follow_ups.q: How often should you re-hedge?
follow_ups.a: It is a trade-off: more frequent rebalancing reduces hedging error (its standard deviation roughly as $1/\sqrt n$, its variance as $1/n$) but increases transaction costs. Desks use time-based rebalancing, delta bands or utility-based rules, and hedge more often when gamma is high.

follow_ups.q: What risks remain after delta hedging?
follow_ups.a: Gamma (large moves, especially jumps and gaps), vega (implied vol changes), discrete hedging error, model risk (wrong delta due to smile dynamics), liquidity and dividend/rate risks.

follow_ups.q: Which delta do you use: at implied or realised vol?
follow_ups.a: Usually implied (the delta from the market vol), which makes daily P&L smooth in expectation but path-dependent. Hedging at the true realised vol would lock in a deterministic P&L but with noisy MtM. In practice desks use implied/smile-adjusted deltas.

cards.topic: Gamma scalping
cards.question: What is gamma scalping? Walk me through a numerical example.
cards.answer: Gamma scalping is **owning options (long gamma) and continually delta-hedging them**, so that each re-hedge sells the underlying after it rises and buys it after it falls, **locking in profits from the moves**. The trader does not bet on direction but on the **size of moves**: the strategy earns about $\frac12\Gamma(\Delta S)^2$ per move and pays theta every day, so it is profitable if **realised vol exceeds the implied vol** paid. Example: long 10,000 one-month ATM calls, stock 100, gamma 0.069, theta about 548 per trading day at 20% implied. Stock goes to 102: calls gain about 11,580, the short hedge of 5,100 shares loses 10,200 - net +1,380; delta rose by 0.138 so sell 1,380 more shares at 102. Stock returns to 100: another +1,380 of gamma P&L, and you buy the 1,380 shares back. The round trip 100 -> 102 -> 100 earns about 2,760 of gamma P&L against two days of theta (about 1,100): net about +1,660, although the stock ended where it started.

follow_ups.q: What is the worst scenario for a gamma scalper?
follow_ups.a: A quiet, range-bound market with small moves: gamma P&L is tiny while theta is paid every day. Also an implied vol collapse, which hits the vega of the options held.

follow_ups.q: Is being short gamma the mirror strategy?
follow_ups.a: Yes: sell options, collect theta, and re-hedge by buying rallies and selling dips (buy high, sell low). It wins when realised vol stays below implied, and loses badly on big moves or gaps.

follow_ups.q: How does a gamma scalper choose when to re-hedge?
follow_ups.a: Fixed time intervals (e.g. end of day), delta bands (re-hedge when delta drifts by a threshold), or move-based rules (every 1% move). Tighter rules lock gains more often but cost more in spreads.

cards.topic: P&L of a delta-hedged option
cards.question: What is the P&L of a delta-hedged option position over its life? Which volatility matters: implied or realised?
cards.answer: If you buy an option at implied vol $\sigma_i$ and delta-hedge it (using the Black-Scholes delta at $\sigma_i$), the P&L over each small interval is approximately $\frac12\Gamma_tS_t^2(\sigma_{r,t}^2 - \sigma_i^2)\,dt$, where $\sigma_{r,t}^2\,dt = (dS/S)^2$ is the realised squared return. Over the whole life: $\text{P\&L}\approx\int_0^T\frac12\Gamma_tS_t^2(\sigma_{r,t}^2 - \sigma_i^2)\,dt$, i.e. **realised minus implied variance, weighted by dollar gamma along the path**. So **both** matter: implied vol is what you pay, realised vol is what you earn, and gamma is the weight. Consequences: the P&L is **path-dependent** (moves near the strike close to expiry count most); a positive average realised-minus-implied spread does not guarantee a profit; and before expiry the MtM also moves with changes in implied vol (vega). Variance swaps were designed to remove this path dependence by paying pure realised variance.

follow_ups.q: Why were variance swaps invented?
follow_ups.a: To get pure exposure to realised variance without the path dependence of gamma scalping: a variance swap pays realised variance minus a strike, and it can be statically replicated by a strip of options weighted by $1/K^2$ plus a delta hedge.

follow_ups.q: Can you lose money if realised vol averaged above the implied you bought?
follow_ups.a: Yes: the P&L is weighted by $\Gamma S^2$, so if the large moves happened when your gamma was small (spot far from the strike) and calm periods coincided with high gamma, you can lose.

follow_ups.q: What is the difference between hedging at implied and at realised vol?
follow_ups.a: Hedging at implied gives a path-dependent but locally smooth P&L; hedging at the (unknown) true realised vol gives a known final P&L $V(\sigma_r)-V(\sigma_i)$ but noisy intermediate MtM.

cards.topic: Dollar Greeks and risk reports
cards.question: How does a trading desk express Greeks in practice (cash delta, dollar gamma, vega per vol point)?
cards.answer: Desks convert Greeks into **currency amounts** so they can be aggregated across positions and compared to limits. **Cash delta** $= \Delta\times S\times N$ (quantity $N$): the equivalent stock position in EUR or USD, e.g. "long 5m EUR of delta". **Cash (dollar) gamma** $= \Gamma\times S^2\times N/100$: the change in cash delta for a **1% move** in the underlying, e.g. "we get 400k longer for every 1% up". The gamma P&L for a move of $x$ (in %) is about $\frac12\times\text{cash gamma}\times x\times x\%$, e.g. a 2% move with 500k cash gamma gives $\frac12\times500\text{k}\times2\times2\% = 10\text{k}$. **Vega** is shown per 1 vol point in currency, bucketed by maturity. **Theta** is shown per day in currency. On a multi-underlying book, deltas are often converted into index-equivalent (beta-weighted) terms, and scenario grids (spot x vol shocks) complement the Greeks since they capture large-move non-linearity.

follow_ups.q: Your book has cash gamma of +500k per 1%. The market drops 2%. What happens?
follow_ups.a: Your cash delta falls by about 1m (you become 1m shorter), and you earned roughly $\frac12\times500\text{k}\times2\times2\% = 10\text{k}$ of gamma P&L. To re-hedge, buy about 1m of the underlying.

follow_ups.q: Why use scenario grids in addition to Greeks?
follow_ups.a: Greeks are local Taylor approximations; large moves (crashes, gaps) and exotic payoffs (barriers) are non-linear, so full revaluation under stressed spot/vol scenarios is needed.

follow_ups.q: What is beta-weighted delta?
follow_ups.a: Each stock's cash delta multiplied by its beta to a reference index, giving the book's equivalent index exposure, useful to hedge a multi-stock book with index futures.

cards.topic: Implied vs realised volatility
cards.question: What is the difference between implied and realised (historical) volatility?
cards.answer: **Realised volatility** is backward-looking: the annualised standard deviation of the underlying's actual log-returns over a past window (e.g. the last 20 or 60 trading days). **Implied volatility** is forward-looking and market-driven: the volatility that, plugged into Black-Scholes, gives the option's market price. It reflects the market's expectation of future volatility **plus a risk premium** and supply/demand (e.g. investors paying up for downside puts). On average, equity index implied vol trades **above** subsequently realised vol - the **variance risk premium** - which is why systematic option selling earns money most of the time but suffers in crashes. The spread between the two is what a delta-hedged option trader bets on: buy options if you expect realised to exceed implied, sell them if you expect it to be lower. Implied vol also varies by strike and maturity (the vol surface); realised vol is a single number per window.

follow_ups.q: How do you annualise daily volatility?
follow_ups.a: Multiply by $\sqrt{252}$ (about 16). Variance scales linearly with time for independent returns, so standard deviation scales with the square root.

follow_ups.q: Why is implied vol usually above realised vol?
follow_ups.a: Investors structurally buy protection (puts) and are willing to pay a premium to hedge crash risk; option sellers demand compensation for tail risk and for being short gamma in bad times. That premium is the variance risk premium.

follow_ups.q: Implied vol is 30 and realised is 15. Should you sell options?
follow_ups.a: Not blindly: check for upcoming events (earnings, elections, central bank decisions) that justify a higher implied, the term structure, skew, and your tail-risk appetite. If no event, selling delta-hedged vol can be attractive but is exposed to gaps.

prerequisites: Why options are quoted in vol

cards.topic: Rule of 16
cards.question: A stock has an implied vol of 32%. What daily move does the market expect? What about a weekly or monthly move?
cards.answer: Use the **rule of 16**: $\sqrt{252}\approx 15.9\approx 16$, so the daily standard deviation is about annual vol / 16. At 32% vol that is **2% per day**. For other horizons, scale by $\sqrt{t}$: weekly $= 32\%\times\sqrt{5/252}\approx 32\%/7.1\approx 4.5\%$; monthly $\approx 32\%/\sqrt{12}\approx 9.2\%$. These are one-standard-deviation moves: roughly two days in three the stock should move less than 2%, and about one day in three more. It is also the **breakeven daily move** for a delta-hedged option position: if you are long options at 32% implied, you need 2% daily moves on average to pay your theta. The expected absolute move is a bit smaller, about 0.8 times the standard deviation (1.6% per day).

follow_ups.q: VIX is at 16. What daily move in the S&P 500 does it imply?
follow_ups.a: About 1% per day (16/16), as a one-standard-deviation move, over the next 30 days.

follow_ups.q: What is the probability of a 3% daily move at 16% vol?
follow_ups.a: A 3-sigma move: about 0.3% under a normal distribution, i.e. roughly once every year and a half. In reality it happens much more often because of fat tails.

follow_ups.q: How do you get the implied earnings move from options?
follow_ups.a: Look at the ATM straddle expiring just after the announcement: its price as a % of spot is roughly the market's expected absolute move. Or back out the event-day variance by comparing expiries before and after the event.

cards.topic: Vol smile and skew
cards.question: What is the volatility smile or skew? What does it tell you about the market's view of the distribution?
cards.answer: If Black-Scholes were right, all options on the same underlying and maturity would have the same implied vol. In practice implied vol **varies with strike**: plotted against strike it forms a **smile** (both wings higher than ATM, typical of FX) or a **skew/smirk** (low strikes much higher than high strikes, typical of equity indices). The smile is how the market corrects BS's lognormal assumption: higher implied vol on OTM puts means the market prices a **fatter left tail** (crash risk) than a lognormal; a symmetric smile means **fat tails on both sides** (excess kurtosis). Traders describe it with the **skew** (slope, e.g. 90% minus 110% strike vol, or the 25-delta risk reversal) and the **curvature** (butterfly). Mathematically, the smile pins down the **risk-neutral distribution** via the second derivative of call prices with respect to strike. It matters for pricing anything strike-dependent: OTM options, digitals, barriers and autocallables.

follow_ups.q: What does a 25-delta risk reversal measure?
follow_ups.a: The difference between the implied vol of the 25-delta call and the 25-delta put: the skew, i.e. which tail the market prices more. Negative for equity indices.

follow_ups.q: How can you extract the risk-neutral distribution from the smile?
follow_ups.a: Breeden-Litzenberger: the second derivative of call prices with respect to strike, times $e^{rT}$, is the risk-neutral density. In practice approximate with butterflies across strikes.

follow_ups.q: How does skew depend on maturity?
follow_ups.a: In equities skew (in vol points per % of moneyness) is steepest for short maturities and flattens roughly like $1/\sqrt T$ for longer ones, because short-term jumps matter more over short horizons.

cards.topic: Why equity skew exists
cards.question: Why do equity index options have a negative skew, i.e. higher implied vol for low strikes?
cards.answer: Four reinforcing reasons. (1) **Crash risk / fat left tail**: equity markets fall faster than they rise ("up the stairs, down the elevator"); large down-jumps like 1987, 2008 or March 2020 are much more likely than a lognormal suggests. (2) **Spot-vol correlation (leverage effect)**: when prices fall, volatility rises - falling equity increases firms' leverage and fear - so low-strike options, which pay off in those high-vol states, deserve a higher vol. (3) **Supply and demand**: investors structurally **buy index puts** to protect portfolios, and **sell OTM calls** (overwriting) for yield, while dealers must be compensated for being short crash risk. (4) **Correlation spikes in crashes**: index vol jumps as all stocks fall together. The skew became pronounced after the **1987 crash**; before it, equity smiles were nearly flat - often cited as the moment the market "learned" crash risk. Structured products (autocallables) partly offset this: investors sell downside puts to banks, which pushes skew the other way.

follow_ups.q: Why is single-stock skew flatter than index skew?
follow_ups.a: Single stocks have upside jump risk (takeovers, earnings beats) and more idiosyncratic, two-sided risk, and there is less systematic put-buying demand. Index skew also reflects correlation spikes in crashes.

follow_ups.q: Which commodities can show an upward (call) skew?
follow_ups.a: Those with upside spike risk from supply shocks, like natural gas, power or some agricultural products: calls are priced at higher vols.

follow_ups.q: When did the equity skew become pronounced?
follow_ups.a: After the October 1987 crash (S&P 500 -20% in a day). Before, equity implied vol smiles were nearly flat.

cards.topic: Volatility term structure
cards.question: What is the term structure of volatility, and what does it look like in calm and stressed markets?
cards.answer: The term structure is implied vol (usually ATM) as a function of **maturity**. In **calm markets** it is typically **upward sloping** (contango): short-dated vol is low, near current realised vol, while long-dated vol is higher because it prices the possibility of future stress and includes a larger risk premium; long-dated vol also mean-reverts toward a long-run average. In **stressed markets** it **inverts** (backwardation): short-dated vol spikes far above long-dated because the market expects the turmoil to calm down eventually. Event dates (earnings, elections, central bank meetings) create **kinks**: the expiry just after the event carries extra variance. Short-dated vols move much more than long-dated ones, which is why vega is bucketed by maturity. You can compute **forward vol** between two expiries from total variances: $\sigma_{fwd}^2 = \frac{\sigma_2^2T_2 - \sigma_1^2T_1}{T_2 - T_1}$.

follow_ups.q: How do you compute forward volatility?
follow_ups.a: From total variances: $\sigma_{fwd}^2 = (\sigma_2^2T_2 - \sigma_1^2T_1)/(T_2-T_1)$. You subtract variances, never vols.

follow_ups.q: What does an inverted vol term structure signal?
follow_ups.a: Current stress: the market expects high volatility now and a calmer future. Typical right after a sharp selloff (e.g. March 2020).

follow_ups.q: Which part of the curve moves most?
follow_ups.a: The short end. Short-dated implied vols can double in days, while 2-5 year vols move much less; long-dated vol is anchored by mean reversion.

cards.topic: VIX
cards.question: What is the VIX? How is it calculated and how can you trade it?
cards.answer: The **VIX** is the CBOE volatility index: the market's **30-day implied volatility of the S&P 500**, often called the "fear gauge". It is not the implied vol of a single option: it is computed model-free from a **strip of OTM S&P 500 puts and calls** across all strikes, weighted by $1/K^2$, which gives the fair strike of a **30-day variance swap**; the VIX is the square root, in vol points. Because OTM puts are included, it embeds the **skew** and typically sits a bit above ATM implied vol. It rises when the market falls (strong negative correlation with the S&P). Its long-run average is around 19-20; below 15 is calm, above 30 stressed; it spiked above 80 in 2008 and March 2020. You **cannot buy the VIX index itself**; you trade **VIX futures**, **VIX options** or ETPs based on futures. VIX futures are usually in **contango** (above spot VIX), so long-VIX products lose money over time through roll-down.

follow_ups.q: Why is the VIX usually above ATM implied vol?
follow_ups.a: Because it integrates all OTM options with $1/K^2$ weights, which captures the expensive downside puts (skew). It measures variance swap-style vol, and variance is convex in tail moves.

follow_ups.q: VIX is 20. What 30-day move does it imply?
follow_ups.a: About $20\%\times\sqrt{30/365}\approx5.7\%$ standard deviation over the month, roughly 1.25% per trading day.

follow_ups.q: Why do long-VIX ETPs lose money over time?
follow_ups.a: They hold VIX futures, which are usually in contango; as futures converge down to the lower spot VIX, the position loses the roll yield. They only pay off in sudden vol spikes.

cards.topic: Variance risk premium
cards.question: Why does implied volatility tend to exceed realised volatility? Is selling options a free lunch?
cards.answer: Historically, index implied vol has exceeded subsequent realised vol most of the time: this gap is the **variance risk premium** (VRP). It exists because option buyers - mainly investors hedging equity portfolios - are **paying for insurance**, and sellers demand compensation for bearing **crash risk**: short options lose most precisely in bad states of the world (market crashes, liquidity crises), when losses hurt most. It is the same logic as an insurance company charging more than expected claims. So selling options (or variance) earns a positive return **on average**, but with **negative skewness**: many small gains and occasional huge losses (1987, 2008, August 2015, February 2018, March 2020). It is **not a free lunch**: it is a risk premium for tail risk, and it can wipe out years of gains in a few days. Careful sellers size positions, hedge tails (e.g. buy far OTM puts) and prefer delta-hedged, diversified exposures.

follow_ups.q: What was 'Volmageddon'?
