The next MPC is 5 November, one week after Chancellor Healey's first Budget on 28 October, and the September CPI release (out 21 October) is the key data point before it.

follow_ups.q: Why does the BoE publish individual votes and does it matter for trading?
follow_ups.a: It is part of its accountability framework. It matters a lot: a shift from 7-2 to 6-3 or 5-4 is itself a signal of where the median is going, so traders price the next move from the vote, not only from the decision.

follow_ups.q: What would make you expect a hike on 5 November?
follow_ups.a: An upside surprise in the 21 October CPI (especially services), stronger pay data, a loose Budget on 28 October, or sterling weakness adding imported inflation. One more hawk switching from the hold camp would make it 5-4 for a hike.

follow_ups.q: How would you trade the view that the BoE hikes less than priced?
follow_ups.a: Receive 1y or 2y SONIA OIS (or buy short-dated gilts / SONIA futures): if hikes fail to materialise, short rates fall. You could also position in 2s10s steepeners. The risk is an inflation surprise; size with DV01 and a stop.

cards.topic: Bank of England QT: active gilt sales, the APF and the new plan to 2034 (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: How does quantitative tightening work at the Bank of England, why is it different from the Fed or the ECB, and what did the MPC decide in September 2026?
cards.answer: The BoE's QE gilts sit in the Asset Purchase Facility (APF). QT shrinks it in two ways: passively, by not reinvesting gilts that mature, and actively, by selling gilts back to the market, which the Fed and the ECB have not done. In the year to September 2026 the stock fell by GBP 70bn: 49bn of maturities and 21bn of sales. In September 2026 the MPC unanimously adopted a multi-year plan: take the APF down to zero apart from about GBP 120bn kept to back banknotes, so about GBP 368bn still to go (APF stock 488bn on 16 September), roughly 222bn through maturities and 146bn through sales, about 46bn a year until September 2034, with active sales of about 20bn a year. The point of a long pre-announced plan is to make QT boring and predictable, so it does not add to term premium, which has risen by about 200bp since 2022. Active sales also crystallise losses, which the Treasury covers under an indemnity, so QT has a fiscal cost too.

follow_ups.q: Why did the BoE choose active sales when the Fed and ECB did not?
follow_ups.a: Its QE book was long-dated and would take decades to run off passively; it wanted to normalise the balance sheet within a reasonable horizon and keep QT in the background by making it gradual and predictable.

follow_ups.q: Does QT raise gilt yields?
follow_ups.a: Somewhat, through term premium: BoE estimates put the effect of announced QT at tens of basis points at most, much smaller than inflation and fiscal news. Execution matters more in stress: sales into a disorderly market could hurt, which is why the BoE keeps the option to pause (it delayed sales in 2022 during the LDI crisis).

follow_ups.q: How do QT sales interact with DMO issuance for a trader?
follow_ups.a: Both add duration supply that dealers must absorb and distribute. Traders track the combined calendar: auctions, syndications and BoE sale operations, often cheapening the relevant maturities into those dates and richening them after.

cards.topic: The 2022 UK LDI crisis: leverage, collateral calls, the gilt doom loop and the BoE intervention
cards.question: What happened in the UK gilt market in September-October 2022? Explain the mechanics of the LDI crisis with numbers and what changed afterwards.
cards.answer: On 23 September 2022 the Truss government's mini-budget announced large unfunded tax cuts and gilt yields jumped: the 30-year rose by about 160bp in a few days, a move far outside historical norms. Many UK defined-benefit pension schemes used liability-driven investment (LDI) funds that hedged their long-dated liabilities with leverage, through gilt repo and swaps. When yields rose, the value of those leveraged gilt positions fell, liabilities also fell so the schemes were not insolvent, but the LDI funds faced immediate collateral and margin calls in cash. To raise cash they sold gilts, mostly long gilts and linkers, which pushed yields up further and triggered more calls: a doom loop. On 28 September the Bank of England stepped in with temporary purchases of long gilts, which ran until 14 October; it bought only GBP 19.3bn out of up to GBP 65bn available, but the backstop stopped the spiral and gave funds time to recapitalise. Afterwards regulators required LDI funds to hold buffers able to withstand a 250bp yield rise, and leverage in the sector fell sharply.

follow_ups.q: Why did yields rise more at the long end than at the short end?
follow_ups.a: Forced sellers held long gilts and linkers, the long end is less liquid, and the fiscal shock raised term premium most. Short yields also rose on BoE hike expectations, but the LDI loop was concentrated beyond 20 years.

follow_ups.q: Was the BoE intervention inconsistent with fighting inflation?
follow_ups.a: The BoE argued no: it was temporary and targeted at market functioning, with a fixed end date and a plan to unwind, while the MPC kept raising Bank Rate. The separation between financial-stability tools and monetary policy was the key message.

follow_ups.q: Could a similar crisis happen today with 30y gilts near 6%?
follow_ups.a: Less likely from LDI because buffers are about 250bp and leverage is lower, but the long end is still thin and sensitive to fiscal news. The risk has shifted to other leveraged players (hedge fund basis trades, repo) and to a fiscal credibility shock around a Budget.

cards.topic: UK inflation now: CPI, CPIH, RPI, services and pay (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: What is UK inflation doing, which measures matter (CPI, CPIH, RPI, core, services) and why does the Bank of England worry more than its peers?
cards.answer: UK CPI inflation was 3.1% in August 2026, up from 2.9% in July, against a 2% target. Core CPI was 2.6% and services 3.4%, goods 2.7%. CPIH, which adds owner-occupiers' housing costs, was 3.3%, and RPI, the old index still used for index-linked gilts, was 3.4%. The pick-up is driven by energy: motor fuel is up about 23% year on year with Brent above USD 100 a barrel, and gas prices have jumped. The worry is persistence: services inflation above 3% and underlying pay growth around 3.5% mean the shock could feed into wages and prices, as it did in 2022-23 when UK inflation peaked above 11%, higher and later than in the US or euro area. With Bank Rate at 3.75%, the real policy rate is only about 0.6%. The next CPI print, for September, is on 21 October, a week before the Budget and two weeks before the 5 November MPC.

follow_ups.q: Why is UK core inflation higher than in the euro area?
follow_ups.a: A tighter labour market after Brexit reduced labour supply, stronger wage indexation habits, and higher services inflation (rents, hospitality) with pay growth above productivity. Energy pass-through also takes longer because of the Ofgem price cap.

follow_ups.q: What happens to RPI in 2030?
follow_ups.a: From February 2030 the RPI methodology will be brought in line with CPIH, so RPI inflation will drop by roughly the historical wedge (about 1 point). There was no compensation for linker holders, which is why long linker breakevens price lower RPI after 2030.

follow_ups.q: How would a strong CPI print move markets?
follow_ups.a: Front-end gilt yields up (more hikes priced), curve flatter, sterling up on higher rate expectations, and short-dated linker breakevens wider. The size depends on services rather than headline.

cards.topic: Gilt-Bund and gilt-Treasury spreads: decomposition, FX-hedged pickup and how to trade them (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: Why do 10-year gilts yield about 180bp more than Bunds and even more than Treasuries? Is that spread attractive for a euro-based investor, and how would you trade a view on it?
cards.answer: On 30 September 2026 the 10y gilt is about 5.42%, the Bund 3.58% and the Treasury 5.26%, so gilt-Bund is about 184bp and gilt-Treasury about +16bp. You can split the gilt-Bund spread into a policy part and a premium part: Bank Rate is 3.75% versus an ECB deposit rate of 2.50%, so 125bp of the spread just reflects higher expected short rates in the UK; the rest, roughly 60bp, is term premium for UK inflation persistence, heavy gilt supply plus active BoE QT sales, and fiscal risk ahead of the 28 October Budget. For a euro investor the headline 184bp is misleading: hedging GBP back to EUR costs roughly the short-rate gap (SONIA 3.73% minus €STR about 2.44%, so about 129bp), which leaves a hedged pickup of about 55bp. To trade it I would do a DV01-matched spread: buy gilts and sell Bunds (or gilt futures against Bund futures) if I think the UK premium compresses, for example after a credible Budget, with the risk that sticky UK inflation forces the BoE to hike.

follow_ups.q: Why does a positive 2y spread and a negative gilt-UST 2y spread matter?
follow_ups.a: It shows what is policy and what is premium. Gilt-UST 2y is negative (UK short rates expected slightly below US), yet the 10y gilt yields more: the whole 10y gap is term premium, a sign the market charges the UK for fiscal and inflation risk.

follow_ups.q: What would widen gilt-Bund?
follow_ups.a: A loose Budget or a hit to fiscal credibility, UK inflation surprises forcing more BoE hikes, faster QT sales, weak auctions or syndications, or ECB cuts. A global risk-off move would normally tighten it as Bunds rally most.

follow_ups.q: Can you trade the spread in futures?
follow_ups.a: Yes: buy ICE Long Gilt futures and sell Eurex Bund futures in DV01 ratio (future DV01 is roughly the cheapest-to-deliver DV01 divided by its conversion factor). It is liquid and cheap on balance sheet, but you carry basis risk between each future and its cash bond.

cards.topic: UK index-linked gilts: RPI indexation, the 3-month lag, breakevens, LDI demand and the 2030 RPI reform
cards.question: How do UK index-linked gilts work, what is a breakeven, and what is special about the UK linker market compared with TIPS or OATi?
cards.answer: Index-linked gilts pay a small real coupon and repay a principal both scaled by the RPI index ratio: today's reference RPI divided by the reference RPI at issue, with a 3-month lag for gilts issued since 2005 (8 months for older ones). So an investor is paid real yield plus realised RPI inflation. The breakeven is the nominal gilt yield minus the linker real yield: if RPI averages more than the breakeven, the linker outperforms the nominal gilt. Three things make the UK market special. First, it is huge and very long: linkers are around a quarter of the gilt stock and go out to about 50 years, because defined-benefit pension schemes have RPI-linked liabilities and were forced buyers through LDI. Second, it is RPI, not CPI: RPI runs above CPI, and from February 2030 its method will be aligned with CPIH, which cuts expected RPI after 2030 with no compensation to holders. Third, the huge real duration: long linkers lost more than half their value in 2022 when real yields jumped from about -2% to positive, which shows that inflation protection is not protection against rising real rates.

follow_ups.q: How would you position for UK inflation surprising up without taking duration risk?
follow_ups.a: Buy breakevens: long linker, short nominal gilt, sized so the real and nominal DV01s match, or receive realised RPI in an inflation swap. You gain if RPI and breakevens rise, with little exposure to a parallel move in nominal yields.

follow_ups.q: Why did the RPI reform matter for pension funds?
follow_ups.a: Many held RPI-linked assets against CPI-linked liabilities or enjoyed the RPI wedge. Aligning RPI with CPIH from 2030 cut the expected value of their linkers by roughly the wedge over the post-2030 cash flows, without compensation.

follow_ups.q: What is the difference between a gilt linker breakeven and an RPI swap rate?
follow_ups.a: Both price expected RPI, but swaps have no funding or balance sheet need and different liquidity; the gap (swap minus bond breakeven) is a traded basis driven by pension demand for swaps and dealers' hedging.

cards.topic: What drives sterling: rate differentials, energy terms of trade, fiscal risk premium (GBPUSD, EURGBP as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: Where is sterling and what drives it? Would you rather be long or short GBP into the Budget and the November MPC?
cards.answer: On 30 September 2026 GBPUSD is about 1.328, in a one-year range of 1.302 (5 November 2025) to 1.383 (29 January 2026), and EURGBP about 0.855 (range 0.847-0.884). Sterling is driven mainly by four things. Rate differentials: the 2-year gilt at 4.77% is 12bp below the Treasury and about 154bp above the Schatz, which supports GBP against EUR more than against USD. Terms of trade: the UK is a net energy importer, so oil above USD 100 and higher gas prices worsen its trade balance and growth. Risk sentiment: GBP is a pro-cyclical currency that tends to fall in global risk-off. And fiscal credibility: normally higher gilt yields support the pound, but when yields rise because of fiscal fear, as in 2022, gilts and sterling fall together, which is the warning sign. Into the 28 October Budget and 5 November MPC I would be cautious: if the Budget is credible and the BoE hikes, GBP should firm against EUR; if the Budget disappoints, the risk is a 2022-style joint sell-off. I would express a view in EURGBP with a stop, or through options to cap the loss.

follow_ups.q: Why did sterling fall in September 2022 even though gilt yields jumped?
follow_ups.a: The yield rise was a fiscal risk premium after unfunded tax cuts, not a sign of stronger growth or a hawkish central bank. Investors sold both gilts and pounds, the pattern of an emerging-market confidence shock; GBPUSD hit about 1.03-1.04.

follow_ups.q: Why does a weaker pound help the FTSE 100?
follow_ups.a: Most FTSE 100 revenues are in foreign currencies (energy, mining, pharma, consumer staples); a weaker pound raises their sterling value. The more domestic FTSE 250 benefits less.

follow_ups.q: What would you look at on the day of the Budget?
follow_ups.a: The OBR forecast and headroom against the fiscal rules, the gilt remit revision (especially long and linker issuance), and the reaction of 30y gilts and GBP together: the sign of the correlation tells you whether the market trusts the plan.

cards.topic: The UK yield curve in Sept 2026: steep 2s10s and 10s30s, long-end supply cuts and the 28 October Budget
cards.question: Describe the shape of the gilt curve today. Why is the UK long end so high, what does the Budget on 28 October change, and what curve trade would you consider?
cards.answer: On 30 September 2026 the 2y gilt is about 4.77%, the 10y 5.42% and the 30y 5.94%: 2s10s is +65bp and 10s30s +52bp, much steeper than in the US (+37bp and +33bp) or Germany (2s10s about +35bp). The 10y touched 5.44% on 28 September, the highest since 2007, and the 30y hit about 5.9% in early September, the highest since 1998. The front end is anchored by Bank Rate at 3.75% plus expected hikes. The long end carries a big term premium: sticky inflation, heavy supply, active BoE QT sales, weaker pension demand after the LDI crisis, and fiscal risk. The Budget on 28 October, the first of Chancellor John Healey, matters through two channels: the fiscal message (tax, spending, headroom against the rules) and the DMO remit revision, which says how much long paper will be sold. If the DMO cuts long issuance further and the fiscal plan is credible, I would expect 10s30s to flatten; a DV01-neutral flattener (sell 10y, buy 30y) expresses that, with the risk of a fiscal disappointment that steepens the curve.

follow_ups.q: Why might the DMO issue fewer long gilts even though long debt reduces rollover risk?
follow_ups.a: Long gilts are expensive now (30y near 5.9%) and demand from pensions is weaker, so forcing supply would raise the term premium and the government's cost. The DMO balances cost and risk; it can issue shorter and rely on Treasury bills while long demand is weak.

follow_ups.q: What is a bear steepener telling you?
follow_ups.a: Long yields rising faster than short ones: the market demands more term premium (inflation risk, supply, fiscal worry) rather than expecting a more hawkish central bank, which would bear-flatten the curve instead.

follow_ups.q: How does the BoE's QT plan affect the curve?
follow_ups.a: Active sales add duration supply; the BoE tilts them away from the long end to limit the impact, and the APF's longest gilt matures in 2049. A slower average pace (about GBP 46bn a year to 2034) is mildly supportive for term premium versus the previous 70bn.

cards.topic: Executing a US bear steepener with Treasury futures: contract DV01, hedge ratio and what can go wrong (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: The US curve is bear steepening: the 10-year is near 5.3% and 2s10s is back around +40bp. You want to put on 100k DV01 of 2s10s steepener with futures rather than cash bonds. How many TU and TY contracts do you trade, and what risks are left?
cards.answer: A steepener makes money if 10-year yields rise **relative** to 2-year yields, so I **buy the 2-year future (TU) and sell the 10-year future (TY)**, sized so a parallel move does nothing. The DV01 of a bond future is roughly the DV01 of its cheapest-to-deliver bond divided by its conversion factor: with yields where they are (2y about 4.9%, 10y about 5.3% on 30 September 2026), that is about **USD 39 per contract for TU** (USD 200k notional) and **about USD 59 for TY** (USD 100k notional); I would take the exact numbers from the screen. For 100k DV01 per leg: **long about 2,580 TU and short about 1,700 TY**, a ratio of about 1.5 TU per TY. Then a 10bp steepening makes about USD 1m, and a parallel 20bp sell-off makes roughly zero. Futures are attractive here because they use little balance sheet and are very liquid, but I keep residual risks: the **CTD can switch** (TY's CTD changes when yields move far from 6%), each future has its own **basis** to cash, I have to **roll** from December to March in late November, and margin is posted daily. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'I am long 2,580 TU / short 1,700 TY, 100k a bp of 2s10s at +41; the curve steepens because the Fed is near the end and the term premium is rising; stop at +30, target +60.'

follow_ups.q: Why use futures rather than cash bonds?
follow_ups.a: Futures need only margin, not a repo-financed bond position, so they use little balance sheet, are very liquid and cheap to trade. The cost is basis risk to cash, CTD switches and the need to roll quarterly.

follow_ups.q: Why is the TY DV01 larger than its CTD's DV01?
follow_ups.a: Because the futures DV01 is roughly the CTD DV01 divided by its conversion factor, and with yields below 6% the conversion factor is below 1 (about 0.91 here).

follow_ups.q: Would you do 2s10s or 5s30s for a term-premium story?
follow_ups.a: 5s30s or 10s30s isolates term premium better, because the 2-year is mostly driven by the next Fed meetings. 2s10s mixes a Fed view with a term-premium view; in a bear steepener driven by supply, the long end moves most.

cards.topic: Conditional curve trades: a bear steepener built with payer swaptions (1y10y vs 1y2y), payoffs and when to prefer it (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: You think that if US rates keep selling off, the curve will steepen, but you are not sure rates will keep rising. How can you express a 'conditional bear steepener' with swaptions, what does it cost, and what is the payoff in each scenario?
cards.answer: A cash steepener bets on the slope whatever the level does. A **conditional bear steepener** only switches on if rates rise: I **buy a 1-year-expiry payer swaption on the 10-year swap (1y10y)** and **sell a 1y2y payer**, both at-the-money forward and weighted to the same DV01. If rates fall, both options expire worthless and I keep or lose only the net premium. If rates rise, I become long the 10-year payer and short the 2-year payer, i.e. a steepener, **exactly in the scenario where I believe in it**. Because front-end vol is usually higher than long-end vol per basis point when the market is debating the next hikes, the package can cost **close to zero or even pay a small premium**: with illustrative normal vols of 120bp (1y2y) and 110bp (1y10y), the ATM premiums are about 48bp and 44bp of running DV01, so on 100k DV01 I receive about **USD 0.4m**. The risk is the scenario I am short: a **bear flattener**, where the Fed hikes more than expected and the 2-year sells off more than the 10-year; then the short 2y payer loses more than the 10y payer earns, without limit. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'I prefer the conditional version because my steepening view comes from term premium in a sell-off, not from Fed cuts; the trade is roughly zero cost and the risk is a hawkish Fed, which I'd cap by buying back the 2-year payer if October gets priced above 60%.'

follow_ups.q: How would you build a conditional bull steepener?
follow_ups.a: Buy a receiver on the short tenor (for example 1y2y) and sell a receiver on the long tenor (1y10y), DV01-matched. If rates fall it becomes a steepener, which is what happens when the Fed cuts; if rates rise both expire worthless.

follow_ups.q: Why is front-end vol often higher than long-end vol in bp?
follow_ups.a: When the market debates the next hikes or cuts, short rates can move a lot on each data print, while long rates also reflect slower-moving expectations and term premium. In calm or 'long end in charge' regimes it can reverse.

follow_ups.q: What is the vega exposure of the package?
follow_ups.a: Before expiry you are long 10-year vol and short 2-year vol. A rise in front-end vol (Fed uncertainty) hurts the mark-to-market even if rates do not move.

cards.topic: Negative USD swap spreads: the carry of a long swap spread trade and its balance-sheet (SLR) cost (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: The 10-year SOFR swap is about 38bp below the 10-year Treasury. A colleague says: 'Buy the Treasury, pay fixed on the swap, you pick up 38bp a year and the spread has to come back.' What is the real carry of this long swap spread trade, why doesn't the street do it in size, and would you put it on?
cards.answer: A **long swap spread** trade means I **buy the 10-year Treasury, finance it in repo, and pay fixed on a 10-year SOFR swap**: I gain if the spread (swap minus Treasury, about **-38bp** at the end of September 2026: swap about 4.91% versus Treasury about 5.29%) moves back towards zero. The carry is **not 38bp**: it is the Treasury yield minus the repo rate, minus the fixed rate I pay plus the SOFR I receive. With repo a few bp above SOFR (about 3.93% versus SOFR 3.88%, illustrative), carry is about **+33bp a year**, so about **USD 330k a year per USD 100m**. In spread terms that is small: with a DV01 of about **USD 77k**, it is only about **1bp of spread per quarter**, while the spread can easily move 8bp in three months. The real reason it stays cheap is **balance sheet**: the Treasury sits on a dealer's balance sheet and consumes leverage capital under the **eSLR**. At about 4% leverage capital (illustrative, after the reform effective April 2026), USD 100m ties up USD 4m of capital for about **8% return**, below a typical 12% hurdle; the carry alone would only clear it with the spread near **-53bp**. So I would only do it small, as a tactical trade with a catalyst. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'Long swap spreads earn about 33bp of carry, 1bp a quarter in spread terms; it is a balance-sheet trade, not free money, so I size it small and want a catalyst like a Treasury SLR exemption.'

follow_ups.q: Why are swap spreads more negative at 30 years than at 2 years?
follow_ups.a: The long end needs the most balance sheet per unit of risk, carries heavy supply, and pension funds and insurers receive fixed in long swaps to hedge liabilities, which pushes long swap rates down relative to Treasuries.

follow_ups.q: How does the trade behave at quarter-end?
follow_ups.a: Repo rates jump above SOFR as banks shrink balance sheets for reporting, so financing the Treasury costs more and daily carry can turn negative; the spread itself can also cheapen for a few days.

follow_ups.q: Would you do it with futures instead of cash?
follow_ups.a: You can: buy TY futures and pay fixed in swaps, a 'futures swap spread'. It uses less balance sheet, but adds CTD and futures-basis risk and depends on the implied repo rate in the futures price (see rfc-740).

cards.topic: Bunds at or above swaps: a near-zero Bund swap spread, German supply, Dutch pensions and how to trade it (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: The 10-year Bund now yields about the same as the 10-year EUR swap, and more than the €STR OIS. For years Bunds traded well through swaps. Why has the Bund swap spread collapsed, what does the asset swap carry, and how would you trade it into year-end?
cards.answer: The **Bund swap spread** (EUR swap minus Bund yield) used to be clearly positive: Bunds were the scarce safe asset and yielded **less** than swaps. On 29 September 2026 the 10-year Bund was at **3.63%** and the 10-year 6-month Euribor swap at about **3.69%**, so the spread was only about **+6bp** (around +12bp on 30 September if the swap was unchanged, with the Bund at 3.57%). Against the €STR OIS (about 3.41%, low-confidence quote) the Bund even yields about **22bp more**. Three forces did it: **German supply** (the 2025 fiscal package, infrastructure fund and defence spending outside the debt brake), **ECB balance-sheet run-off** so collateral is no longer scarce, and **receiving demand in swaps** from the Dutch pension reform (about EUR 34bn of swaps under 25 years bought at the January 2026 transition, with ABP's switch on 1 January 2027). The trade is an **asset swap**: buy the Bund, repo it, pay fixed. Carry is about **+39bp a year** (illustrative repo 2.40% and 6-month Euribor 2.85%), mostly the Euribor-repo gap, only about **1.2bp of spread per quarter**. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'Bund swap spreads at +6 price a lot of German supply already; I'd buy Bund asset swaps small for the year-end collateral bid and a slower ABP transition, stop at -2, target +15.'

follow_ups.q: Why compare the Bund with Euribor swaps rather than €STR swaps?
follow_ups.a: Euribor swaps are still the most liquid EUR benchmark and the standard for asset swaps. But €STR is the risk-free rate, so Bund minus €STR OIS tells you the pure duration-supply premium; quote both and say which one you trade.

follow_ups.q: Why did Dutch pensions matter for EUR swap spreads?
follow_ups.a: Under the new contracts funds need less long-dated hedging: they receive fixed in shorter maturities and unwind receivers beyond 25 years. That moves swap rates, not Bund yields, so it shifts swap spreads and the 10s30s swap curve.

follow_ups.q: Is a negative Bund swap spread a sign of German credit risk?
follow_ups.a: No. Germany's CDS stays very low; the move is about supply, the end of ECB buying and swap flows. It is a liquidity and balance-sheet premium, not a default premium.

cards.topic: Carry and roll-down on the EUR €STR OIS curve, tenor by tenor, and the carry-to-vol ratio (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: Your PM asks: 'Where is the best carry on the EUR curve for the next three months if nothing moves?' The €STR OIS curve is roughly 2.52% at 3 months, 2.98% at 1 year, 3.16% at 2 years and 3.41% at 10 years, with €STR at 2.44%. Compute 3-month carry and roll-down for receivers, scale them by volatility, and tell me what the answer really means.
cards.answer: For a **receiver** (receive fixed, pay €STR), 3-month **carry** is the fixed rate minus the floating I expect to pay, scaled into rate bp by the swap's annuity: $(S_n - r_{3m}) \times 0.25 / A_n$. **Roll-down** is what I gain as the swap ages down an unchanged curve: $S_n - S_{n-0.25}$. With €STR at 2.44% and the curve of 30 September 2026 (2.52% 3m, 2.98% 1y, 3.16% 2y, 3.41% 10y, 3.42% 30y, medium-to-low confidence quotes; 5y at an illustrative 3.30%, a straight line between 2y and 10y would give 3.25%), I get about **27bp for the 1-year, 13bp for the 2-year, 5.5bp for the 5-year, 3bp for the 10-year and 1bp for the 30-year**. Divided by an illustrative 3-month normal vol (35-45bp), the carry-to-vol ratio is about **0.78 at 1 year and 0.30 at 2 years**, but below 0.12 beyond 5 years. So the best carry is at the **front end**, because the curve is steep there. But that steepness is the market pricing **ECB hikes** (roughly four more over the next year after September's move to 2.50%): the carry is exactly what I earn if the ECB delivers **less than priced**, and what I lose if it delivers more. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'Best carry-to-vol is receiving 1y to 2y €STR, about 0.8 and 0.3 a quarter, but it is a short hike-risk position, not free carry; I'd only do it with a view that the energy shock fades before the ECB delivers four hikes.'

follow_ups.q: Why divide carry by volatility instead of comparing raw bp?
follow_ups.a: Because 5bp of carry on a tenor that moves 20bp a quarter is better than 10bp on one that moves 80bp. Carry-to-vol puts tenors on the same risk scale and is the closest thing to a Sharpe ratio for one horizon.

follow_ups.q: Is carry the same as the expected return?
follow_ups.a: Only if the curve really stays unchanged. Under the expectations hypothesis forwards are unbiased and expected carry is zero; carry trades work historically because forwards include a term premium, which is not guaranteed.

follow_ups.q: Where would a payer have the best carry?
follow_ups.a: Where the curve is flattest or inverted, here the 10s30s area, which costs almost nothing to pay; it is a cheap way to be short duration, while paying the 1-2 year area costs the full hike premium.

cards.topic: Fed-ECB divergence or convergence through 1y1y forwards: SOFR vs €STR, sizing and the EURUSD link (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: Both the Fed and the ECB are in hiking mode. A macro client asks: 'Is the market pricing the Fed and the ECB to diverge further or to converge, and how do I trade a view on it?' Use 1y1y forwards on SOFR and €STR, size a DV01-neutral trade and explain what it means for EURUSD.
cards.answer: The cleanest way to read a policy gap is the **1y1y forward**: the 1-year rate starting in 1 year, $F = (1+S_2)^2/(1+S_1) - 1$. It strips out the next few meetings and shows where the market thinks each central bank will be in a year. With SOFR 2-year swaps about **4.69%** and an illustrative 1-year at 4.40%, the SOFR 1y1y is about **4.98%**; with €STR OIS at 2.98% (1y) and 3.16% (2y), the €STR 1y1y is about **3.34%** (medium-to-low confidence quotes). The gap is about **164bp**, against **144bp** today (SOFR 3.88% minus €STR 2.44%) and 142bp at 1 year. So the market prices **more divergence**: the Fed keeps hiking in year two (about +58bp versus +36bp for the ECB). If I think the energy shock hits Europe harder and the ECB has to catch up, I **receive SOFR 1y1y and pay €STR 1y1y**, DV01-matched: for USD 100k per bp, about **USD 1.1bn** of SOFR 1y1y against about **EUR 0.94bn** of €STR 1y1y (EUR 88.5k per bp at EURUSD 1.13). A 30bp convergence makes about USD 3m. For FX, a narrower gap is **EURUSD-positive**; the 1-year forward at today's rates is about 1.1146, about **154 pips** below spot (illustrative, before cross-currency basis). **What I'd say on the desk:** 'The 1y1y gap is 164bp versus 144 spot: the curve prices the Fed outrunning the ECB. I'd fade it, receive SOFR 1y1y, pay €STR 1y1y, 100k a bp, target 135, stop 180.'

follow_ups.q: Why use 1y1y rather than 2-year swaps?
follow_ups.a: The 2-year includes the next few meetings, which are mostly known; the 1y1y isolates the policy rate expected a year ahead, where views differ and where term premium is still small.

follow_ups.q: How do you hedge the FX risk of the EUR leg?
follow_ups.a: The swap itself has no principal, only P&L in EUR. You can sweep EUR P&L into USD periodically or buy a small EURUSD forward against the expected P&L; the main FX effect is translation, not principal.

follow_ups.q: How would you express the same view in FX?
follow_ups.a: Buy EURUSD or EURUSD calls: if the forward rate gap narrows, the carry against the euro shrinks and the euro tends to rise. But FX also depends on growth, terms of trade and risk sentiment, so the rates spread is the purer expression.

cards.topic: Reading ECB pricing for the 29 October meeting with meeting-dated €STR OIS, and HICP flash scenarios for 2 October (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: The ECB meets on 29 October after raising the deposit rate to 2.50% in September. €STR is 2.44%. How do you read from the meeting-dated €STR OIS what the market prices for that meeting, and how could the September HICP flash on 2 October (consensus 3.6% after 3.2%) move that pricing and your P&L?
cards.answer: A **meeting-dated OIS** (an ECB-dated €STR swap) covers exactly the period between two policy meetings, so its rate is the market's expected average €STR over that period. A decision on Thursday 29 October takes effect on **Wednesday 4 November**, so I look at the swap from 4 November to the December meeting. If €STR stays about **6bp below the deposit rate** (2.44% versus 2.50%), the priced move is simply the dated rate minus today's €STR: with an illustrative dated rate of **2.58%**, that is **+14bp, or about 56%** of a 25bp hike. It is consistent with the 3-month OIS at about 2.52% (my blend gives 2.53%). Published readings disagree (from about 40% to 75% in late September), so I always rebuild it myself. For HICP on 2 October, I map scenarios to pricing: a print **at or above 3.9%** (France 3.4% and Italy 4.1% already beat forecasts) could take hike odds to about **85%**, i.e. **+7bp** on the dated swap; in line at **3.6%** leaves it near unchanged; **3.3%** could cut odds to about 35%, **-5bp**. Paying EUR 1bn of the dated swap (DV01 about EUR 13.6k) makes about EUR +99k, 0 or -71k; with illustrative weights of 30/50/20 the expected gain is only about EUR 15k. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'October is priced at about 56% of a hike, 14bp in the dated OIS; the risk into HICP is skewed up, but much of it is priced after the country prints, so I'd only pay small, and prefer options for the tails.'

follow_ups.q: Why compare with today's €STR rather than with the deposit rate?
follow_ups.a: Because the dated swap is on €STR, which trades about 6bp below the deposit rate. If you subtracted 2.50% you would understate the priced hike by 6bp; the assumption is that the spread stays stable through the meeting.

follow_ups.q: How would you trade the flash if you thought core would be soft?
follow_ups.a: Receive the October dated swap or buy a call spread on December Euribor futures. If headline is high but core is soft, the ECB may look through energy, so odds could fall even on a strong headline.

follow_ups.q: How does this differ from fed funds futures?
follow_ups.a: Fed funds futures settle on a monthly average, so you must weight days before and after the meeting (rfc-747). ECB-dated OIS already align with the effective dates, which makes the probability calculation more direct.

cards.topic: FOMC 28 October 2026: reading fed funds futures (October, November and December contracts) and the 35% hike probability
cards.question: The market prices about a one-in-three chance that the Fed hikes on 28 October. Show me how you get that number from fed funds futures, which contract you would look at, and what you would tell the desk about the meeting.
cards.answer: As of 30 September 2026 the Fed funds target is 3.75-4.00% and the effective rate (EFFR) prints about 3.88%. A 30-day fed funds future settles on 100 minus the **average** EFFR of its month, so I read the meeting from the **November contract**: the October meeting decision takes effect on 29 October, so November is the first full month after it and there is no meeting in November. If November trades at about 96.03, the implied average rate is 3.97%, i.e. about 9bp above today's 3.88%; divided by a 25bp hike, that is a **35% probability**. The October contract is almost useless for this: only 3 of its 31 days come after the decision, so even a certain hike moves it by just 2.4bp. The number is a risk-neutral price, not a forecast, and it moved a lot: about 70% before John Williams said on 29 September there is 'no need for urgency' and before the soft August core PCE (3.0%). **What I'd say on the desk:** 'October is a live meeting but not the base case at 35%; the real swing factor is the September payrolls on 2 October, consensus about 90k. A strong number re-prices October toward 50-60%, and 2-year yields would move most. December stays priced for a hike, so the debate is timing, not direction.'

follow_ups.q: Why not read the October contract?
follow_ups.a: Because it settles on the average EFFR of October and the decision only applies from 29 October, 3 days out of 31. A certain 25bp hike moves it by only 2.4bp, the same order as month-end noise in the EFFR.

follow_ups.q: Is 35% the market's forecast?
follow_ups.a: No, it is a risk-neutral price. It includes any premium investors pay to hedge a hike, and positioning: after a big repricing, the number can overshoot. I use it as 'what is priced', then state my own probability.

follow_ups.q: What would make the probability jump back to 60-70%?
follow_ups.a: A strong September payrolls report (2 October) with falling unemployment, a hot September CPI in mid-October, or Fed speakers pushing back on Williams. Oil above 100 again would also help.

cards.topic: Trading your FOMC view against the market: expected value, sizing, asymmetry and options (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: The market prices roughly a one-in-three chance of a Fed hike on 28 October. You think it is more like 60%. How do you turn that view into a trade: which instrument, how much expected value, how big, and would you use options instead?
cards.answer: A view is only worth trading if it differs from the price, so I start from what is priced. With EFFR at about 3.88% and a 35% hike probability, the **November fed funds future** trades near **96.03** (the maths of reading it is in rfc-747). If the Fed hikes, November settles near 95.87; if it holds, near 96.12. So **selling** November makes **+16.25bp** if they hike and loses **8.75bp** if they don't: about **USD +677 / -365 per contract** (USD 41.67 per bp). At my 60% the **expected value is +6.25bp, about USD 260 per contract**. I size from the loss I accept if I am wrong, not from the expected gain: a USD 500k budget gives **about 1,370 contracts**, which makes about USD 930k on a hike and has an expected value of about USD 360k. Careful: another FedWatch reading on 30 September showed **47%**, not 35%. At 47% the payoff is +13.25 / -11.75bp, my edge falls to 3.25bp and the same budget buys only about 1,020 contracts. So I check the live price before anything else. Options (for example a put spread on December SOFR futures) are better if I am right on direction but unsure of **timing** (October or December), because the loss is capped at the premium. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'I think October is closer to 60% than 35%; I'd sell November fed funds, sized to lose 500k on a hold, and add a December SOFR put spread in case they wait until December.'

follow_ups.q: Why size from the loss rather than the expected gain?
follow_ups.a: Because the outcome is binary: you either lose the full 8.75bp or gain 16.25bp. The risk budget is what you can lose on one meeting; the EV only tells you whether the trade is worth doing.

follow_ups.q: Why not just trade the 2-year Treasury?
follow_ups.a: The 2-year mixes October with the whole path of rates, term premium and supply. The November fed funds future isolates the October decision, so the P&L matches the view.

follow_ups.q: Why did the probability move from about 70% to 35% in a few days?
follow_ups.a: Fed speakers (Williams said there was no urgency on 29 September) and a soft August core PCE. A binary price reacts strongly to news, which is why entry level matters.

prerequisites: Fed funds futures and implied probabilities

cards.topic: European investor in US Treasuries: FX hedging cost, hedged yield and hedge ratio (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: A French insurer sees the 10-year Treasury at about 5.3% against roughly 3.6% on the Bund and wants to buy USD 100m. It must hedge the dollar. What yield does it really get in euros, how do you compute the hedging cost, and what hedge ratio would you suggest?
cards.answer: The 5.3% is a dollar yield; an insurer that hedges the dollar earns roughly the **Treasury yield minus the hedging cost**. Hedging means selling USD forward, usually 3 months at a time. By covered interest parity, the cost is about the **gap between 3-month USD and EUR rates plus the cross-currency basis**: with an illustrative 3-month USD OIS of 3.95% (SOFR is 3.88% and some hike risk is priced), 3-month €STR OIS around 2.52% and an illustrative EURUSD basis of -15bp, the cost is about **1.58% a year**. So the hedged yield is about **5.29 - 1.58 = 3.71%**, only about **10bp above the Bund** and about **1% below the OAT**. On USD 100m, the hedge costs about USD 1.6m a year, paid about USD 0.4m every quarterly roll. Two traps. First, the hedged yield is a **carry number, not a locked return**: if the Fed hikes in October, the cost rises by about 25bp and the hedged yield falls toward 3.5%. Locking it with a 10-year cross-currency swap gives about the same 3.7% today. Second, the **hedge ratio**: a 100% hedge kills the pickup; a 50% hedge gives about 4.5% of carry but leaves half the position exposed to EURUSD (spot about 1.13). Most insurers stay close to fully hedged because of solvency capital on FX. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'Hedged Treasuries yield about 3.7% in euros, Bund plus 10; the case is curve and diversification, not carry. If the client wants pickup, show OATs or a partial hedge, with the FX risk spelled out.'

follow_ups.q: Why does a negative basis make the hedge more expensive for a European investor?
follow_ups.a: Because the investor is effectively borrowing dollars through the FX swap, and a negative EURUSD basis means dollars borrowed this way cost more than USD OIS. Here it adds about 15bp a year.

follow_ups.q: Is the hedged yield the return the insurer will earn?
follow_ups.a: No. It is today's carry. The hedging cost resets every roll with short rates and the basis, and the bond price moves with US yields. Only a cross-currency swap to maturity locks the euro yield.

follow_ups.q: When does hedged UST beat Bund clearly?
follow_ups.a: When the US curve is much steeper than the euro curve, or when Fed cuts lower the hedging cost. With 10-year yields above 5% but the Fed still hiking, the gap is small.

prerequisites: Covered interest parity and FX forwards

cards.topic: US investor in hedged Bunds and OATs: when the FX hedge pays you, and what it does to flows (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: A US asset manager can buy the 10-year Treasury at about 5.3%. You pitch French OATs hedged back into dollars instead. Why does the hedge pay the investor, what hedged yield do they get on Bunds and OATs, and what are the risks they take on?
cards.answer: It is the mirror of the European investor's problem (rfc-749). A US investor buys EUR spot, buys the bond and **sells EUR forward**, so in effect it lends dollars and borrows euros for 3 months. It **receives** the short USD rate and pays the short EUR rate, and with a negative EURUSD basis it also earns the basis. With illustrative 3-month USD OIS at 3.95%, 3-month €STR OIS around 2.52% and a basis of -15bp, the hedge **pays about 1.58% a year**. So a Bund at an illustrative 3.60% becomes about **5.18% in dollars**, roughly 11bp below the Treasury, but an OAT at about 4.75% (Bund plus 111-121bp at end September) becomes about **6.33%**, about **104bp above the Treasury** and above a rough US IG yield (Treasury plus 84bp). On USD 100m that is about USD 1m a year of extra carry. What the investor really buys is **French spread risk and EUR duration**, not FX risk: with a duration of about 8, the carry is wiped out if OATs underperform Treasuries by about **3bp a quarter** or 13bp over a year. Catalysts are close: Moody's review on 23 October (Aa3 negative), the ECB on 29 October, the budget vote on 17 November. Flows like this, plus US companies issuing in euros (cf-922), are why there are natural dollar lenders in the FX swap market. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'Hedged OATs yield about 6.3% in dollars, Treasuries plus 100; you are paid for French politics and the rating, so size it on spread risk, not on the carry.'

follow_ups.q: Why does the Bund hedged into dollars yield about the same as the Treasury?
follow_ups.a: Because hedging adds the short-rate gap plus basis, about 1.58%, and the Bund plus that is about 5.18%. Covered parity makes safe assets look similar once hedged; what remains is the slope of each curve and credit.

follow_ups.q: Does a Fed hike hurt this trade?
follow_ups.a: Not the carry: the investor lends dollars in the FX swap, so a higher USD short rate raises the hedge pickup on the next roll. It hurts only through any broad sell-off in yields.

follow_ups.q: Why compare with the CDS?
follow_ups.a: To show how much of the pickup is pure French credit. Taking off the 65bp CDS still leaves about 39bp over Treasuries, so part of the gain comes from the euro curve and the basis.

cards.topic: The EURUSD cross-currency basis today: where it shows up in prices and how the year-end turn distorts it (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: It is 1 October. A client asks why the 3-month EURUSD FX swap looks more expensive than the rate gap, and why a 1-month swap starting mid-December is quoted much worse still. Where does the cross-currency basis enter prices today, and how does the year-end turn work?
cards.answer: The basis is the extra cost of getting dollars through an FX swap rather than at USD OIS; for EURUSD it is negative, so dollar borrowers pay more and dollar lenders earn more. Today it enters three places. First, **hedging costs**: of the about 1.58% a year a European pays to hedge Treasuries, about 15bp is basis (rfc-749), and a US buyer of OATs earns it (rfc-750). Second, **funding**: the implied dollar rate in the swap is about 4.10% against an illustrative 3.95% OIS. Third, **issuance**: a US company issuing in euros and swapping back saves the basis (cf-922). The year-end part: banks shrink balance sheets at 31 December because regulatory scores (G-SIB, leverage) use year-end data, so dollar lending over the turn is scarce. In 2026 the turn runs from Thursday 31 December to Monday 4 January, **4 nights**. With an illustrative ex-turn basis of -6bp and a turn premium of 200bp annualised, a 1-month swap from mid-December to mid-January trades about **-32bp**, a 3-month from 5 October (maturing 5 January) about **-15bp**, of which about 9bp is the turn, and a 1-year about -8bp. On USD 1bn the turn alone costs about **USD 222k for 4 days**. All basis levels are illustrative: take them from the screen. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'Quote the 3-month ex-turn and the turn separately; for clients who must hedge across year-end, roll early or extend past mid-January, and don't annualise a 4-day premium into a view on dollar funding stress.'

follow_ups.q: Why do banks care about year-end specifically?
follow_ups.a: Many regulatory measures, such as G-SIB scores for several jurisdictions and leverage disclosures, use year-end or quarter-end data. Banks shrink balance sheets on those dates, so lending dollars over them is more expensive.

follow_ups.q: What limits how negative the basis can go?
follow_ups.a: For banks with access, the Fed swap lines through the ECB offer dollars at USD OIS plus 25bp, a ceiling on the short-term cost. Longer tenors have no such ceiling.

follow_ups.q: Is the basis a measure of dollar shortage?
follow_ups.a: Partly: it reflects demand for dollar hedges and funding against the balance sheet available to arbitrage it. Use ex-turn tenors for that read; turn-crossing quotes mostly price calendar effects.

prerequisites: Bank balance sheet constraints (leverage ratio, G-SIB)

cards.topic: French sovereign CDS: level, implied default probability, why it is quoted in dollars, and the quanto effect (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: France 5-year CDS is quoted around 65bp in dollars, above Italy. What default probability does that imply, why is a French CDS quoted in USD rather than EUR, and how would you read the level ahead of Moody's review on 23 October?
cards.answer: The quick rule is **spread ≈ default intensity × (1 - recovery)**. With 65bp and a standard 40% recovery, the intensity is about **1.08% a year**, so the market-implied probability of a French credit event within 5 years is about **5.3%**. It is a **risk-neutral** number: it includes a risk premium and the cost of hedging demand, so it is much higher than any rating-based estimate. Why dollars: protection on a euro-area sovereign pays out exactly when the euro is likely to fall, so buyers want to be paid in USD; a EUR-denominated contract trades lower. That gap is the **quanto effect**: if you think the euro would drop about 20-30% on a French default (illustrative), the EUR CDS should be about **(1 - d) × 65 ≈ 45-52bp**. This matters when you compare with a EUR bond spread (rfc-753). On sizing: a USD 10m position has a CS01 of about **USD 4.4k per bp**, and the contract trades with the standard 100bp coupon plus an upfront (at 65bp the protection buyer receives about 1.5 points). The level has moved fast: 39bp on 16 September, 56bp on 23 September, 65bp on 29 September (investing.com), while press reports cite about 52bp as the highest since 2017, so I'd check the dealer quote. A Moody's downgrade from Aa3 is **not a credit event**; it matters through flows and sentiment. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'At 65 in dollars France prices about a 5% five-year risk-neutral default probability, more than Italy; in euro terms it is nearer 50, so it is a hedge for French political risk, not a default call.'

follow_ups.q: Why is the risk-neutral default probability higher than the historical one?
follow_ups.a: Because the spread also pays for a risk premium, for uncertainty on recovery and for hedging demand. Historical default rates for sovereigns rated around AA/A are tiny; CDS prices insurance, not frequency.

follow_ups.q: Is a rating downgrade a credit event?
follow_ups.a: No. Sovereign credit events are failure to pay, repudiation or moratorium, and restructuring. A downgrade moves the CDS only through market risk appetite and hedging demand.

follow_ups.q: Why can France trade above Italy despite a better rating?
follow_ups.a: Spreads price direction and uncertainty: France's deficit and political risk are rising, and French CDS is used as a proxy hedge for European exposure. Ratings lag and move in steps.

cards.topic: The CDS-bond basis on French OATs: which spread to use, the quanto trap and why the basis is not arbitraged (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: France 5-year CDS is about 65bp in dollars. A 5-year OAT yields about 4.2% against a 5-year euro swap around 3.6%. Is the CDS-bond basis on France positive or negative, what drives it right now, and is there a trade?
cards.answer: The basis is **CDS spread minus the bond's spread over a risk-free-ish curve**, usually the asset-swap spread (ASW). Roughly, the 5-year OAT is about **58bp over 6-month Euribor swaps** (4.18 - 3.60, an approximation; levels of medium confidence). The trap is the CDS: 65bp is a **USD** contract. Against it the basis looks **+7bp**. But the bond is in euros, and the USD CDS includes the quanto premium (rfc-752): with an illustrative 25% euro fall on default, the euro-equivalent CDS is about **49bp**, and the basis is about **-9bp**. Against €STR OIS (about 3.25% interpolated) the bond spread is about 93bp and the basis about **-44bp**. So the sign depends on the currency and the benchmark: say which one you use. What drives it now: **hedging demand** lifts CDS (it rose from 39 to 65bp in two weeks), which pushes the basis up; **rating-driven selling** before Moody's on 23 October and heavy OAT supply cheapen bonds, which pushes it down. Is there a trade? A negative basis package (buy the OAT on asset swap, buy protection) earns the basis, here only about 9bp, about **EUR 45k a year on EUR 50m**, while the balance sheet it uses costs an illustrative **60bp** at a 12% return on 5% capital. That is why the basis is not arbitraged away. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'On a like-for-like euro basis, OATs trade slightly cheap to CDS, about -10; it is too small to pay for balance sheet, so I'd use it as a signal: CDS is leading, driven by hedgers.'

follow_ups.q: Why not compute the basis as CDS minus the OAT-Bund spread?
follow_ups.a: Because the Bund is not a risk-free benchmark for this purpose: it trades rich to swaps for its own reasons (safe-haven demand, collateral value). OAT-Bund mixes French credit with German technicals.

follow_ups.q: Why is a negative basis not arbitraged away?
follow_ups.a: Because the package uses balance sheet and funding, which cost far more than a few basis points a year, and because the basis can widen further in stress before converging.

follow_ups.q: What does it mean when CDS rises faster than the bond spread?
follow_ups.a: Hedgers are buying protection as the quickest unfunded hedge. The basis turns more positive; if bonds later cheapen (rating-driven selling, supply), it can move back.

cards.topic: Moody's on France, 23 October: the mechanics of a sovereign downgrade (ECB collateral, mandates, indices) (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: Moody's reviews France on 23 October; it is Aa3 with a negative outlook, while S&P and Fitch are already at A+. A client asks whether a downgrade to A1 would trigger forced selling of OATs. Walk me through what actually changes: ECB collateral, index ratings, investor mandates, and what you expect for OAT-Bund.
cards.answer: Very little changes **mechanically**, which is why I would not expect a big forced-selling wave. **ECB collateral**: the Eurosystem uses the **best** rating among its accepted agencies for public sector assets. DBRS still has France at **AA** (trend negative since 18 September 2026), so France stays in credit quality step 1; and even at A+ everywhere it would be step 2, which for central government bonds carries the **same haircuts** as step 1. **Indices**: Bloomberg uses the **middle** of Moody's, S&P and Fitch. Today that is Aa3/A+/A+, so the index rating is already **A+**; after a cut to A1 it is still A+. **Mandates**: the only real sellers are mandates with an "AA by any agency" or "lowest rating" rule, and most of those had to act when Fitch and S&P moved in 2025. Capital rules barely care: euro area sovereigns in euro keep a 0% risk weight for banks. So the effect is mostly **signal and headline**: France would be single A at the three big agencies. The market already prices worse than Aa3: OAT-Bund 10y is about **111-121bp** and France 5y CDS about **65bp**, above Italy. A one-notch cut is probably worth **a few basis points**, and with an OAT DV01 of about EUR 73k per EUR 100m, 5bp costs about EUR 0.36m. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'A Moody's cut is mostly priced and does not change ECB eligibility or the index rating; I'd fade any spike above 120bp in OAT-Bund unless the budget vote on 17 November goes wrong.'

follow_ups.q: Why does the ECB use the best rating and not the worst?
follow_ups.a: For public sector assets the Eurosystem applies the first-best rule among its accepted agencies, to avoid one agency alone pushing a sovereign out of the collateral framework. Since 2025 it moves to the second-best rating for private sector assets only.

follow_ups.q: What would really trigger forced selling of OATs?
follow_ups.a: A fall below the thresholds written into rules: for example the index middle rating dropping to A- or BBB, or a sovereign losing ECB eligibility (below BBB-). France is many notches away from those.

follow_ups.q: How would you hedge an OAT long into the review?
follow_ups.a: Sell Bund futures against it (OAT-Bund spread) or buy 5y France CDS. The spread hedge removes the rate risk; the CDS also covers a deeper fiscal crisis, but it is quoted in USD and has basis risk to the bond.

cards.topic: US investment grade spreads against Treasuries versus against swaps: why credit is less tight than it looks (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: US investment grade trades at an OAS of about 84bp over Treasuries, close to the tights of the last 25 years. A client says credit is 'priced for perfection'. But 10y Treasuries yield more than 10y SOFR swaps. How does that change the picture, and what spread does a swapped investor actually earn?
cards.answer: The 84bp is measured against **Treasuries**, and Treasuries are unusually **cheap** right now: the 10y SOFR swap is about **4.91%** against a 10y Treasury near **5.29%**, a **swap spread of about -38bp**. A corporate bond's spread to swaps is its spread to Treasuries **minus** the swap spread, so: 84 - (-38) = **about 122bp over SOFR swaps** at the 10y point. The IG index has a duration of roughly 7 years, where the swap spread is about -32bp by interpolation (2y about -21, 10y about -38), so the **index is about 116bp over swaps**. That is the number an investor who swaps fixed into floating (a bank treasury, a foreign buyer, an insurer with floating liabilities) actually earns: about **SOFR + 115-120bp**, which is not tight at all. So part of the "tightness" is not credit getting expensive, it is **Treasuries getting cheap**: heavy supply, bank balance sheet limits (SLR) and the term premium push Treasury yields above swaps. The right comparison depends on the investor: a total-return buyer funded in cash compares with Treasuries, a swapped buyer with swaps. The breakeven is also better: 116bp over 7 years of duration means spreads can widen about **16-17bp** in a year before the spread carry is lost, versus 12bp on the Treasury measure. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'IG at 84 over Treasuries looks tight, but it is SOFR + 116 on an asset-swap basis, because Treasuries are 30-40bp cheap to swaps; for swapped buyers credit is fair, not rich.'

follow_ups.q: Why are USD swap spreads so negative?
follow_ups.a: Heavy Treasury issuance must be absorbed by dealers and investors, and holding Treasuries uses bank balance sheet (leverage ratio, SLR), while a swap uses very little. Investors also demand a term premium on bonds that swaps, being unfunded, do not need to carry.

follow_ups.q: What is the asset swap spread in one sentence?
follow_ups.a: It is the floating spread over SOFR that an investor earns after buying the fixed bond and paying fixed / receiving floating on a swap with the same cash flows; it is close to the bond's spread to the swap curve.

follow_ups.q: If swap spreads normalise to -20bp at 10y, what happens to the IG OAS?
follow_ups.a: Treasuries richen by about 18bp versus swaps; if the corporate yield is unchanged against swaps, its spread to Treasuries widens by about 18bp, from 84 to about 102bp, with no change in credit risk.

cards.topic: AT1 call or extension with US yields above 5%: reset coupon versus new-issue cost and what it does to prices (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: A bank's USD AT1 has its first call in a year. If not called, the coupon resets to 5y Treasury + a fixed reset spread. With the 10y Treasury near 5.3%, how do you decide whether the bank will call, and how should the bond be priced: to call or to extension?
cards.answer: An AT1 is a **perpetual** bank bond: the bank **may** call it at par on the call date, otherwise the coupon **resets** to the 5y Treasury (or mid-swap) plus the original reset spread. The bank calls when refinancing is **cheaper** than keeping the bond: it compares the **reset coupon** with the yield of a **new AT1**. Higher Treasury yields make calls **more** likely, because the reset coupon rises one for one with the 5y rate. With a 5y Treasury around **5.06%** (illustrative, about 25bp over the 4.81% SOFR 5y swap), a bond with a **2.75% reset spread** would reset to **7.81%**; if the bank can issue a new AT1 at **7.25%** (illustrative), calling saves **56bp a year**, about USD 5.6m per USD 1bn: it calls. A bond with a **1.75% reset spread** resets to **6.81%**, below the new-issue cost, so the bank saves 44bp a year by **not** calling: extension. The investor holds a short option, so the price is the **lower** of the two scenarios: at 7.25%, about **96.97 to call** for the first bond and about **94.60 to extension** for the second (python-checked). The bank also needs the **regulator's permission** to call (it must replace the capital or show a surplus), and it weighs **reputation**: missing a call can raise the cost of all its future AT1s. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'With 5y Treasuries above 5%, most high-reset AT1s are calls; the extension risk is in the low-reset 2020-21 vintage, and I price those to extension.'

follow_ups.q: Why do higher Treasury yields reduce extension risk?
follow_ups.a: Because the reset coupon is the 5y Treasury plus a fixed spread. When the 5y rises, the reset coupon rises one for one, so keeping the bond becomes more expensive for the bank relative to a new issue, as long as AT1 spreads do not widen as much.

follow_ups.q: How do you price a callable bond when the call is uncertain?
follow_ups.a: Price both scenarios and take a weighted view, but the issuer's option means the market tends to the worse case for the investor: yield-to-worst. A full approach models the call as an option on the bank's refinancing spread.

follow_ups.q: Why can't a bank simply call whenever it is economic?
follow_ups.a: AT1 is regulatory capital. The supervisor must approve the call, and usually wants it replaced by capital of equal or better quality, or proof that the bank stays well above its requirements.

prerequisites: Callable bonds and yield to worst

cards.topic: Japanese investor: FX-hedged Treasuries versus JGBs, hedge cost and repatriation (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: A Japanese life insurer asks whether it should keep buying 10y Treasuries hedged into yen, or bring money home into JGBs now that the BoJ is at 1.25%. The 10y Treasury is about 5.29% and SOFR about 3.88%. How do you compare, and what would make it repatriate?
cards.answer: A yen investor who hedges USD with rolling 3-month FX forwards earns the Treasury yield **minus the hedge cost**, and the hedge cost is roughly the **3m rate gap** plus the cross-currency basis: about 3.88% (SOFR) - 1.25% (yen 3m rate, illustrative, at the BoJ rate) + about 0.15% of basis (illustrative) = **about 2.78% a year**. So the hedged 10y Treasury yields about **5.29 - 2.78 = 2.51%**. Against a 10y JGB at about **3.07%** (30 September), the hedged Treasury yields about **56bp less**, while carrying more risk: US duration, a hedge that is rolled every 3 months, and margin on the forwards. It gets worse if the Fed hikes 25bp on 28 October (odds about 35%): the hedge cost rises and the gap widens to about **81bp**; another BoJ hike lowers the hedge cost a little but also tends to lift JGB yields. **Repatriation** happens when the hedged pick-up is zero or negative, as it is now: insurers then sell (or simply stop reinvesting in) hedged foreign bonds and buy JGBs, which **supports the yen** and can push up long US yields. Alternatives: **lower the hedge ratio** (a 50% hedge yields about 3.90%, but with FX risk), or look at **hedged euro bonds**: the EUR hedge costs only about 1.3% because €STR is 2.44%, so a hedged OAT at an illustrative 4.85% gives about **3.56%**, still about 49bp over JGBs. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'Hedged Treasuries give about 2.5% against about 3.1% on JGBs, so hedged they lose; I'd stop adding hedged USTs and put new money in long JGBs and hedged euro govvies, which still pay about 3.5%.'

follow_ups.q: Why is hedging euros cheaper than hedging dollars for a yen investor?
follow_ups.a: Because the hedge cost is mostly the 3m rate gap: €STR at about 2.44% is much closer to yen rates than SOFR at about 3.88%, so the EUR hedge costs about 1.3% against about 2.8% for USD.

follow_ups.q: What is the cross-currency basis doing in the formula?
follow_ups.a: It is the deviation from covered interest parity. When it is negative, dollars are scarce in the FX swap market, and a yen investor who needs to hedge USD pays more than the pure rate gap.

follow_ups.q: How would large-scale repatriation show up in markets?
follow_ups.a: A stronger yen, lower demand for long Treasuries and euro bonds (which can steepen those curves), and more demand for long JGBs; insurers would also lower their hedge ratios on what they keep abroad.

prerequisites: Covered interest parity and FX forwards

cards.topic: Quarter-end in USD funding: SOFR, repo and the Standing Repo Facility (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: It is 30 September 2026, quarter-end. SOFR printed 3.88% on 29 September with fed funds at 3.75-4.00%. Overnight repo is trading higher this morning. Why does repo spike at quarter-ends, where are the Fed's floor and ceiling, and what does a spike cost a repo desk and a SOFR futures position?
cards.answer: At quarter-end, **cash lenders stay the same but balance sheet shrinks**: many banks, especially non-US banks, report balance sheets on quarter-end dates, so they cut repo intermediation for a day or two, while demand for funding is high (Treasury coupon settlements at month-end, dealer inventories after heavy issuance). Repo rates rise until someone with spare balance sheet lends. The Fed's **corridor** frames the move: the **ON RRP** rate at the bottom of the range (**3.75%**) is the floor for money funds; **IORB** for banks sits normally 10bp below the top, so about **3.90%**; the **Standing Repo Facility (SRF)** lends against Treasuries and agencies at the **top of the range, 4.00%**, which is the soft ceiling. SOFR at 3.88% on 29 September was already **just 2bp below IORB**, a sign that reserves are no longer abundant. If repo trades above 4.00%, dealers should borrow from the SRF and lend on, so usage of the SRF is the signal to watch. Costs are small but real: a one-day **15bp** spike (illustrative) on a USD 10bn repo funding book costs about **USD 42k**; it moves the **September 1-month SOFR future** by only **0.5bp** and a 3-month SOFR future by about **0.16bp**, because SOFR futures average or compound daily rates. The bigger risk is **year-end**, when the same effect is larger. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'Quarter-end SOFR prints above IORB are balance-sheet noise, not policy; I'd watch SRF usage, and I would not fade the December turn because year-end is always worse.'

follow_ups.q: Why are quarter-ends worse for non-US banks?
follow_ups.a: Many non-US banks report leverage ratios on quarter-end snapshots rather than daily averages, so they shrink repo books on those dates; US banks use averages for most measures, but year-end matters for G-SIB scores.

follow_ups.q: Why does SOFR near IORB matter?
follow_ups.a: Banks earn IORB risk-free on reserves; if they lend repo below it, reserves are plentiful. When SOFR trades at or above IORB, reserves are getting scarcer and repo becomes more sensitive to shocks.

follow_ups.q: How would you protect a funding book over year-end?
follow_ups.a: Term out the funding across 31 December with term repo or FX swaps, or hedge with SOFR futures or OIS covering the turn; the turn premium is the cost of that insurance.

cards.topic: French corporate pre-hedging a bond: forward-start payer swap versus payer swaption (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: A French corporate plans to issue a EUR 500m 7-year fixed-rate bond in about 12 months to refinance a maturing one. The treasurer fears higher rates. Compare locking the rate with a 1y-forward 7y payer swap versus buying a 1y x 7y payer swaption: levels, costs, and when each is the right choice.
cards.answer: Both hedges protect against **higher swap rates**, the part of the future coupon that the company can hedge; the credit spread on top stays open. **Forward-start payer swap**: the company pays fixed from 12 months for 7 years. With 6m Euribor swaps at about **3.53% (2y), 3.60% (5y), 3.69% (10y)** and an illustrative 1y at 3.25%, the forward 1y x 7y rate is about **3.72%** (python-checked), about 8bp above the spot 7y because the curve slopes up. It costs **nothing upfront** and locks 3.72% plus the credit spread, but if rates **fall** the company loses on the swap: with a DV01 of about **EUR 294k**, a 100bp rally costs about **EUR 29m** at issue, offset by a cheaper bond. **Payer swaption 1y x 7y**: the right to pay 3.72% in a year. With an illustrative normal vol of **85bp**, the at-the-money premium is about **1.99% of notional, EUR 10m, or 34bp a year** over 7 years. All-in: about **4.06%** if rates rise, and market minus 34bp of cost if they fall, so the swaption beats the swap only if rates fall by **more than 34bp**. Rule: if issuance is **certain** and the company has a view that rates go up, the swap; if issuance is **uncertain** (acquisition, rating, market window) or the treasurer cannot accept a big loss on the hedge, the swaption, or a cheaper **collar**. **What I'd say on the desk:** 'For a certain refinancing I'd lock 1y x 7y at about 3.72% in a forward-start swap; if the deal can slip, I'd buy the payer swaption for about 34bp a year.'

follow_ups.q: Why is the forward 7y rate above the spot 7y rate?
follow_ups.a: Because the curve slopes up between 1 and 8 years: the forward rate is the rate that makes investing for 1 year then 7 years equal to investing for 8 years, so it sits above the spot 7y when longer rates are higher.

follow_ups.q: How do you choose the swaption strike?
follow_ups.a: At the forward (ATM) for the standard case; out of the money (for example 4.00%) to cut the premium if the company only fears a big rise; the premium falls quickly as the strike moves away from the forward.

follow_ups.q: What happens at issuance if rates have fallen 100bp?
follow_ups.a: With the swap, the company pays about EUR 29m to unwind it, but issues 100bp cheaper, so its all-in rate stays near 3.72% plus spread. With the swaption, it lets it expire, has spent about EUR 10m, and issues at about 2.72% plus spread, 3.06% all-in.

cards.topic: Global Markets overview
cards.question: What is Global Markets and how does it fit inside an investment bank?
cards.answer: Global Markets is the division of the bank that **trades financial instruments with clients**: it quotes prices, executes orders, provides financing and designs hedging or investment solutions. It sits next to Investment Banking (M&A advisory and capital raising, i.e. IBD/Corporate Finance) and is usually split into **FICC** (Fixed Income, Currencies and Commodities) and **Equities** (cash equities, equity derivatives, prime brokerage). Inside each business you find sales, trading, structuring and research, supported by middle and back office. The division earns money mainly from **bid/ask spreads on client flow, financing revenue, and structuring margins** rather than from betting on market direction. In short: IBD helps companies raise money once; Markets serves investors and corporates every day, in the secondary market.

follow_ups.q: What is the difference between FICC and Equities in revenue terms?
follow_ups.a: At most large banks FICC generates more revenue than Equities, because rates, FX and credit markets are huge and corporate/institutional hedging needs are constant. Equities is very large at US banks (Morgan Stanley, Goldman) thanks to prime brokerage and derivatives.

follow_ups.q: Where does DCM/ECM sit?
follow_ups.a: They are usually part of or jointly run between IBD and Markets: they originate new bond/share issues with issuers and rely on Markets sales to place them with investors.

cards.topic: Sales vs trading vs structuring vs research
cards.question: What are the roles of sales, trading, structuring and research, and how do they interact?
cards.answer: **Sales** own the client relationship: they understand what the client needs, bring ideas, take orders and relay prices. **Traders** own the risk: they make the prices, manage the book (the inventory of positions) and hedge it; their P&L is measured daily. **Structurers** design tailored products (for example a capital-protected note or an autocall) by combining vanilla building blocks, and work on pricing, documentation and regulatory constraints. **Research and strategy** produce analysis and trade ideas (economists, rates/FX strategists, equity analysts) that sales use to engage clients. The loop is: research gives the view, sales turn it into a client conversation, structuring shapes the product, trading prices and warehouses the risk.

follow_ups.q: Which role would you choose and why?
follow_ups.a: Give a reason tied to your strengths: for trading, quick decision-making, comfort with numbers and risk; for sales, communication, curiosity about clients and ability to explain complex products simply. Show you understand the downside (traders live with daily P&L; sales live with client demands).

follow_ups.q: What is a sales-trader?
follow_ups.a: In equities, a sales-trader takes client orders and manages execution during the day (working large orders, using algos, finding liquidity), sitting between sales and the trading desk.

cards.topic: Buy side vs sell side
cards.question: What is the difference between the buy side and the sell side?
cards.answer: The **sell side** sells financial services: investment banks and brokers who make markets, provide liquidity, research, execution and structured products. The **buy side** buys those services to invest money: asset managers, hedge funds, pension funds, insurers, sovereign wealth funds, private equity. The sell side earns mainly spreads and fees and is supposed to be roughly neutral on market direction; the buy side earns returns on the capital it manages and takes directional views. The sell side's product is liquidity and ideas; the buy side's product is performance for its investors. Global Markets at a bank is sell side, and the buy side are its clients.

follow_ups.q: Why would a hedge fund trade through a bank rather than directly?
follow_ups.a: Banks provide liquidity (they take the other side immediately), leverage and financing via prime brokerage, access to many markets, research and derivatives the fund cannot create itself.

follow_ups.q: What is a mandate?
follow_ups.a: The set of rules under which an asset manager invests: benchmark, allowed instruments, risk limits, leverage, ESG constraints. It determines what trades a salesperson can pitch.

cards.topic: Front, middle and back office
cards.question: What are the front office, middle office and back office?
cards.answer: The **front office** generates revenue and faces clients or markets: sales, trading, structuring, and research. The **middle office** controls and measures the risk the front office takes: market risk (VaR, limits), credit risk, product control (which validates the daily P&L and marks), model validation and compliance. The **back office** makes trades actually happen after execution: confirmation, settlement (exchange of cash and securities), collateral management and reconciliations. The separation exists so that the people who take risk are not the ones who measure it or book the cash, which is a lesson from rogue-trading scandals like Kerviel at Société Générale in 2008.

follow_ups.q: What is P&L explain?
follow_ups.a: A daily breakdown of the P&L into sources: delta (market moves), gamma, vega, theta, new trades, carry. If a big unexplained part remains, product control and the trader investigate.

follow_ups.q: Why did settlement move to T+1 in the US?
follow_ups.a: To reduce counterparty risk and margin needs between trade and settlement, following the volatility episodes of 2020-21. It went live in May 2024.

cards.topic: Market making vs proprietary trading
cards.question: What is the difference between market making and proprietary trading?
cards.answer: A **market maker** continuously quotes a bid and an offer to clients and earns the **spread** by facilitating their trades; the risk it takes is a by-product of serving client flow, and it tries to recycle it quickly. A **proprietary trader** uses the firm's own capital to take **directional views** to profit from price moves, with no client on the other side. Since the Volcker rule (part of the US Dodd-Frank Act, fully effective 2015), US banks and their affiliates are essentially banned from proprietary trading, and Europe has similar ring-fencing ideas, so bank trading desks are designed as market makers and hedgers. Prop trading moved to hedge funds and proprietary trading firms like Jane Street, Optiver or Citadel Securities (which themselves are also huge market makers).

follow_ups.q: Can a market maker have a view?
follow_ups.a: Yes: it uses its view to decide how to skew prices and how quickly to hedge, but the positions must originate from client activity and be sized relative to expected client demand.

follow_ups.q: Who does prop trading today?
follow_ups.a: Hedge funds, proprietary trading firms (Jane Street, Optiver, IMC, Jump), and family offices. Many of them are also electronic market makers.

cards.topic: Bid/ask and market maker revenue
cards.question: What is the bid/ask spread and how does a market maker make money?
cards.answer: The **bid** is the price at which the market maker is willing to buy, the **ask (offer)** the price at which it is willing to sell; ask minus bid is the spread, and the **mid** is the average. A market maker earns money by buying at the bid and selling at the offer, so each round trip captures the spread, and each single trade earns half-spread versus mid. The spread compensates for three costs: **inventory risk** (price may move before the position is offloaded), **adverse selection** (the client may know more than you), and **operating/capital costs**. So spreads widen when volatility is high, when the product is illiquid, when the trade is large, and when the counterparty is likely informed.

follow_ups.q: Why do spreads widen in a crisis?
follow_ups.a: Volatility rises (inventory riskier), dealers have less balance sheet capacity, and flow becomes one-directional (everyone wants to sell), so market makers protect themselves with wider quotes.

follow_ups.q: What is the difference between quoted and effective spread?
follow_ups.a: Quoted spread is the displayed ask minus bid; the effective spread measures what trades actually paid versus mid (2 x |trade price - mid|), which can be smaller (price improvement) or larger (walking the book).

cards.topic: Inventory risk and skewing
cards.question: You are a market maker and a client just sold you a large block. What risk do you have and how do you manage it?
cards.answer: I now hold **inventory risk**: I am long the asset and lose if the price falls before I get rid of it. I would manage it in three ways. First, **hedge** the main risk immediately with a liquid proxy (index futures for a stock basket, a Bund future for a bond, interest rate swaps for a corporate bond's rate risk).
