cards.answer: On a 1 SOL position in the moderate scenario: the pool fee is 0.5% per leg, so 1% round trip. Slippage is 2% per leg, so 4%. The priority fee is 0.002 SOL per transaction, two transactions, so 0.4% of the position. That is about 5.4% round trip before the small base network fee. In the low scenario it is about 1.5%, and in the high one about 22%. So the trade must be expected to return more than 5.4% on average just to break even in normal conditions. My raw model edge was 2.7%, so it loses money unless costs are at the low end. Sizing up does not help much. The priority fee shrinks as a percentage, but slippage grows with size in a thin pool. Scaling down makes the fixed priority fee proportionally heavier. There is a narrow band where the trade can make sense, and the edge was not large enough to fit in it.

follow_ups.q: What's the equivalent on an equity desk?
follow_ups.a: Commission plus half the bid-ask spread per leg plus market impact, which grows roughly with the square root of size relative to daily volume. The same logic applies: fixed costs favour bigger trades, impact favours smaller ones.

follow_ups.q: Would limit orders help?
follow_ups.a: On an AMM there are no resting limit orders in the classic sense; you can cap slippage tolerance, but then some trades fail to fill, typically the ones where price is running away, which is adverse selection on fills.

cards.topic: Portfolio caps and path dependence
cards.question: Your ENR filter improved the numbers, but adding portfolio position caps made the system negative. Why would a risk limit destroy the edge?
cards.answer: On the 927 out-of-sample signals, the ENR filter alone took the low-cost scenario from +1.2% to +3.6% net expectancy. But without limits, tens of positions could be open at the same time on overlapping tokens, so I added portfolio-level concurrent-position caps, and the full system fell to -0.09% under low costs and -5.31% under moderate costs. The caps do not remove trades at random: they keep whichever signals arrive first while capacity is free. So the edge in this sample sat in a few trades that a realistic, capped book would not have been able to take. It is also path-dependent. When I recalibrated the holding time honestly, positions stayed open for different lengths of time, which changed which later signals found a free slot. That moved the low-cost number from -0.09% to -4.57%. My conclusion was that on 5 days and 927 signals the backtest could not give a stable number, so I stopped refining it.

follow_ups.q: Why not just raise the cap?
follow_ups.a: Raising the cap after seeing the results is threshold-shopping on the test set, which is the same leak I had already fixed twice. It also concentrates risk on correlated positions in the same token. The cap is a risk decision and has to be set before looking.

follow_ups.q: What would you do with more data?
follow_ups.a: Treat capacity explicitly: simulate the book at several caps chosen in advance, on a fresh walk-forward window, and report the whole curve rather than one point.

follow_ups.q: Is path dependence a bug in your backtest?
follow_ups.a: No. It is how the real system would behave. The problem is only that 5 days is too short for the path-specific noise to average out.

cards.topic: Stopping backtest refinement
cards.question: At some point you deliberately stopped improving your backtest. Why? Isn't more analysis always better?
cards.answer: No. Past a certain point, more analysis on the same data only produces more overfitting. By then the 927-signal, 5-day test window had been looked at many times: to find the clustering issue, the model mix-up, the exit-calibration leak, the cost scenarios and the caps. Every reasonable modelling choice moved the net expectancy, sometimes past a sign change, from -0.09% to -4.57% just by recalibrating the holding time. That told me the sample could not produce a stable number. Each further tweak would effectively be fitting to that window. So I froze the methodology and chose to wait for fresh data that no analysis had touched: first live paper trading, then a new pre-registered Stage 1 cycle on post-audit data.

follow_ups.q: How do you tell a robustness check apart from tuning?
follow_ups.a: A robustness check is reported whatever it shows and does not change the decision rule. Tuning changes the rule because of the result. I reported every variant, including the bad ones, and never changed frozen components on the test window.

follow_ups.q: Isn't waiting for new data slow?
follow_ups.a: Yes, but it is the only honest source of evidence. The plan was 5 days of clean data plus 1 day for labels to mature, which is cheap compared with trading real money on a mirage.

cards.topic: First reported vs corrected expectancy
cards.question: Give me the headline numbers: what did you first report, and what was the corrected figure?
cards.answer: On the same 927 out-of-sample signals, with the same code, the full system first showed +7.5% net expectancy per trade in the low-cost scenario and -17.7% in the moderate-cost scenario. After correcting the model-artifact mix-up, the full system was -0.09% under low costs and -5.31% under moderate costs. On the raw model edge, the mix-up had inflated expectancy from a true +2.7% to a reported +5.39%. The significance followed the same path: a naive z of 10.02, then 4.08 and 2.52 once clustered by wallet and by wallet-token pair, and finally 3.91 with negative expectancy on the cleaned 5-wallet pool, which is a FAIL. So the honest one-liner is: a strong-looking PASS turned into a documented FAIL, and my own process caught it.

follow_ups.q: Which single number summarises the project?
follow_ups.a: Net expectancy of the full system under low costs: about -0.09% corrected against +7.5% first reported. The edge does not survive realistic execution in a capped book.

follow_ups.q: Why did you trust z = 10 at first?
follow_ups.a: I didn't for long. Within about 24 hours I checked concentration and found one wallet was 34.7% of signals, which is what triggered the cluster bootstrap.

follow_ups.q: What's net expectancy -0.022 in the replay?
follow_ups.a: About -2.2% per trade after costs on the 435 signals from the cleaned 5-wallet pool: negative, so it fails even though z = 3.91 passes.

cards.topic: Stage 2 paper trading design
cards.question: What is paper trading, and why did you treat it as stronger evidence than your backtest?
cards.answer: Paper trading means running the real live system on real-time data with a fixed decision rule, and simulating only the money moving. Every decision is made before the price outcome exists, so it cannot be contaminated by hindsight, however careful or careless the backtest was. That is why it was Stage 2 of my gate. I ran 5 days immediately after the Stage 1 backtest, fully in simulation mode, without touching any execution code. The criteria were fixed in advance: at least 30 to 50 simulated trades, positive net expectancy within 50% of the Stage 1 estimate, and at least 3 of 5 days net positive. The 50% band matters: a bigger gap between paper and backtest points to a modelling or execution problem, not just noise.

follow_ups.q: What does paper trading NOT tell you?
follow_ups.a: Real fill quality: slippage, failed or late transactions, the priority-fee auction and market impact. Those are still modelled. Only small real trades would measure them.

follow_ups.q: Why 50% tolerance and not 20%?
follow_ups.a: With 30-50 trades and very dispersed returns, the sampling noise is large, so a tight band would fail a real edge by chance. 50% was the level at which a gap starts to suggest a structural modelling problem. It was fixed in advance.

cards.topic: Stage 2 result: FAIL
cards.question: So what happened in live paper trading?
cards.answer: It failed. After 5 days in simulation, the verdict I pre-registered and published at the end of the window was FAIL on net expectancy. After a correction, the net expectancy was essentially zero, +0.001505%, against a Stage 1 estimate of about +2.7% per trade. That is a 94.4% deviation, far outside the 50% tolerance. Only 1 of 5 days was net positive against a required 3 of 5. So the live evidence did not confirm the backtest, and that is exactly what the gate is for: it stopped the process before any real capital was involved. No real money was ever at risk.

follow_ups.q: Could the edge still exist?
follow_ups.a: Possibly. 5 days is a small sample, which is why the next step is a fresh pre-registered cycle on clean data. But the burden of proof is on the strategy, and today the evidence says no.

follow_ups.q: How many trades did paper trading produce?
follow_ups.a: 1,019 simulated buys over the 5 days (226, 255, 156, 234 and 148 per day), all with a resolved label at evaluation, against a pre-registered minimum of 30. So the count was not what failed: the failing criteria were net expectancy, the 94.4% deviation from the backtest and the 1-of-5 day robustness. Those 1,019 are the model's buy signals; only about 40 of them would also have passed the cost filter, even in the low-cost scenario.

cards.topic: Race condition and the addendum
cards.question: You found a bug after publishing the paper-trading verdict. What did you do?
cards.answer: The day after the verdict, I found a race condition that affected 4 trades in the paper-trading simulator. I corrected it, but I did not rewrite the published verdict. I kept the original report exactly as it was and added a dated addendum with the recount. On the corrected data, one of the three failing criteria flipped: net expectancy went from -0.000187% to +0.001505%, so from FAIL to PASS. The overall verdict stayed FAIL, because the 94.4% deviation from the backtest and the 1-of-5 day robustness were unchanged. While checking the recount, I found a second, unrelated anomaly: 4 different trades changed status between two database snapshots. It had no effect on any verdict, and I flagged it for investigation instead of fixing it silently or ignoring it.

follow_ups.q: Why not just update the report?
follow_ups.a: Because the value of a pre-registered verdict comes from it being immutable. If I edit results after the fact, even for good reasons, nobody, me included, can tell a correction from a convenient revision.

follow_ups.q: What could cause trades to change status between snapshots?
follow_ups.a: Likely candidates are a labelling job running at the same time as the snapshot, or a label maturing (the 24h window) between the two reads. I flagged it rather than guess, since it had no effect on any verdict.

cards.topic: Spam and dust parser bug
cards.question: Tell me about the data-quality bug in your parser.
cards.answer: My transaction parser recorded a "buy" whenever a tracked wallet's token balance went up. On Solana, though, people constantly send unsolicited spam or dust tokens to active wallets, and those are plain transfers with no swap behind them. So some recorded "buys" were not trades at all. Measured over the full history, this affected every wallet to some extent, from 1.7% up to about half of a wallet's recorded buys: the report text says 51.5%, and the per-wallet chart shows Rilsio at 48.4% and Tom at 40.6%. I fixed the parser for all future collection with a check that a buy must have a matching counter-leg, the `_a_une_contrepartie` function, merged with 18 dedicated tests. The two most contaminated wallets were also the only two whose measured performance got worse once the contamination was removed, so part of their apparent edge was a data artifact, and they were excluded.

follow_ups.q: How did you notice it?
follow_ups.a: Through an anomaly I chose to dig into: one wallet (smart_money_07) had 32 recorded "buys" with an amount of exactly 1.0 token. I pulled a few of those transactions directly from Helius and saw plain incoming transfers with no swap leg behind them, and measuring it across wallets showed a pool-wide contamination, strongest for Tom and Rilsio. The day-long audit then measured the contamination wallet by wallet, and the same day it also caught a silent desynchronisation between the VPS and local databases.

follow_ups.q: Why was 07 kept at 21% contamination?
follow_ups.a: Because the criterion fixed for exclusion was that cleaning hurts measured performance, meaning the edge depended on the artifact. For 07 it didn't, so a high but harmless contamination rate isn't grounds for exclusion.

cards.topic: Not reprocessing the history
cards.question: You fixed the parser but did not reprocess the 40,000+ trades already in the database. Isn't that sloppy?
cards.answer: It was a deliberate trade-off. Reprocessing the whole history in the middle of the analysis would have changed the data underneath the already-published, frozen Stage 1 result, so nobody could reproduce or audit that verdict any more. Instead, the fix applies to all future collection, and I measured the contamination over the full history so I knew its size wallet by wallet. The excluded wallets' histories are kept in the database for audit; the code paths that decide, train and trade simply stop using them. The next Stage 1 cycle is planned on clean, post-audit data: 5 days of fresh collection plus a 1-day label-maturation margin. So the clean result will come from genuinely new data, not a rewritten past.

follow_ups.q: Wouldn't the next training window include old dirty trades?
follow_ups.a: The plan guarantees that the 5-day test window is entirely post-fix, which is what matters for an honest verdict. A 25-day training window necessarily reaches back before the fix, so I reclassified the whole history in a separate table (`classification_spam`, all 20,196 buys re-checked) without touching the frozen trades table, and the next-cycle script excludes the confirmed spam tokens by default (it can only be switched off explicitly). Either way the test data is clean and never seen.

follow_ups.q: What's point-in-time data?
follow_ups.a: Data exactly as it was available on a given date, before any later revision. Backtests must use it to avoid look-ahead bias.

cards.topic: Silent database desynchronisation
cards.question: What was the database desynchronisation issue?
cards.answer: I had two PostgreSQL databases: one on the VPS, where the live collector writes, and one local, which every analysis script used by default. They were never continuously synchronised, and the local one had stopped receiving live data for several days without anyone noticing. Left uncaught, the next validation cycle would have trained and tested on stale data while I believed it was fresh post-cleanup data. I first took a full database backup, then re-ran an idempotent backfill directly from Helius, which is the on-chain source of truth. That recovered 5,215 trades the same evening with no risk of duplicates. The lesson for me is that silent failures are the dangerous ones, which is why monitoring checks things like the time since the last trade was inserted.

follow_ups.q: How would you prevent it structurally?
follow_ups.a: A single database for analysis that reads from the VPS, or a scheduled replication, plus a pre-flight check in every analysis script asserting the latest trade timestamp is recent.

follow_ups.q: Why is idempotency so important here?
follow_ups.a: Because the backfill and the live collector can both see the same trade. Dedup on (signature, token) lets me re-run safely at any time without inflating counts.

cards.topic: Wallet pool 9 to 5 in one day
cards.question: Your active wallet pool went from 9 to 5 in a single day. Doesn't dropping wallets look like cherry-picking?
cards.answer: It would be cherry-picking if I had dropped wallets because they hurt the result. Every exclusion followed a criterion fixed before it was applied and recorded with its date and evidence in a standing registry. That afternoon, I removed one wallet under a pre-registered performance criterion: near-zero precision on two independent stages, 0.0% on 31 signals and then 1.3% on 75. I removed another because over 98% of its apparent edge came from a single calendar day. That evening, I removed the two wallets whose measured performance got worse once the spam and dust contamination was removed. The key test is the outcome: after the exclusions, the frozen Stage 1 method gave a FAIL. If I had been cherry-picking, the numbers would have gone up, not down.

follow_ups.q: Why exclude a wallet whose regime was authentic?
follow_ups.a: Because authentic isn't the same as repeatable. A one-day concentration can't be told apart from luck at this sample size, so copying it means copying noise.

follow_ups.q: Isn't 5 wallets too few?
follow_ups.a: Yes. That fragility is one of my main findings. Leave-one-out showed no single wallet was solely responsible either way, and the open decision is whether to rebuild the pool before the next cycle.

cards.topic: Post-audit replay: z = 3.91 but FAIL
cards.question: After the audit you reran Stage 1 and got z = 3.91, which is still above 1.96. Why is that a FAIL?
cards.answer: Because Stage 1 was never "just be significant". It had several pre-registered criteria that all had to pass together, and an economic sanity check. I reran the exact, unmodified Stage 1 code on the cleaned 5-wallet pool and the freshest walk-forward window. z = 3.91 passed the 1.96 bar and n = 435 passed the minimum of 300. But directional robustness was 3 of 5 days against the required 4 of 5, and net expectancy was -0.022, about -2.2% per trade after costs. So the model still picks winners more often than the base rate, but not by enough to pay for execution. Statistical significance is not the same as profitability, and that is probably the most important lesson of the project.

follow_ups.q: Would you reconsider the robustness criterion since 3/5 is close?
follow_ups.a: No. Relaxing a frozen criterion after seeing it fail is exactly the threshold-shopping the gate exists to prevent. And expectancy was negative anyway.

follow_ups.q: Is z = 3.91 itself trustworthy?
follow_ups.a: It's the naive version. On the original sample, clustering by wallet cut 10.02 to 4.08, so the clustered replay z would likely be well below 3.91.

cards.topic: Independent stress test
cards.question: How did you stress-test the post-audit result?
cards.answer: The same night as the replay, I ran an independent stress test from a separate terminal as a cross-check, looking at four angles. First, leave-one-out: removing each wallet in turn showed the 5-wallet pool is fragile in both directions, with no single wallet uniquely responsible or uniquely at fault. Second, shifting the test window by ±1 to 2 days: net expectancy stayed negative in every variant. Third, costs: every scenario except the most favourable admitted zero or negative-expectancy signals. Fourth, and most telling, I re-scored the actual Stage 2 live paper decisions, which no retrospective analysis had touched. 83.3% of the full system's admitted trades came from three wallets that have since been excluded. All four angles agreed with the FAIL. I deliberately did not let the stress test itself decide stop or continue; that decision stayed with me as a separate step.

follow_ups.q: Why run it from a separate terminal?
follow_ups.a: As an independent cross-check: a separate process and session, so it doesn't share state or assumptions with the replay I had just run.

follow_ups.q: Why didn't the stress test decide whether to stop?
follow_ups.a: My governing rule keeps go/no-go decisions separate from analysis tools. The stress test produces evidence; the decision is explicit and human.

cards.topic: Governance: simulation by default
cards.question: How did you make sure the system could never lose real money by accident?
cards.answer: I built safety into the architecture, not into good intentions. The trading mode defaults to simulation everywhere in the codebase, and no code path switches it to real execution automatically, under any condition. Any change touching the execution module, or any run with the trading mode set to real, requires my explicit sign-off given at that specific moment, never inferred from an earlier approval or from how good the results look. The execution module is fully specified on paper but contains zero lines of code, by design, until the validation gate justifies building it. Secrets live only in a git-ignored environment file, and nothing sensitive has ever been committed. These rules held even at the moment the headline result looked strongest, with z = 10.02.

follow_ups.q: What would go into the execution module's pre-trade checks?
follow_ups.a: As specified: pool liquidity not trivially removable (rug-pull check), holder concentration, and a simulated sell before buying to detect honeypots. Plus capped slippage and priority fees as explicit parameters, never permissive defaults.

follow_ups.q: Isn't approving your own trades pointless?
follow_ups.a: It's a forced pause: a deliberate decision at that moment, instead of a system drifting into real trading. On a real desk the equivalent is a second person or a risk function.

cards.topic: Kill-switch design
cards.question: Describe your kill-switch. How is it like a desk's stop-loss limit?
cards.answer: For production, I specified an automatic kill-switch: three consecutive days of negative expectancy trigger an immediate fallback to simulation mode, plus an alert. It is deliberately one-way. The automatic logic can only stop the system, never start or resume it, and resuming after a kill-switch event needs the same fresh sign-off as a first launch. That asymmetry is the point: switching off on a false alarm costs little, but trading on after a real breakdown costs a lot. It works like a loss limit on a desk. When a trader hits the limit, risk is cut automatically and the conversation about resuming happens afterwards with risk management, not in the heat of the moment.

follow_ups.q: Why 3 days and not a P&L threshold?
follow_ups.a: Both are valid. A days-based rule is scale-free and simple while position sizes are tiny. In a real deployment I'd add a hard cumulative-loss cap in SOL on top.

follow_ups.q: What's a circuit breaker in markets?
follow_ups.a: An exchange-level halt when prices move beyond a threshold, for example market-wide halts on US equities after large index drops. Same philosophy: pause automatically, restart deliberately.

cards.topic: Champion/challenger model replacement
cards.question: How would a new model replace the one in production?
cards.answer: I specified a conservative champion/challenger rule. A candidate model, the challenger, only replaces the live model, the champion, if it beats it by at least 20% relative expectancy, with statistical significance at p < 0.05, with at least 30 trades on each side, and over two consecutive rolling evaluation windows. When in doubt, the incumbent is kept. The goal is to avoid thrashing: with noisy, small samples, the model that did best on the last window is often just the luckiest. Requiring a material margin, significance and persistence makes a lucky promotion much less likely.

follow_ups.q: Why 30 trades minimum?
follow_ups.a: It's the rough point where the sample mean's distribution is closer to normal, so a t-test is less unreliable. With fat-tailed memecoin returns, I'd prefer a bootstrap too.

follow_ups.q: Is 20% arbitrary?
follow_ups.a: It's a judgement call, fixed in advance, meant to demand an economically meaningful improvement. What matters is that it's set before seeing the challenger's results.

cards.topic: Keeping the leaky exit policy frozen
cards.question: You found a leak in your exit policy but chose not to fix it in the code. Explain that.
cards.answer: The three exit parameters of POLITIQUE_SORTIE_V1 (2.0x take-profit, 0.6573x stop-loss, 11,458-second max hold) had been calibrated on a distribution that included the test window. The measured deviation against an honest, train-only calibration was +7.5% on the stop-loss and +9.2% on the max hold. The obvious fix would have been to recalibrate. But the only data available was that same test window, already compromised by being analysed, so recalibrating on it would just create a third generation of the same leak. I documented it in full the moment I found it, ran the honest recalibration only as a separate analysis exercise, which made results worse (-0.09% to -4.57% under low costs), and left the live code frozen pending an explicit decision. The clean fix is to recalibrate on fresh data.

follow_ups.q: Isn't leaving a known bias in the code worse?
follow_ups.a: It's documented and quantified, so every result carries it transparently. A silent re-tune on a seen window would create an unknown bias. A known bias beats an unknown one.

follow_ups.q: When is a trade outcome exact under your two-point limitation?
follow_ups.a: A confirmed loss when the 24h peak never reaches the stop level, and a confirmed win when the peak clears the target before the max hold. Everything else is an explicit approximation.

cards.topic: Current status and the open decision
cards.question: Where is the project today, and what will you do next?
cards.answer:
*Open question (mock interview): no single right answer. Below is how to build yours, using only facts you've confirmed.*

**Structure: the status (facts, as of September 2026), the open decision, your position (about 60 seconds).**
1. **Status** (report): ongoing but deliberately idle since the data-quality audit (last commit 22 September 2026). The plan fixed then: 5 days of clean, post-fix data collection plus a 1-day label-maturation margin, then a fresh, pre-registered Stage 1 cycle. Launch script and checklist prepared and structurally tested, never run for real. The trading mode has never left simulation; no real money risked.
2. **The open decision** (report): run that cycle as a genuinely independent test on new data, or first revisit the wallet pool and the acceptance criteria, given how fragile both proved to removing a single wallet.
3. **Your position** (yours to choose; arguments for each side):
   - run it unchanged: cheap, uncontaminated, and any change to the criteria now would be shaped by results already seen;
   - revisit first: 5 wallets is a fragile pool, and a power calculation says five days can hardly confirm a small edge;
   - a middle path: run the pre-registered cycle as planned, and separately design a larger pool under criteria written before any new data arrives.
4. **What would change your mind**: give a concrete, pre-stated criterion, for example a PASS on fresh data with clustered z above 1.96 and positive net expectancy under the moderate cost scenario.

**Avoid**: implying the new cycle has already run, or giving a date you haven't fixed.

follow_ups.q: What result would make you abandon it?
follow_ups.a: State your stopping rule in advance; a natural one is another FAIL on clean, independent data, after which the hypothesis that this wallet set carries a cost-robust signal is rejected and written up as the final result.

follow_ups.q: Would you ever put real money in?
follow_ups.a: Use the gate: only after Stage 1 and Stage 2 pass on independent data, with your explicit sign-off at that moment, tiny capped size and the kill-switch live, mainly to measure real execution against the modelled costs.

cards.topic: Project timeline and scale
cards.question: 277 commits and 21,000 lines of Python — how long did this take, and how is that possible?
cards.answer:
*Open question (mock interview): no single right answer. Below is how to build yours, using only facts you've confirmed.*

**Structure: three beats, about 40 seconds.**
1. **The duration, straight away**: the repository was started on 9 September 2026, so about three weeks of intense work. How many hours that represented is for you to say.
2. **How it was possible** (pick two):
   - an AI coding assistant used as an implementation and documentation collaborator, under constraints you set (acceptance criteria, safety rules, exclusion criteria), as the report states;
   - data that already existed: a 30-day backfill of on-chain history gave 40,000+ trades, enough for a 25-day train / 5-day test walk-forward without months of live collection; the live collector then added 11,000+ trades on the VPS.
3. **The redirect**: the code volume isn't the achievement; the method and the handling of the negative result are.

**Material (sourced)**: report figures: 277 commits, about 21,000 lines of Python, 430+ automated tests, 5 database migrations. Your final CV gives about 22,000 lines and 460+ tests (the repository count on 22 September): pick one set and match the document the interviewer has in front of them.

**Avoid**: playing down the assistant's role; giving an hours figure you can't stand behind; letting the numbers become the story.

follow_ups.q: What exactly did the AI do versus you?
follow_ups.a: Start from the report's division: you designed the research and fixed the acceptance criteria, safety rules and exclusion criteria; the assistant implemented and documented code to those specifications. Then give one example you can explain in detail, for instance the two collector bugs found by testing on real trades (transactions fetched at the default finalized commitment level, so freshly notified ones weren't found yet; subscription acknowledgements that could be mistaken for notifications), or the two leaks and the survivorship bias in the win rate caught by your own checks. Only claim what you personally verified.

follow_ups.q: Why only 30 days of history?
follow_ups.a: Material: the backfill window defaulted to 30 days, with one very active wallet limited to 15 days to fit the API retry budget. Enough for a 25/5 walk-forward, and also the reason the sample is small. Whether you'd extend it, and how, is your call.

cards.topic: Using an AI coding assistant
cards.question: Did you actually write this code yourself?
cards.answer:
*Open question (mock interview): no single right answer. Below is how to build yours, using only facts you've confirmed.*

**Structure: answer first, then the split, then an offer.**
1. **Direct answer** (1 sentence): you owned the project end to end and used an AI coding assistant heavily for implementation and documentation; the report says so explicitly, and your CV lists AI coding agents.
2. **The division of labour** (2 sentences): what you set (the hypothesis, the principle of targeting the 5-60 second human reaction gap rather than speed, the four-stage gate, the safety rules, every exclusion criterion, every decision when a result came in) versus what the assistant did (much of the code, to those specifications, reviewed and tested by you against real data).
3. **One verification example** you can tell in detail (see the follow-ups).
4. **The offer**: invite questions on any part of the pipeline, but only parts you can explain unaided.

**Your choice**: whether to add a view on these tools as a desk skill, and in what terms.

**Avoid**: hesitating or minimising; claiming you typed everything; the opposite excess of presenting yourself as a mere reviewer.

follow_ups.q: What's one thing the AI got wrong that you caught?
follow_ups.a: Pick one you can tell in detail. Candidates: the collector bugs found by testing on real trades (default finalized commitment instead of confirmed, so just-notified transactions weren't found yet; subscription acknowledgements mistaken for notifications), or the model-artefact mix-up on the analysis side (validation numbers produced by a model trained on train plus test, which inflated net expectancy from +2.7% to +5.39%). Describe it as a bug you caught, without deciding who 'caused' it if you don't know.

follow_ups.q: Would you use AI tools on a desk?
follow_ups.a: Material for your answer: within the bank's policies only, with human review of every output, and never with confidential data in unapproved tools. Where you think they help most (code, documentation, analysis drafts) is your view to give.

cards.topic: What I would do differently
cards.question: If you started this project again, what would you do differently?
cards.answer:
*Open question (mock interview): no single right answer. Below is how to build yours, using only facts you've confirmed.*

**Structure: 3 or 4 changes, each = one-line cause + one-line fix, then one sentence on which mattered most.**

**Material (pick the ones you genuinely believe):**
- **Audit data quality before modelling.** The parser counted plain transfers (spam, dust) as buys: 1.7% to 51.5% of a wallet's recorded buys; a single day of auditing found three separate problems under the headline numbers.
- **Make leaks structurally impossible.** Both leaks were bookkeeping errors: validation numbers from a model trained on train plus test (+5.39% reported versus +2.7% honest), and an exit policy calibrated on a distribution that included the test window. Possible fix: a test window the calibration code cannot read, and every reported number tied to a model artifact ID.
- **Store full price paths.** Labels used 15-minute candle closes (entry price, highest close over 24 h), so the triple-barrier outcome was approximated, not exact.
- **Start from a larger, more diversified wallet pool with pre-registered concentration limits.** One wallet supplied 34.7% of the 927 selected signals, two wallets 59.7%.

**Your choices**: which 3-4 you keep, their order, and the one you call most important.

**Avoid**: a list without causes; changes that are hindsight with no fix; inventing figures beyond these.

follow_ups.q: Which one mattered most?
follow_ups.a: Your call, with an argument. For data quality: every later statistic inherits the raw-data errors, and contamination reached 51.5% of one wallet's recorded buys. For the leaks: they are what turned an apparent PASS into a FAIL once corrected. Choose one and say why.

follow_ups.q: Would you still use LightGBM?
follow_ups.a: Material: 4 features, about 16,000 training rows with only around 5% wins, and no hyperparameter search was run. A defensible answer is that a simple model was appropriate, possibly benchmarked first against a logistic regression to check the extra complexity earns its keep. Whether you'd keep it is your view.

cards.topic: What the project taught me about trading
cards.question: What did this project teach you about trading?
cards.answer:
*Open question (mock interview): no single right answer. Below is how to build yours, using only facts you've confirmed.*

**Structure: two or three lessons, each anchored by one number, then one sentence on what changed in how you work.**

**Material (sourced):**
- **Costs decide.** Three sourced cost scenarios (slippage per leg 0.5%, 2%, 8%); the ENR filter helps under low and moderate costs, but adding position caps brings the full system close to breakeven or negative.
- **Significance is not an edge.** The post-audit replay had z = 3.91 (passing the z criterion) but net expectancy of −0.022 per trade: a FAIL.
- **Concentration is hidden risk.** 34.7% of the 927 "independent" signals came from one wallet, 59.7% from two; reclustering by wallet cut z from 10.02 to 4.08, then 2.52 at wallet-and-token level. The desk analogy: a book that looks diversified but is one bet.
- **Process.** Rules frozen before looking; a negative result reported as such.

**Your choices**: which lessons, in what order, and which one matters most to you for the role.

**Avoid**: generic lessons with no number; implying the strategy nearly worked; claiming trading experience beyond the simulation.

follow_ups.q: Which lesson applies most to a sales role?
follow_ups.a: Possible thread: explaining a result honestly, costs and risks included, to someone who wants a simple answer. If you link it to your client-facing experience (Polifeb: 3 clients signed; BNP Paribas: 2 partnerships), use only those confirmed facts and say in your own words what it taught you.

follow_ups.q: What's transaction cost analysis?
follow_ups.a: Definition to have ready: measuring what execution actually cost against a benchmark (arrival price, VWAP), to improve execution and evidence best execution to clients and regulators. Link to the project if you wish: the ENR filter is a pre-trade cost estimate, whereas TCA is mostly post-trade measurement.

cards.topic: Relevance to Sales & Trading
cards.question: This is a crypto side project. Why is it relevant to a Sales & Trading desk?
cards.answer:
*Open question (mock interview): no single right answer. Below is how to build yours, using only facts you've confirmed.*

**Structure: one sentence conceding the niche, then 2-3 mappings to desk problems, each with one project example, then one sentence tying it to the role.**

**Material (mappings, sourced):**
- **Is a flow signal real?** Testing whether observed wallet activity carries information is the question a trader asks of client flow.
- **Does it survive costs?** A cost model from sourced, dated inputs (pool fee tiers, priority-fee percentiles, slippage from live Jupiter quotes): close to transaction cost analysis.
- **Liquidity and impact**: slippage of up to 8% per leg in the high-cost scenario on thin pools.
- **Risk controls**: a kill-switch that only ever de-risks, position caps, explicit sign-off before any real money.
- **Communicating a disappointing result** clearly and honestly, a daily sales skill.
- **Tools**: Python, SQL (PostgreSQL), statistics.

**Your choices**: which mappings fit the desk you're interviewing for (QIS or derivatives → backtesting rigour; flow → costs and liquidity; sales → communication), and your closing link.

**Avoid**: overselling crypto as equivalent to a bank desk; listing every mapping; jargon you can't define.

follow_ups.q: How does client flow give a desk information?
follow_ups.a: Definition to have ready: client orders reveal demand and positioning; a market maker adjusts quotes and hedges accordingly, within strict rules on confidentiality and front-running. You can then link it to the project's question (does observed flow carry a signal?), in your own words.

follow_ups.q: Would you rather be in sales or trading?
follow_ups.a: Give the same answer as in your fit preparation (fit-007) and keep it consistent across interviews. Material for either side: trading → costs, sizing, risk limits; sales → explaining a disappointing result clearly; your client-facing roles at Polifeb and BNP Paribas, using only confirmed facts.

cards.topic: Skeptic: isn't this just gambling?
cards.question: Isn't copy-trading memecoins just gambling?

follow_ups.q: Would you trade memecoins with your own money?
follow_ups.a: Your personal answer. Facts to anchor it: the measured net expectancy is negative; the gate only allows tiny, capped real size after a clean pass, with explicit sign-off and a kill-switch, as a way of measuring real execution.

follow_ups.q: Why did you pick memecoins then?
follow_ups.a: Material: free and complete on-chain data (every trade is public), fast feedback, and a clear hypothesis about the 5-60 second human reaction lag. Add your own motivation if it's real; it can be a good lab without being an asset you'd defend.

cards.topic: Skeptic: why care about a negative result?
cards.question: Your strategy doesn't work. Why should we care about a negative result?
cards.answer:
*Open question (mock interview): no single right answer. Below is how to build yours, using only facts you've confirmed.*

**Structure: acknowledge, reframe, transfer (under 45 seconds).**
1. **Acknowledge** (1 sentence): the strategy failed its pre-registered gate.
2. **Reframe** (2 sentences): the process turned an impressive first result into a correct "no" before any money was at risk. Material: first backtest z = 10.02; reclustering by wallet brought it to 4.08 and 2.52; two leaks and a data-quality bug found by your own checks; the clean replay gave z = 3.91 but net expectancy −0.022 and robustness 3/5, a FAIL. Under low costs, net expectancy per trade went from a first-reported +7.5% to −0.09% once the model-artefact leak was corrected.
3. **Transfer** (1 sentence): what a desk needs from someone who finds the problem in their own backtest or P&L before it becomes a loss.

**Your choice**: whether to say that a pretty backtest alone should earn less trust, and how.

**Avoid**: apologising; implying the strategy "almost" worked; overselling the negative result as a success.

follow_ups.q: What would you have done if it had passed?
follow_ups.a: What the gate says: Stage 2 live paper trading, then tiny real size only with explicit sign-off, a kill-switch and capped positions. Add, if true for you, that a pass would have raised your scrutiny rather than lowered it.

follow_ups.q: Isn't it just that you gave up?
follow_ups.a: Material: the project is paused before a fresh pre-registered cycle on untouched data. Stopping further tuning on data already seen was a methodological decision, since it would only manufacture a false positive. Say what would make you restart, in your own words.

cards.topic: Skeptic: how do you know you didn't overfit?
cards.question: How do you know you didn't overfit?
cards.answer: The honest answer is that my result isn't a claim of edge, so the risk runs the other way: overfitting would have produced a false positive, and I ended with a negative. But I built specific defences. The model is small: LightGBM with only 4 features, buy/no-buy only, with no sizing or exit timing learned. Validation is walk-forward, 25 days of training and the next 5 days of testing, never random splits. The decision threshold of 0.5 was chosen on an internal split of training data only. The Stage 1 criteria (z ≥ 1.96, n ≥ 300, at least 4 of 5 days) were frozen before the first run. I corrected significance for clustering with a cluster bootstrap, and I kept a live paper-trading stage that hindsight can't reach. Where I did find overfitting-like leaks, I documented them, and I stopped refining once the test window was worn out.

follow_ups.q: Did you tune LightGBM hyperparameters?
follow_ups.a: No. There was no hyperparameter search: the configuration was small and fixed in advance (shallow trees, a low learning rate, 100 rounds). The only free parameter I chose was the 0.5 decision threshold, set on an internal split of the training window, never on the test window. The model is small by design (4 features, a binary target), so capacity is limited without any tuning. I can give the exact configuration (see the LightGBM configuration card, prj-127).

follow_ups.q: Why is shuffled cross-validation wrong here?
follow_ups.a: Future trades would train a model that is scored on the past. Also, signals from the same wallet and token are correlated across neighbouring times, so random folds leak information between train and test.

cards.topic: Skeptic: what's your edge vs HFT?
cards.question: Professional bots are faster than you. What edge could you possibly have?
cards.answer: None on speed, and I designed the project around that. Professional sniping infrastructure works at millisecond latency with colocated setups; a solo VPS can't compete there and doesn't try. The hypothesis was different. Many human traders copy these same wallets manually through a leaderboard app, with a realistic reaction time of 5 to 60 seconds. If there's any edge, it's in being systematic within that human gap, not beating the bots. That also drove my vetting: I excluded bot-like wallets, and one wallet whose median holding time was 2 seconds, because its edge depended on beating my reaction gap by two orders of magnitude and couldn't be copied. The test said the gap edge doesn't survive realistic costs, which is a coherent answer to exactly this question.

follow_ups.q: How would crowding show up in your data?
follow_ups.a: As slippage worse than the quotes: if many copiers buy right after a tracked wallet, the price has moved by the time I'd fill. My slippage inputs came from live Jupiter quotes on comparable sizes, so crowding is only partly captured; the high scenario (8% per leg) is the stress case that covers it.

follow_ups.q: Why not just pay higher priority fees?
follow_ups.a: Higher fees raise the fixed cost per trade (0.02 SOL in my high scenario) and still wouldn't beat colocated bots. It moves you up the queue, not to the front.

cards.topic: Label quality and price data
cards.question: How exactly did you label a trade as a win, and what's wrong with your labels?
cards.answer: For every observed buy, I stored raw observations, not a verdict: the maximum price ratio reached within 24 hours of the buy, and the time to that peak. I took prices from DexPaprika OHLCV candles at 15-minute granularity, with the entry baseline as the nearest candle within 30 minutes of the buy. Wins and losses were then defined downstream by the frozen triple-barrier exit: 2.0x target, 0.6573x stop and 11,458-second max hold. The weaknesses are real, and I document them. Fifteen-minute candles are coarse for trades whose edge plays out in seconds to minutes. Only two price points are stored, so the order in which the barriers were hit is approximated except for confirmed wins and losses. And tokens that never graduate from their bonding curve often have no price history at all, which caused a survivorship bias I had to correct by treating them properly in the denominator.

follow_ups.q: How would you get better prices?
follow_ups.a: Derive prices from the swap transactions themselves (the executed amounts in each swap give a trade-level price), instead of candles from a third-party indexer.

follow_ups.q: Why store raw ratios instead of a win flag?
follow_ups.a: So the win/loss definition can be chosen later from the real distribution, and changed without re-downloading the whole price history.

cards.topic: Capacity and market impact
cards.question: Suppose the strategy worked. How much money could it run?
cards.answer: Very little, and I'd say so upfront. Memecoin pools are thin, so slippage grows fast with order size. My moderate scenario already assumes 2% slippage per leg and the high one 8% per leg, based on observed Jupiter quotes for comparable trade sizes. Scaling up would push costs into the high scenario, where even the raw +2.7% edge is wiped out. Signals are also clustered: several tracked wallets buy the same token within seconds, so adding size means competing with the wallets I'm copying and with other copiers. So the capacity is a small personal book at most, and I'd have to measure it with tiny real trades. That's a key difference from institutional strategies, where capacity is usually one of the first questions asked.

follow_ups.q: Why is exit liquidity worse?
follow_ups.a: Memecoins often crash after the peak, liquidity providers and holders rush out at the same time, and your sell hits a thinning pool. That's asymmetric impact.

follow_ups.q: How does a bank handle impact on large client orders?
follow_ups.a: It prices it into the spread or executes over time with algorithms (VWAP, TWAP, implementation shortfall), and measures the result with TCA.

cards.topic: Multiple testing and p-hacking
cards.question: You tried rules, then ML, then several fixes and clusterings. Isn't your significance p-hacked?
cards.answer: It's a fair concern, and it's why I never treated any single z as the final word. The acceptance criteria were fixed before the first real test, so I couldn't pick the criterion after seeing the results. I reported every variant, including the ones that hurt: the naive z of 10.02, the clustered 4.08 and 2.52, the replay at 3.91, and the expectancy under all three cost scenarios. Most of my later analyses were robustness checks that could only lower confidence, and they did. The final conclusion is a FAIL, and p-hacking produces false positives, not negatives. The deeper lesson is that each look at the same test window uses up its evidential value, so the decisive evidence has to come from fresh data, which is why the next step is a new pre-registered cycle.

follow_ups.q: What's the deflated Sharpe ratio?
follow_ups.a: A Sharpe ratio adjusted for the number of strategies tried and for non-normal returns. It estimates the probability the best backtest is genuinely positive, not the luckiest of many (Bailey & López de Prado).

follow_ups.q: Why is fresh data the only real fix?
follow_ups.a: Because corrections like Bonferroni need you to count your tests honestly, and informal looks are hard to count. New untouched data resets that.

cards.topic: Explaining the result to a non-specialist
cards.question: Explain your project and its result to me as if I were a client with no technical background.
cards.answer:
*Open question (mock interview): no single right answer. Below is how to build yours, using only facts you've confirmed.*

**Structure: plain words, under 60 seconds, ending on a recommendation.**
1. **The question** (1 sentence): would copying a handful of apparently successful crypto traders make money once every cost is counted?
2. **What you built** (1 sentence, no jargon): a system that watches their trades live, learns which ones tend to work, and simulates copying them, without real money.
3. **What happened** (2 sentences): the first results looked excellent; careful checks found that part of it came from the system accidentally seeing answers it shouldn't have (a data leak), and that one trader supplied about a third of the signals (34.7%).
4. **The result and the advice** (1-2 sentences): with that fixed and realistic costs included, roughly breakeven at best (net expectancy −0.09% per trade under low costs) and losing under moderate costs (−5.31%); so: don't do it.

**Your choices**: the one number you keep, your analogy for the leak, and how you close (for instance, the value of getting to the answer before anyone put money in).

**Avoid**: z-scores, "walk-forward", "LightGBM"; more than one number; hedging the recommendation.

follow_ups.q: Now explain data leakage to that client.
follow_ups.a: Use one everyday analogy of your own. A classic is the student who sees the exam answers while practising: the practice score looks brilliant but says nothing about the real exam. Then one sentence linking it back: the system had seen some of the answers, so its good score was misleading.

follow_ups.q: What does the client really want to hear?
follow_ups.a: Three things, in this order and briefly: what to do, what it costs, what can go wrong. Check your answer against that list.

cards.topic: Execution risks and pre-trade checks
cards.question: If you had built execution, what could go wrong when actually buying these tokens?
cards.answer: A lot, which is one reason execution was the last thing to build. First, rug pulls: the token creator removes the pool's liquidity and the price collapses to zero. Second, honeypots: contracts where you can buy but not sell. Third, holder concentration: one wallet holding a huge share of supply can dump on you. My execution specification requires three pre-trade checks before any real buy: liquidity not trivially removable, holder concentration below a limit, and a simulated sell before buying to detect honeypots. On top of that come market risks: slippage beyond tolerance, which is why slippage must be an explicit capped parameter and never a permissive default, and transactions failing or landing late under congestion, which is what priority fees try to address. Execution would go through the Jupiter aggregator, which routes across pools for the best quote.

follow_ups.q: How do you simulate a sell before buying?
follow_ups.a: Most Solana RPCs can simulate a transaction without sending it. You simulate the swap route for selling (or run a quote check) and reject the token if the sell would fail or be heavily taxed.

follow_ups.q: What's an OMS?
follow_ups.a: An Order Management System: the software that routes orders and enforces pre-trade checks such as limits, restricted lists and fat-finger checks before anything reaches the market.

cards.topic: Conditions for going live
cards.question: What exactly would need to happen before you put a single real euro into this?
cards.answer: Four sequential stages, each with criteria frozen before the results. Stage 1: a walk-forward backtest on data untouched by any earlier decision, passing z ≥ 1.96 on precision against the base rate, n ≥ 300 signals, at least 4 of 5 days directionally robust, and a positive expectancy per trade under the exit policy (before execution costs). I'd now also require the clustered significance and positive net expectancy after realistic costs. Stage 2: five days of live paper trading with positive net expectancy within 50% of the Stage 1 estimate and at least 3 of 5 positive days. Stage 3: real capital, never automatic, only with my explicit sign-off at that moment, at tiny capped size, mainly to measure real fills against modelled costs. Stage 4: production, with the kill-switch after 3 negative days and champion/challenger rules for model changes. And before Stage 3, the execution module has to be written, with pre-trade checks against rug pulls, honeypots and holder concentration.

follow_ups.q: What's the Kelly criterion?
follow_ups.a: The bet size that maximises long-run log growth. For a small edge, approximately mean over variance. Practitioners use a fraction of it because the edge estimate is noisy.

follow_ups.q: Wouldn't changing criteria be inconsistent?
follow_ups.a: Not if the changes are declared for a new cycle before its data exists. What's forbidden is changing the rules for a test whose results you've already seen.

cards.topic: Regime change and non-stationarity
cards.question: Memecoin markets change every week. How does your approach deal with regime change?
cards.answer: Non-stationarity was built into the design and it's also part of why the result is fragile. The model is retrained on a rolling window, 25 days of training and 5 days of testing, rather than trained once and frozen, so it adapts to recent behaviour. Model replacement goes through the champion/challenger rule, so the system doesn't chase every short-lived regime. In production, the kill-switch would catch a regime break quickly: 3 consecutive days of negative expectancy send the system back to simulation. My own data showed the risk concretely. One wallet's apparent edge came over 98% from a single calendar day in one narrow regime, and it made up 34.7% of the original signals. The trade-off is that shorter windows adapt faster but give noisier estimates, and with only 5 test days, my evidence can't cleanly separate a regime shift from noise.

follow_ups.q: How would you detect a regime change formally?
follow_ups.a: Monitor live against expected performance with a control-chart or CUSUM-style test on trade returns, and alert when the cumulative deviation passes a threshold set in advance.

follow_ups.q: Why not use a longer window to reduce noise?
follow_ups.a: Older memecoin data likely reflects dead regimes and a different set of active tokens. A longer window lowers variance but raises drift bias. With 30 days of backfill, 25/5 was also the practical maximum.

cards.topic: Label construction: which way are your labels biased?
cards.question: Your labels come from 15-minute candle closes. The entry price is the nearest close within 30 minutes of the wallet's buy, and the peak is the highest close over the next 24 hours. In which direction does each of those choices bias your win rate?
cards.answer: There are four biases and they don't all go the same way. First, the peak uses closes, not highs, so it underestimates the true intraday peak: a take-profit that was touched inside a candle can be missed, which biases wins down. Second, the entry is the nearest close within ±30 minutes, which can be before or after the buy. On tokens that pump in the minutes before a smart wallet buys, a pre-buy close understates the real entry price and overstates the ratio, so wins are biased up. Third, and most important, the entry is the leader's time, not mine: a follower buys 5 to 60 seconds later at a worse price, so labels describe the leader's opportunity, not the follower's, which is biased up. Fourth, the price comes from the pool that is most active at labelling time, which can differ from where the trade actually happened. Net, I believe the labels are optimistic for a copy trader, and that's consistent with paper trading, which used real timing, deviating 94.4% from the backtest.

follow_ups.q: Why not simply use the leader's own execution price from the transaction?
follow_ups.a: That's the better fix: a swap transaction contains both legs, SOL out and tokens in, so the executed price is exact. The early labeller used candles because price history was needed anyway for the peak. The report still describes only two stored price points per trade, the entry price and the 24-hour peak, and doesn't claim transaction-level entries, so moving the entry to the executed swap price is the first labelling fix I'd make.

follow_ups.q: Does label noise or label bias hurt you more?
follow_ups.a: For the model, noise mostly costs power. For the evaluation, bias is worse, because it can create a fake edge that survives every significance test, since the test measures precision against labels that are themselves wrong in one direction.

follow_ups.q: Is quoting a max hold of 11,458 seconds sensible?
follow_ups.a: Not to the second: time-to-peak comes from 15-minute candle close times, so the right statement is 'about three hours, the 75th percentile of time-to-peak'.

cards.topic: Setting a stop-loss from the peak distribution: is that logical?
cards.question: Your stop-loss is 0.6573× entry, the 5th percentile of the peak-price-ratio distribution. But a stop is about how far the price falls, not how high it rises. Why calibrate a stop on the peak?
cards.answer: It's a fair criticism, and the honest answer is that I calibrated it on the data I had, not the data I needed. The database stores only two prices per trade: the entry and the highest close within 24 hours. With only the peak, the one thing I can say for sure is that trades whose peak stays below 0.6573× entry were losers whatever path they took, because the price never got back above the stop. So the stop was placed below the roughly 46% of trades that never move meaningfully from entry, and the 5th percentile marks the 5% that only ever went down. But the right statistic for a stop is the distribution of the trough, or maximum adverse excursion, before the peak. A trade can dip 40% and then triple, and my data can't see that dip, so I can't tell whether the stop or the target was hit first. That's why the report says only two outcomes are exact, and why storing the full path is my first fix.

follow_ups.q: How would you calibrate the stop properly?
follow_ups.a: Store the full price path, compute each trade's maximum adverse excursion before its peak, and set the stop so that it cuts the losers' tail without cutting too many eventual winners, all on training data only, then evaluate once on a later holdout.

follow_ups.q: Break-even hit rate for a 2× target and a 0.6573 stop?
follow_ups.a: Loss 0.3427, gain 1.0, so p* = 0.3427 / 1.3427 ≈ 25.5% before costs, if every trade ends at one of the two barriers. The ambiguous trades, scored at their peak or at breakeven, change that.

follow_ups.q: Was the stop itself leaky?
follow_ups.a: Yes: the exit parameters were calibrated on a distribution that included the test window, and an honest train-only calibration moved the stop by 7.5% and the max hold by 9.2%. I documented it and froze it rather than retuning on an already-seen window.

cards.topic: The 'trade amount' feature: in which units?
cards.question: One of your four features is 'trade amount: the raw size of the observed buy'. Raw in what unit? SOL, dollars, or tokens? And does it matter?
cards.answer: It matters a lot, and the honest answer is token units. In the final code, the parser stores the amount as the absolute change in the wallet's token balance (Helius `uiTokenAmount.uiAmount`, decimal-adjusted), and the model's `montant` feature reads that field directly. The SOL leg is read only to check that the buy had a counterpart (the spam filter); it is never stored. The report just says "the raw size of the observed buy". Token units are not comparable across tokens: one token can have a supply of a billion and another a million, so '10 million tokens' says nothing about the money at risk. So the feature partly acts as a token identifier rather than a size, and a tree model can overfit to that. The economically meaningful size is the notional in SOL, the quote currency, which the swap transaction gives exactly because it contains the SOL leg. The relative-size feature, current size divided by the median of the wallet's earlier buys, has the same issue, since that median mixes quantities of different tokens. So the fix is to compute notional in SOL for both features and to check that feature importance doesn't collapse after the change.

follow_ups.q: Trees are invariant to scaling a feature, so why does the unit matter?
follow_ups.a: Invariance holds for a monotone transform applied to the whole feature. Token units apply a different, time-varying scale per token, so the ordering of trades by 'size' changes, and that's not something a tree can undo.

follow_ups.q: How do you get the SOL amount from a Solana transaction?
follow_ups.a: From the wallet's native SOL balance change between pre- and post-balances, corrected for the network and priority fees, or from the wrapped-SOL token leg if the route used WSOL.

follow_ups.q: Could token quantity still carry signal?
follow_ups.a: Yes, because more tokens per SOL means an earlier, cheaper entry in the launch. But then it's a timing feature and should be built explicitly, like time since launch or market cap at entry.

cards.topic: Transaction parser edge cases
cards.question: Your parser calls any increase in a wallet's token balance a buy and any decrease a sale. Beyond the spam bug you found, give me three more cases where that rule gets it wrong.
cards.answer: The balance-delta rule is simple and robust to routing, but it breaks whenever a balance moves without a trade. First, outgoing transfers: if a wallet sends tokens to its own second wallet, that's recorded as a sale, which also matters because many traders split across wallets. Second, liquidity operations: adding liquidity to a pool reduces the token balance without selling, and removing it increases the balance without buying. Third, token-to-token swaps without SOL: the parser records one sale and one buy in the same transaction, which is correct in direction but has no SOL price attached. Fourth, native SOL was not read at all in the original version, and even after the fix it is only used as a counterpart signal, so I don't store what was paid. Fifth, it is keyed on the owner, so if a wallet trades through a token account it doesn't own directly, like some program-controlled accounts, the trade is missed. The spam fix, `_a_une_contrepartie`, requires a counterpart leg before calling it a buy, which also fixes the airdrop case, and it shipped with 18 tests. The report describes the fix for incoming transfers, but in the code the rule is symmetric: a token leaving the wallet with no SOL or other token coming back is ignored too, so a plain transfer out is no longer recorded as a sale, and there's a dedicated test for it. What stays open is liquidity: adding or removing liquidity moves several balances at once, so it can still pass the counter-leg check without being a trade. That's next on the list.

follow_ups.q: Why not decode each DEX program's instructions instead?
follow_ups.a: It's more precise but brittle: routes change, aggregators split orders across pools, and new programs launch constantly. Balance deltas work for any route; you then add rules, like requiring a SOL or WSOL counterpart, to reject non-trades.

follow_ups.q: How would you detect wallet-to-wallet transfers?
follow_ups.a: Check whether the counterpart of the token movement is another wallet with no swap program invoked and no SOL leg. If the destination is a known sibling wallet, you could even merge the two into one trader.

follow_ups.q: Does summing deltas within a transaction lose anything?
follow_ups.a: You lose intra-transaction fills and gross volume, but for a follower what matters is the net position change, so it's acceptable.

cards.topic: Idempotent writes: select-then-insert and the race condition
cards.question: You say your inserts are idempotent. How exactly? And what happens if the live listener and the backfill write the same trade at the same moment?
cards.answer: A trade is identified by the pair (transaction signature, token mint), and there's a unique constraint on that pair in PostgreSQL. In the early code, the store function first selects on that pair and inserts only if nothing is found, so replaying the same data, like re-running the backfill after the desync, never creates duplicates. But select-then-insert is not atomic: if the listener and the backfill both check at the same instant, both see nothing and both insert. The unique constraint then rejects the second insert with an integrity error, so the database stays correct, but that process's transaction fails, and if it isn't handled it can lose the other trades in the same batch. The clean fix is a single atomic statement, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, which makes the database arbitrate. Separately, the report documents a race condition that affected 4 paper trades, found and corrected the next day. The published verdict stayed as it was, and a dated addendum documented the recount.

follow_ups.q: Why is (signature, token) the key and not just the signature?
follow_ups.a: One Solana transaction can change the balances of several tokens for the same wallet, for example a token-to-token swap, and the parser emits one trade per mint whose balance changed.

follow_ups.q: What does 'read committed' isolation guarantee?
follow_ups.a: Each statement sees only data committed before it began, so no dirty reads. It doesn't stop two transactions from both seeing 'no row' and both trying to insert; only a unique constraint or serializable isolation stops that.

follow_ups.q: Why did you publish an addendum instead of correcting the verdict?
follow_ups.a: Rewriting a published verdict after the fact is how results quietly drift. The addendum keeps the original, shows the recount, and in this case the overall verdict didn't change: FAIL.

cards.topic: WebSocket subscriptions vs polling, and what happens on reconnect
cards.question: Why a WebSocket and not polling the RPC every second? What latency does your pipeline really have, and what do you lose when the connection drops?
cards.answer: Polling means asking 'anything new?' every second for every wallet, which wastes rate limit and still adds up to a second of delay on average. A WebSocket subscription pushes a notification when something happens. I subscribe with logsSubscribe, one subscription per wallet, filtered on transactions that mention the wallet, at 'confirmed' commitment. But the notification only carries the signature, so I then fetch the full transaction by RPC and parse it, which adds a round trip. So my latency is roughly confirmation time, plus the notification, plus the fetch: well under the 5 to 60 seconds of human reaction I was targeting, but far from sniper bots. The weakness was reconnection: the listener reconnects with exponential backoff from 2 to 60 seconds, but it didn't backfill the gap, so trades during a disconnection were missed until a backfill was re-run. The robust fix is to record the last processed signature and, on reconnect, fetch everything since it before resuming.

follow_ups.q: Why 'confirmed' rather than 'finalized'?
follow_ups.a: Finalized can take several more seconds, eating the reaction-time advantage. Confirmed transactions are voted on by a supermajority of stake and are very rarely rolled back, so for a signal it's the right trade-off; for accounting you'd reconcile at finalized.

follow_ups.q: How would you get lower latency?
follow_ups.a: Use a streaming service that pushes full transactions (a Geyser-based gRPC stream offered by RPC providers) to skip the extra fetch, co-locate near the RPC, and pre-build the swap transaction. But the thesis was never speed, so I didn't.

follow_ups.q: Can the gap bias your data?
follow_ups.a: Yes, because outages cluster in congestion, which is when these tokens trade most. Missing data is not missing at random, so gap recovery matters for statistics, not just completeness.

cards.topic: Scaling the system from 5 wallets to 500
cards.question: Suppose you want to track 500 wallets instead of 5. What breaks first in your system, and what would you change?
cards.answer: Three things break, roughly in this order. First, API limits. Each notification triggers a transaction fetch from Helius, and labelling calls DexPaprika, which allows about 50 requests a minute with a key and 300,000 a month. With 500 active wallets, the labelling queue grows faster than it drains, so labels lag and my labelling-lag alarm fires. Second, the subscription model: one logsSubscribe per wallet over a single connection hits provider limits on subscriptions per connection, so I'd shard across connections or use a streaming service that filters many accounts server-side. Third, statistics rather than engineering: with 500 wallets, most are noise, so the vetting and multiple-testing problem gets 100 times worse. The database is the least of my worries: PostgreSQL handles millions of rows easily with the indexes I have. I'd also cache price history per token, because many wallets buy the same token, so one price series can label many trades.

follow_ups.q: What is 'equal jitter' in your retry logic?
follow_ups.a: The wait is half the exponential delay plus a random amount up to the other half. Without randomness, requests that were rate-limited together retry together and hit the limit again; jitter spreads them out.

follow_ups.q: How many false positives would you expect among 500 no-skill wallets?
follow_ups.a: At a 5% significance level, about 25. That's why scaling needs pre-registered vetting rules and a multiple-testing correction, or shrinkage of each wallet's estimated edge towards the pool average.

follow_ups.q: Would PostgreSQL cope?
follow_ups.a: Easily: tens of thousands of rows a day is small. The indexes on wallet, token, timestamp and the unique key are what matter, plus partitioning by time if it ever grew to hundreds of millions of rows.

cards.topic: 430+ tests: what do they test, and why didn't they catch the leaks?
cards.question: You have 430+ automated tests. Yet two data leaks and a parser bug got through. So what are those tests worth?
cards.answer: They're worth a lot, but they test a different thing. Most of my tests are unit tests: given this input, the code produces that output. They check the parser on real transaction fixtures, that inserts are idempotent, that retries back off, that labelling picks the right candle, that monitoring alarms fire. They catch regressions, which is why every bug I found became new tests, like the 18 tests for the spam fix. But a leak is not code doing the wrong thing; it's code doing exactly what I told it to do on the wrong data, like calibrating on a window that included the test period. Unit tests don't catch methodological errors unless you write tests for the methodology itself. Now I would add invariant tests: every feature for a trade at time t must be computable from data strictly before t; every calibration function must fail if it receives a date inside the test window; every scored model must have a training window that ends before the test starts.

follow_ups.q: What's the difference between testing and model validation?
follow_ups.a: Testing checks the implementation matches the specification. Model validation, usually by an independent team, challenges the specification itself: assumptions, data, calibration, performance and limitations.

follow_ups.q: Did you use an AI assistant to write tests?
follow_ups.a: Yes, as an implementation collaborator, under rules I set, like 'every bug becomes a regression test' and the pre-registered criteria. The methodological constraints were mine; the tool doesn't discover them.

follow_ups.q: How do you test for look-ahead bias automatically?
follow_ups.a: Perturb every record after the decision time and check that no feature changes; and assert that every model's training window ends before its test window starts.

cards.topic: Multiple testing with your own numbers: does z = 3.91 survive?
cards.question: Count honestly how many tests you ran on this data: rule variants, thresholds, ML, clusterings, cost scenarios, window shifts, wallet removals. Then tell me what z you actually needed.
cards.answer: Counting generously, I ran on the order of 20 to 50 distinct looks at the data: the rule's threshold scan, the rule versus ML, two clustering levels, three cost scenarios, the ENR filter with and without caps, window shifts of ±1-2 days, leave-one-wallet-out on 5 wallets, and the post-audit replay. With a Bonferroni correction at a 5% family-wise level, the two-sided threshold is about 3.0 for 20 tests and 3.3 for 50 tests, instead of 1.96. The naive 10.02 clears that easily, the clustered 2.52 doesn't, the clustered 4.08 does, and the post-audit 3.91 still does, because its p-value is about 0.0001, which would survive up to roughly 500 tests. So the precision edge is not a pure multiple-testing artefact. The real point is that the economic result, negative net expectancy, doesn't depend on significance at all. And the frozen Stage 1 criteria were set before the first test, which is the best protection: the replay was one pre-specified test, not a search.

follow_ups.q: Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg here?
follow_ups.a: Bonferroni, because the question is 'is there any real edge at all?', a single family-wise claim. BH controls the share of false discoveries when you expect many, like screening hundreds of wallets or factors.

follow_ups.q: Your tests are correlated. Is Bonferroni too harsh?
follow_ups.a: Yes, it's conservative under positive correlation. A permutation or bootstrap approach that recomputes the maximum statistic over all variants gives the exact family-wise threshold, which would be lower. I use Bonferroni as an upper bound.

follow_ups.q: Why did the wallet-token clustering give a smaller z than wallet clustering?
follow_ups.a: The report gives the two results (4.08 clustering by wallet, 2.52 by wallet and token), not a decomposition. Normally finer clusters give a smaller correction, so the reversal is itself a warning: with only 9 wallet clusters the wallet-level bootstrap probably underestimates the variance, so 4.08 is likely the optimistic figure and the truth may be closer to 2.5. Either way both are above 1.96, and the economic verdict doesn't depend on it.

cards.topic: Leaderboard selection bias and regression to the mean
cards.question: You picked wallets because a leaderboard showed them as recently profitable. Why should their future performance be anything like their past? Quantify the problem.
cards.answer: It shouldn't be, fully, and that's the core weakness of any copy-trading strategy. A leaderboard ranks wallets by recent profit, and recent profit is skill plus luck. Selecting the top of the ranking selects both, so on average the selected wallets' future performance falls back towards the mean: regression to the mean. The expected future edge is the past edge multiplied by a shrinkage factor, the share of past variance that comes from skill. In memecoins, with fat-tailed outcomes and short windows, that share is small, so the shrinkage is severe: if luck accounts for 80% of the variance, a wallet that showed +50% keeps only +10% in expectation. That's exactly why I didn't trust the leaderboard: I used it only for sourcing, excluded wallets on pre-registered criteria, and required out-of-sample and live evidence. And the live paper trading, the only test on data after the selection, failed.

follow_ups.q: How would you shrink a wallet's win rate?
follow_ups.a: Use a beta prior centred on the pool's win rate: with prior Beta(a, b), a wallet with w wins in n trades gets (a + w)/(a + b + n). A wallet with 3 of 5 barely moves from the prior; one with 60 of 100 moves a lot.

follow_ups.q: Is the leaderboard itself biased in other ways?
follow_ups.a: Yes: it shows survivors and only recent windows, it may rank on unrealised gains, and wallets know they're watched, so some may trade to attract followers and then sell to them.

follow_ups.q: Why not pick wallets with the longest track record instead?
follow_ups.a: Better in principle, but memecoin wallets are short-lived and regimes change fast, so long records are rare. That trade-off between sample length and relevance is the same as choosing a lookback window on a desk.

cards.topic: In-sample wallet selection: the backfill overlaps the leaderboard window
cards.question: You chose wallets because they looked good on a leaderboard, then backfilled their trades over the previous 30 days to train and test. Isn't your whole backtest in-sample by construction?
cards.answer: Largely yes, and I think it's the single best explanation for why the backtest looked better than live trading. In my early code, the wallets were added on 9 September 2026 and backfilled 30 days back. The leaderboard picked them because of how they'd traded recently, which is the same period I then used for training and for the first Stage 1 test windows. So even with a perfect walk-forward split in time, the universe of wallets was chosen using information from the test period. It's a look-ahead in the universe, not in the features. The backfill covered about 30 days before the 9 September import and the walk-forward used 25 training days plus the next 5 test days, so the first test window sits in the last days before selection; if the leaderboard ranks on recent profits, whether over 7 or 30 days, it overlaps that window. The walk-forward split protects against the model seeing the future; it doesn't protect against the selection of what to model seeing the future. The clean test is on data after the selection date, which is live paper trading, and that failed. For the next cycle, the fix is to freeze the wallet list first and only evaluate on trades that happen afterwards.

follow_ups.q: Then is your Stage 1 result meaningless?
follow_ups.a: Not meaningless, but biased upwards, and I'd weight it much less than the live paper trading, which is clean and failed. The Stage 1 result is best read as an upper bound.

follow_ups.q: What's the equity-market equivalent?
follow_ups.a: Backtesting on today's index constituents: stocks are in the index because they did well, so the backtest inherits their past success. The fix is point-in-time constituents, including the companies that dropped out or went bankrupt.

follow_ups.q: Why didn't you see this earlier?
follow_ups.a: Because I focused my leakage checks on features and labels, where walk-forward protects you. Universe selection sits upstream of the whole pipeline, which is exactly why it's easy to miss.

cards.topic: Power analysis: how many trades did you need?
cards.question: Before you started, how many signals or trades would you have needed to detect a realistic edge? Was your five-day test ever going to be conclusive?
