cards.answer: There are two different sample-size questions. For the precision test, detecting a lift from a 5% base rate to 7% with 80% power at the 5% level needs about 1,000 selected signals; my 927 were close, but only if they were independent, and they weren't. For the economic question, net expectancy, it's far worse, because per-trade returns are very noisy. If the true edge is +2.7% per trade and the standard deviation per trade is around 40%, you need about 1,700 independent trades for 80% power. The 40% is an illustrative assumption, not a figure from the report, but it is consistent with the exit barriers: roughly a 12% chance of about +100% against mostly small losses gives $\sigma \approx \sqrt{0.12 \times 0.88} \times 105\% \approx 34\%$. The pre-registered minimum was only 30 to 50 trades, and at 40 trades the standard error on the mean is about 6 percentage points, so you can't tell +2.7% from −10%. In fact the model made 1,019 simulated buys over the five days: that brings the naive standard error down to about 1.3 points, but it's still below the 1,700 needed, roughly 58% power, before accounting for the fact that those trades came from a handful of wallets. And after my cost filter, only about 40 of them would have been admitted, which puts you back at a 6-point standard error. So no: five days of paper trading could reject a clearly bad strategy, but could hardly confirm a small real edge. If I restarted, I'd compute this first and set the Stage 2 length to reach the needed sample, not to a fixed number of days.

follow_ups.q: So was your FAIL verdict just low power?
follow_ups.a: Partly for Stage 2, which couldn't confirm a small edge either way. But the post-audit point estimate was negative, the clean live re-scoring showed concentration in excluded wallets, and every cost scenario except the most favourable admitted zero or negative-expectancy signals. That's evidence against, not just absence of evidence.

follow_ups.q: What is a design effect?
follow_ups.a: The factor by which clustering inflates the variance relative to independent sampling: about 1 + (m − 1)ρ for clusters of size m and intra-cluster correlation ρ. You divide n by it to get the effective sample size.

follow_ups.q: How does a sequential test help?
follow_ups.a: It lets you look at the data as it arrives and stop early for a clear success or failure, with boundaries set in advance so peeking doesn't inflate the false-positive rate.

cards.topic: Cluster bootstrap with only a handful of clusters
cards.question: You clustered your bootstrap by wallet. But you had 9 wallets, and now only 5. Is a cluster bootstrap with 5 clusters meaningful?
cards.answer: Barely, and I'd say so upfront. The cluster bootstrap's validity is asymptotic in the number of clusters, not the number of observations. With 5 wallets, resampling 5 with replacement gives only 126 distinct combinations, so the bootstrap distribution is coarse, and with few clusters it systematically underestimates the true variance, so it's anti-conservative. With one wallet carrying 34.7% of signals, it's worse, because whether that wallet is drawn zero, one or two times dominates every resample. So a clustered z of 4.08 on 9 wallets should be read as optimistic. Better tools for few clusters exist: use a t-distribution with G − 1 degrees of freedom, so the 5% critical value is 2.78 with 5 clusters instead of 1.96, or a wild cluster bootstrap. But the honest conclusion is that with 5 wallets, wallet-level inference is weak whatever the method, which is why leave-one-wallet-out, showing the pool is fragile in both directions, was the more informative check.

follow_ups.q: How many clusters do you want for cluster-robust inference?
follow_ups.a: Rules of thumb say at least 30 to 50 roughly balanced clusters. Below that, use small-sample corrections, a t with G − 1 degrees of freedom, or a wild cluster bootstrap.

follow_ups.q: Should you cluster by wallet or by token?
follow_ups.a: Both correlations exist: a wallet's signals share its style, and several wallets buying the same token share that token's fate. Two-way clustering handles both but needs many clusters in each dimension; with 5 wallets, the wallet dimension is the binding weakness.

follow_ups.q: What is the wild cluster bootstrap in one sentence?
follow_ups.a: Instead of resampling clusters, you keep them all and randomly flip the sign of each cluster's residuals, which preserves within-cluster correlation and behaves much better when clusters are few.

cards.topic: Which z-test exactly? One-sample vs two-proportion
cards.question: You call it a 'z-test for two proportions', but your selected signals are a subset of the population you compare them with. Those samples aren't independent. Which test did you actually run, and does the choice change the answer?
cards.answer: Good catch. The 5.0% reference is the win rate of all 4,011 candidates, and the 927 selected signals are inside that set, so a textbook two-independent-sample test would be wrong. The code runs a one-sample test: selected precision 12.2% against a fixed reference of 5.0%, with the standard error computed under the null, root of 0.05 × 0.95 over 927, which gives about 10.06 before rounding. The correct two-sample version compares selected against non-selected: the 3,084 non-selected candidates had about 2.8% wins, which gives a z around 11.4 with a pooled standard error; the Stage 1 report ran that check too. And if you use the selected sample's own variance, 12.2% × 87.8%, instead of the null variance, you get about 6.7. So the choice moves z between roughly 7 and 11, but it never crosses 1.96. The much bigger issue is independence, which the cluster bootstrap addressed: that took it down to between 2.5 and 4.1.

follow_ups.q: Why do the null-SE and Wald-SE versions differ so much?
follow_ups.a: Because the variance of a proportion p(1 − p) is much larger at 12.2% than at 5%. The null-based SE uses 5%, giving a smaller SE and a bigger z; the Wald SE uses 12.2%.

follow_ups.q: How would a permutation test work here?
follow_ups.a: Randomly choose 927 of the 4,011 candidates many times, compute the win rate of each random selection, and see where 12.2% falls in that distribution. It's exact under exchangeability, but, like the z-test, it assumes candidates are exchangeable, which clustering violates.

follow_ups.q: Is the z-test even the right test for a model?
follow_ups.a: It tests precision at one threshold. I'd also look at ranking metrics like the area under the precision-recall curve on the test window, and ultimately at net expectancy, which is what pays.

cards.topic: Is your acceptance gate powerful enough to pass a real edge?
cards.question: Your Stage 2 required live expectancy within 50% of the backtest estimate and at least 3 of 5 positive days. Suppose the strategy genuinely had a +2.7% edge. What's the probability it passes?
cards.answer: It depends on a number I never fixed in advance, the trade count, and that's the real design flaw. The pre-registered minimum was only 30 to 50 trades. At 40 trades, with a per-trade standard deviation of around 40%, the standard error on the live mean is about 6.3 percentage points. The 'within 50%' band around +2.7% is +1.35% to +4.05%, only 2.7 points wide, so even a true +2.7% strategy lands inside it only about 17% of the time; add 3 of 5 positive days, about 68% if each day is positive with 60% probability, and a genuine edge passes roughly one time in ten. The live run actually produced 1,019 simulated buys, which helps a lot: the standard error falls to about 1.25 points, the band is hit about 72% of the time, and the combined pass probability is roughly 70%. But those trades came from a handful of wallets over five days: with a design effect of about 6, it falls back to roughly 25%. These numbers use an illustrative 40% per-trade standard deviation, which the barrier structure makes plausible. So the gate is tuned to reject, which is the safe side for capital, but I never computed its power. And the Stage 1 criterion of 4 of 5 positive days is weak in the other direction: a strategy with no edge passes it about 19% of the time by chance. I'd redesign both with the sample size chosen from a power calculation.

follow_ups.q: So was the Stage 2 FAIL uninformative?
follow_ups.a: Not entirely: 1 positive day of 5 happens with only about 8% probability if each day is 60% likely to be positive, and a 94.4% deviation is large. It's weak evidence against the edge, not proof, which is why the post-audit replay and live re-scoring matter too.

follow_ups.q: Why is a relative band like 'within 50%' a bad criterion?
follow_ups.a: Its absolute width scales with the backtest estimate, so a small estimated edge gives a tiny band that noise almost always misses. A one-sided test of live versus backtest, with a sample size chosen in advance, is better.

follow_ups.q: Why tune a gate towards rejection?
follow_ups.a: Because the costs are asymmetric: a false positive loses capital, a false negative loses an opportunity you can retest. But you should still know the false-negative rate, or you'll reject every good idea.

cards.topic: Probability calibration and the 0.5 threshold with a 5% base rate
cards.question: Only 5% of candidates are wins, yet your model's 0.5 threshold selected 927 of 4,011, about 23%. A calibrated model would almost never output 0.5 at that base rate. What's going on, and why does it matter for your ENR filter?
cards.answer: It means the scores aren't calibrated probabilities, and the code says why: the LightGBM model was trained with class weighting, scale_pos_weight = n_neg/n_pos, about 19.88 for the deployed model. Weighting the wins by w multiplies the model's odds by roughly w, so a score of 0.5 (odds of 1) corresponds to true odds of about 1/19.88, a real probability of about 4.8%. The 0.5 threshold therefore sits roughly at the base rate, which is why it lets about 23% of candidates through. The realised precision among the 927 selected was 12.2%, well above the base rate, so the ranking carries information; the score level doesn't. That's fine for ranking trades, but not for the ENR filter, which turns the model's probability into an expected return under the exit policy and subtracts costs. That is exactly what happened in the first version of ENR: plugging in the raw probability gave an expected gross return of +32.9% at p = 0.5, while the realised return in the lowest probability bucket was negative (−8.05% on [0.50, 0.55) in the internal validation), so the filter admitted almost everything. It was replaced by an empirical calibration: the average realised return per probability bucket (0.50, 0.55, 0.60, 0.65, 0.70), built only on the internal validation split of the training window (599 signals), never on the test window. After that, the filter actually discriminated. A cleaner alternative would be an analytic prior correction (divide the odds by the weight) or Platt or isotonic calibration, checked with a reliability plot. The 0.5 threshold itself was chosen on a 20-day / 5-day internal split of the training data, which avoided a leak, but it isn't a meaningful probability.

follow_ups.q: Platt or isotonic?
follow_ups.a: Platt scaling has two parameters and works with little data; isotonic is more flexible but overfits with few positives. With a few hundred positives per window, I'd start with Platt and check the reliability diagram.

follow_ups.q: Does calibration change the model's ranking of trades?
follow_ups.a: No, both are monotone transformations of the score, so the ordering and metrics like AUC are unchanged. What changes is the probability level, which is what ENR needs.

follow_ups.q: Why not just choose the threshold that maximises backtest expectancy?
follow_ups.a: That's the calibration/evaluation leak again unless it's done on training data only. And with ENR, you don't need a separate threshold: calibrated probability plus costs decides.

cards.topic: Copy-trading, front-running and MEV: where are the ethical and legal lines?
cards.question: Your strategy trades on other people's flow. On our desk, trading on client flow is front-running and gets you fired. Why is your project any different, and would you be the victim of front-running on Solana?
cards.answer: The difference is the source of the information and the duty attached to it. On a desk, a client's order is confidential information given to you in a relationship of trust; trading ahead of it, for yourself or the bank, abuses that trust and is market abuse. My project only used public data: on a public blockchain, every confirmed transaction is visible to everyone at the same time, and I had no relationship with those wallets and no privileged access. It's closer to reading public filings of what a famous fund bought, which is legal, than to front-running. That said, I'd still clear it with compliance as a personal activity, and it has never traded real money. And yes, on Solana I'd be the potential victim: MEV searchers can see pending or just-landed transactions and sandwich a buy, buying just before it and selling just after, so the follower pays more. That's one reason my cost scenarios include up to 8% slippage per leg.

follow_ups.q: What is a sandwich attack?
follow_ups.a: A searcher sees a pending swap, buys the same token just before it to push the price up, lets the victim buy at the worse price, then sells right after to capture the victim's price impact. The victim's slippage is the attacker's profit.

follow_ups.q: Is copying a public fund's 13F holdings legal?
follow_ups.a: Yes, 13F filings are public, delayed by up to 45 days after quarter-end in the US, and anyone can replicate them. The delay is part of why the edge is small.

follow_ups.q: What would you do if a colleague traded ahead of a client order?
follow_ups.a: Escalate to compliance or my manager immediately. It's a conduct breach that harms the client and the bank, and staying silent makes you part of it.

cards.topic: Adverse selection: are you the exit liquidity?
cards.question: If a wallet is on a public leaderboard, thousands of followers see its trades. Why wouldn't the wallet's owner buy, let followers push the price up, and sell to them? How would you know you're not the exit liquidity?
cards.answer: That's the key adverse-selection risk in copy trading, and a leaderboard makes it worse, because visibility is exactly what lets a wallet monetise its followers. If the owner knows followers buy after him, his best strategy is to buy, wait for the followers' buying to lift the price, and sell into it. Then the followers' losses are his profit, and the signal I'm copying is negatively correlated with my own P&L. I'd look for it in the data: the time between the leader's buy and his sale relative to follower inflows, whether his sells cluster right after spikes in other wallets' buying, and whether his profitable trades come from tokens where he was early and followers were many. Some of my exclusions were in that spirit: bot-like wallets, a 2-second-hold wallet, and a wallet whose edge was one day. But I never built a direct test for 'leader sells to followers'. I don't have a direct measurement of how fast the leaders sold after buying, so I wouldn't claim one; the peak-timing data (the 75th percentile of time-to-peak is about 3h11, which set the maximum hold) at least shows that many peaks came hours after the buy, not seconds. The live result, positive precision but negative expectancy, is consistent with this story.

follow_ups.q: What does Glosten-Milgrom say?
follow_ups.a: A market maker facing a mix of informed and uninformed traders sets a bid-ask spread so that profits from the uninformed cover losses to the informed. The more informed flow, the wider the spread.

follow_ups.q: How would you measure the follower-delay curve?
follow_ups.a: Recompute each signal's outcome assuming entry at the leader's time plus 5, 15, 30 and 60 seconds, using trade-level prices, and plot net expectancy against the delay. A steeply falling curve means the edge is a race, not information.

follow_ups.q: Could wallets deliberately game the leaderboard?
follow_ups.a: Yes: a wallet could build a good-looking public record to attract followers and then monetise them. That's why I treated the leaderboard as a sourcing tool, not a data feed or a quality label.

cards.topic: Alpha decay and implementation shortfall for a follower
cards.question: Your edge is supposed to live in a 5-to-60-second reaction gap. How fast does that edge decay with delay, and how would you measure what you lose between the signal and your fill?
cards.answer: I'd measure it as implementation shortfall: the difference between the price at the moment the signal fires, the leader's execution, and the price I actually get, plus fees, plus the cost of trades I miss. For a follower it has three parts: the delay cost, the price move during my 5 to 60 seconds, which is where copy-trading edge goes to die; my own price impact on a thin AMM pool; and fixed costs like network and priority fees. My labels were measured from the leader's time, so they ignore the delay cost entirely, which is why I think the backtest was optimistic and why paper trading deviated 94.4% from it. The right analysis is an alpha-decay curve: recompute the expectancy of each signal as if I entered 5, 15, 30 and 60 seconds after the leader, with trade-level prices, and see where it crosses zero. If the edge only exists in the first few seconds, it belongs to bots, not to my design. The report doesn't document a decision-to-fill latency measurement in paper trading, so that is the first thing I'd log in the next cycle.

follow_ups.q: What is implementation shortfall in one line?
follow_ups.a: The return you'd have made trading instantly at the decision price with no costs, minus what you actually made: delay, impact, fees and missed trades.

follow_ups.q: How does alpha decay affect execution choice?
follow_ups.a: Fast-decaying signals must be executed aggressively, accepting more impact; slow ones can be worked patiently to reduce impact. The optimal speed balances the two.

follow_ups.q: How would you reconstruct prices at second resolution?
follow_ups.a: From on-chain swaps in the same pool: each swap's two legs give an executed price and time. You don't need candles at all.

cards.topic: AMM math: constant product, price impact and the follower's entry
cards.question: Take a constant-product pool with 50 SOL and 1 billion tokens. What happens to the price if you buy with 1 SOL? And what if the leader buys 5 SOL just before you?
cards.answer: In a constant-product AMM the pool keeps x times y constant, with x tokens and y SOL, so the spot price is y over x: 50 SOL for a billion tokens is 5 × 10⁻⁸ SOL per token. If I put in 1 SOL, after a 0.25% fee about 0.9975 SOL enters, and I get x·Δy/(y + Δy), about 19.56 million tokens. My average price is about 2.25% above the pre-trade spot, and the spot after my trade is about 4% higher. That's price impact: for small trades, the impact on the spot is about twice my trade as a fraction of the SOL reserve. Now if the leader buys 5 SOL first, the SOL reserve becomes 55 and the token reserve falls to about 909 million, so the spot rises 21% before I trade. My 1 SOL then costs me about 23.5% above the price the leader saw. And if the leader sells his tokens before me, I get back only about 0.82 SOL, a 17.8% loss, while he makes about 3%: my buying funded his exit. That's why following is expensive.

follow_ups.q: Why does the spot move about twice as much as your average price?
follow_ups.a: Because along the curve you buy the first tokens near the old price and the last ones near the new price; the average is roughly the midpoint, so about half the spot move. Exactly, P1/P0 = (1 + γΔy/y)².

follow_ups.q: Who bears the loss in an AMM when the price moves?
follow_ups.a: Liquidity providers: arbitrageurs trade against the pool until its price matches the market, and LPs end up holding more of the asset that fell. That's impermanent loss, or loss-versus-rebalancing.

follow_ups.q: How do concentrated-liquidity pools change this?
follow_ups.a: Liquidity is concentrated in price ranges, so near the current price the pool is deeper and impact is smaller, but once the price leaves the range, depth collapses. The formula becomes piecewise.

cards.topic: Kill-switch false alarms: how often would a good strategy be stopped?
cards.question: Your kill-switch stops the system after three consecutive days of negative expectancy. If the strategy genuinely had a positive edge, how often would it be stopped by bad luck in its first month?
cards.answer: Very often, which is by design but worth quantifying. Suppose the true edge is +2.7% per trade with a standard deviation around 40%, and the system does about 10 trades a day. The daily mean then has a standard error of about 12.6%, so a day is negative with probability around 42%, even though the edge is real. The probability of at least one run of three negative days in 30 days is then roughly 75%, and near certain over a year. (Both inputs are illustrative: 40% is consistent with the exit barriers, and about 10 trades a day is roughly what my cost filter admitted in paper trading, about 41 of the 1,019 simulated buys over 5 days.) So the kill-switch as designed would almost certainly stop a genuinely good strategy within weeks. That's acceptable only because it's one-way and cheap: it falls back to simulation, and resuming needs my fresh sign-off. But as a production rule it's too sensitive. I'd base it on cumulative drawdown or a sequential test on the running mean, with a false-alarm rate I choose in advance, rather than on runs of daily signs.

follow_ups.q: How did you compute the run probability?
follow_ups.a: With a Markov chain whose state is the current number of consecutive negative days (0, 1 or 2), absorbing at 3. Iterating it 30 times gives the probability of having hit 3 at least once.

follow_ups.q: How would you set a drawdown limit?
follow_ups.a: Model cumulative P&L as a drift plus noise and choose the drawdown level so that a strategy with the target edge breaches it with only a small, pre-chosen probability over the horizon, then check it on the backtest.

follow_ups.q: What's the VaR backtesting analogy?
follow_ups.a: With a 99% one-day VaR you expect about 1% exceptions, roughly 2.5 in 250 days. Too many exceptions means the risk model underestimates risk; regulators use that count in a traffic-light test.

cards.topic: Champion/challenger rule: can it ever detect a better model?
cards.question: Your challenger model must beat the champion by 20% relative expectancy, with p < 0.05, at least 30 trades per side, over two consecutive windows. What's the power of that test?
cards.answer: Essentially zero at those sample sizes, which I'd happily admit. If the champion makes +2.7% per trade, a 20% relative improvement is 0.54 percentage points. With a per-trade standard deviation around 40% and 30 trades on each side, the standard error of the difference is about 10 percentage points, so the expected z is about 0.05. The power is barely above the 5% false-positive rate, and requiring it twice in a row makes it smaller still. To have 80% power you'd need around 86,000 trades per side. So in practice the rule means 'the incumbent is kept', which is what the report says: when in doubt, keep the champion. That's a defensible anti-thrashing choice, but it's really a lock, not a test. I'd improve it by comparing the two models on the same signals, since both can score every candidate: the paired difference has far lower variance, and you can use thousands of shadow decisions instead of 30 executed trades.

follow_ups.q: What is shadow mode?
follow_ups.a: The challenger runs on live data and records its decisions without trading. Because it faces exactly the same candidates and outcomes as the champion, you can compare them fairly and at no risk.

follow_ups.q: Why are relative thresholds dangerous?
follow_ups.a: Because they scale with the base: 20% of a tiny or noisy expectancy is a tiny absolute difference, and if the champion's expectancy is near zero or negative, a relative improvement is meaningless.

follow_ups.q: How do banks govern model changes?
follow_ups.a: Through model risk management: the developer documents the change, an independent validation team reviews it, the model inventory is updated, and material changes need approval before use, often with parallel runs of the old and new models.

cards.topic: Changing base rates: comparing precision to the right reference
cards.question: Your reference was a 5.0% win rate across all candidates. But in a hot market day maybe 15% of tokens pump, and on a dead day 1%. If your model just selects more on hot days, is 12.2% precision an edge at all?
cards.answer: That's a real concern: a model can beat a pooled base rate simply by trading more on days when everything wins. If 60% of my selections came from a 15%-base-rate day and the rest from a 2% day, a random selector with the same daily timing would already show about 10% precision against a pooled 5%. So the fair comparison is precision against the base rate of the same day, or the same hour, weighted by where the model actually selected. Technically, that's a stratified test: compare selected versus non-selected within each day and combine, for instance with a Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test, or compute the expected wins under the day-matched base rates and test against that. My robustness criterion, direction right on 4 of 5 days, partly addresses it, because it compares within each day. If the daily comparisons used each day's own base rate, that criterion is already a crude stratified test; if they used the pooled 5%, it isn't, so I'd make this explicit. I'd make the day-matched reference the primary test next time. And for the economics, timing the market is fine if it's real, but then the claim is 'market timing', not 'wallet skill'.

follow_ups.q: What is Simpson's paradox?
follow_ups.a: A trend present in every subgroup can disappear or reverse when groups are pooled, because group sizes differ. Classic example: a treatment better in every hospital but worse overall because it was used more in the hospital with sicker patients.

follow_ups.q: Was the post-audit base rate the same 5%?
follow_ups.a: The report doesn't publish it, and it very likely differs: a different window, a smaller pool and cleaned data. That is another reason to always compare to the same-window, ideally same-day, reference.

follow_ups.q: How is this like alpha versus beta?
follow_ups.a: A fund that beats cash in a rising market may just have market exposure. You measure alpha after removing beta; here, you measure selection skill after removing the day's base rate.

cards.topic: Why no Sharpe ratio? Risk-adjusted performance of the strategy
cards.question: You report expectancy per trade but no Sharpe ratio. Any desk would ask for one. What would your Sharpe have been, and why is it misleading here?
cards.answer: I chose expectancy per trade because the question was whether each trade pays for its costs, and the corrected answer was no: −0.09% in the low-cost scenario and −2.2% after the audit, so the Sharpe is negative and there's nothing to annualise. But the more interesting point is why a Sharpe would have misled on the initial numbers. With +2.7% per trade, a standard deviation around 40% and about 185 signals a day, a naive calculation gives a daily Sharpe near 0.9 and an annualised Sharpe around 17, which is absurd. It's absurd because it assumes trades are independent, when many are in the same token at the same time; it ignores capacity, since pools are too thin to trade 185 positions a day; and returns are extremely fat-tailed, so standard deviation misdescribes the risk. If the edge had survived, I'd compute Sharpe on the daily P&L of the actual capped portfolio, with realistic sizes, and add drawdown and tail measures like the worst day.

follow_ups.q: What's the standard error of an estimated Sharpe ratio?
follow_ups.a: For i.i.d. normal returns over T periods, about the square root of (1 + S²/2)/T. With 5 daily observations, it's about 0.45 or more on a daily Sharpe, so the estimate says almost nothing.

follow_ups.q: Why √365 rather than √252?
follow_ups.a: Because crypto markets trade every day of the year. For equities you'd use about 252 trading days. Either way, annualising by the square root assumes independent returns.

follow_ups.q: Sharpe or Sortino for a strategy with positive skew?
follow_ups.a: Sortino, or better, look at the full distribution. Sharpe penalises big wins as much as big losses, which misrepresents a positively skewed strategy, but it also hides how often you lose small amounts.

cards.topic: Kelly sizing for your strategy, and why estimation error kills it
cards.question: Suppose the initial numbers had been right: +2.7% expectancy per trade. What fraction of capital would Kelly tell you to put on each trade, and would you follow it?
cards.answer: For small edges, the Kelly fraction is approximately the mean divided by the variance of the per-trade return. With +2.7% and a standard deviation around 40%, that's 0.027 over 0.16, about 17% of capital per trade. I wouldn't follow it, for three reasons. First, estimation error: the +2.7% came from 927 clustered signals over 5 days, so its real uncertainty is several percentage points, and the corrected full-system number was −0.09%, for which Kelly says bet zero. Betting full Kelly on an overestimated edge is the fastest way to ruin, since at twice the true Kelly fraction your expected growth is zero. Second, trades are correlated: many positions in the same token are open together, so per-trade Kelly overstates what the portfolio can carry. Third, fat tails and capacity: returns aren't normal and pools are thin. In practice I'd use a small fraction of Kelly, a quarter or less, cap exposure per token and per wallet, and size down automatically when live results diverge from the backtest.

follow_ups.q: Why is overbetting worse than underbetting?
follow_ups.a: Growth is a concave function of the bet: half Kelly keeps 75% of the maximum growth with half the volatility, while double Kelly gives zero growth. The penalty is asymmetric, so with an uncertain edge you shade down.

follow_ups.q: How would correlation change the sizing?
follow_ups.a: For a portfolio, Kelly becomes the inverse covariance matrix times the mean vector. Correlated positions, like several wallets buying the same token, get much less combined weight than independent ones would.

follow_ups.q: What does full Kelly feel like in practice?
follow_ups.a: Very volatile: under standard assumptions there's about a 50% chance of losing half your capital at some point, which is why professionals use fractions.

cards.topic: Why paper trading is still optimistic: fills, fees, MEV and failed transactions
cards.question: You say paper trading can't be contaminated by hindsight. Fine, but it still assumes you get filled. What does paper trading get wrong compared with real execution on Solana?
cards.answer: Paper trading removes look-ahead, but it keeps the fill model, and every fill model is optimistic. The paper system decides in real time, but it simulates the transaction, so it doesn't face what a real order faces: latency between decision and landing, priority-fee competition in busy blocks, transactions that fail or expire, sandwich attacks by MEV searchers, the real depth of the pool at that second, and the sell side, where exits in a collapsing token can be much worse than any quote. In my design, costs are not guessed per trade: they come from the three sourced scenarios (priority fee, pool fee and slippage per leg, with slippage taken from live Jupiter quotes on comparable sizes), applied on top of the observed price. So a paper result is an upper bound on live performance, especially for small illiquid tokens. In my case, it didn't matter much in the end, because paper trading already failed: 94.4% deviation from the backtest and 1 of 5 days positive. But if it had passed, I'd have treated the gap between paper and real as the next thing to measure, with a tiny real-money pilot at Stage 3, precisely to calibrate the fill model.

follow_ups.q: Why do failed transactions bias paper results?
follow_ups.a: Because failures cluster in fast moves: a fast pump makes your buy exceed its slippage limit, so you miss winners, while a crash still lets you sell at bad prices. A 100% fill assumption overweights the good outcomes.

follow_ups.q: What would you log in a real-money pilot?
follow_ups.a: Decision time and price, quote, send and landing times, executed price, fees paid including priority fees, and success or failure, so I can decompose implementation shortfall and fix the fill model.

follow_ups.q: How does a stop-loss behave in a rug pull?
follow_ups.a: It gaps: the price can jump far below the stop between two observations, so the exit fills far worse than the stop level, like a stock gapping down overnight through a stop order.

cards.topic: LightGBM configuration on a small, imbalanced dataset
cards.question: Tell me your LightGBM configuration: number of trees, leaves, learning rate, minimum samples per leaf, early stopping. With 4 features and maybe a few hundred positive examples, how did you avoid overfitting?
cards.answer: The configuration was small and fixed, not tuned: binary objective, num_leaves 15, max_depth 4, learning rate 0.05, 100 boosting rounds, min_data_in_leaf 20 (the LightGBM default), and class weighting with scale_pos_weight equal to negatives over positives, about 19.9 on the deployed model. No early stopping, no row or feature subsampling, no L1/L2 penalty, no monotone constraints, no explicit seed. With hindsight, the weak points are min_data_in_leaf 20, which holds about one win per leaf at a 5% base rate, and class weighting without recalibration, which is why a 0.5 score meant only about 12% precision. What I'd change, given the data: with four features and about 5% positives, the model can't need much depth, so I'd keep trees shallow, a few leaves or a maximum depth of 3 or 4, and a large minimum number of samples per leaf, so each leaf holds enough positives to mean something. A small learning rate with a moderate number of trees, and early stopping on a validation slice taken from the end of the training window, never the test window. Subsampling rows and features adds regularisation. Class weighting helps the model see the rare class but ruins calibration, so it must be followed by calibration if the probabilities feed the ENR filter. And monotone constraints are a good idea: a higher historical win rate, or more simultaneous buyers, should never lower the score. The real protection against overfitting, though, was walk-forward evaluation on unseen days, and the paper-trading stage.

follow_ups.q: Why is leaf-wise growth risky on small data?
follow_ups.a: LightGBM splits the leaf with the biggest loss reduction wherever it is, so trees can become deep and narrow, fitting a few examples. On small data you limit num_leaves and max_depth and raise min_data_in_leaf.

follow_ups.q: Did LightGBM beat logistic regression?
follow_ups.a: The report doesn't include that comparison, so I wouldn't claim it. The project's own rules allowed gradient boosting or logistic regression, and a logistic regression on the same walk-forward windows is the first benchmark I'd add: with four features it should be close, and if it is, it's the better choice because it is calibrated and interpretable.

follow_ups.q: What's the risk of a monotone constraint on 'simultaneous buyers'?
follow_ups.a: Crowding can be bad: many buyers in the same minute may mean you're late and the price already moved. Forcing monotonicity would hide that; I'd test both and keep the constraint only if it doesn't hurt out of sample.

cards.topic: Model artefact controls: making the 'wrong model' mix-up impossible
cards.question: Your first leak was that the validation numbers were produced by a model trained on train plus test data. How can that even happen, and what controls would make it impossible?
cards.answer: It happens because a model file is just a file. At one point the model used to produce the retrospective validation numbers was the one trained on the combined train and test data, the kind of refit on all data that is normal for a production model, instead of the genuine out-of-sample one. Nothing in the pipeline checked which data the model had seen. That inflated net expectancy from a true +2.7% to +5.39%. The controls are the ones a bank's model risk function would ask for. Every model gets a registry entry with its version, the start and end of its training window, the code version and a hash of the artefact; my schema already had a models table with training window start and end and an active flag. Then the scoring code must assert, before producing any validation number, that the model's training window ends before the test window starts, and refuse to run otherwise. Validation reports must record which model version produced them. And production models trained on everything are stored under a different name, so they can't be confused with validation models.

follow_ups.q: Is it wrong to retrain the final model on all data?
follow_ups.a: No, it's common for production, because more data usually helps. But that model has no out-of-sample performance of its own; its expected performance is the walk-forward estimate, and it must be labelled so it's never used to report validation numbers.

follow_ups.q: What is model risk management in a bank?
follow_ups.a: The framework that inventories every model, requires independent validation before use, sets usage limits, and monitors performance over time. US guidance SR 11-7 is the classic reference.

follow_ups.q: How did you discover the mix-up?
follow_ups.a: Within 24 hours of the Stage 1 PASS, while re-checking how the headline result had been computed, I traced which model artefact had produced the validation numbers: it was the model trained on train plus test data, which inflated net expectancy from a true +2.7% to a reported +5.39%.

cards.topic: The triple-barrier exit as an exotic option, and why it can't create edge
cards.question: Think of your exit rule as a derivative. What exotic option is a triple barrier, and can a clever exit policy turn a no-edge entry into a profitable strategy?
cards.answer: The position with a triple-barrier exit is like holding the token with a double knock-out attached: at the 2.0× barrier you're knocked out with a gain, at the 0.6573× barrier you're knocked out with a loss, and if neither is hit you're closed at maturity, 11,458 seconds later. So its payoff is a double-barrier, path-dependent claim, and its value depends on volatility and time to the barriers, like any barrier option. But it can't create edge. If the token price is a martingale after my entry, meaning no drift, the optional stopping theorem says the expected price at any bounded stopping time equals the entry price. So any exit rule, barriers or not, has zero expected return before costs, and negative after. With only up and down barriers, the probability of hitting the target first is exactly (1 − 0.6573)/(2 − 0.6573), about 25.5%, which is the break-even hit rate. The exit reshapes the distribution, it doesn't change the mean. The edge must come from the entry.

follow_ups.q: Why does optional stopping need a bounded stopping time?
follow_ups.a: Without it, strategies like 'double down until you win' seem to beat a fair game, because they can run forever with unbounded losses. With a bounded time, like the 11,458-second barrier, or bounded positions, the theorem holds.

follow_ups.q: Where do barriers appear in real products?
follow_ups.a: Autocallables knock out and pay a coupon when the underlying is above a level on an observation date; reverse convertibles and knock-in puts expose the investor to losses below a lower barrier; FX clients buy knock-out forwards to cheapen hedges.

follow_ups.q: Can an exit policy ever add value, then?
follow_ups.a: Yes, if the entry has an edge that plays out over a specific horizon: a well-chosen time barrier captures the drift before it decays, and barriers can control risk so you can size up. But it harvests an existing edge; it can't create one from a fair game.

cards.topic: Boosting maths for log-loss: gradients, Hessians, leaf values, gain
cards.question: Your model is a binary LightGBM classifier. Write down what one boosting iteration actually computes: the loss, the gradients and Hessians, the value put in each leaf, and the criterion used to choose a split.
cards.answer: The model outputs a raw score $F(x)$ that is a log-odds, turned into a probability by the sigmoid $p=1/(1+e^{-F})$, and it minimises the binary log-loss. At each iteration it computes, for every training candidate, the gradient $g_i=p_i-y_i$ and the Hessian $h_i=p_i(1-p_i)$ of the loss with respect to the current score. A new tree is grown on these numbers: for any candidate leaf, the optimal value is the Newton step $w^*=-G/(H+\lambda)$, where $G$ and $H$ are the sums of gradients and Hessians of the samples in the leaf, and a split is chosen to maximise the gain $\tfrac12\big[G_L^2/(H_L+\lambda)+G_R^2/(H_R+\lambda)-G^2/(H+\lambda)\big]-\gamma$. The tree's output is multiplied by the learning rate and added to the score. On my data the starting score is the log-odds of the 5.0% base rate, about $-2.94$, and every tree nudges candidates up or down from there.

follow_ups.q: Why does LightGBM use the Hessian at all? Gradient boosting in Friedman's original paper uses only gradients.
follow_ups.a: Using the Hessian gives a Newton step instead of a gradient step, so leaf values are automatically scaled by the local curvature. For log-loss the curvature $p(1-p)$ varies a lot across samples, so the Newton version adapts step sizes per leaf and converges in fewer trees. XGBoost introduced this second-order form and LightGBM uses it too.

follow_ups.q: What happens to $h_i$ for a candidate the model is already very sure about, and why does it matter?
follow_ups.a: If $p_i$ is near 0 or 1, $h_i=p_i(1-p_i)$ is near 0, so the sample adds almost nothing to $H$. A leaf full of such samples has tiny $H$ and the Newton step $-G/H$ can explode. That is exactly what `min_sum_hessian_in_leaf` and $\lambda$ guard against.

follow_ups.q: What is the starting score $F_0$, and does it matter?
follow_ups.a: LightGBM starts from the log-odds of the training base rate when `boost_from_average` is on (the default for binary). With 5% that is $-2.94$. Starting from 0 (p = 50%) would waste the first trees just learning the base rate.

follow_ups.q: How is a multiclass or a regression version different?
follow_ups.a: Only $g$ and $h$ change. For squared loss $g=F-y$, $h=1$, so the leaf value is the mean residual, shrunk by $\lambda$. Multiclass uses a softmax and one tree per class per iteration.

cards.topic: What is specific to LightGBM: histograms, leaf-wise growth, GOSS, EFB
cards.question: Why LightGBM rather than XGBoost or scikit-learn's gradient boosting? What does LightGBM actually do differently, and which of those differences matter on a problem with four features and a few thousand candidates per 5-day window?
cards.answer: LightGBM differs in four ways. It bins each feature into at most 255 histogram buckets and searches splits over bins rather than over every raw value, which is fast. It grows trees leaf-wise: it always splits the leaf with the largest gain, wherever it is, instead of filling a whole level at a time. It has GOSS, which keeps the samples with large gradients and subsamples the others, and EFB, which bundles sparse features that are never non-zero together. On my problem, with four numeric features and a few thousand rows, GOSS and EFB are irrelevant and the speed advantage doesn't matter much. The difference that does matter is leaf-wise growth, because it reaches a given training loss with fewer leaves but overfits faster on small data, so the leaf-count and minimum-leaf-size limits become the main safeguards. Honestly, XGBoost or logistic regression would have been a reasonable choice too. The project's rules capped model complexity at "gradient boosting or logistic regression", and LightGBM is a standard, well-tested implementation of the first.

follow_ups.q: If leaf-wise growth overfits on small data, why not just use depth-wise growth?
follow_ups.a: You can approximate it by setting `max_depth` and `num_leaves = 2^max_depth`. The real point is the complexity budget, not the growth order. A shallow tree with a large minimum leaf size is stable either way.

follow_ups.q: What does the histogram trick do to split quality?
follow_ups.a: It restricts thresholds to bin edges, which loses a little resolution on large datasets and almost nothing on a few thousand rows. It is a mild regulariser. The subtraction trick (child = parent − sibling) halves the histogram work.

follow_ups.q: How does GOSS keep the gradient estimate unbiased?
follow_ups.a: The small-gradient samples it keeps are a random fraction $b$ of a population of size $(1-a)n$. Multiplying their gradients and Hessians by $(1-a)/b$ makes their sums unbiased estimates of the full sums.

follow_ups.q: Would you put wallet ID in as a categorical feature?
follow_ups.a: No. With nine then five wallets, the model would learn a per-wallet win rate, which is what the win-rate feature already does in a point-in-time way. It would also make generalisation to a new wallet impossible to assess and would reinforce the concentration problem (34.7% of the 927 signals came from one wallet).

cards.topic: Regularisation terms inside the boosting objective
cards.question: Name the LightGBM regularisation parameters and tell me exactly where each one enters the maths. Which ones matter most on a problem where only 5% of candidates are wins?
cards.answer: There are three groups. The first is the learning rate and the number of trees: each tree is shrunk by $\eta$, and early stopping on a time-ordered validation split chooses how many trees to keep. The second is penalties inside the objective: `lambda_l2` adds $\lambda$ to the denominator of the leaf value $-G/(H+\lambda)$, `lambda_l1` soft-thresholds $G$ before dividing, and `min_gain_to_split` is a fixed cost $\gamma$ that a split's gain must exceed. The third is structural limits: `num_leaves`, `max_depth`, `min_data_in_leaf` and `min_sum_hessian_in_leaf`. Row and feature subsampling add randomness on top. With a 5% base rate, the minimum-leaf constraints matter most. A leaf needs enough wins for its win rate to mean anything, and the Hessian $p(1-p)$ is small where $p$ is near zero, so leaves of confident losers have tiny Hessian sums and unstable Newton steps. The report doesn't list the values, but the code does: 15 leaves, depth 4, at least 20 samples per leaf, learning rate 0.05, 100 trees with no early stopping, and no L1, L2 or subsampling. So the structural limits did all the regularising, and 20 samples per leaf is thin at a 5% base rate: that's the first lever I'd revisit.

follow_ups.q: L1 or L2 on leaf values: which would you pick here and why?
follow_ups.a: L2 by default: it shrinks every leaf smoothly and especially the low-Hessian ones, which is the failure mode with rare wins. L1 zeroes weak leaves, which makes the model sparser but doesn't handle the small-denominator problem as directly. Both are cheap to include and should be chosen on the inner time split.

follow_ups.q: Is a lower learning rate always better?
follow_ups.a: In the limit of infinitely many trees, a lower $\eta$ usually generalises slightly better, but it needs proportionally more trees and makes early stopping noisier to read. Below about 0.01 the gain is usually negligible for the cost.

follow_ups.q: How do you know regularisation is working?
follow_ups.a: Compare training and validation log-loss curves across iterations, and check that the precision on the out-of-time window is stable when you change the settings slightly. If precision swings a lot with small changes, the model is fitting noise whatever the settings.

follow_ups.q: Where does `min_data_in_leaf` interact with class imbalance?
follow_ups.a: It counts samples, not wins. A 20-sample leaf holds about one win on average at a 5% base rate. A win-count constraint doesn't exist directly, so you raise `min_data_in_leaf` or `min_sum_hessian_in_leaf` so that each leaf has enough expected positives.

cards.topic: Feature importance: split, gain and permutation importance
cards.question: Which of your four features mattered most? How would you measure it, which importance measure would you trust, and on which data would you compute it?
cards.answer: The report doesn't give feature importances, so I won't make up a ranking. I'd measure it three ways. Split importance counts how many times a feature is used in splits. It's biased towards continuous, high-resolution features like raw trade amount, which offer many candidate thresholds. Gain importance sums the loss reduction from those splits, which is better, but it's still measured on the training data, so it rewards features the model overfits on. The one I'd trust is permutation importance on the out-of-time test window. You shuffle one feature across candidates, rescore, and measure how much the precision or log-loss drops. That tells you what the model actually relies on out of sample. Two caveats apply. Relative position size is trade amount divided by the wallet's median size, so the two are correlated, and permuting one while keeping the other lets the model partly recover the information. And with about 113 wins among 927 selected signals, the drops are noisy, so I'd repeat the shuffles and report an interval.

follow_ups.q: Why does split importance favour continuous features, precisely?
follow_ups.a: A continuous feature offers many candidate thresholds, so by chance one of them usually has some positive gain, and in deep leaf-wise trees these small, noisy splits accumulate. An integer feature with three or four values simply has fewer opportunities.

follow_ups.q: Permutation importance says 'trade amount' is useless but gain importance says it's the top feature. What's going on?
follow_ups.a: Most likely the model uses trade amount to fit noise in training (high gain), and those splits don't generalise (no out-of-time drop). Another possibility is that relative size carries the same information, so shuffling trade amount alone costs nothing. Permuting them as a group separates the two explanations.

follow_ups.q: Would you drop a feature that has zero permutation importance?
follow_ups.a: Not on one 5-day window. I'd check it across several walk-forward folds first. If it's consistently zero, dropping it reduces variance, and with only four features and a small sample, simpler is better.

follow_ups.q: What's drop-column importance and why is it more expensive?
follow_ups.a: You retrain the model without the feature and compare out-of-time performance. It answers 'how much would I lose if I never had this feature', including the model's ability to compensate with others, but it needs one retrain per feature and is noisy across retrains.

cards.topic: SHAP values for a boosted-tree trading signal
cards.question: Suppose I ask why the model wanted to buy one particular trade. How would you explain a single LightGBM prediction? What is a SHAP value, what does it add up to, and where does it mislead you?
cards.answer: I'd use SHAP values. For a given candidate, each feature gets a contribution $\phi_j$, and the contributions add up exactly: the baseline score plus the sum of the $\phi_j$ equals the model's raw output. For a binary LightGBM that output is in log-odds, not probability. The $\phi_j$ are Shapley values from cooperative game theory: a feature's average marginal contribution over all orders in which features can be added to the prediction. TreeSHAP computes them exactly and quickly for tree ensembles. So for one trade I could say something like "the baseline is the model's average score, three simultaneous buyers added this much log-odds, and a small relative size took some away". Where it misleads is correlated features. Trade amount and relative position size are mechanically linked, and SHAP can split their joint effect between them in an arbitrary way. It also explains the model, not the market: a large contribution says what the model uses, not what causes the price to move. The report doesn't include a SHAP analysis. I'd add it as a check that the model isn't just a proxy for one wallet.

follow_ups.q: Why are Shapley values the 'fair' attribution?
follow_ups.a: They're the unique attribution satisfying efficiency (contributions sum to the total), symmetry (identical features get the same share), dummy (a feature that never changes the output gets zero) and additivity across models. That uniqueness theorem is why SHAP chose them.

follow_ups.q: How is TreeSHAP fast when Shapley values need all $2^n$ subsets?
follow_ups.a: For a tree, the expected output given a subset can be computed by walking the tree and weighting branches by the fraction of training samples going each way. TreeSHAP tracks all subsets at once along each root-to-leaf path, which gives a cost polynomial in depth and leaves. With four features, brute force is also trivial.

follow_ups.q: What are SHAP interaction values?
follow_ups.a: They split each prediction into main effects plus pairwise interaction terms $\phi_{ij}$. With trees they can be computed exactly. They would show, for example, whether simultaneous buyers only matter when the wallet's win rate is high.

follow_ups.q: Can SHAP detect leakage?
follow_ups.a: Sometimes. A leaked feature typically gets huge, uniform contributions. But a leak in the evaluation pipeline, like the model-artefact mix-up in the report, is invisible to SHAP, because the model is internally consistent. You catch that with process controls, not interpretability.

cards.topic: Tree models: invariance to scaling, heavy tails and no extrapolation
cards.question: Did you normalise or winsorise your features before LightGBM? Your 'trade amount' and 'relative size' are heavy-tailed. And what does the model do on a candidate whose feature values are outside anything it saw in training?
cards.answer: Trees don't need normalisation. A split only asks whether a value is above or below a threshold, so any strictly increasing transformation of a feature (log, rank, scaling) gives exactly the same partitions and the same model, up to how histogram bins are placed. Heavy tails are therefore not a problem for the fit, unlike in a linear or logistic model where an extreme value can dominate. The flip side is extrapolation. A tree's prediction is constant beyond the last threshold, so a trade ten times larger than anything seen gets the same score as the largest training trade. That's safe in one sense, since nothing blows up, but it means the model silently treats unseen regimes like the edge of the known one. The real risk in my setting is drift rather than scale. Trade amount is a token quantity (the parser stores the change in token balance, not SOL), so a shift in which tokens the wallets buy, and at what prices, moves its whole distribution. I'd monitor the share of live candidates falling in the extreme bins and prefer relative features.

follow_ups.q: Is there any case where transforming a feature changes a LightGBM model?
follow_ups.a: Yes, through binning: histogram bins are built on quantiles of the values, so a monotone transform leaves them almost unchanged, but a non-monotone one or a combination of features (like dividing by the median) creates a genuinely new feature. Linear-tree options (`linear_tree`) also break invariance.

follow_ups.q: If trees can't extrapolate, is that a safety feature for trading?
follow_ups.a: Partly. It prevents extreme predictions from extreme inputs, but it also hides the fact that you're outside your data. A human-readable flag ('feature outside training range') is safer than trusting a flat prediction.

follow_ups.q: How would you make 'trade amount' more stable?
follow_ups.a: Express it in a stable numeraire (euro or USD value at trade time), or replace it by a rank within the wallet's history or within the day. Relative size already does part of this, which is also why the two features are redundant.

cards.topic: The wallet win-rate feature as target encoding: noise, shrinkage and label timing
cards.question: Your strongest-looking feature is each wallet's historical win rate. In ML terms that's a target encoding. What statistical problems does it have for a wallet with few past trades, how would you fix them, and is 'strictly before t' really enough to avoid leakage?
cards.answer: It is a target encoding: the feature is a running average of the label for the same wallet, so it carries the target into the inputs and has to be built carefully. It has three problems. The first is noise. A wallet with 10 past resolved trades and 2 wins shows 20%, but with a 5% base rate that estimate has a standard error of about 13 points, so the feature is mostly noise early on. The standard fix is empirical-Bayes shrinkage: use $(k+\alpha)/(n+\alpha+\beta)$ with a Beta prior centred on the population rate, so small samples are pulled towards 5%. The second is timing. 'Strictly before t' has to refer to when the earlier trade's label became known, not when that trade happened. A buy an hour before t isn't resolved yet, since the peak is measured over 24 hours and the max hold is about 3h11, so using its label at t would be a leak. The third is that the denominator must follow the survivorship fix: unresolved or never-graduated tokens count as failures where appropriate, and pending labels are excluded. In my code, 'strictly before t' was keyed on trade time, not on label availability: prior buys with a timestamp before t, excluding only labels still pending in the database when the script ran. In the backtest the labels had been filled in afterwards, so a buy an hour before t carried its future outcome. That's a leak, and the fix is to filter on trade time plus 24 hours. Live, recent buys were still pending, so the live feature differed from the backtest one.

follow_ups.q: How big could the label-timing leak be here?
follow_ups.a: It only affects prior trades of the same wallet that were placed within the label horizon before $t$ (up to 24 hours for the peak). For active wallets trading several times an hour, that's a meaningful share of the recent history, and it's the most recent, most regime-relevant part. So it could inflate the feature's apparent predictive power, especially in bursts.

follow_ups.q: Why not use a leave-one-out target encoding instead?
follow_ups.a: Leave-one-out uses future rows of the same wallet, which is fine for cross-sectional data but a leak in a time series. Worse, it can leak the current label through the encoding itself (the LOO mean is a deterministic function of the current label and the group mean).

follow_ups.q: How would you choose the prior strength $s$?
follow_ups.a: By method of moments on training data: the variance of observed wallet win rates equals the Beta-binomial variance, which depends on $s$. Or by maximising the out-of-time log-loss of the shrunk feature over a small grid on an inner time split.

follow_ups.q: Does shrinkage matter for a tree, or only for linear models?
follow_ups.a: It matters for both. The tree can't see sample size, so an unshrunk 20% from 10 trades lands in the same leaf as a reliable 20% from 200 trades. Shrinkage moves the noisy values towards the base rate before the tree ever sees them.

cards.topic: Benchmarks: what should the model be compared against?
cards.question: Your Stage 1 test compares the model's precision with the unconditional 5.0% base rate. Is that the right benchmark? What else should the model have been compared against before you can say that LightGBM adds value?
cards.answer: The base rate answers only one question: is the selection better than picking candidates at random? That's a low bar. A selection rule can beat it without any machine learning, because some wallets are simply better than others. To claim the model adds value I'd want a ladder of benchmarks, all evaluated on the same 5-day out-of-time window and at the same selection rate of 927 of 4,011, about 23%. First, random selection at that rate, which gives the exact hypergeometric null. Second, 'best wallets only', which selects every trade of the wallets with the highest training-window win rate. Third, the report's own three-signal boolean rule. Fourth, a logistic regression on the same four features. LightGBM earns its place only if it beats the logistic regression and the rule out of time, by more than the noise. With a cluster-adjusted standard error of a couple of points on precision, the margin has to be several points. The report compares only against the base rate, so the incremental value of the model over simpler rules isn't established. That's a gap I'd close in the next cycle.

follow_ups.q: Why fix the selection rate when comparing models?
follow_ups.a: Precision depends on how many candidates you select: a stricter threshold usually gives higher precision on fewer trades. Comparing at the same $k$, or comparing whole precision-recall curves, removes that confound.

follow_ups.q: How would you test whether LightGBM beats logistic regression on the same window?
follow_ups.a: A paired cluster bootstrap. Resample wallets (or days), recompute both precisions at equal $k$ on each resample, and look at the distribution of the difference. Because both models share the same candidates, the difference is much less noisy than each precision alone.

follow_ups.q: If the top-wallets rule matched LightGBM, is the project dead?
follow_ups.a: Not necessarily. It says the value is in wallet selection, which is a much simpler strategy to run and validate. But it also means the edge depends on a handful of wallets, which the report showed is fragile to removing a single wallet.

cards.topic: Class imbalance: weights, resampling, or nothing?
cards.question: Only 5% of your candidates are wins. How should you deal with that imbalance: class weights, oversampling, SMOTE, undersampling, or nothing? What does each choice do to the probabilities that your ENR cost filter consumes?
cards.answer: The honest default is to do nothing to the data. Log-loss is a proper scoring rule, so an unweighted model trained on the true 5% mix estimates the actual win probability. That's exactly what the ENR filter needs, because it multiplies probabilities by payoffs. Imbalance is mainly a problem for the metric, not the loss. Accuracy is useless when 'always no' is 95% accurate, which is why the report uses precision against the base rate. If the model struggles to learn the rare class, class weights (`scale_pos_weight` around 19, the ratio of losers to wins) or undersampling of losers can help the trees focus on wins. Both distort the output: the model's odds are multiplied by the weight, so a weighted 0.5 corresponds to a true probability of only about 4.8% when the weight is about 19.88. You must either correct the probabilities analytically or recalibrate them before computing expected returns. SMOTE-style oversampling I'd avoid here. It interpolates synthetic candidates between real ones that may come from different wallets and different days, and if it's done before the time split it leaks. In my project the code did use class weights: scale_pos_weight = n_neg/n_pos, about 19.88 in the deployed model, so the 0.5 threshold sat roughly at the base rate. The first version of the ENR filter took that raw score at face value and promised a +32.9% gross expected return at p = 0.5, while the lowest probability bucket actually lost money. It was replaced by an empirical calibration of the realised return per probability bucket (0.50 to 0.70) on the internal validation split of the training window, never on the test window.

follow_ups.q: Derive the odds relation for class weights.
follow_ups.a: In a leaf, the weighted log-loss is minimised where the weighted gradient sum is zero: $w\,n_+(p_w-1)+n_-p_w=0$, so $p_w/(1-p_w)=w\,n_+/n_-$. The unweighted optimum has odds $n_+/n_-$, so the weighted odds are $w$ times the true odds.

follow_ups.q: Does class weighting change the ranking of candidates?
follow_ups.a: For the exact optimum, no: the map from $p$ to $p_w$ is strictly increasing. In practice the trees are built differently (splits are chosen with different gradient weights), so the ranking can change, sometimes for the better on rare classes. That's why it's a legitimate hyperparameter.

follow_ups.q: What metric would you optimise when choosing the weight?
follow_ups.a: Out-of-time log-loss or Brier score after recalibration, or directly the net expectancy on an inner time split if you accept a noisier criterion. Not precision on the test window, which is where the gate is evaluated.

cards.topic: Evaluation metrics: the full confusion matrix from your numbers
cards.question: Using only the numbers in your report, rebuild the confusion matrix of the Stage 1 model. What are its accuracy, recall and false-positive rate? Why did you evaluate on precision against the base rate rather than accuracy or ROC-AUC?
cards.answer: There are 4,011 candidates and a 5.0% base rate, so about 200 wins. The model selected 927 at 12.2% precision, so about 113 true positives and 814 false positives. That leaves about 87 missed wins and roughly 2,997 correctly rejected losers. Recall is therefore about 56%, the false-positive rate is about 21%, and accuracy is about 77.5%, which is worse than the 95% of a model that never buys. That's exactly why accuracy is the wrong metric. ROC-AUC isn't great either: it rewards ranking over the whole population, including thousands of hopeless candidates, while a trader only cares about the trades actually taken. Precision at the chosen selection rate is what connects to money. With the payoffs fixed by the exit policy, expectancy per trade is roughly a function of the hit rate among selected trades. The fair summary number is the lift, 12.2% / 5.0% = 2.44 times the base rate. If I wanted a threshold-free metric, I'd use precision-recall AUC, whose random baseline is the 5% prevalence, not 0.5.

follow_ups.q: What's the precision-recall AUC of a random classifier here?
follow_ups.a: About 0.05, the prevalence. A random ranking gives the same precision at every recall level, equal to the share of wins in the population.

follow_ups.q: Is a 56% recall good or bad?
follow_ups.a: For a copy-trading filter it's secondary. It means the model catches a bit more than half of the wins while rejecting about 79% of the losers. What matters is whether the selected set pays after costs.

follow_ups.q: Why is the win rate among rejected candidates (2.8%) useful?
follow_ups.a: It's a sanity check: the rejected set should be worse than the base rate, and it is (2.8% against 5.0%). It also gives the 'selected versus rest' two-sample comparison, which is a cleaner test than comparing a subset with a population that contains it.

follow_ups.q: Would you ever optimise F1 here?
follow_ups.a: No. F1 weights precision and recall equally and ignores payoffs and costs. The threshold should maximise expected net return per trade or total, on an inner time split.

cards.topic: Measuring calibration: reliability diagrams, Brier score and ECE
cards.question: Your ENR filter multiplies the model's probability by the payoff, so the probabilities have to be right, not just well ordered. How would you actually measure whether they're calibrated, with how much data, and what would you do if they're not?
cards.answer: Calibration means that among candidates given a probability around $p$, a fraction $p$ actually win. I'd measure it three ways on the out-of-time window. First, a reliability diagram: bin candidates by predicted probability, plot the observed win rate against the average prediction, and look for the diagonal. Second, the Brier score, the mean squared error between probability and outcome, which decomposes into reliability minus resolution plus uncertainty, so it separates calibration error from discrimination. Third, the expected calibration error, the weighted average gap between predicted and observed rates across bins. The difficulty is sample size. With about 200 wins among 4,011 candidates, a bin of 93 candidates at a 12% true rate has a standard error of about 3.4 points on its observed rate, and clustering by wallet makes it worse. So I'd use few bins, quantile bins and bootstrap bands. If the model is miscalibrated, I'd fit an isotonic regression or a Platt (logistic) map on a later slice of the training window, never on the test window, and feed the corrected probabilities to the ENR filter. The report doesn't show a calibration check. In the code, this problem did come up: the first ENR version multiplied the raw probability by the payoff and gave about +32.9% expected gross return already at p = 0.5, while the realised P&L in that range was negative. I replaced it with an empirical calibration: for each probability bucket (0.50, 0.55, 0.60, 0.65, 0.70), the average return actually observed on the internal validation split of the training window, never the test window. What I'd add is the out-of-time reliability diagram, Brier score and ECE.

follow_ups.q: Can a model be perfectly calibrated and useless?
follow_ups.a: Yes: always predicting the 5% base rate is perfectly calibrated and has zero resolution. Calibration is necessary for ENR to be right, but discrimination (resolution) is what creates the edge.

follow_ups.q: Why is the Brier score better than ECE for comparing models?
follow_ups.a: Brier is a proper scoring rule and doesn't depend on binning. ECE depends on the number and placement of bins and can be gamed. ECE is a readable diagnostic; Brier or log-loss is the comparison metric.

follow_ups.q: How does miscalibration bias the ENR filter specifically?
follow_ups.a: ENR is roughly $\hat p\times$ win payoff minus $(1-\hat p)\times$ loss minus costs. If $\hat p$ is too high by a few points near the admission boundary, many trades with true negative expected value are admitted. Overconfidence biases ENR upwards exactly where the filter decides.

follow_ups.q: What would you do if isotonic and Platt disagree strongly?
follow_ups.a: Treat it as a sign that the calibration slice is too small or that the distortion isn't sigmoid-shaped. I'd look at the reliability diagram with bootstrap bands, and if in doubt use the more conservative (lower) probabilities for ENR.

cards.topic: Aggregating out-of-time results across days: pooled precision, heterogeneity and 'robustness'
cards.question: Your test window is 5 days. How do you combine the 5 daily results into one number: pooled precision or the average of daily precisions? How do you test whether the edge is the same every day? And what is your 'robustness on at least 4 of 5 days' criterion really measuring?
cards.answer: Pooled precision is total wins over total selected signals, so it weights each day by its number of signals. The average of daily precisions weights each day equally. They differ when signal counts vary across days, and a busy day dominated by one wallet can drive the pooled number. I'd report both. To test whether the edge is stable, I'd use a chi-square test of homogeneity: a 5-by-2 table of wins and losses among selected signals per day, or better, a test on the daily excess over that day's own base rate. With about 185 selected signals per day, each daily precision has a naive standard error of about 2.4 points, so day-to-day swings of several points are expected even with a constant edge. The '4 of 5 days' criterion is a sign test, and a weak one. If there were no edge and each day were a coin flip, 4 or more positive days out of 5 would happen with probability 6/32, about 19%. So it isn't significance evidence on its own. It's a guard against a result made by one extraordinary day, which is exactly the failure mode later found with the wallet whose edge came over 98% from one day.

follow_ups.q: With 5 days, how much power does the homogeneity test have?
follow_ups.a: Very little: four degrees of freedom and daily SEs of about 2.4 points mean only large differences (say 12% vs 4% on some days) would be detected. Not rejecting homogeneity is not evidence of stability.

follow_ups.q: Why would a desk still use 'positive in k of n periods' rules?
follow_ups.a: They're easy to communicate and they catch results driven by a single period. They should be read alongside a proper test of the mean and a look at the worst period.

follow_ups.q: How would you make robustness a real test?
follow_ups.a: Use more, shorter periods (for example 20 half-days with a purge gap) or a block bootstrap by day of the excess precision. Better still, more walk-forward windows, so that robustness is measured across independent model fits.

cards.topic: Combinatorial purged cross-validation and the probability of backtest overfitting
cards.question: You tested on a single 5-day path. Could you have got a distribution of out-of-sample results from the same 30 days? Explain combinatorial purged cross-validation and the probability of backtest overfitting, and say whether they fit a market like yours.
cards.answer: Yes. A single walk-forward split gives one out-of-sample path, so one draw of the result. Combinatorial purged cross-validation, from López de Prado, splits the period into $N$ blocks, uses every combination of $k$ blocks as the test set and the rest as training, and purges and embargoes around each test block. With 30 days in 6 blocks of 5 days and 2 test blocks, that's $\binom62=15$ train-test splits, which can be recombined into 5 complete out-of-sample paths. You get a distribution of precision and expectancy instead of a single number. The probability of backtest overfitting uses a similar combinatorial split to ask a different question: if I pick the best of my model variants in-sample, how often is it below the median of those variants out of sample? A high value means the selection process is fitting noise. The catch for my market is that combinatorial CV trains on the future to test the past. That's only legitimate if the relationship is stationary, and memecoin regimes change weekly. So I'd use it as a stability diagnostic, and keep a forward-only walk-forward and live paper trading as the verdict.

follow_ups.q: Why is the number of paths $\frac kN\binom Nk$?
follow_ups.a: There are $\binom Nk$ splits, each testing $k$ of the $N$ blocks, so $k\binom Nk$ block-tests in total. Each full path needs $N$ block-tests (every block once), giving $k\binom Nk/N$ paths.

follow_ups.q: How is PBO different from a p-value?
follow_ups.a: A p-value tests one strategy against a null. PBO evaluates the selection procedure: whether choosing the best of many configurations in-sample picks something that holds up out of sample. It can be high even when every individual p-value looks small.

follow_ups.q: Would you use CPCV to choose hyperparameters?
follow_ups.a: Only inside the training period, with purging. The test period used for the final verdict must stay untouched, and for this market the verdict should come from forward-only data.

cards.topic: Purging, embargo and the label horizon, done formally
cards.question: Your labels depend on prices up to 24 hours after entry and your exit policy can hold for 11,458 seconds. Define purging and embargo precisely, compute what they would remove in your 25-day/5-day setup, and tell me where else in your pipeline a purge is needed besides the main train/test boundary.
cards.answer: Each candidate $i$ has a label interval from its entry time to the time its label is fully determined: up to 24 hours for the peak-based label, up to the barrier hit or 11,458 seconds for the exit-policy outcome. Purging removes from the training set every sample whose label interval overlaps the test period, because its label was computed with prices from the test window. In a forward walk-forward, that's the training candidates from roughly the last 24 hours before the test starts, about 1 day out of 25, so 4% of the training window. The embargo removes training samples just after a test block. It only matters when training data can come after the test, as in k-fold or combinatorial CV, or with features whose look-back reaches into the test. Beyond the main boundary, three more places need the same treatment: the inner split used to choose the 0.5 threshold and any early stopping, the calibration window of the exit-policy percentiles, and the win-rate feature, whose prior labels must be resolved before the decision time. My Stage 1 code had no purge gap: training ended exactly where the test began, and the inner split had no gap either. The planned one-day label-maturation margin is a related but different control: it waits until the test window's own labels are resolved before scoring.

follow_ups.q: How large should the embargo be?
follow_ups.a: At least the longest horizon through which test-block information can reach a later sample: the label horizon for labels, and the feature look-back for features. López de Prado suggests a small fraction of the sample (about 1%) as a default, but here the 24 h label horizon and the win-rate feature's look-back are the real constraints.

follow_ups.q: Isn't a 24-hour purge overkill if most tokens resolve within minutes?
follow_ups.a: Purge by each sample's actual label end time, not the maximum. If most labels are determined early, the purge removes few samples. But the label as defined uses the peak within 24 h, so strictly its end time is 24 h after entry unless the definition is changed.

follow_ups.q: If you didn't purge, in which direction is the bias?
follow_ups.a: Upwards. Training samples near the boundary carry labels computed with test-period prices, so the model partly learns the test period's regime. The effect is small when the purged share is 4%, but it's systematically optimistic.

follow_ups.q: How does maturation interact with the survivorship fix?
follow_ups.a: An unresolved candidate at scoring time is 'pending', not a failure. If you score before maturation and count pending as failures, you reintroduce a denominator error in the opposite direction to the survivorship bias. The status field (pending, labeled, confirmed no price history) exists to keep these apart.

cards.topic: Group generalisation: will the model work on a wallet it has never seen?
cards.question: Your model was trained and tested on the same handful of wallets. When you replace a wallet or add a new one, does the model still work? How would you test generalisation across wallets, and how do you combine that with the time ordering?
cards.answer: A walk-forward split tests generalisation in time, but every test candidate comes from wallets the model has already seen in training. If the model mostly learned 'this wallet is good', it will look strong out of time and fail on a new wallet. To test transfer across wallets, I'd use a group split combined with time. Train on days 1 to 25 using all wallets but one, then test on days 26 to 30 of the held-out wallet only, and rotate over wallets, like leave-one-group-out cross-validation.
