The held-out wallet's own win-rate feature is still available, because it's computed point-in-time from that wallet's own history. What's being tested is whether the mapping from features to outcomes transfers. With 5 wallets that gives 5 folds, each noisy, so it's a diagnostic rather than a precise estimate. The report's leave-one-wallet-out stress test answers a related but different question: how much the pooled result depends on each wallet. It found the pool 'fragile in both directions', and a group-held-out test is the natural next step. It matters in practice because the vetting keeps changing the pool (15, then 9, then 5), so the model will keep facing wallets it wasn't trained on.

follow_ups.q: Isn't holding out a whole wallet too harsh? In production you'd have its history.
follow_ups.a: It's a different question. In production you do have the wallet's history through the win-rate feature, and the held-out test keeps that. What it removes is the model's training on that wallet's outcomes. That's exactly the situation every time vetting brings in a new wallet.

follow_ups.q: What if out-of-group precision is good for 4 wallets and zero for one?
follow_ups.a: Look at that wallet's base rate and trading style. It may be a different kind of trader (for instance an execution-speed edge) for which the features don't mean the same thing. That's an argument for vetting criteria, not for tuning the model to fit it.

follow_ups.q: How does this relate to leave-one-wallet-out in the report's stress test?
follow_ups.a: The stress test removed a wallet from the pooled evaluation to measure its influence on the aggregate. The group split removes it from training to measure transfer. One is about the fragility of the statistic, the other about the generality of the model.

cards.topic: Adversarial validation: are training and test windows the same world?
cards.question: Your training window is 25 days, your test window the next 5, and paper trading came after. How would you check, quantitatively, that these windows come from the same distribution? What would you do with the result?
cards.answer: I'd use adversarial validation. Label every candidate from the training window 0 and every candidate from the test window 1, remove anything that encodes time directly, and train a classifier to tell them apart using the model's four features. If its out-of-fold AUC is close to 0.5, the feature distributions are indistinguishable, which is reassuring. If it's well above 0.5, the windows differ, and the classifier's feature importances say how. In my setting I'd expect a few mechanical sources of shift: the number of simultaneous buyers depends on how many wallets are tracked, which fell from 9 to 5; trade amount depends on SOL's price and on wallet habits; and win rates evolve as wallets accumulate history. I'd use the result three ways. It's a diagnostic that tells me whether a backtest number is relevant to the next period. It can give importance weights $p/(1-p)$ from the adversarial classifier's probability, to reweight training candidates towards the test distribution. And I'd rerun it on live paper-trading candidates against the backtest, to explain gaps like the 94.4% deviation between paper expectancy and the Stage 1 estimate. It only detects shift in the features, though. A change in the relationship between features and outcomes, for example because bots start front-running these wallets, is invisible to it.

follow_ups.q: What AUC would worry you?
follow_ups.a: Anything clearly above 0.5 out of fold, say 0.6 or more, deserves an explanation. Above 0.7 the periods are clearly different and the backtest number should be discounted or the model retrained on more recent data.

follow_ups.q: Can adversarial validation choose the training window length?
follow_ups.a: Yes, indirectly. Compare, for several candidate window lengths, how distinguishable the training data is from the most recent data, and prefer windows that are both large and similar. It's a principled version of 'why 25 days and not 60'.

follow_ups.q: How would you detect concept drift then?
follow_ups.a: Monitor calibration and precision of live decisions against backtest expectations over time, with control-chart or sequential tests. A stable feature distribution with a falling hit rate is the signature of concept drift.

cards.topic: Meta-labelling: your model is a secondary model on the wallets' bets
cards.question: In López de Prado's vocabulary, what kind of model is your LightGBM classifier? Explain meta-labelling, why it fits a copy-trading setup, and what it would let you do with the model's probability beyond a yes/no decision.
cards.answer: It's a meta-labelling model. In meta-labelling there are two layers. A primary model decides the side of a bet. Then a secondary model, trained on whether the primary's bets worked out, decides whether to act on each one and how big to go. In my project the primary model isn't mine: it's the tracked wallet. Its buy gives me the side, always long, and the moment. The LightGBM classifier only answers 'is this particular buy worth copying?'. That's why the model is binary and why the report insists its job is narrow. Meta-labelling has two advantages. It separates the direction problem, which I delegate to the wallet, from the precision problem, which is what the model learns, so the model can trade some recall for precision. My numbers show that: recall of about 56% in exchange for precision rising from 5.0% to 12.2%. And its probability can be used for sizing, for example a bet size increasing in $p$ above the breakeven probability, instead of a flat size with a 0.5 cut. I didn't do the sizing part: the report deliberately keeps sizing rule-based. Doing it would require calibrated probabilities first, and my sample of about 113 wins was too small to trust them.

follow_ups.q: Why can a meta-model raise precision without being able to forecast prices?
follow_ups.a: It only needs to learn when the primary signal is reliable: which wallet, which conviction level, whether other wallets confirm. It's conditional on a signal that already contains information. It learns the primary model's error pattern, not the market.

follow_ups.q: What's the downside of meta-labelling here?
follow_ups.a: You inherit the primary signal's biases and its concentration. If one wallet dominates the signals, the meta-model mostly learns that wallet. Latency too: the primary signal is someone else's trade, so you're always entering after them.

follow_ups.q: How would you size from p concretely?
follow_ups.a: Compute the expected net return from p, the frozen payoffs and the cost scenario, then size proportionally to it with a cap, and a hard floor at zero. I'd use a fraction of Kelly because the p and payoff estimates are noisy.

cards.topic: Overlapping labels, concurrency and sample uniqueness
cards.question: Your 927 selected signals came in 5 days and each position can stay open for up to 11,458 seconds. How many positions overlap at a time? Why do overlapping outcomes matter for training a model and for testing it, and what is 'average uniqueness'?
cards.answer: By Little's law, the average number of open positions is the arrival rate times the average holding time. 927 signals in 5 days is about 185 a day, or 7.7 an hour. With holds of up to about 3.2 hours, that means up to about 25 positions open at once, which matches the report's remark that 'tens of positions can otherwise be open simultaneously'. Overlap matters because overlapping outcomes aren't independent. Several wallets buying the same token within 60 seconds produce nearly identical labels, and all positions open during the same market mood share the same common shock. For training, those samples are over-represented: the trees see the same event several times and give it too much weight. That's why López de Prado weights each sample by its average uniqueness, which is one over the number of concurrent labels, averaged over its life. For testing, overlap shrinks the effective sample size, which is another reason the naive z of 10.02 was too high. I'd at least collapse same-token co-buys into one event, or weight by uniqueness, and cluster the test on token as well as wallet, which the wallet-plus-token bootstrap partly did.

follow_ups.q: Isn't collapsing co-buys throwing away the co-buyer signal?
follow_ups.a: No, you keep it as a feature of the event: the number of tracked wallets that bought the token within 60 seconds. What you remove is the triple counting of the same outcome as three training rows.

follow_ups.q: How does uniqueness weighting interact with LightGBM's min_data_in_leaf?
follow_ups.a: Leaf-size constraints count rows, not weights. LightGBM has min_sum_hessian_in_leaf, which does account for weights, so with uniqueness weights you'd constrain the Hessian sum rather than the row count.

follow_ups.q: Does overlap bias the precision estimate or just its variance?
follow_ups.a: Mostly the variance: the estimate stays roughly unbiased, but it's much noisier than the naive formula says. It can bias the estimate when overlapping duplicates are unevenly spread, for example when one wallet's co-buys make up a big block of wins.

cards.topic: Binary target versus return target: how p becomes an expected return
cards.question: Your model predicts a binary win/no-win label, but you trade on expected return. Why classify rather than regress the return directly? How exactly does the ENR filter turn a probability into an expected net return, and what assumption is hidden in that step?
cards.answer: A classifier was the robust choice for this data. The returns are extremely heavy-tailed: most trades drift down or sideways, and a few go up many times. Squared-error regression would chase those few outliers, and with about 200 wins in the sample it would be very unstable. A binary label, 'hits the 2.0× target before the stop or the 3h11 max hold', is bounded, so a single outlier can't dominate the fit. The price is that the ENR filter has to rebuild the expected return from the probability. In the first version of the code the formula was $\text{ENR}=p\cdot R_W+(1-p)\cdot R_L-c$: the win payoff $R_W$ is fixed by the target, +100% before costs, and every non-win is counted as a stop-out at −34.3%. Two assumptions are hidden there. First, the raw probability is taken at face value, although class weighting inflates it: at $p=0.5$ the formula promised +32.9% gross while the trades actually seen in that range lost money, so the code later replaced it with an empirical calibration, the average return actually observed in each probability bucket on an internal validation split of the training window. Second, the non-win payoff is the same for every candidate. In reality non-wins mix stop-outs and time exits, and the mix depends on the features: a trade the model rates at 0.4 that doesn't win probably exits at the time barrier near breakeven, while one rated 0.05 more likely hits the stop. If I had more data, I'd either model the non-win payoff too, with a second model or a three-class label (target, stop, time exit), or regress a transformed, bounded return directly, and compare.

follow_ups.q: Why not predict the return quantiles instead?
follow_ups.a: Quantile regression is robust to tails and would give a distribution, not just a mean. But the ENR needs the mean, and recovering a mean from a few quantiles in a heavily skewed distribution is itself unstable with this little data.

follow_ups.q: Is the +100% win payoff before or after costs?
follow_ups.a: Before. The ENR subtracts costs separately under each scenario, which is the point of keeping costs downstream of the model. In practice the realised win is lower because the sell into a pump pays slippage.

follow_ups.q: What would a proper scoring check look like for the ENR itself?
follow_ups.a: Bin admitted trades by predicted ENR and compare with realised net return per bin, like a reliability diagram for expected values. A flat or inverted relation means the ENR ranks badly even if p is calibrated.

cards.topic: Reconciling 12.2% precision with +2.7% expectancy
cards.question: Your barriers pay +100% on a win and −34% on a stop. With a 12.2% hit rate, that should lose money. Yet you report a raw edge of +2.7% per trade. Reconcile the two numbers. What do they imply about the non-winning trades, and what hit rate do you need to break even?
cards.answer: If every trade ended at the target or the stop, the expectancy would be $0.122\times100\%-0.878\times34.3\%\approx-17.9\%$ per trade, and the breakeven hit rate would be $34.3/134.3\approx25.5\%$. So +2.7% can only hold if most non-wins don't reach the stop. They exit at the 3h11 time barrier somewhere between −34% and +100%. Solving $0.122\times100\%+0.878\,\bar m=2.74\%$ gives an average non-win return of about −10.8%. That's consistent with the report's remark that about 46% of trades never move much from entry. Given that mix, breakeven before costs is a hit rate of about 9.7%, and with a round-trip cost of about 1.5% in the low scenario it's about 11.1%. The 12.2% is only about one percentage point above that. That's the arithmetic reason the edge disappears under moderate costs: at about 5% round trip, you'd need about 14%. Two caveats. The −10.8% is implied, not measured: the database only stores entry and peak, so time-exit prices are partly approximated. And the +100% win payoff ignores sell-side slippage.

follow_ups.q: What single number would you most like to have measured better?
follow_ups.a: The average time-exit return, because it drives the breakeven hit rate. It needs the price at the max-hold time, which the two-point database doesn't store.

follow_ups.q: If sell slippage on wins were 8%, what's the effect?
follow_ups.a: The win payoff drops from +100% to about +84% after one leg of 8%, so the expectancy drops by 0.122 × 16 points, about 2 points per trade. That's most of the +2.7% edge.

follow_ups.q: Is 12.2% vs 11.1% a significant margin?
follow_ups.a: No. The precision's standard error is about 1.1 points naively (Wald). The wallet-clustered z of 4.08 implies an SE of about 1.8 points on the 7.2-point gap (7.2/4.08), and inflating the 1.1 by the same factor 10.02/4.08 gives about 2.6. Either way, the one-point margin over low-cost breakeven is less than one clustered standard error.

cards.topic: Two price points only: bounding the barrier outcome
cards.question: Your database stores only the entry price and the peak within 24 hours, plus the time to peak. List every case, say which barrier outcomes are actually identifiable, and bound the expectancy. Is the report's 'confirmed win' really confirmed?
cards.answer: Compare the peak ratio $M$ with the barriers, and the time to peak $\tau$ with the max hold. Case one: $M<0.6573$. The price was below the stop level for the whole 24 hours, so the stop was hit and the trade is a sure loss of 34.3%, plus slippage. Case two: $M\ge2$ and $\tau\le$ 11,458 seconds. The report calls this a confirmed win, but strictly it isn't: the price could have dipped below 0.6573 before rallying, and the stop would have fired first. For a pumping memecoin that's not absurd. So 'confirmed win' really means 'win if the stop wasn't touched first', and it's an upper bound. Case three is everything else: the peak lies between the barriers, or it's above 2× but arrives after the max hold. The outcome is then either a stop, which needs the unknown minimum, or a time exit at an unknown price no higher than the peak. So the return is bounded between −34.3% and $\min(M,2)-1$. Aggregating, you get a best-case and a worst-case expectancy. I would report that interval instead of one approximated number, and fix the data by storing the minimum before the peak, or better, the full path at a few fixed times.

follow_ups.q: Which direction is the report's approximation likely biased?
follow_ups.a: Optimistic, mainly through case 2: treating every early 2× as a win ignores dips below the stop first, which are common in memecoins. The direction for cases 3 and 4 depends on the fill-in rule used, which the report doesn't detail.

follow_ups.q: Can simulation help without path data?
follow_ups.a: Partly. Fit a price-path model (for example a jump-diffusion calibrated to the entry-peak-time data) and simulate the conditional probability of a stop-first given M and tau. But that replaces missing data with model assumptions, so I'd present it as a sensitivity, not a fix.

follow_ups.q: Why not simply take the 24h close as the time-exit price?
follow_ups.a: Because the max hold is 3h11, not 24 hours. The price at 24 hours is a different quantity, and in this market usually much lower. It would bias time exits downward.

cards.topic: Calibrating barriers from empirical quantiles: sampling error, censoring and what the leak implies
cards.question: Your stop is the 5th percentile and your max hold the 75th percentile of distributions estimated on 9,629 labelled outcomes. How precise are those quantiles? What censoring issues affect them? And what does it tell you that removing the test window shifted them by 7.5% and 9.2%?
cards.answer: With 9,629 outcomes the quantiles themselves are precise. The standard error of the rank of a 5th-percentile estimate is $\sqrt{0.05\times0.95/9{,}629}\approx0.22$ points, so the true 5th percentile is somewhere between the empirical 4.6th and 5.4th. That's a tiny move in price terms. The time-to-peak distribution has two censoring problems. The peak is taken inside a 24-hour window, so a token that peaks later is recorded with a 24-hour-capped peak. And for the roughly 46% of trades that never move much, 'time to peak' is close to meaningless, so the 75th percentile mixes two populations. The 7.5% and 9.2% shifts are far larger than sampling error. That's the interesting part. If the test window was about one sixth of the pooled data, removing it can only move the pooled quantile a lot if the test window's distribution was very different from the training window's. So the leak also revealed a regime difference between training and test, which is itself a warning about stationarity. The honest calibration is train-only, with a bootstrap interval on each barrier. I'd also check how sensitive expectancy is across that interval.

follow_ups.q: How would you calibrate the max hold instead?
follow_ups.a: On the distribution of time to first hitting the target, among trades that do hit it, estimated on train only, with a Kaplan-Meier estimator to handle censoring at 24 hours. Then pick the hold that captures, say, 90% of target hits, and check the expectancy sensitivity around it.

follow_ups.q: Why does the extra precision of 0.6573 not matter much?
follow_ups.a: Because expectancy is flat-ish in the stop level near that point and because the regime shift moves the quantile by several percent. Four significant digits are false precision. Two would be honest.

follow_ups.q: Could you have seen the regime change directly?
follow_ups.a: Yes: a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of peak ratios in the train versus test windows, with clustering in mind, or an adversarial classifier. Either would flag the shift before anything is tuned.

cards.topic: Precision is a ratio estimator: cluster-robust standard errors and the bootstrap
cards.question: Precision is wins divided by selected signals, summed over wallets of very different sizes. Write the cluster-robust standard error of that ratio, back out what the report's z values imply for it, and explain how a cluster-bootstrap z is actually formed.
cards.answer: Precision is a ratio estimator, $\hat p=\sum_w y_w/\sum_w n_w$, where $y_w$ is the number of wins and $n_w$ the number of selected signals of wallet $w$. By the delta method, its cluster-robust variance is roughly $\frac{m}{m-1}\sum_w(y_w-\hat p\,n_w)^2/N^2$, with $m$ wallets and $N=927$. Each wallet contributes its residual wins, what it won minus what it would have won at the pooled rate, and large wallets dominate. Backing out from the report: the naive z of 10.02 corresponds to a null standard error of about 0.72 points. A z of 4.08 means a standard error of about 1.76 points, so a design effect of about 6 and an effective sample of about 154. The wallet-and-token z of 2.52 means about 2.86 points, a design effect of about 16, and about 59 effective signals. The bootstrap z is $(\hat p-0.05)$ divided by the standard deviation of $\hat p$ across resamples of whole wallets. Two caveats: with 9 wallets that bootstrap distribution is lumpy and understates the variance. And the 5.0% reference comes from the same clusters, so strictly one should bootstrap the difference, not treat 5% as known.

follow_ups.q: Why does part of the 10.02 to 4.08 drop not come from clustering at all?
follow_ups.a: Because the naive z uses the null standard error at p = 5%, while a bootstrap measures spread around the observed 12.2%, where Bernoulli variance is larger. The Wald naive z is already 6.7. So roughly 10 to 6.7 is convention and 6.7 to 4.1 is clustering.

follow_ups.q: Is an intracluster correlation of about 0.03 to 0.05 plausible?
follow_ups.a: Yes. It only needs a wallet's hit rate to differ from the pool's by a few points on average, which the report's per-wallet vetting (one wallet at 0.0% and 1.3% precision) shows is the case.

follow_ups.q: What bootstrap interval would you report?
follow_ups.a: A percentile or BCa interval for the precision difference, from 10,000 cluster resamples, alongside the wild cluster bootstrap p-value. With so few clusters, also a leave-one-wallet-out table, because it shows the dependence on each wallet directly.

cards.topic: Confounding by wallet: stratified tests and Simpson's paradox
cards.question: Your model selected 34.7% of its signals from one wallet. Suppose that wallet simply has a higher base rate. How much of the model's apparent lift could come from 'pick that wallet' rather than from learning anything? How would you test the model's lift within wallets?
cards.answer: Potentially a lot, and my z-test couldn't tell the difference. It compares selected precision with the pooled 5.0%. If one wallet has a much higher base rate and the model mostly selects that wallet, precision rises even if the model has no skill within any wallet. Take a hypothetical case where the big wallet has 800 candidates at a 12% base rate and the rest have a 3.2% base rate. If the model selects 322 signals from the big wallet and 605 from the others, at random within each wallet, precision is about 6.3% against 5.0%, and the naive z is about 1.8, all from composition. The right test compares selected and rejected candidates within each wallet, then combines across wallets: the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test, or a logistic regression with wallet fixed effects. The same logic applies to days: a hot day with many signals and a high base rate can inflate pooled precision. The wallet win-rate feature makes this concern concrete. It's partly a wallet identifier, so the model's lift is probably a mix of 'which wallet' and 'which trade of that wallet'. A stratified test measures only the second part.

follow_ups.q: If the lift is all between-wallet, is the strategy worthless?
follow_ups.a: Not necessarily, but it becomes 'copy the best wallet', which needs no model and whose risk is the concentration itself. Its edge disappears if that wallet changes behaviour, which is what happened when smart_money_03 was excluded.

follow_ups.q: Can Simpson's paradox reverse the sign here?
follow_ups.a: Yes. If within every wallet the model picks worse-than-average trades but tilts heavily toward the best wallet, pooled precision can be above 5% while the within-wallet effect is negative. Only the stratified test reveals it.

follow_ups.q: What's the stratified analogue for expectancy rather than precision?
follow_ups.a: A regression of net return on 'selected' with wallet (and day) fixed effects and clustered standard errors, or a permutation test that shuffles the selection flag within wallets.

cards.topic: The Stage 1 gate's real false-pass rate under clustering
cards.question: Your Stage 1 gate required z ≥ 1.96, at least 300 signals, at least 4 of 5 positive days and positive net expectancy. If the model had no edge at all, how often would that gate pass, given that your signals were clustered by wallet? Which criterion actually protects you?
cards.answer: With independent signals, a model with no edge passes the z criterion about 2.5% of the time, one-sided. With clustering it's much worse. A simple simulation of a no-edge world gives the order of magnitude (a back-of-the-envelope check, not a result from the project), using the report's concentration: nine wallets, the largest two holding 34.7% and 25% of signals, and wallet-level noise sized to reproduce the design effect of about 6 implied by the wallet-clustered z. In that simulation, the naive z clears 1.96 about 20% of the time. Adding the 4-of-5-days criterion barely helps, 18.5%, because the days aren't independent: the same wallets drive every day, so a lucky wallet makes all days look good together. The criterion that does the work is positive net expectancy. With the payoffs implied by the report, breakeven precision before costs is about 9.7%. A no-edge model sitting at 5% has to be lucky by almost five points to cross it, and in the simulation the full gate passes about 1.4% of the time. The n ≥ 300 criterion never binds. So the significance test gave false comfort. The economic criterion was the real guard, and it's exactly the one that failed after the audit, with −0.022.

follow_ups.q: Why doesn't n ≥ 300 matter?
follow_ups.a: Because the model selected 927, and under the null the selection count doesn't change. It protects against tiny samples, but it counts correlated signals, so it overstates the evidence: 927 was worth about 154 independent signals.

follow_ups.q: How would you choose the wallet-level noise without the report's z?
follow_ups.a: Estimate it from pre-test data: the between-wallet variance of hit rates, net of binomial noise, from the training window. That's exactly the random-effects variance a meta-analyst would estimate.

follow_ups.q: What's the gate's power against a true 12.2% precision?
follow_ups.a: The z criterion passes almost always, but the expectancy criterion needs realised precision above about 9.7% before costs and about 11% in the low-cost scenario. With a clustered standard error of about 1.8 points, the low-cost version passes only around 70% of the time, less with moderate costs.

cards.topic: Leave-one-wallet-out and the jackknife
cards.question: Your stress test removed wallets one at a time. What does a leave-one-out analysis estimate formally? Write the jackknife variance, explain what 'fragile in both directions' means, and show how much one wallet with 34.7% of the signals can move the pooled precision.
cards.answer: Leave-one-out recomputes the statistic $m$ times, each time dropping one cluster, here a wallet. It answers two questions. Influence: how much does each wallet move the result? Variance: the jackknife estimate is $\frac{m-1}{m}\sum_i(\hat\theta_{(-i)}-\bar\theta)^2$, which for a pooled precision is close to the cluster-robust variance. With a wallet holding 34.7% of the signals, the leverage is big. Pooled precision without it is $(\hat p-s\,p_w)/(1-s)$. If that wallet ran at 20%, removing it takes the pool from 12.2% to about 8.1%. At 25%, to about 5.4%, almost the base rate. 'Fragile in both directions', from the report's stress test, means that on the 5-wallet pool removing some wallets pushes expectancy up and removing others pushes it down, and no single wallet is uniquely responsible. With only 5 wallets, that's what you expect when the result is noise around zero. I'd make it a gate criterion: the pass must survive removing the largest contributor. The report's own diagnosis, that 34.7% of the original signals came from the wallet later excluded, is a leave-one-out statement in disguise.

follow_ups.q: Why is dropping the most influential wallet after the fact dangerous?
follow_ups.a: It turns a diagnostic into selection on the outcome. The report handles this by using criteria fixed in advance for exclusions, so a wallet is removed because it met a pre-registered rule, not because it moved the number.

follow_ups.q: Jackknife or bootstrap with 5 clusters?
follow_ups.a: Both are shaky. With 5 clusters the jackknife is at least transparent: 5 numbers you can show in a table. I'd report it alongside a wild cluster bootstrap and use t with 4 degrees of freedom for any interval.

follow_ups.q: How does LOO relate to group k-fold?
follow_ups.a: Leave-one-group-out cross-validation is LOO applied to model training: train without wallet w and test on w. It asks whether the model generalises to an unseen wallet, which is a stricter question than whether one wallet drives the pooled test result (prj-215).

cards.topic: Concentration metrics: HHI, effective number of wallets and a concentration limit
cards.question: One wallet produced 34.7% of the selected signals and two produced 59.7%. The live Stage 2 trades were 83.3% concentrated in three wallets that were later excluded. How would you measure concentration formally, and what limit would you put in the gate?
cards.answer: The standard measure is the Herfindahl-Hirschman index, the sum of squared shares. Its inverse is the effective number of independent sources. With 9 wallets and shares of 34.7% and 25%, the HHI is at least 0.347² plus 0.25² plus the smallest possible contribution of the other 40.3%, which is when it's spread evenly over seven wallets. That gives at least 0.206, so at most about 4.9 effective wallets out of 9. In other words, the nine wallets weighed like at most five wallets of equal size. The HHI also links directly to the statistics: under a wallet random effect, the variance of pooled precision is roughly the between-wallet variance times the HHI, plus binomial noise. Concentration and the design effect are the same problem seen from two sides. The 83.3% for Stage 2 says the same thing about live trades: the admitted flow came almost entirely from wallets that later failed vetting. For the gate, I'd require the largest wallet to be below about 25% of signals, or at least five effective wallets, and I'd require that the pass survives removing the top contributor. That's the equivalent of a desk's single-name concentration limit.

follow_ups.q: Why is the HHI a lower bound here?
follow_ups.a: Because only the two largest shares are known. The HHI is smallest when the rest is spread evenly, so any real unevenness among the other seven wallets raises it.

follow_ups.q: Is concentration always bad?
follow_ups.a: No, if the concentrated source is genuinely skilled and stable. But you can't distinguish skill from luck with one dominant source and 5 days, and its failure takes the whole strategy with it. That's the same reason desks cap single names even when they like them.

follow_ups.q: Would you cap per wallet or per token?
follow_ups.a: Both. Per-wallet caps limit dependence on one trader. Per-token caps matter because several wallets buying the same memecoin is one risk, not several.

cards.topic: Placebo tests: label shuffling and random entries to test the pipeline itself
cards.question: Suppose you want a test that would have caught your model-artefact leak automatically. Describe a label-shuffle placebo test for the full pipeline and a random-entry placebo for the exit policy. What should they show if everything is clean, and what does a leak look like?
cards.answer: The idea is to feed the pipeline data where the true answer is known to be 'no edge', and check that it says so. For the model: shuffle the win labels within each day, and ideally within each wallet, so every feature-label link is destroyed but base rates are kept. Then run the whole pipeline end to end: training, threshold choice, test scoring, z-test. Repeat, say, 200 times. On clean code the z-scores should look like draws from the null, centred near zero, and about 2.5% should exceed 1.96 under independence, more under clustering. A leak shows up as placebo z-scores that are systematically positive. That's exactly what the model-artefact mix-up would have produced: a model trained on train plus test memorises the shuffled test labels and scores well on them, even though there's nothing to learn. For the exit policy: replace the model's selections with random entries at the same rate and times, and run the frozen barrier and cost code. Before costs, expectancy should match the unconditional candidate population, and after costs it should be negative. A placebo that shows positive edge means the exit, cost or cap code is creating P&L out of nothing, for example through a look-ahead in the barrier evaluation.

follow_ups.q: Why shuffle within wallet and not only within day?
follow_ups.a: Because wallets have different base rates and the win-rate feature partly identifies the wallet. Shuffling within each wallet keeps each wallet's base rate, so the placebo data still look like the real data and the test asks the right question: does the pipeline find edge where there is none? Shuffling across wallets would erase those base-rate differences, so the placebo would no longer resemble the real data and its result would be harder to compare with the observed lift.

follow_ups.q: Could a placebo pass while the pipeline still leaks?
follow_ups.a: Yes, if the leak doesn't depend on labels, for example a price feature taken a few seconds after the decision time. Label shuffles test label leakage. Timestamp audits and shifted-feature placebos test feature timing.

follow_ups.q: How many placebo runs do you need?
follow_ups.a: Enough to estimate the tail you care about. For a p-value near 0.05, about 200 to 1,000 runs. For a smoke test that the lift is centred at 1, 50 runs are already informative.

cards.topic: Data snooping across variants: White's Reality Check, SPA and Romano-Wolf
cards.question: You looked at a rule, several thresholds, an ML model, three cost scenarios, filters with and without caps, window shifts and clusterings. Bonferroni is very conservative with correlated variants. What do White's Reality Check, Hansen's SPA test and Romano-Wolf stepdown do, and how would you apply one here?
cards.answer: All three answer the question 'is the best of my variants better than the benchmark, once I account for having searched?'. They do it by bootstrapping the whole set of variants jointly, so the correlation between them is kept, which is why they're less conservative than Bonferroni when variants are similar. White's Reality Check takes the maximum, across variants, of the standardised performance difference against the benchmark. It builds the null distribution of that maximum by a block bootstrap of the time series, recentred so that no variant has an edge. If the observed maximum is in the tail, at least one variant beats the benchmark. Hansen's SPA improves it by not letting clearly bad variants inflate the critical value. Romano-Wolf goes further and says which variants are significant, controlling the family-wise error rate. For me, the performance series would be daily net expectancy per variant over the test days, with the benchmark 'copy every candidate' or 'do nothing'. The catch is that five days is far too short for a block bootstrap. So on this data the honest version is simpler: count the variants and use a max-statistic critical value. For 20 independent variants it's about 2.8 one-sided at 5%, versus 1.96, and a bit lower when variants are correlated.

follow_ups.q: What's the deflated Sharpe ratio and how does it relate?
follow_ups.a: Bailey and López de Prado's deflated Sharpe ratio adjusts an observed Sharpe for the number of trials, their variance, and non-normal returns. It answers the same data-snooping question with a closed form instead of a bootstrap, but needs an estimate of the number of effectively independent trials.

follow_ups.q: Are the three cost scenarios multiple tests?
follow_ups.a: Not if you pre-register which scenario is the decision scenario. They're sensitivity analyses of one strategy. They become multiple tests if you report whichever scenario looks best.

follow_ups.q: What if variants were tried sequentially over time?
follow_ups.a: Then the family is still all of them. Sequential trying doesn't reduce snooping, it just makes it easier to forget. A research log of every variant looked at is the practical defence.

cards.topic: Was the +2.7% expectancy ever statistically significant?
cards.question: Your z-test was on precision, not on money. Take the +2.7% raw edge on 927 signals. Estimate the per-trade standard deviation from your barrier structure and tell me whether the expectancy itself was significant, with and without clustering.
cards.answer: No, and that's one of the most important lessons of the project. The payoff is roughly a Bernoulli bet: +100% on a win, and about −10.8% on average otherwise, which is what the report's numbers imply. The Bernoulli part alone gives a standard deviation of $\sqrt{0.122\times0.878}\times1.108\approx36$ points per trade. Adding spread among non-wins, say 10 to 15 points, gives 37 to 39 points. With 927 independent trades, the standard error of the mean is about 1.25 points, so the t-statistic on +2.74% is about 2.2. Barely significant, and that's before costs. With the wallet design effect of about 6, it drops to about 0.9. With wallet and token clustering, about 0.55. So even at the moment Stage 1 passed with z = 10.02 on precision, the thing that pays, net expectancy, was statistically indistinguishable from zero. Precision can be very significant while expectancy isn't, because a win is a rare, large payoff and most of the variance is in whether you catch it. To detect +2.7% with this volatility you need about 700 independent trades for t = 1.96, so about 4,200 signals at a design effect of 6.

follow_ups.q: Why not test the median return instead?
follow_ups.a: Because the median non-win is negative and the median trade is a non-win: the median is negative even for a profitable strategy. The strategy's profit lives in the mean, driven by rare wins, so the mean is the right target even though it's noisy.

follow_ups.q: How would you get a tighter estimate without more data?
follow_ups.a: Variance reduction: use precision (well estimated) times the average win and non-win payoffs, which are each estimated with less noise, instead of the raw mean return. It's a control-variate style decomposition, but the payoffs still have to be measured, not assumed.

follow_ups.q: What's the Sharpe-like number per trade?
follow_ups.a: About 2.74/37 ≈ 0.074 per trade. Annualising needs the number of independent bets per year and the correlation between them, which is where concentration and concurrency kill the naive calculation (prj-124).

cards.topic: Sequential testing: peeking, alpha spending and SPRT for the next cycle
cards.question: In the next Stage 1 cycle and in live monitoring, you'll be tempted to look at the results every day. What happens to the false-positive rate if you test daily and stop at the first z ≥ 1.96? How do Pocock, O'Brien-Fleming and Wald's SPRT fix it, and what breaks with clustered data?
cards.answer: If I test after each of 5 days and stop the first time z crosses 1.96 one-sided, the false-positive rate isn't 2.5% any more. It's about 7.1%, about 14% two-sided. Each look is another chance to cross by luck. Group sequential designs fix this by spending the error rate across looks. Pocock uses a constant boundary, about 2.41 two-sided for 5 looks at a 5% overall level. O'Brien-Fleming uses boundaries that start very high and fall toward normal: about 4.56, 3.23, 2.63, 2.28 and 2.04. It barely penalises the final analysis, and early stopping needs overwhelming evidence, which I prefer here. Wald's sequential probability ratio test goes signal by signal. It accumulates the log-likelihood ratio of 'precision 12.2%' against 'precision 5%': plus 0.89 per win, minus 0.079 per loss. It stops at log(16), about 2.77, for the edge and at about −1.56 for no edge, with 5% and 20% error rates. Under independence it decides after about 50 signals on average, but it assumes independent signals. With my clustering, a burst of wins from one wallet would cross the boundary spuriously, so I'd run it on daily or wallet-day aggregates, or with inflated boundaries.

follow_ups.q: Why prefer O'Brien-Fleming to Pocock here?
follow_ups.a: Early data are the most fragile: few wallets, few days. O'Brien-Fleming only stops early on overwhelming evidence and keeps the final boundary close to 1.96, so the final analysis loses little power.

follow_ups.q: Does stopping early bias the estimate?
follow_ups.a: Yes. Trials stopped at an interim look tend to overestimate the effect, because they stop when noise happens to be favourable. Report a bias-adjusted estimate or at least the full-period number.

follow_ups.q: How does the kill-switch relate to this?
follow_ups.a: It's a sequential test for harm with a very simple boundary (three negative days). Its false-alarm rate is high for a real but noisy edge. A CUSUM with a target run length would make that trade-off explicit.

cards.topic: Survivorship as missing-not-at-random: what the 27.3% to 6.3% flip reveals
cards.question: Your first backtest showed 27.3% against 16.3% on the 46% of trades with a resolved price. Counting unresolved tokens as failures gave 6.3% against 7.9%. What do these four numbers tell you about how the rule selected trades? Classify the missingness and give bounds.
cards.answer: If unresolved trades are counted as failures, the win rate becomes the resolved share times the win rate among resolved trades. So the four numbers pin down the resolved shares. For the reference, 7.9 divided by 16.3 is about 48.5%, consistent with the report's 'roughly 46% resolved'. For the rule, 6.3 divided by 27.3 is about 23%. The rule picked tokens that resolved half as often as average. That's why it looked good on the survivors and bad overall: it was selecting heavily among tokens that never graduated. That's missing-not-at-random. Whether a token gets a price label depends on its outcome, since tokens that never graduate are almost always worthless, and the rule's features correlate with that. Ignoring the missing ones is then biased, not just noisy. Bounds: if every unresolved trade were a win, the rule would be at 83%, and if every one a loss, 6.3%. That's Manski's worst-case interval, useless on its own. The domain fact that non-graduated tokens are near-certain losses justifies taking the lower bound as the estimate, which is what the fix did. The fix also added a third state, 'confirmed no price history', so pending labels aren't counted as failures too early.

follow_ups.q: Would inverse-probability weighting have fixed it?
follow_ups.a: Not reliably. IPW corrects missingness that depends on observed variables. Here it depends on the outcome itself, so weighting by observed features can't recover the missing wins and losses.

follow_ups.q: How does this relate to the later model's 12.2%?
follow_ups.a: The report says every downstream statistic now uses the corrected denominator, so the 12.2% should treat 'confirmed no price history' tokens as failures; the report doesn't restate it for Stage 1 specifically, so I'd say 'should' and check it in the code. The same MNAR logic still matters for the barrier calibration, whose 9,629 outcomes are labelled trades only.

follow_ups.q: Is there a finance analogue?
follow_ups.a: Delisted stocks and dead hedge funds. Databases that drop them overstate returns. Here it's more extreme because most tokens die and death is the missing label.

cards.topic: Stage 2's '94.4% deviation': units, relative error near zero, and noise
cards.question: Your Stage 2 addendum says net expectancy went from −0.000187% to +0.001505% and that the deviation from the backtest was 94.4%. Check those numbers against the +0.027 backtest estimate. What are the units, is 'within 50% of the backtest' a sensible criterion, and was a 94% gap evidence of an execution problem?
cards.answer: The numbers only fit if the addendum's values are fractions, not percentages. $1-0.001505/0.027=0.944$, which is exactly the 94.4% deviation. So +0.001505 means +0.15% per trade, and the '%' sign in the addendum is a unit slip. Read literally, +0.0015% would be a 99.99% deviation. The pre-fix value, −0.000187, means −0.019% per trade, a deviation of about 100.7%. So the 94.4% is the post-correction figure. It 'stayed a FAIL', but the number itself did change. The criterion has two problems. First, relative deviation is unstable near zero: a live expectancy of −0.1% or +0.1% gives deviations of 104% or 96% for economically identical results, and a negative backtest would make the band meaningless. Second, it ignores the noise. The live expectancy was computed on 1,019 simulated buys. With a per-trade standard deviation around 37%, the standard error of the live mean is about 1.2 points if trades were independent, and about 2.8 points with the wallet design effect of about 6. The gap of 2.55 points between +2.7% and +0.15% is about 2.2 naive standard errors, but only about 0.9 once clustering is counted. So the 94% deviation was a weak signal, not proof of an execution-modelling problem. I'd replace it with a test of whether live and backtest expectancy differ, with cluster-robust standard errors, plus a direct comparison of simulated versus quoted fills.

follow_ups.q: Then why did Stage 2 fail meaningfully?
follow_ups.a: On the pre-registered rules it failed, and the decision to not proceed stands. But the information content was low: live expectancy of about zero on 1,019 clustered simulated buys is still consistent with both +2.7% and a negative edge once the clustering is counted. The later post-audit replay and stress test carry more of the evidence.

follow_ups.q: What's the day criterion's content, 1 of 5 positive days?
follow_ups.a: More informative than it looks, but still noisy. With about 200 simulated buys a day and 37% per-trade volatility, a day's mean has a naive standard error of about 2.6 points, the same size as the +2.7% edge. If trades were independent, a true +2.7% edge would make about 85% of days positive, so 1 of 5 would be unlikely. But trades on the same day share the market mood and cluster by wallet, so the real day-level noise is larger (prj-121).

follow_ups.q: How would you word the correction in the report?
follow_ups.a: A dated erratum: the addendum's expectancy values are fractions per trade (−0.0187% and +0.1505% per trade); the 94.4% deviation is computed from the corrected value. No verdict changes.

cards.topic: Reverse-engineering the cost chart: additive costs plus a fixed fee
cards.question: Your cost scenarios give per-leg pool fees and slippage and a priority fee in SOL. Starting from the +2.74% raw edge, rebuild the 'cost only' bars of your chart, +1.2%, −2.6% and −18.7%. What does the fit imply about trade size, and what's wrong with modelling costs this way?
cards.answer: Per-leg percentage costs are 0.75% low, 2.5% moderate and 9% high, so 1.5%, 5% and 18% round trip. Subtracting them additively from +2.74% gives +1.24%, −2.26% and −15.26%. The chart shows +1.2%, −2.6% and −18.7%, so something fixed is missing, and the gap grows with the priority fee. If the priority fee is paid on both legs and divided by a trade size of about 1.17 SOL, all three bars come out exactly: +1.21%, −2.60% and −18.68%. So the chart is consistent with additive percentage costs plus a fixed fee on a trade of roughly 1.2 SOL. The report doesn't state it, but the code confirms it: those bars use a 100 € stake at 85.57 € per SOL, which is 1.17 SOL. A multiplicative model, $(1.0274)(1-c)^2-1$, fits the low bar but needs different trade sizes for the other two, so the additive reading is the coherent one. The weaknesses are real. Slippage isn't a constant percentage: on an AMM it grows with trade size relative to pool depth, and it's worst exactly when many wallets are buying at once. The fixed fee's weight depends on each trade's size, and averaging fee over size isn't fee over average size. And the scenario is applied uniformly, when costs are correlated with the signal.

follow_ups.q: How would trade size change the picture?
follow_ups.a: Smaller trades suffer more from the fixed fee: at 0.2 SOL, the high scenario's priority fee alone costs 20% round trip. Larger trades suffer more from slippage. There's an optimal size per pool, and it's small in thin memecoin pools.

follow_ups.q: Should costs be in the model's target after all?
follow_ups.a: No, but the cost estimate should be per trade, with features like pool depth and co-buyer count, and it can be a separate model. Keeping it outside the classifier keeps the scenarios swappable, which is the report's point.

follow_ups.q: Is the additive model wrong?
follow_ups.a: For costs of a few percent, additive and multiplicative differ by about 2 × cost × return, negligible. For the high scenario (18%) the difference is a few tenths of a point. The fixed fee matters much more.

cards.topic: Stop-loss gap risk and costs that are correlated with the outcome
cards.question: Your stop is at 0.6573× entry, so you assume a −34.3% loss on a stop-out. In a memecoin crash, where would a stop actually fill? How much would realistic gap risk cost per trade, and why are execution costs correlated with the trade's outcome here?
cards.answer: A stop on a DEX isn't a resting order. The system sees the price cross 0.6573, then sends a sell that executes at whatever the pool gives. In a crash that can be well below the level: the price may already have gapped through by the time you're in a block, and your sell pushes the price down further in a thin pool. So the realised stop loss is the level minus gap minus sell slippage. If stops fill at 0.55 instead of 0.6573, each stop costs 10.7 extra points. From the report's numbers, between a fifth and a third of non-wins can be stop-outs, which is 17% to 27% of all selected trades. That's 1.9 to 2.9 points per trade, the size of the whole +2.7% edge. Costs are also correlated with outcomes. On entry, the model likes co-bought tokens, where several wallets buy within 60 seconds, so you enter in a rising pool and pay more slippage. On exit, stops happen in panics and targets in pumps, both one-sided markets. A cost model with constant per-leg slippage misses both effects, and both push the same way, making real P&L worse than the scenario.

follow_ups.q: Would a limit order help?
follow_ups.a: A limit sell at the stop level guarantees the price but not the fill. In a crash it may not execute at all, leaving you with the full downside. It trades gap risk for non-execution risk.

follow_ups.q: How would you measure stop slippage without real money?
follow_ups.a: Log the pool state at the trigger time and simulate the swap against the reserves, adding a latency of a few blocks. Compare with Jupiter quotes captured at the same time. It won't include MEV but it gets the price-impact part.

follow_ups.q: Does gap risk change your ranking of cost scenarios?
follow_ups.a: It shifts all of them down, but it matters most in the low-cost scenario, the only one where the edge was near breakeven. A two-point hit there turns −0.09% into about −2%.

cards.topic: The ENR admission threshold and the winner's curse
cards.question: Write the ENR admission rule as a threshold on the model's probability. What threshold does each cost scenario imply with your numbers? Then explain why trades admitted because their estimated ENR is positive will, on average, do worse than their estimated ENR says.
cards.answer: Admission is $p\,R_W+(1-p)\bar m-c>0$, which is $p>p^*=(c-\bar m)/(R_W-\bar m)$. With $R_W=+100\%$ and the implied $\bar m\approx-10.8\%$, the thresholds are about 11% for a 1.5% round trip, about 14.5% for moderate costs, and about 29% for the high scenario once fixed fees are included. The chart only partly fits this simple reading. The high scenario admits nothing, but the low and moderate scenarios admit the same 74.5% of signals, which end at +3.6% and −0.2% net. That's because the code doesn't use a probability threshold with a constant $\bar m$. Its first version used the raw scores, which are at least 0.5 for every selected trade, and counted every non-win at the stop: +32.9% expected at $p=0.5$, so even the high scenario admitted almost everything. It was then replaced by an empirical calibration: the average return actually observed in each probability bucket, on an internal validation split of the training window. Those bucket returns sat above the moderate cost and below the high one, hence the same trades admitted under low and moderate costs and none under high costs. The second point is the winner's curse. The estimated ENR is the true ENR plus estimation error. Selecting trades where the estimate exceeds zero keeps trades with positive errors more often than negative ones. So the realised ENR of admitted trades is biased below the estimate, and the more the filter cuts, the bigger the bias. The fix is to shrink estimates before filtering, or to evaluate the filter out of sample, never on the data used to estimate the probabilities.

follow_ups.q: Where else do you see the winner's curse in the project?
follow_ups.a: In wallet selection from the leaderboard: the wallets that look best are partly the luckiest, so their future performance regresses toward the mean (prj-110). And in choosing the best rule threshold by scanning (prj-245).

follow_ups.q: How would you size the shrinkage?
follow_ups.a: Estimate the dispersion of true ENRs (tau) from the between-bin variance of realised returns net of sampling noise on training data, then apply the empirical-Bayes factor tau²/(tau²+sigma²). With little data the factor is small and the filter should be conservative.

follow_ups.q: Would a higher ENR threshold than zero help?
follow_ups.a: Yes, as a crude safety margin: admit only if ENR exceeds, say, one standard error of its estimate. It lowers the number of trades but protects against admitting trades whose positive ENR is mostly noise.

cards.topic: A taxonomy of the project's leaks, and one control for each
cards.question: You've had a survivorship error, a threshold leak, a model-artefact mix-up, an exit-policy calibration leak, a parser bug and a stale database. Classify them. Which are genuine information leaks, which are data-quality problems, and what single control would have prevented each?
cards.answer: I'd sort them into three families. First, information leaks, where the evaluation uses information not available at decision time. The threshold leak and the exit-policy leak are the same pattern: a free parameter fitted on data that included the evaluation set. The fix is a pipeline where every fitted object, including thresholds, quantiles and barrier levels, is fitted inside the training fold, with a test that fails if the fitting data overlaps the test window. The model-artefact mix-up is train-test contamination of the model itself. The control is an artefact registry that stores each model with the hash and date range of its training data, and refuses to score a window that overlaps. Second, selection and denominator errors. Survivorship was a biased sample, not future information. The control is labelling states and an explicit denominator for every statistic. Third, data-quality failures. The parser bug created fake events and the desync meant stale data. Controls: invariants, such as every buy having a matching swap, and freshness monitoring, meaning an alarm if the latest trade in the database is older than a few minutes. The common theme is that none of these was caught by the 430+ automated tests before it had affected a result. The controls that work are structural and automated.

follow_ups.q: Which one would you worry about most in a bank?
follow_ups.a: The frozen-component leak, because it's invisible: people audit the model and trust the 'fixed' parameters around it. In banks, the equivalent is a calibration input or a curve built from data that included the backtest period.

follow_ups.q: How do you test for label-maturation leaks?
follow_ups.a: Rebuild each feature from the labels as they were known at decision time, using label timestamps, and compare with the backtest features. Any difference means the backtest saw labels that didn't exist yet.

follow_ups.q: Why not simply reprocess everything when a leak is found?
follow_ups.a: Because re-fitting on data you've already looked at creates a new leak. The report's choice was to document, not re-fit, and wait for fresh data. Reprocessing is fine for data-quality fixes when the decision code is untouched and the evaluation is rerun on new data.

cards.topic: How clean was the 'clean' replay? Biases in the post-audit rerun
cards.question: After the audit you reran the frozen Stage 1 code on the 5-wallet pool: 435 signals, z = 3.91, expectancy −0.022, robustness 3/5, FAIL. Play devil's advocate: in what ways is that replay not a clean out-of-sample test? And what does z = 3.91 on 435 signals imply about precision?
cards.answer: It's much cleaner than the original PASS, but not clean in three ways. First, the pool was chosen using the data. Two wallets were excluded because removing their spam made their numbers worse, which is an outcome-based criterion, and another because its edge was concentrated in one day. Pre-registered or not, the 5 remaining wallets were chosen after looking at performance. Second, the historical trades weren't reprocessed. The parser fix applies to future collection, so unless the replay window is entirely post-fix, the remaining wallets still carry some spam buys, since even the least contaminated of the five kept wallets had 3.1% spam buys and one had 21%. Third, the window and the methodology had been looked at many times, so the analyst's choices aren't independent of the data, even though the code was frozen. On the number: if the base rate was still around 5%, z = 3.91 on 435 signals means precision about 9.1%, since the null standard error is about 1.05 points. That's below the roughly 9.7% breakeven before costs implied by the Stage 1 payoffs, so a negative expectancy is exactly what you'd expect. The FAIL isn't in conflict with the z. It's the same arithmetic as the original PASS with less lift. Only the fresh-data cycle can give a clean test.

follow_ups.q: Does the co-buyer feature break when the pool shrinks?
follow_ups.a: Its distribution shifts: with 5 wallets there are fewer possible co-buyers, so values drop mechanically. A model trained on a 9-wallet world may misread it. Retraining on 5-wallet data, or normalising by pool size, fixes that.

follow_ups.q: Why not reprocess history now?
follow_ups.a: For a clean fresh-data test it isn't needed, and reprocessing would change the frozen historical record. But for understanding, a reprocessed copy in a separate schema would be useful, as long as it's clearly labelled and not used to re-tune anything.

follow_ups.q: Could the true answer be that the edge exists but is smaller?
follow_ups.a: Yes. A few points of lift over the base rate with negative net expectancy is consistent with a small real selection skill that costs eat. The data can't distinguish that from noise yet.

cards.topic: Reproducibility: bitemporal data, snapshots and the four trades that changed status
cards.question: While verifying the Stage 2 recount you found 4 trades that changed status between two database snapshots, unexplained. Why is that a serious reproducibility problem, and how would you design the storage so that any past result can be reproduced exactly and such changes are always explainable?
cards.answer: It's serious because a verdict is only auditable if you can rerun it on exactly the data it was computed on. If rows can change silently, a published number can't be reproduced, and you can't tell a legitimate update, such as a label maturing, from a bug. The fix is bitemporal storage. Each fact carries two time axes: valid time, when the event happened in the market, and transaction time, when the system learnt or changed it. Rows are never updated in place. A change inserts a new version with its transaction time and a reason code, such as 'label matured', 'parser fix' or 'manual correction'. Then any analysis can be rerun 'as of' a timestamp and gives the same answer, and a diff between two snapshots lists every change with its cause. The four mysterious trades would then have a history that explains them. I'd add three things around it: a manifest for every published result, with the code commit, model artefact ID, query and data watermark; a hash of the input dataset; and a CI check that recomputes one published number from its manifest. That's the same discipline banks apply to risk and P&L reporting.

follow_ups.q: How do banks do this for market data?
follow_ups.a: Market data and trade stores keep official end-of-day snapshots and versioned corrections, so a VaR or P&L figure can be recomputed as it was reported, and separately as corrected. Regulators expect that audit trail.

follow_ups.q: Isn't this over-engineering for a solo project?
follow_ups.a: The minimum version is cheap: never update in place, add a recorded_at and a reason to each row, and save a manifest per result. It would have made both the race condition and the four-trade anomaly explainable in minutes.

follow_ups.q: How does this interact with the decision not to reprocess history?
follow_ups.a: With versioning, you can reprocess into new versions without destroying the frozen record: the Stage 1 result stays reproducible as of its watermark, and the corrected history exists alongside it.

cards.topic: How stable is the number? Seeds, small perturbations and the noise floor
cards.question: If you rerun your Stage 1 pipeline with a different LightGBM seed, or shift the window by a day, how much should precision and expectancy move just from noise? How would you measure the stability of the result, and what would count as 'unstable'?
cards.answer: First, the sampling noise floor. Precision of 12.2% on 927 signals has a binomial standard error of about 1.1 points, and roughly 1.8 to 2.6 clustered by wallet, depending on the convention. Expectancy with about 37% per-trade volatility has a standard error of about 1.2 points naive, and closer to 3 points clustered. Any perturbation that moves results by less than that isn't informative. Second, algorithmic noise. LightGBM is deterministic for a fixed seed, but row and feature subsampling, and bagging if enabled, depend on the seed. Different seeds give slightly different scores, and a threshold at 0.5 turns small score changes into different selected sets. I'd measure it directly: run 20 to 50 seeds, and for each, record precision, expectancy and the set of selected trades. Then report the spread and the overlap between selected sets, for example the Jaccard index. Third, the portfolio caps amplify everything, because a different early trade changes which later trades fit under the caps. The report saw this with the exit recalibration moving low-cost expectancy from −0.09% to −4.57%. I'd call the result unstable when the spread across seeds and one-day window shifts is comparable to the effect itself. For full-system expectancy that was clearly the case, which is why stopping the backtest refinement was the right call.

follow_ups.q: Would averaging over seeds fix instability?
follow_ups.a: It reduces the algorithmic part, like bagging, and is worth doing. It does nothing to sampling noise or to specification sensitivity, which dominate here.

follow_ups.q: How would you make the caps less path-dependent?
follow_ups.a: Evaluate them by Monte Carlo over arrival-order tie-breaks and random admission among simultaneous signals, and report the distribution (prj-244). Or replace hard caps with proportional sizing so that one early trade doesn't block a later one entirely.

follow_ups.q: Is the 0.5 threshold part of the instability?
follow_ups.a: Yes. Many candidates near the threshold means small score changes flip selections. Reporting results across a band of thresholds, or using a top-k rule, reduces that sensitivity.

cards.topic: Inconsistencies in my own report, and how I'd answer if challenged
cards.question: I've read both versions of your report carefully and some numbers don't add up. Before I point them out: are there inconsistencies you know about? Go through them.
cards.answer: Yes, a few, and I'd rather name them myself. First, wallet arithmetic. The vetting list sums to 6 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 11 exclusions, but 15 to 5 is only 10. The chart also shows 7 wallets before the audit, while the text says 9 were active before it. One count is off by one. Second, the Stage 1 section says 'all four pre-registered criteria passed', while the gate is described with three criteria, z, n and day robustness. Net expectancy was the fourth line of the replay table, so it was treated as a criterion in practice. Third, units in the Stage 2 addendum. −0.000187% and +0.001505% are fractions, not percentages, since 1 − 0.001505/0.027 is exactly the 94.4% deviation. And that deviation did move with the recount, from about 101% to 94.4%, even if the verdict didn't. Fourth, the short report says 'correcting both' leaks, while the long report's corrected column fixes only the model-artefact leak, and the exit leak was deliberately not corrected. Fifth, the spam contamination text says up to 51.5% while the chart's maximum is 48.4%. Sixth, the kill-switch is 'negative expectancy' in one version and 'loss-making days' in the other. None of these changes a verdict, but I'd correct them in a dated erratum rather than let a reader find them.

follow_ups.q: Which inconsistency is the most serious?
follow_ups.a: 'Correcting both' in the short report, because it claims more correction than was done: the exit-policy leak was documented but not corrected, and correcting it moved results further down. A reader could think the −0.09% is fully clean.

follow_ups.q: How did these get through?
follow_ups.a: The two reports were written separately from the same material, and numbers were retyped rather than generated from one source. The fix is to generate every number in both reports from the same results file.

follow_ups.q: Why didn't you fix them before sending the report?
follow_ups.a: Some I only found when re-reading closely afterwards. The honest route is an erratum rather than a silent replacement, the same principle as the Stage 2 addendum.

cards.topic: Writing the pre-registration for the next Stage 1 cycle
cards.question: You're about to run a fresh Stage 1 cycle on clean data. Write me the pre-registration, what exactly you would freeze before collecting the data, knowing everything you learnt from the first cycle.
cards.answer: I'd freeze six things. The data: the collection window dates, the parser version, the wallet pool and the rule for handling a wallet that stops trading, all decided before day one, with a one-day label-maturation margin. The model: code commit, features, hyperparameters, training window of 25 days, and how the threshold and the probability calibration are fitted, on inner training folds only. The exit and costs: barrier parameters recalibrated on pre-window data only, and the decision cost scenario, not three to choose from. The primary hypothesis: net expectancy per trade after low-scenario costs is positive, tested with a cluster-robust statistic, clustered by wallet and token, with few-cluster corrections. Not precision, because precision can be significant while money isn't. Secondary checks: precision lift, a within-wallet stratified test, survival after removing the largest wallet, and a concentration limit such as no wallet above 25% of signals. Finally the decision rule and power. The minimum sample follows from a power calculation on expectancy, which with realistic volatility means thousands of signals, so five days won't be enough. That leads to the most important pre-registered statement: if the sample falls short, the verdict is 'inconclusive', not PASS or FAIL. And any look before the end follows an O'Brien-Fleming schedule.

follow_ups.q: Why fix the pool even if a wallet turns bad during the window?
follow_ups.a: Because dropping it mid-window is selection on the outcome. The pre-registered alternative is a mechanical criterion applied by script, like bot-like volume, which doesn't look at P&L.

follow_ups.q: Why not make precision primary since it has more power?
follow_ups.a: Because it answers the wrong question. The project's own history shows precision can be very significant while the strategy loses money. Power on the wrong endpoint isn't useful.

follow_ups.q: Where would you register it?
follow_ups.a: A dated, committed file in the repository with a tag, and ideally a timestamp outside my control, such as a hash posted publicly or emailed to someone. The point is that nobody, including me, can edit it after the data arrive.

cards.topic: Per-trade expectancy versus return on capital
cards.question: You quote expectancy as a percentage per trade. A PM wants return on capital per day or per year. Convert your +2.7% raw edge into a return on capital, using Little's law and the trade size your cost chart implies, and explain why the answer is both huge and meaningless.
cards.answer: Return on capital is total P&L divided by capital tied up. The P&L is trades per day times size times return per trade. The capital is the average number of open positions times size. By Little's law, open positions equal arrivals times average holding time. So return on capital per day is $E[R]\times 24/W$, with $W$ the average hold in hours, whatever the trade size. With +2.74% per trade and an average hold between 2 hours and the 3.2-hour maximum, that's about 20% to 33% per day on capital, before costs. In absolute terms, with 185 signals a day and the roughly 1.2 SOL size used in the cost chart (a 100 € stake), it's about 6 SOL a day of gross P&L on 20 to 30 SOL of capital. It's huge because capital turns over about ten times a day. It's meaningless for three reasons. It's gross of costs, and after costs and caps the full system was around −0.1%. It isn't significant (prj-230). And it doesn't scale: slippage grows with size in thin pools, so the return on capital falls fast as capital grows. The right way to present a strategy like this is P&L per day, capacity, and the return-on-capital curve as a function of size.

follow_ups.q: Why does size cancel in the return on capital?
follow_ups.a: Both P&L and capital are proportional to size at constant costs, so size scales both. It stops cancelling as soon as costs depend on size, which is exactly the capacity limit.

follow_ups.q: How does the portfolio cap change the calculation?
follow_ups.a: The cap limits concurrent positions, so capital is capped at K × S and some signals are dropped. Return on capital then depends on which trades are kept, which is the path-dependence problem (prj-035, prj-244).

follow_ups.q: What's a realistic capacity estimate?
follow_ups.a: Order of a SOL per trade and tens of SOL in total, from pool depth. In other words a personal-scale strategy, not a desk strategy, which is a fair thing to say openly.

cards.topic: Making path dependence measurable: Monte Carlo over the portfolio caps
cards.question: Changing the max hold moved your full-system expectancy from −0.09% to −4.57%, because the caps admitted a different subset. That's a single draw of a very noisy process. How would you turn it into a distribution, and what would the distribution tell you that the single number can't?
cards.answer: The caps admit trades first come, first served while slots are free, so the system's result depends on arrival order and on which early trades block later ones. To get a distribution, randomise the parts of that process that are arbitrary. Break ties among signals arriving at the same moment at random. Randomly delay each decision by a realistic latency of a few seconds. Randomly admit among candidates competing for the last slot. And, as a second layer, bootstrap wallet-days. Run the full system a thousand times and look at the distribution of net expectancy. It tells you two things a single number can't. First, how much of the result is order noise: if the 5th to 95th percentile under low costs spans, say, −5% to +3%, then −0.09% and −4.57% are both ordinary draws, and the recalibration didn't necessarily make things worse. Second, whether the caps have a systematic effect: compare with an uncapped or randomly capped book. If admitted trades under caps are systematically worse than random subsets of the same size, the caps are biasing toward bad trades, for example because early trades in a burst are the worst-priced. That would argue for a different cap design, such as proportional sizing instead of hard slots.

follow_ups.q: Why not just remove the caps?
follow_ups.a: Because they're a real constraint: without them, tens of positions on overlapping tokens would be open, a concentration no risk manager accepts. The goal is to measure their effect and choose a design that doesn't select badly, not to pretend they don't exist.

follow_ups.q: What's proportional sizing and why would it help?
follow_ups.a: Instead of admitting a trade at full size or not at all, size each new trade by available capacity, for example total exposure divided by the number of open positions. Every admitted signal gets some weight, so one early trade doesn't block a later one entirely, and the result is smoother in the parameters.

follow_ups.q: Is this simulation expensive?
follow_ups.a: No. The full-system replay on 927 signals is milliseconds of logic per run once model scores and prices are precomputed. A thousand runs is seconds.

cards.topic: The threshold-scan leak in numbers: max statistics and combining 0.54 and 1.49
cards.question: Your rule's threshold was first chosen by scanning the full data, which gave z = 1.35. The honest split gave z = 0.54 on the 2/3 calibration part and z = 1.49 on the 1/3 holdout. Explain why the scanned z is biased, whether it's odd that the holdout z is higher than the calibration z, and what a combined z would be.
cards.answer: The scanned z is the maximum over thresholds, and the maximum of several noisy statistics is biased upward even when nothing is there. For ten roughly independent thresholds, the 5% critical value of the maximum is about 2.57 instead of 1.64, one-sided. Correlated thresholds give less inflation, but still some. So 1.35 at the best threshold is weaker evidence than a single pre-chosen 1.35. The holdout being higher than calibration is less strange than it looks. If there were a constant true effect, the expected z grows with the square root of sample size, so a holdout with half the calibration's data should show a smaller z, about 0.71 times. Seeing 1.49 against 0.54 is the opposite, but z-statistics have a standard deviation of 1 each, so a difference of about 0.95 is well within noise. It's consistent with a weak or zero effect and luck in the holdout. Combining them with Stouffer's method, weighting by sample share, gives $\sqrt{2/3}\times0.54+\sqrt{1/3}\times1.49\approx1.30$, below 1.96. That's close to the full-sample figure. The 'plausible, not proven' conclusion in the report is exactly right.

follow_ups.q: How would you correct a scanned z properly?
follow_ups.a: Permutation: shuffle labels within days, redo the whole scan each time, and compare the observed maximum with the distribution of maxima. That automatically accounts for the correlation between thresholds.

follow_ups.q: Why is 2/3–1/3 a reasonable split here?
follow_ups.a: It keeps enough data to estimate the threshold while leaving a holdout that can detect a moderate effect. With a weak effect, neither part has much power, which is what the z values show. Walk-forward with several folds would use data more efficiently.

follow_ups.q: Does z = 1.49 on the holdout mean p ≈ 0.07?
follow_ups.a: One-sided, yes, about 0.068. But that's a single pre-planned test only if the threshold was fixed before looking at the holdout, which the fix ensured. Its evidence is weak but honest.

cards.topic: Wallet exclusion as a statistical test: 0 of 31 and 1 of 75
cards.question: One wallet was excluded for 'near-zero precision': 0.0% on 31 signals, then 1.3% on 75 signals, under a pre-registered criterion. Is that statistically strong evidence the wallet is bad? Against what benchmark? And does looking at nine wallets change the answer?
cards.answer: It depends entirely on the benchmark. Against the model's overall precision of 12.2%, it's strong. Zero out of 31 has probability $0.878^{31}\approx1.8\%$, and one or fewer out of 75 about 0.07%. That wallet clearly didn't perform like the average selected signal. Against the 5% base rate, the evidence is weak. Zero out of 31 happens 20% of the time for a wallet with no edge at all, and one or fewer out of 75 about 11% of the time. Pooled, one out of 106 has a probability of about 2.9% at 5%. Looking at nine wallets matters: if all nine were average 5% wallets, the chance that at least one shows one or fewer wins in 106 is about 23%. So the data say this wallet was worse than the model's average, but not clearly worse than random. That's fine for the decision, because the pre-registered question was 'does following this wallet add value', and with a 95% upper confidence bound of about 7% on its precision, it can't reach the roughly 10 to 11% breakeven. So exclusion is justified on economic grounds, not because it was proven bad. The criterion being fixed in advance is what keeps this from being cherry-picking.

follow_ups.q: How would you write the exclusion criterion formally?
follow_ups.a: Exclude a wallet if the one-sided 95% upper bound on its selected precision, from at least N signals, is below the low-cost breakeven precision. It's mechanical, it has a known false-exclusion rate, and it can be applied by script.

follow_ups.q: What's the false-exclusion rate of that rule for a good wallet?
follow_ups.a: For a wallet truly at 12.2%, the probability that its 95% upper bound falls below about 11% is small but not zero, about 1.4% with 75 signals (one-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson bound below 11%), so the rule is conservative. It can be computed exactly from the binomial.

follow_ups.q: Should the same logic apply to the fragile-regime wallet?
follow_ups.a: Yes, but with a different statistic: the share of its edge from one day. With 98% from a single day, its effective sample is one day, so no significance is possible. That's a sample-size argument, not a performance one.

cards.topic: How often do the caps bind? Little's law and the Erlang loss formula
cards.question: With about 185 signals a day and holds up to 3h11, how often would a cap on concurrent positions reject a signal? Use a queueing model to size the cap, and say where the model is too optimistic.
cards.answer: A book with at most $K$ positions and no waiting line is a loss system, like a telephone exchange with $K$ lines. Signals arrive at a rate λ, about 7.7 an hour. Each occupies a slot for its holding time, and a signal that finds all slots full is dropped. The offered load is $a=\lambda W$, Little's law: about 15 positions for a 2-hour average hold, about 25 at the maximum hold.
