The Erlang B formula gives the fraction rejected, and it holds for any holding-time distribution, which suits barrier exits. With $a=15.5$, a cap of 10 rejects about 42% of signals, 15 rejects about 20%, 20 about 5%. At the maximum hold, a cap of 10 rejects about 62%. So any cap well below the offered load drops a large share of trades, which is why caps changed the result so much. The code's cap is 6 concurrent positions, far below that load. The model is optimistic because signals aren't Poisson: they come in bursts. Several wallets buy the same token within 60 seconds, and busy market hours cluster. Bursty arrivals increase rejections at the same average rate. They also mean that the rejected signals are exactly the ones in bursts, which are often the co-bought signals the model likes most.

follow_ups.q: Why is insensitivity useful here?
follow_ups.a: Because the holding-time distribution is a messy mix of early stops, target hits and full 3h11 holds. Erlang B only needs the mean, so the sizing doesn't depend on modelling that mix exactly.

follow_ups.q: How would you handle burstiness quantitatively?
follow_ups.a: Simulate with the empirical arrival times instead of Poisson, replaying the real sequence of signals against the cap. Or use an over-dispersed arrival model. Both give higher blocking than Erlang B.

follow_ups.q: Would a queue help, admitting a signal a bit later when a slot frees up?
follow_ups.a: Only if the edge survives the delay, which it doesn't in a 5-to-60-second reaction-gap strategy. A delayed entry is a different, worse trade.

cards.topic: Two-way clustering: wallets and days at the same time
cards.question: You clustered by wallet and by wallet-token. But all positions on a hot day share the same market mood, whatever the wallet. How would you cluster by wallet and by day at the same time, and what goes wrong with only 5 days and 5 to 9 wallets?
cards.answer: Two-way clustering, from Cameron, Gelbach and Miller, allows correlation within the same wallet across days and within the same day across wallets. The variance estimate is the wallet-clustered variance plus the day-clustered variance minus the variance clustered on wallet-day cells, which would otherwise be counted twice. It's the natural structure here: wallet effects capture skill and style, and day effects capture the memecoin market factor, the days when everything pumps or everything dies. The problem is the number of clusters. Cluster-robust methods are asymptotic in the number of clusters in each dimension, and the smaller dimension drives the reliability. Five test days means the day component is estimated from five numbers, so it's very noisy and biased downward, and the combined variance can even come out negative. With 5 days I'd report it as a sensitivity, use t critical values with 4 degrees of freedom, and prefer a design-based alternative, such as permutations within days or a wild bootstrap over the smaller dimension. The real solution is more days. Across a few months, the day dimension becomes usable and the market factor can be estimated explicitly, for example by including the day's base rate as a control.

follow_ups.q: Is day clustering the same as a time-series correction like Newey-West?
follow_ups.a: Related but different. Day clustering allows arbitrary correlation within a day and none across days. Newey-West allows correlation decaying over lags. With labels overlapping across midnight (24-hour peak window), a small cross-day correlation also exists, which Driscoll-Kraay style estimators handle.

follow_ups.q: Would day fixed effects remove the need for day clustering?
follow_ups.a: They remove the day mean, the common shock to the level. They don't remove within-day correlation of residuals from other sources, so some clustering may still be needed, but much of the problem disappears.

follow_ups.q: Which clustering would you pre-register?
follow_ups.a: Wallet clustering with day fixed effects as primary, two-way clustering as a sensitivity, and the smallest cluster count's t distribution for critical values.

cards.topic: From zero: standard error and the z-score (z = 10.02)
cards.question: What is the z you report? Explain it to me from scratch: what is z = 10.02, and what is a standard error?
cards.answer: z is a distance measured in units of noise. My model selected 927 of the 4,011 test candidates and 12.2% of them won, while the win rate of all candidates was 5.0%. If the model were useless, a random batch of 927 candidates would still not win exactly 5.0% of the time: it would wobble around 5% with a standard deviation, called the standard error, of $\sqrt{0.05 \times 0.95 / 927} \approx 0.72$ percentage points. So z = (12.2% − 5.0%) / 0.72% ≈ 10: the gap is about ten times the size of normal luck. Under the no-edge hypothesis that is essentially impossible by chance. The caveat, which is the real story of the project, is that the formula assumes the 927 trades are independent, and they were not: re-estimated with clustering it fell to 4.08 and 2.52.

follow_ups.q: Why does the standard error shrink like 1/√n?
follow_ups.a: Because the variance of a sum of n independent terms is n times the variance of one term, so the variance of the average is σ²/n and its standard deviation σ/√n. Quadrupling the sample halves the noise.

follow_ups.q: Why use p₀ in the standard error and not p̂?
follow_ups.a: Under the null hypothesis the true rate is p₀, so the noise we compare against is the noise of a no-skill selection. Using p̂ (a Wald-type test) is also common and gives 0.072/0.0107 ≈ 6.7 here; both are clearly significant, but the null-based version is the textbook one-sample test.

follow_ups.q: Is z = 10 a measure of how good the model is?
follow_ups.a: No. It measures how surprising the gap is given the sample size, not how large or profitable it is. With a million trades, a tiny useless edge would also give a huge z.

follow_ups.q: What would z be for the post-audit replay?

cards.topic: From zero: p-values, 1.96 and what 'significant' means
cards.question: What is a p-value? Why is 1.96 your threshold, and what p-value goes with your z of 10.02, 4.08, 2.52 and 3.91?
cards.answer: A p-value is the probability, if the null hypothesis were true, of seeing a result at least as extreme as the one observed. Here the null is 'the model has no skill, its picks win at the base rate'. 1.96 is the z beyond which a standard normal falls only 5% of the time on both sides together, so z ≥ 1.96 means p < 0.05 two-sided. My naive z of 10.02 gives a p-value around 10⁻²³, the clustered 4.08 about 5 × 10⁻⁵ and 2.52 about 0.012, two-sided. The post-audit 3.91 is about 10⁻⁴. The key thing is that a p-value is not the probability that my model is useless, and it says nothing about profit: 3.91 was highly significant and the verdict was still FAIL because net expectancy was negative.

follow_ups.q: Why two-sided 1.96 if you only care whether the model is better?
follow_ups.a: Conventional and conservative: a two-sided 5% cutoff is the same as a one-sided 2.5% cutoff. A one-sided test at 5% would use 1.645. Using 1.96 made the bar slightly stricter, which is fine for a pre-registered gate.

follow_ups.q: Is p < 0.05 enough to trade?
follow_ups.a: No. It says the precision differs from the base rate, not that the edge covers costs, is stable, or survives many tests. My gate also required n ≥ 300, 4 of 5 positive days and positive expectancy, and then live paper trading.

follow_ups.q: What is statistical power?
follow_ups.a: The probability of rejecting H₀ when a real edge of a given size exists. It depends on effect size, noise and n; with clustering the effective n is much smaller, so power drops.

follow_ups.q: What's the difference between the p-value and α?
follow_ups.a: α is the false-alarm rate you fix before looking (5%); the p-value is computed from the data. You reject when p < α.

prerequisites: Type I and type II errors

cards.topic: From zero: one-sample versus two-sample tests (why 'two proportions' is the wrong label)
cards.question: Your report calls it a 'z-test for two proportions'. Is it? What's the difference between a one-sample and a two-sample test, and which did your code run?
cards.answer: A one-sample test compares one estimated proportion with a reference treated as a known constant; a two-sample test compares two estimated proportions from two separate groups, each with its own noise. My code ran the one-sample version: (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n), with p̂ the 12.2% precision of the 927 selected trades and p₀ the 5.0% win rate of all 4,011 candidates, which includes those 927. So the report's box label 'two proportions' is wrong and I say so. The proper two-sample comparison is selected versus not selected, 12.2% against 2.9% on the other 3,084, which gives z = 11.4 with a pooled variance, the ~11.4 in my Stage 1 notes. Treating the selected set and the whole population as independent groups would be a mistake, since one contains the other. None of these changes the verdict, but the honest statement is 'one-sample test against the base rate'.

follow_ups.q: Why is selected-vs-not-selected the right two-sample comparison?
follow_ups.a: The two groups are disjoint, so their sampling errors are independent (under the i.i.d. assumption) and the variance of the difference is the sum of the two variances. That is the assumption the two-proportion formula needs.

follow_ups.q: Which is more relevant economically?
follow_ups.a: The one-sample comparison with the base rate: the alternative to following the model is taking every signal, whose win rate is the base rate. Selected-vs-rejected measures ranking power.

follow_ups.q: Could you have used a chi-square test instead?
follow_ups.a: Yes. A 2×2 chi-square test on selected/not selected × win/loss is equivalent to the pooled two-proportion z-test: χ² = z² ≈ 130.

cards.topic: From zero: clustered standard errors (why wallets and tokens are clusters, 10.02 → 4.08 / 2.52)
cards.question: Why aren't your 927 signals independent? What is a cluster, and why did clustering take your z from 10.02 to 4.08 and 2.52?
cards.answer: A cluster is a group of observations that share a common shock, so they tend to succeed or fail together. My signals come from a handful of wallets: 34.7% from one wallet and 59.7% from two. If a wallet is skilled, or just lucky that week, all its signals win together; and when several wallets buy the same pumping token, those signals share one outcome. So 927 signals carry much less information than 927 independent coin flips, and the naive standard error is too small. Allowing for correlation within wallets, z fell from 10.02 to 4.08; within wallet-token pairs, to 2.52. Compared like for like with an ordinary, non-clustered bootstrap of the same gap (about 0.86 points of noise), the variance was inflated about 4 times by wallet and 11 times by wallet-token, so the 927 signals were worth very roughly 220 to 85 independent ones.

follow_ups.q: What's the intra-cluster correlation implied by a DEFF of about 4?
follow_ups.a: If clusters had equal size m, ρ = (DEFF − 1)/(m − 1). The wallet clusters were built on all 4,011 candidates, about 450 per wallet, so ρ ≈ 3.2/445 ≈ 0.007. A correlation below 1% between trades of the same wallet is enough to cut the evidence by a factor of about 4, because the clusters are so large.

follow_ups.q: Why cluster on wallet-token rather than just token?
follow_ups.a: The project tested wallet and wallet-token granularities. Wallet-token groups repeated buys by one wallet on one token, the most obviously duplicated information; clustering on token alone would also merge co-buyers across wallets.

follow_ups.q: Does clustering change the 12.2% precision?
follow_ups.a: No. It changes the uncertainty around the estimate, not the estimate itself.

follow_ups.q: Where else do clustered errors appear in finance?
follow_ups.a: Panel regressions of returns (firm and time clustering, Petersen 2009), overlapping returns, trades from the same client or the same day.

cards.topic: From zero: the bootstrap and the cluster bootstrap
cards.question: What is a bootstrap, and what is a cluster bootstrap? Walk me through how you would compute the clustered z by resampling.
cards.answer: The bootstrap estimates how noisy a statistic is by pretending the sample is the population: you redraw a sample of the same size with replacement, recompute the statistic, repeat thousands of times, and the spread of those recomputed values is the standard error. The plain bootstrap resamples individual trades, so it assumes they are independent and gives about the same noise as the textbook formula around the observed value. A cluster bootstrap resamples whole clusters instead, all of a wallet's trades, or all of a wallet-token pair's trades, so that correlated trades stay together, the way they would if the world were rerun. I formed the clusters over all 4,011 test candidates, redrew them 5,000 times, recomputed on each draw both the precision of the selected trades and the base rate, and took the spread of the gap as the standard error: z became 4.08 by wallet and 2.52 by wallet-token. The limitation is that with only 9 wallets you are resampling 9 units, so the bootstrap distribution itself is coarse.

follow_ups.q: Why draw with replacement?
follow_ups.a: Drawing n from n without replacement just gives back the same sample. With replacement, each resample is a new plausible sample from the empirical distribution, which mimics drawing a fresh sample from the population.

follow_ups.q: How many resamples do you need?
follow_ups.a: For a standard error, a few thousand is plenty; for extreme percentiles more. The number of clusters, not B, is the real limit on precision.

follow_ups.q: What's the jackknife?
follow_ups.a: Leave one cluster out at a time, recompute the statistic, and use the spread of those G values to estimate the variance. Your leave-one-wallet-out stress test is exactly that idea (prj-226).

cards.topic: From zero: multiple testing (why trying many things inflates false discoveries)
cards.question: What is the multiple-testing problem? Explain it from scratch and tell me where it shows up in your own project.
cards.answer: A 5% significance level means that if there is no effect, a single test still says 'significant' 5% of the time by luck. If I run many tests and report the best one, the chance that at least one is a false alarm grows fast: with 20 independent tests it is $1 - 0.95^{20} \approx 64\%$. That is the multiple-testing problem. In my project it appeared concretely: the rule's win-rate threshold was first chosen by scanning the whole dataset and reporting the best z (1.35), and the model's probability threshold was chosen as the best of 8 candidates on an internal split. The honest fixes are to choose on one sample and test once on another, which I did for the model, to pre-register the criteria, and, when several tests remain, to raise the bar, for example with Bonferroni: for 20 tests, 3.02 instead of 1.96.

follow_ups.q: Why is choosing a threshold on a calibration split and testing once enough?
follow_ups.a: Because the selection bias (picking the best of 8) is spent on the calibration data. The test data only sees one pre-chosen rule, so its p-value is a genuine single-test p-value.

follow_ups.q: Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg?
follow_ups.a: Bonferroni controls the probability of any false positive: right for a go/no-go decision like deploying capital. BH controls the share of false positives among discoveries: right for screening many signals where some false positives are acceptable.

follow_ups.q: Does z = 3.91 survive a correction?
follow_ups.a: Its two-sided p-value is about 9.2e-5, so a naive Bonferroni at 5% would tolerate about 540 tests. But that p-value assumes independent trades; with clustered standard errors (z between 2.5 and 4 in Stage 1) the margin is far thinner. And the verdict was FAIL on money anyway.

follow_ups.q: What is the 'garden of forking paths'?
follow_ups.a: The idea that data-dependent analysis choices act like hidden tests even if you only formally run one test. Pre-registration is the cure.

cards.topic: From zero: base rate, precision, recall and lift (the confusion matrix of your model)
cards.question: What are precision, recall and the base rate? Which one matters for your strategy and why is your 12.2% 'good'?
cards.answer: The base rate is how often a random candidate wins: 5.0% of my 4,011 test candidates. Precision is how often the trades I actually select win: 12.2% of the 927 the model picked. Recall is the share of all winners that I caught: about 113 of 201, so 56%. Lift is precision divided by the base rate, about 2.4: my selection is 2.4 times richer in winners than random. For a trading strategy precision and payoff matter most, because I pay costs on every trade I take, not on the ones I skip. Accuracy is useless here: saying 'never buy' would be 95% accurate and make nothing. And 12.2% is only 'good' relative to 5%; the economics depend on whether that hit rate times the payoff beats the losses and costs, which it did not after costs.

follow_ups.q: What is the precision-recall trade-off?
follow_ups.a: Raising the probability threshold makes the model buy only its most confident picks: precision tends to rise, but it catches fewer winners (recall falls) and trades less. The right threshold depends on payoff and costs, not on a metric like F1.

follow_ups.q: Why not ROC-AUC?
follow_ups.a: AUC measures ranking quality over all thresholds and is insensitive to the base rate, so it can look fine at 5% positives while precision is poor. For a strategy that trades a top slice, precision at the operating threshold (or a precision-recall curve) is more relevant.

follow_ups.q: What would a useless model's precision be?
follow_ups.a: About the base rate, 5%, whatever its selection rate: selecting at random keeps the winner share unchanged.

follow_ups.q: Is the 113 a published number?
follow_ups.a: No. The report gives 12.2% of 927 and 5.0% of 4,011; 113 and 201 are the integer counts consistent with those rounded figures and with z = 10.02.

cards.topic: From zero: class imbalance and scale_pos_weight (why 0.5 did not mean 50%)
cards.question: Only about 5% of your candidates were winners. What did you do about the imbalance, what does scale_pos_weight = 19.88 do, and what does it imply for your 0.5 threshold?
cards.answer: With 5% winners, a model can reach 95% accuracy by never predicting a win, so the positives get drowned out. I used LightGBM's scale_pos_weight set to negatives over positives, 19.88 in the deployed model: each winner counts about 20 times in the loss, so the two classes weigh the same. The side effect is that the output is no longer a real probability: the model behaves as if half the data were winners. Undoing the weighting, a raw score of 0.5 corresponds to a true probability of $0.5/(0.5 + 19.88 \times 0.5) \approx 4.8\%$, the base rate. So my 0.5 threshold was really 'select trades the model ranks above average', and when my first cost filter read 0.5 as a 50% chance of doubling, it predicted +32.9% expected return on trades that actually lost money. I replaced it with an empirical calibration.

follow_ups.q: Why not just oversample the winners?
follow_ups.a: Duplicating positives is almost equivalent to weighting them for trees, but it creates exact copies that can end up in the same leaf and encourage overfitting; SMOTE-style synthetic points make little sense for a few noisy tabular features.

follow_ups.q: Would you use weighting again?
follow_ups.a: For ranking, yes or no makes little difference. Given the ENR filter needs probabilities, I would train unweighted or recalibrate on held-out data, and check with a reliability diagram.

follow_ups.q: Does weighting change which trades are ranked highest?
follow_ups.a: It can, slightly, because the tree splits are chosen with different gradient weights, but its main effect is a monotone distortion of the score scale.

follow_ups.q: Where does 19.88 come from exactly?
follow_ups.a: It is n_neg / n_pos in the data the saved model was trained on: about 1 winner per 20.88 rows, i.e. a 4.8% positive share, consistent with the 5.0% base rate of the test window.

cards.topic: From zero: decision trees (how one tree splits your trades)
cards.question: Before boosting: what is a decision tree? How does it choose a split, and what would a tree on your four features look like?
cards.answer: A decision tree is a sequence of yes/no questions on the features, like 'is the wallet's past win rate above 7.6%?' then 'is the trade size above 3.3 times its usual size?', ending in leaves that each give a prediction, for example the win rate of the training trades that landed there. To grow it, the algorithm tries every feature and every cut point, and keeps the one that makes the two groups purest, measured by how much it reduces the loss, Gini impurity or log-loss. It then repeats inside each group until a limit is hit: in my model depth 4, at most 15 leaves and at least 20 trades per leaf. Trees are attractive for my data because they don't care about the scale of a feature, handle heavy tails like token amounts, and capture interactions. A single tree is unstable and coarse, which is why I used boosting, many small trees added together.

follow_ups.q: Gini or log-loss for the split?
follow_ups.a: They almost always choose similar splits. LightGBM with a binary objective actually uses the gradient-based gain of the log-loss (prj-310), not Gini.

follow_ups.q: Why is min_data_in_leaf important at a 5% base rate?
follow_ups.a: A leaf of 20 trades contains on average one winner; with fewer, a leaf's win rate is almost pure noise and the tree would chase lucky clusters.

follow_ups.q: Why not one big tree?
follow_ups.a: A deep tree fits the training data perfectly and generalises badly; small trees combined by boosting or bagging are both more accurate and more stable.

follow_ups.q: Is the 0.0756 threshold meaningful?
follow_ups.a: It is where the first tree found the best split on the training data. It tells you the win-rate feature carries the most immediate information, not that 7.6% is a law of nature.

cards.topic: From zero: gradient boosting step by step (gradient, Hessian, leaf value, learning rate)
cards.question: Explain gradient boosting from scratch. What does one iteration of your LightGBM do, with actual numbers?
cards.answer: Boosting builds the prediction as a sum of small trees. It works on the log-odds scale: it starts from the base rate, 5%, i.e. log-odds of about −2.94. At each round it computes, for every trade, how the loss would change if the prediction moved: for log-loss the gradient is simply $p - y$, the prediction minus the outcome, and the curvature is $p(1-p)$. A new small tree groups trades with similar errors, and each leaf gets the Newton step $-\sum g / \sum h$. That step is shrunk by the learning rate, 0.05 in my model, and added. After 100 such rounds the log-odds pass through a sigmoid to give a score. Concretely, a leaf with 5 winners and 20 losers, starting from 5%, moves to about 5.8% after one round without weighting, and to about 10.7% with my positive weight of 19.88. I checked that exact number against LightGBM itself.

follow_ups.q: Why use the Hessian and not only the gradient?
follow_ups.a: The Hessian rescales the step by the curvature: for trades with p near 0 or 1 the loss is flat in F and a gradient-only step would be badly sized. Newton steps make one leaf value near-optimal for log-loss.

follow_ups.q: Gradient boosting versus random forest?
follow_ups.a: A forest averages independent deep trees to reduce variance; boosting adds dependent shallow trees to reduce bias, each one correcting the current errors. Boosting is usually more accurate but easier to overfit.

follow_ups.q: What does the learning rate trade off?
follow_ups.a: Smaller steps need more trees but generalise better; 0.05 with 100 trees is a common conservative choice. With early stopping one would let the validation loss choose the number of trees.

follow_ups.q: Where do the 4 features enter?
follow_ups.a: Only in the splits: the tree chooses which feature and threshold maximise the gain computed from the gradients and Hessians.

cards.topic: From zero: the LightGBM hyperparameters you used and what each one controls
cards.question: Tell me your LightGBM configuration and explain each hyperparameter from scratch. Did you tune them?
cards.answer: Binary objective with log-loss; 15 leaves maximum, depth at most 4, learning rate 0.05, 100 boosting rounds, at least 20 trades per leaf, and scale_pos_weight equal to negatives over positives, 19.88. Leaves and depth limit how complex each tree is; min_data_in_leaf stops a leaf from being built on a handful of trades; the learning rate and number of rounds set how far the model moves toward the training data; scale_pos_weight rebalances the 5% winners. I did not tune them: no hyperparameter search, no early stopping, no subsampling, no L1 or L2 penalty, and no fixed random seed. With four features and about 16,000 training rows, conservative defaults were deliberate, since tuning is another way to overfit. The only choice tuned on data was the probability threshold, on an internal split of the training window. If I did it again I'd add early stopping on a time-ordered validation set and fix the seed.

follow_ups.q: Why would a threshold at the edge of the grid worry you?
follow_ups.a: If the best value is the largest one tried, the true optimum may lie beyond it, and the choice may reflect a trend in noise. One should widen the grid, pre-declared, and check that the internal result is stable.

follow_ups.q: What's the difference between leaf-wise and level-wise growth?
follow_ups.a: Level-wise (XGBoost default) splits all leaves at a given depth; leaf-wise (LightGBM) always splits the single best leaf, producing deeper, lopsided trees that fit faster, hence the need for num_leaves and min_data_in_leaf limits.

follow_ups.q: What would early stopping need here?
follow_ups.a: A validation set that comes after the training data in time, never the test window; e.g. the last 5 days of the 25-day train, the same internal split used for the threshold.

follow_ups.q: Is 100 trees a lot?
follow_ups.a: No: with depth-4 trees and a learning rate of 0.05 it is a modest model, consistent with the small dataset.

cards.topic: From zero: overfitting and the train / validation / test split
cards.question: What is overfitting, and why do you need three data sets, train, validation and test? How were they organised in your project?
cards.answer: Overfitting is when a model learns the noise of its training sample rather than the pattern, so it looks great on data it has seen and disappoints on new data. The defence is to keep data the model and I have never touched. Training data fits the model; validation data is where I make choices, like the probability threshold; the test data is used once, at the end, to measure. In my Stage 1 the last 30 days were split in time: 25 days of training, of which the first 20 trained an internal model and the last 5 chose the 0.5 threshold, and then 5 never-seen days of test. Two of my errors were exactly violations of this: a rule threshold chosen by scanning the full data, and validation numbers produced by a model that had been retrained on train plus test, which inflated expectancy from +2.7% to +5.39%.

follow_ups.q: Isn't retraining on train + test before deployment itself a leak?
follow_ups.a: No, as long as nothing measured afterwards is reported as a test result. The leak was using that retrained model to produce validation numbers on days it had seen.

follow_ups.q: Why not k-fold cross-validation?
follow_ups.a: Random folds mix past and future in time-ordered data with overlapping labels; one needs time-ordered or purged schemes (prj-313, prj-314).

follow_ups.q: How big should the test set be?
follow_ups.a: Big enough that the metric's noise is smaller than the effect you care about; 927 selections gave a precision SE of about 1 point but clustering made the effective size much smaller (prj-304).

follow_ups.q: What's the bias-variance trade-off?
follow_ups.a: Simple models miss real patterns (bias); flexible ones fit noise (variance). Test error is minimised in between; regularisation and more data move the sweet spot.

cards.topic: From zero: walk-forward validation (and what yours really was)
cards.question: What is walk-forward validation, why can't you split time-series data at random, and how exactly did you do it?
cards.answer: Walk-forward means you always train on the past and test on the period right after, the way a live system would have lived it. A random split would put Tuesday's trades in training and Monday's in test, so the model would learn from the future, for example from market mood or from a wallet's later results. In my Stage 1 I trained on 25 days, from 11 August to 5 September 2026, and tested once on the next 5 days, to 10 September, which the model had never seen. The report calls it a rolling window: the window is anchored on the most recent data and each new cycle moves forward. In Stage 1 itself that was a single fold, one train-test pair, so one path of 5 days, not an average over many periods. The next real forward step was the live paper trading from 11 to 16 September.

follow_ups.q: How would you get more than one out-of-sample result from 30 days?
follow_ups.a: Roll the window: e.g. train on 15 days, test on the next 3, move forward 3 days, repeat, with purging between train and test. Or use combinatorial purged CV. You'd then report the distribution of results, not one number.

follow_ups.q: Expanding or rolling window for memecoins?
follow_ups.a: Rolling, because the regime changes fast and old data may mislead; but a shorter window means fewer winners to learn from. It's an empirical trade-off to decide in validation, not on the test.

follow_ups.q: Was your walk-forward leak-free?
follow_ups.a: The split was, but two subtler leaks remained: no purge between train and test (last ~24 h of train labels use test-period prices) and the label-maturity leak in the win-rate feature.

follow_ups.q: Why is paper trading the best walk-forward?
follow_ups.a: Because the decision is logged before the price outcome exists, so no hindsight can enter, whatever the bugs in the backtest.

cards.topic: From zero: purging and embargo (the gap your train/test split didn't have)
cards.question: What are purging and embargo? Did your train/test split need them, and did it have them?
cards.answer: A label is not known at the moment of the trade: mine is whether the price reaches 2x within the next hours, looking at up to 24 hours of prices. So a trade at the very end of the training window has a label computed from prices that fall inside the test window. The model is then trained on information from the test period. Purging means removing from training every trade whose label window overlaps the test period, here the last 24 hours of the training window. Embargo means also dropping a buffer of trades just after a test block, which matters when training data can come after the test, as in cross-validation. My split had neither: training ended exactly where the test began. The affected share is roughly one day of 25, about 4% of the training rows, so probably a small effect, but it is a real leak and the fix is trivial: stop training 24 hours before the test starts.

follow_ups.q: Why is an embargo unnecessary in a pure forward split?
follow_ups.a: Because no training data comes after the test period; the embargo protects training observations that follow a test block, as in k-fold or combinatorial CV.

follow_ups.q: How would you check whether the missing purge mattered?
follow_ups.a: Rerun Stage 1 with the last 24 hours of training removed and compare precision, z and expectancy. If the change is within the noise, the leak was harmless; it's a cheap, pre-declarable check.

follow_ups.q: Is 24 hours the right horizon?
follow_ups.a: It's the maximum time the label looks ahead. For confirmed winners the outcome is known earlier, but you don't know which trades those are at training time, so you purge the full horizon.

follow_ups.q: Was it in the report?
follow_ups.a: No. The report doesn't mention purging; I found it when re-reading the code, and I'd raise it myself as a known limitation.

cards.topic: From zero: data leakage in general, and the leaks of your project
cards.question: What is data leakage? Give me the general types and then list the leaks you had in your own project.
cards.answer: Leakage is when information that would not be available at decision time sneaks into the model or into its evaluation, so the backtest looks better than reality. There are four families: the future leaking into features, the test data leaking into training or choices, the labels themselves leaking through, and the sample being selected in a biased way. I had one of each. Survivorship: my first win rate ignored tokens that never got a price, which flipped the conclusion. A calibration leak: a threshold chosen and reported on the same data. A model artefact mix-up: validation run with a model retrained on the test days, +5.39% instead of +2.7%. And the exit policy was calibrated on data including the test window. Re-reading the code later, I found two quieter ones: no purge between train and test, and the wallet win-rate feature using labels that would not yet be known live.

follow_ups.q: Which leak was the worst?
follow_ups.a: By effect on the headline, the model-artefact mix-up (expectancy halved from 5.39% to 2.7%) and the survivorship error (sign flip). By subtlety, the label-maturity leak, because even an internal audit judged that code leak-free.

follow_ups.q: Why didn't you fix the exit-policy leak?
follow_ups.a: Re-calibrating on the same, already-examined test window would itself be tuned on test data, a third generation of the same leak. The clean fix is a new calibration on train-only data and a new, untouched test period.

follow_ups.q: How do you find leaks systematically?
follow_ups.a: For each feature, label and choice, write down when the information becomes available and compare it with the decision time; then run placebo and shift tests. And treat any result that is too good as a bug until proven otherwise.

follow_ups.q: Are leaks only an ML problem?
follow_ups.a: No, the first two appeared in a simple rule-based backtest.

cards.topic: From zero: the label-maturity leak in the wallet win-rate feature
cards.question: Your wallet win-rate feature only uses trades before the current one. Why can it still leak?
cards.answer: Because 'before' was measured on the trade time, not on the time the outcome became known. A trade's label, did it reach 2x within 24 hours, is only settled up to a day later. In the backtest, all labels had been filled in afterwards, so when the code computed a wallet's win rate for a trade at 14:00, it included that wallet's buy from 13:00 together with its outcome, which in reality nobody could have known at 14:00. In live paper trading the same function saw that recent buy as still pending and left it out. So the feature was computed with hindsight in the backtest and differently live: a classic training-serving skew. The fix is to use only past trades whose label was already resolved at the decision time, for example trades older than 24 hours. I haven't quantified the effect; I found it on re-reading the code, and the project's own audit had called that filter leak-free.

follow_ups.q: How would you measure its impact?
follow_ups.a: Recompute the win rate with only labels resolved before each decision, retrain and rescore Stage 1 on the same windows, and compare precision, z and expectancy with the original run.

follow_ups.q: Could a win be known before 24 hours?
follow_ups.a: In principle a doubling is visible the moment it happens, but the system stored only the 24-hour peak and wrote labels after the window, and losses are only certain at the end. Using the full horizon is the safe rule.

follow_ups.q: Is this the same as the missing purge?
follow_ups.a: Related but different: the purge problem is about the label of a training row crossing into the test period; this one is about a feature built from other trades' labels that weren't known yet.

follow_ups.q: Why did the audit miss it?
follow_ups.a: Because it checked event times (strictly before the trade) and the pending filter, both of which look correct; the problem only appears when you ask when the database was filled.

cards.topic: From zero: how your labels were defined (triple barrier, 15-minute closes, the code's rule)
cards.question: Define precisely what a 'win' was in your data. What is a triple barrier, and how was it turned into labels and P&L with only two price points?
cards.answer: A triple-barrier exit sells at whichever comes first: a take-profit, here 2 times the entry price; a stop-loss at 0.6573 times entry, so −34.27%; or a maximum holding time of 11,458 seconds, about 3 hours 11. Those levels came from the distribution of 9,629 labelled outcomes. My price data were 15-minute candle closes: entry is the close nearest the buy, within 30 minutes, and for each trade I stored only the peak close over the next 24 hours and when it happened. A trade is labelled a win if that peak is at least 2x and it occurs within the 3h11 window: that's a confirmed take-profit, +100%. A confirmed loss is a peak that never exceeds the stop level, or a token that never got a price at all: −34.27%. Everything else is approximated: sold at the peak if the peak is inside the window, which is optimistic, or breakeven if it's later.

follow_ups.q: Why not store the full price path?
follow_ups.a: Price-API quotas on about 40,000 trades, and it wasn't needed for the first analysis. With the path, the barriers could be simulated exactly; it's the first data improvement I'd make.

follow_ups.q: Why does a stop at the 5th percentile of the peak make sense?
follow_ups.a: The peak ratio says how high a trade ever got; 5% of trades never rose above 0.6573× entry at any 15-minute close, so for them the stop surely fired. Tighter levels sit on the huge mass of flat trades at 1.0×.

follow_ups.q: Is the label the same as the win in the wallet win-rate feature?
follow_ups.a: Not exactly: the feature counts a past buy as a win if its 24-hour peak reached 2.0×, without the 3h11 condition.

follow_ups.q: What's the net bias of the labels?
follow_ups.a: Unknown: closes and peak timing understate wins, while peak exits and invisible stops overstate P&L. Only full paths would settle it.

cards.topic: From zero: probability calibration (why +32.9% was wrong and how you fixed it)
cards.question: What does it mean for a model's probabilities to be calibrated? What went wrong in your first cost filter, and what did you replace it with?
cards.answer: A model is calibrated if its probabilities mean what they say: among trades it scores 30%, about 30% should win. A model can rank trades well and still be badly calibrated. Mine was, mainly because I weighted the rare winners about 20 times during training, which inflates the scores. My first cost filter took the raw score as a real probability and plugged it into the payoff: $p \times (+100\%) + (1-p) \times (-34.27\%)$. At a score of 0.5 that promises +32.9% expected return before costs, while the trades in that score range actually lost money. So the filter would have admitted almost everything. I replaced the formula with an empirical calibration: on the internal validation days of the training window, I grouped the selected trades into score buckets, 0.50 to 0.55, 0.55 to 0.60, and so on up to 0.70 and above, and used the average P&L actually observed in each bucket, falling back on the overall average when a bucket had fewer than 30 trades.

follow_ups.q: How would you check calibration properly?
follow_ups.a: Out-of-sample, bucket predictions (e.g. deciles), plot mean score versus realised win rate with confidence bands, and compute the Brier score; with few positives, use wide buckets and bootstrap the bands.

follow_ups.q: Platt, isotonic or bins?
follow_ups.a: Platt is smooth and needs little data but assumes a sigmoid shape; isotonic is flexible but overfits small samples; bins are transparent. With a few hundred trades, Platt or coarse bins are the safer choices.

follow_ups.q: Why calibrate expected return rather than probability?
follow_ups.a: Because the payoff isn't binary: the P&L of non-winners varies widely. Averaging realised returns per bucket captures both the hit rate and the real payoff distribution in one number.

follow_ups.q: Would an unweighted model have been calibrated?
follow_ups.a: Closer, since log-loss is minimised on the true class balance, but boosted trees can still be over- or under-confident; you'd still check a reliability diagram.

cards.topic: From zero: expectancy and the breakeven hit rate (25.5%, and why 12.2% still made +2.74%)
cards.question: What is expectancy? With a +100% target and a −34% stop, what hit rate do you need to break even, and how could 12.2% precision give a positive expectancy?
cards.answer: Expectancy is the average P&L per trade: probability of winning times the average win, plus probability of losing times the average loss, minus costs. If every trade ended exactly at my barriers, +100% or −34.27%, the breakeven hit rate would be $0.3427 / 1.3427 \approx 25.5\%$. At my 12.2% precision that binary picture gives about −17.9% per trade, a disaster. Yet the measured raw expectancy of the 927 selected trades was +2.74%. The reason is that most non-winners did not lose 34%: they were exited near their peak or at breakeven under the exit rule. Solving backwards, the average non-winner must have been around −10.8%. Two cautions: the report's 'net expectancy +0.027' is in fact this gross figure before costs, and after realistic costs it was barely positive in the best case and negative otherwise.

follow_ups.q: How does expectancy relate to the Sharpe ratio?
follow_ups.a: Sharpe is mean over standard deviation (annualised). Expectancy is only the numerator per trade; a positive expectancy with huge dispersion can still have a poor Sharpe and a high chance of ruin (prj-124).

follow_ups.q: Why do trend-following strategies have low hit rates?
follow_ups.a: They cut losers small and let winners run, so a 30-40% hit rate is enough; the same logic as a +100% / −34% payoff with a 25.5% breakeven.

follow_ups.q: What does −10.8% implied average loss tell you?
follow_ups.a: That the exit approximations matter enormously: the expectancy depends on how non-winners are valued, which is exactly where the labels are least reliable.

follow_ups.q: Would you size by Kelly with +2.74%?
follow_ups.a: No; the estimate is too uncertain and costs erase it. Kelly with estimation error overbets (prj-125).

cards.topic: From zero: execution costs on Solana (pool fee, slippage, priority fee) and your three scenarios
cards.question: What does it cost to execute one of your trades? Walk me through the components and compute the round-trip cost for your low, moderate and high scenarios.
cards.answer: Four components, paid on both the buy and the sell. The pool fee, a percentage taken by the liquidity pool on each swap. Slippage, the price moving against me because my own order shifts the pool price and because the price moves before I'm filled. The priority fee, a tip in SOL to get included quickly during congestion. And Solana's base fee, 5,000 lamports, 0.000005 SOL, per signature. Percentages scale with the trade; the fixed fees in SOL hurt small trades. For a 100 EUR stake, about 1.17 SOL at the 85.57 EUR per SOL I used, the round trip is about 1.5% in the low scenario, 5.3% moderate and 21.4% high. Against a raw edge of +2.74%, that leaves +1.21%, −2.60% and −18.68%. So the whole strategy lived or died on execution costs, which is why I modelled them explicitly in the ENR filter rather than ignoring them.

follow_ups.q: Where does slippage come from in an AMM?
follow_ups.a: The pool keeps x·y = k: buying tokens removes them from the pool and raises the price along the curve, so the average fill is worse than the pre-trade price; add price moves during your delay and other bots trading ahead of you.

follow_ups.q: Why is the sell leg often worse for memecoins?
follow_ups.a: Liquidity can collapse after the initial hype, and everyone exits at the same time; your stop-loss sell may execute far below the stop level.

follow_ups.q: How would you get real cost data?
follow_ups.a: Record live Jupiter quotes and, better, tiny real fills: quoted versus executed price, fees paid and failed transactions, then fit slippage as a function of size and liquidity.

follow_ups.q: Why keep the SOL price at 85.57 EUR?
follow_ups.a: It's the project's frozen input (Coinbase, 11 Sept 2026) so results are reproducible; only the fixed fees depend on it, and they're small except for tiny stakes or the high scenario.

cards.topic: From zero: paper trading, and what your 1,019 live decisions showed
cards.question: What is paper trading, why is it stronger evidence than a backtest, and what exactly happened in your Stage 2?
cards.answer: Paper trading means running the real live system, real-time data, the frozen model and rules, and recording every decision at the moment it's made, but without sending real orders. Its strength is that the outcome doesn't exist yet when the decision is logged, so no hindsight, no leak and no tuning can creep in. My Stage 2 ran for five days, 11 to 16 September 2026, and the model made 1,019 simulated buys, all eventually labelled. The pre-registered bar was at least 30 trades, positive expectancy, within 50% of the backtest's +2.7%, and at least 3 of 5 positive days. The result was an expectancy of essentially zero, −0.0002 per trade, a deviation of about 100% from the backtest, and only 1 day out of 5 positive: FAIL. After a race-condition fix on 4 trades, expectancy became +0.0015, but the other two criteria still failed. And applying my cost filter, only about 41 of the 1,019 would have been admitted, with negative net results.

follow_ups.q: Why require the live result within 50% of the backtest?
follow_ups.a: To check that the backtest is a reliable model of reality; a large gap signals leakage or mis-modelled execution, even if the live number is positive.

follow_ups.q: Is 1,019 trades a lot?
follow_ups.a: In count yes, but they come from a handful of wallets over five days, so the effective sample is much smaller; day-level robustness (1 of 5) is the weaker, more honest view.

follow_ups.q: What would you add to paper trading next time?
follow_ups.a: Live Jupiter quotes at decision time logged for every signal, simulated fills with realistic delay, and the complete system (ENR filter and caps) scored live, not afterwards.

follow_ups.q: Why keep the original report after finding the race condition?
follow_ups.a: Rewriting a published verdict erodes trust; a dated addendum shows both numbers and why they differ, and here the verdict didn't change.

cards.topic: From zero: survivorship bias (27.3% vs 16.3% became 6.3% vs 7.9%)
cards.question: What is survivorship bias? Explain it from scratch and walk me through the example in your project.
cards.answer: Survivorship bias is drawing conclusions from the cases that survived long enough to be observed while silently dropping the others. The classic story is the Second World War bombers: the returning planes had holes in the wings, and the right conclusion was to armour the engines, because planes hit there never came back. In my project, a token only gets a price, and so an outcome, once it 'graduates' from its launch bonding curve to a real trading pool; most never do. My first backtest measured win rates only on trades with a resolved price, about 46% of them, and my rule looked great: 27.3% against 16.3% for the reference. Counting the tokens that never got a price as failures, which is economically what they are, both numbers collapsed to 6.3% versus 7.9%, and the rule became worse than the reference. The implied reason: the rule's picks got a price only about 23% of the time, against about 48% for the reference.

follow_ups.q: Why count an unresolved token as a failure and not drop it?
follow_ups.a: Because a copier would have bought it too and been unable to sell into a liquid market: economically it's a loss. Dropping it measures a strategy nobody can execute.

follow_ups.q: Is counting it as −34.27% right?
follow_ups.a: It's a bounded assumption: the real loss could be larger (up to −100%) or smaller if some exit existed on the bonding curve. It's documented as an approximation.

follow_ups.q: Where else does survivorship appear in finance?
follow_ups.a: Fund and hedge-fund databases, stock indices (delisted companies), backtests on today's index constituents, and track records of traders who are still in the business.

follow_ups.q: How do you detect it?
follow_ups.a: Ask what happened to the cases that are missing, and compare the characteristics of observed and missing cases; if the selection correlates with the outcome, you have a bias.

cards.topic: From zero: pre-registration and your four-stage validation gate
cards.question: What is pre-registration, why did you fix your criteria in advance, and what exactly was your four-stage gate?
cards.answer: Pre-registration means writing down, before looking at the results, what you will test, on which data, and what counts as success. It protects you from yourself: after seeing results it is always tempting to move the threshold, pick the flattering window or the best cost scenario. I fixed four stages. Stage 1, an out-of-sample backtest: z at least 1.96 against the base rate, at least 300 selected signals, the right direction on at least 4 of 5 test days, and positive expectancy. Stage 2, five days of live paper trading: at least 30 trades, positive expectancy, within 50% of the backtest, at least 3 of 5 positive days. Stage 3, real money, only with my explicit sign-off at that moment, never automatic. Stage 4, a production loop where a challenger model replaces the champion only if it beats it by 20% with p below 0.05 over two consecutive windows, and a kill-switch after three negative days. Stage 1 passed, Stage 2 failed, and I stopped there.

follow_ups.q: Isn't pre-registration too rigid for research?
follow_ups.a: Exploration is fine, as long as it's labelled as exploration and the final claim is tested on fresh data under criteria fixed before. The rigidity is the point for the decision to risk money.

follow_ups.q: Why a 20% improvement and two windows for the challenger?
follow_ups.a: To avoid 'thrashing': swapping models on noise. A new model must be clearly and repeatedly better; by default you keep the incumbent.

follow_ups.q: Why can the kill-switch only stop?
follow_ups.a: Automatic actions should reduce risk; starting or resuming trading is a judgement call that needs a human, so the automation is deliberately one-way.

follow_ups.q: What would you change in your Stage 1 criteria?
follow_ups.a: Replace the naive z by a wallet-clustered test, add a net-of-cost expectancy criterion with its own uncertainty, require a minimum number of distinct wallets, and compute the gate's power beforehand.

cards.topic: Score z versus Wald z: which standard error, and the duality between a test and an interval
cards.question: Your z of 10.02 divides by a standard error computed at 5.0%, but if I put a confidence interval around your 12.2% I use a standard error computed at 12.2%, and then z is only about 6.7. Which one is right, and why don't your test and your interval agree?
cards.answer: Both numbers are correct; they use the variance at a different point. A proportion's standard error is the square root of p(1 − p)/n, and it depends on which p you plug in. My test plugs in the null value, the 5.01% base rate: that gives 0.72 percentage points and z = 10.02. This is called the score test, and it is the standard choice for a test, because under the null hypothesis the variance is known exactly. If you plug in the observed 12.19% instead, the standard error is 1.07 points and z = 6.68: that is the Wald version, and it is what the textbook interval 12.19% ± 1.96 × 1.07, so [10.1%; 14.3%], is built on. The link between the two is duality: a 95% interval is the set of null values a 5% test would not reject. The interval that matches my score test is not the Wald one but the Wilson interval, [10.2%; 14.5%]. Here the choice changes z from 10 to 6.7 but never the verdict, since 5% is far outside every interval. The much bigger correction is clustering, which takes z to between 2.5 and 4.1.

follow_ups.q: Which one would you report in a paper?
follow_ups.a: For the test, the score version with the null variance, which is standard for a one-sample proportion. For the interval, Wilson or Clopper-Pearson rather than Wald, so that test and interval agree (prj-325). And both clustered, since independence is the assumption that actually fails.

follow_ups.q: Can the two versions ever give opposite verdicts?
follow_ups.a: Yes, when the result is close to the threshold. For example a z near 2 with the null SE can become below 1.96 with a larger estimated SE. Here 10.02 versus 6.68 are both far above 1.96, so the choice is cosmetic.

follow_ups.q: Why is the Wilson centre 12.35% and not 12.19%?
follow_ups.a: Because the interval is built from the score equation, which adds the equivalent of about z squared over 2 pseudo-wins and pseudo-losses. That pulls the centre slightly towards 50%. With 927 trades the shift is small, 0.16 point.

cards.topic: Wilson and Clopper-Pearson intervals for your precision (12.2% and 10.3%), and how clustering widens them
cards.question: Give me a proper 95% confidence interval for your Stage 1 precision of 12.2%, and for the 10.3% of the post-audit replay. Which method do you use, and how does clustering change those intervals?
cards.answer: For a proportion I'd use Wilson or Clopper-Pearson rather than the textbook plus-or-minus 1.96 standard errors. For Stage 1, 113 wins out of 927, Wilson gives about 10.2% to 14.5% and Clopper-Pearson, the exact binomial interval, about 10.2% to 14.5% as well; the base rate of 5.0% is far outside. For the post-audit replay, about 45 wins out of 435, so 10.3%, Wilson gives 7.8% to 13.6% and Clopper-Pearson 7.6% to 13.6%; the 5.9% base rate is still outside. But all of these assume 927 or 435 independent trades, and they were not: the trades come in bursts from a few wallets. Clustering by wallet multiplies the variance by about 6, which is like having only about 154 independent trades. With that effective size the Stage 1 interval becomes roughly 8% to 18%. If the same factor applied to the replay, its interval would be roughly 5% to 19.5% and would contain the 5.9% base rate, so the replay's z of 3.9 would not survive clustering. That last number is an extrapolation, not a measured result, but it is the honest way to read 10.3%.

follow_ups.q: Why not just use the bootstrap interval directly?
follow_ups.a: I can: the wallet bootstrap gave an interval on the excess over the base rate of about 2.9 to 9.9 points, and the wallet-and-token one about 2.2 to 13.3 points. The Wilson-with-effective-size shortcut is a sanity check that gives the same picture. With 9 wallets, both are probably too narrow (prj-113).

follow_ups.q: Is it legitimate to transfer the deff from Stage 1 to the replay?
follow_ups.a: Only as an order of magnitude. The deff depends on how concentrated the selected trades are; the replay had 5 wallets instead of 9, so if anything I'd expect concentration to be at least as strong. The right thing is to rerun the cluster bootstrap on the replay.

follow_ups.q: Why is the Clopper-Pearson interval slightly wider?
follow_ups.a: Because the binomial is discrete, an exact interval cannot hit 95% coverage exactly for every true p, so it is built to have at least 95% everywhere. That conservativeness costs a little width.

cards.topic: A sample drawn from its own reference population: finite-population correction, the hypergeometric law and the permutation test
cards.question: Your 927 selected trades are drawn from the very 4,011 candidates whose win rate is your reference. A binomial test treats the reference as an infinite population. What is the exact null distribution of your number of wins, and what does the right test give?
cards.answer: Exactly: the 927 are a subset of the 4,011, drawn without replacement, and the 201 winners are a fixed number. If the model had no skill, its 927 picks would be like a random draw of 927 cards from a deck of 4,011 containing 201 winners. The number of winners in such a draw follows a hypergeometric law: mean 927 × 5.01% = 46.5, and standard deviation 5.83, smaller than the binomial 6.64 because drawing without replacement removes some noise. That reduction is the finite-population correction, a factor of the square root of (N − n)/(N − 1), about 0.877. With it, z goes from 10.02 to 11.42, and that is exactly the z of the two-sample test 'selected versus not selected', 12.2% against 2.85%: the two are the same test written differently. The exact probability of 113 or more winners is about 2 in 10 to the 25. The same thing can be done by simulation: shuffle the win labels among the 4,011 candidates many times and count the winners among the selected; that is a permutation test. But shuffling individual labels assumes all candidates are exchangeable, which clustering breaks. A permutation within each wallet already brings z down to about 6.3, and the trades within a wallet are not independent either.

follow_ups.q: So is 10.02, 11.42 or 6.3 the right z?
follow_ups.a: 11.42 is the exact answer to the question my code asked, under independence. 10.02 is a slightly conservative approximation of it. 6.3 answers a different, better question, skill within wallets. None of them handles clustering within a wallet; for that, the cluster bootstrap (4.08 and 2.52) is the reference.

follow_ups.q: How would you run a cluster permutation test here?
follow_ups.a: Keep the selection fixed and permute labels in blocks, for example reassign whole wallet-token bursts, or permute within each wallet and day. With only 9 wallets, permuting whole wallets gives very few distinct permutations, so permuting within strata is more practical.

follow_ups.q: Why is the binomial standard deviation larger than the hypergeometric one?
follow_ups.a: With replacement, the same winner can be drawn several times, which adds variability. Without replacement, each winner you draw leaves fewer in the deck, which pulls the count back towards the average. The factor (N − n)/(N − 1) measures that.

cards.topic: What z = 10 means in trades: 66.5 extra winners, and how many of them you could lose before the result fails
cards.question: Forget the z for a moment. In plain counts, how many more winning trades did your model find than chance would, and how many of those winners would have to be flukes for the result to stop being significant?
cards.answer: In counts, chance would have given about 46 winners among my 927 picks, since the base rate was 5.01%. I got 113. So the whole 'z = 10' is about 66.5 extra winners over five test days, roughly 13 a day out of about 185 picks a day. The z is that excess divided by the noise of the count, about 6.6 winners for independent trades, which gives 10. Turned around: under independence, I'd need only about 60 winners to pass the 1.96 bar, so I could lose 53 of my 113 winners and still pass, which sounds very solid. But with the noise measured by clustering by wallet, the count's standard deviation is about 16 winners, the bar is about 78 winners, and the margin is only about 35. With wallet-and-token clustering it is about 26, the bar is about 98, and the margin is about 15 winners. One hot day, the fifth, produced about 52 winners on its own. So the result that looks overwhelming as 'z = 10' rests, once correlation is counted, on a margin smaller than a single day's burst. That is why I translate z into counts before trusting it.

follow_ups.q: Why is the excess 66.5 and not 113 − 46 = 67?
follow_ups.a: The expected count is 46.45, not 46, so the excess is 66.55. I keep the decimal because the expectation is not an integer; rounding both sides would hide that.

follow_ups.q: Would you rather have z = 10 on 927 trades or z = 4 on 100 trades?
follow_ups.a: It depends on what produced them. z = 4 on 100 independent trades means a bigger effect per trade. z = 10 on 927 correlated trades may be a smaller effect with an overstated sample. I'd compare effect sizes and effective sample sizes, not the z values.

follow_ups.q: How does this connect to the money?
follow_ups.a: It doesn't directly. An extra winner is worth about +100% of the stake before costs, but what the model selects also changes the non-winners. The +2.74% raw expectancy, about 25 position sizes over five days, is the money figure, and it was not statistically significant on its own (prj-230).

cards.topic: One hot day? How much of the Stage 1 result came from day 5
cards.question: Your test window had five days. Show me the result day by day. Was it one hot day, and what happens to your z if you take that day out?
cards.answer: Day by day, precision against that day's base rate was: 9.5% against 2.7%, 3.3% against 3.7%, 5.7% against 2.8%, 10.3% against 5.7%, and 35.9% against 11.6% on day 5. So four days out of five were above, which is the 'robustness 4 of 5' criterion, and day 2 was slightly below. Day 5 is clearly special: it has 15.6% of the selected trades but about 46% of the winners, about 52 of 113, and its base rate, 11.6%, was itself more than twice the others: it was a hot day for every candidate, not only for my picks. Without day 5, precision falls to 61 out of 782, 7.8%. Comparing each day with its own base rate and summing, the z is 9.2 with all days and about 4.9 without day 5, still above 1.96 but under independence. If I treat each day as one observation, the mean daily excess has a t of 1.77 on 4 degrees of freedom, below the 2.78 bar. On a ratio scale it is more regular: the log-lift has a t of 2.96. So my reading is: the model roughly multiplied the base rate, and day 5's high base rate turned that into many winners. It is not only one day, but one day carries a large share, and five days are too few to say more.

follow_ups.q: Was day 5 the day of the excluded wallet's burst?
follow_ups.a: The report says the wallet with 34.7% of the signals was later excluded because over 98% of its apparent edge came from one calendar day; I would check in the data whether that is day 5 rather than assume it. A wallet-by-day table of selected trades and winners answers it directly.

follow_ups.q: Why does the stratified z (9.2) come out below the pooled one (10.02)?
follow_ups.a: Because the model selected more trades on days with a higher base rate. The pooled test compares them with the average 5.01%, so part of the excess is just 'trading more on hot days'. Stratification removes that, about 3.7 winners.

follow_ups.q: What would you pre-register for the next cycle?
follow_ups.a: A minimum number of days, a stratified test by day as the primary statistic, a leave-one-day-out check with a pre-set bar, and the scale, ratio or difference, chosen in advance.

cards.topic: Why the finer clustering (wallet × token, z = 2.52) gave a lower z than the coarser one (wallet, z = 4.08)
cards.question: Wallet-token pairs sit inside wallets, so clustering by wallet should be the more conservative choice. Yet your wallet bootstrap gave z = 4.08 and the finer wallet-and-token bootstrap gave z = 2.52. How is that possible, and which one do you believe?
cards.answer: You're right that it's the opposite of what theory suggests. With nested clusters, the wallet-level variance equals the pair-level variance plus the covariances between different tokens of the same wallet. If those covariances are positive, as you'd expect from bursts, clustering by wallet should give the larger standard error and the lower z. Getting the reverse tells me the wallet-level estimate is unreliable, for two reasons. First, there are only 9 wallets, and a standard error estimated from 9 clusters is itself very noisy, roughly 25% relative error, and biased downward, especially when one wallet carries 34.7% of the signals. Second, aggregating at the wallet level nets out opposite results inside a wallet: a winning burst on one token and a losing one on another cancel, and with only nine sums left, the estimate can come out low by chance. The wallet-and-token version has 2,427 clusters, so its standard error is estimated far more precisely, and adding the day as well barely changes it: 2,505 clusters, z = 2.45. So I believe the lower number, about 2.5, and I read 4.08 as optimistic. If anything, the true wallet-level z is probably below 2.5, which I can't measure well with 9 wallets.

follow_ups.q: Which population did the bootstrap resample?
follow_ups.a: All 4,011 candidates, grouped into clusters, with both the selected precision and the reference rate recomputed in each draw. That is why there can be 2,427 wallet-token clusters, more than the 927 selected trades. An earlier attempt that clustered only the 927 selected trades against a fixed reference gave 2.65 by wallet and 1.87 with 409 pairs: a different estimand.

follow_ups.q: How would you get a reliable wallet-level answer with 9 wallets?
follow_ups.a: Not with an asymptotic method. I'd use a wild cluster bootstrap with a t(G − 1) reference, report leave-one-wallet-out results, and above all collect more wallets. With 9, the honest answer is a wide range.

follow_ups.q: Does this change the PASS verdict of Stage 1?
follow_ups.a: Not by itself: 2.45 to 2.52 is still above 1.96. But the margin is thin, about 15 winners (prj-327), and it was later overturned by the leaks and the post-audit replay.

cards.topic: Per-wallet contributions: share of signals is not share of P&L
cards.question: One wallet produced 34.7% of your 927 signals. Does that mean it drove 34.7% of your +2.7% expectancy? Which wallet actually carried the result?
cards.answer: No. Share of signals and share of P&L are different things, because each wallet's trades have a different average outcome. The contribution of a wallet is its number of signals times its expectancy per trade, divided by the total. Done that way, the wallet with 34.7% of the signals, smart_money_03, gives 27.5% of the P&L, even though it has the best precision and about half of all the wins. The real driver is smart_money_04: 12.3% of the signals but 40.1% of the P&L, because its winners were big, and those wins were concentrated on a few tokens (one token is 26.3% of its signals). Four wallets were net negative and together subtract about 24% of the total. Two wallets, smart_money_04 and smart_money_02, make 72% of the result; without them the expectancy falls from +2.7% to about +1.2%. So the headline number rests on very few independent bets, which is exactly why the wallet-clustered tests mattered.

follow_ups.q: How does contribution relate to signal share?
follow_ups.a: Contribution equals signal share times the wallet's expectancy divided by the overall expectancy. smart_money_04: 12.3% × 0.0895/0.0274 ≈ 40%.

follow_ups.q: Why can the wallet with the best precision pull the average down?
follow_ups.a: Precision counts wins; expectancy also counts how big they are and how bad the losers are. smart_money_03's expectancy, +2.17%, is below the +2.74% average, so removing it raises the average to +3.05%.

follow_ups.q: What would you report alongside the headline?
follow_ups.a: The per-wallet contribution table, leave-one-out expectancies and a wallet-clustered interval. If one or two removals change the conclusion, the headline isn't robust.

follow_ups.q: Is the +1.2% without the two top wallets meaningful?
follow_ups.a: Only as a sensitivity check. It is chosen after seeing the results, so it is not a test; it shows how much of the result rests on two wallets.

cards.topic: Stage 2 after costs: does −5.44% on about 41 trades prove a loss?
cards.question: After your cost filter, about 41 paper trades were admitted, with a net expectancy of −5.44%. Does that prove the strategy loses money after costs?
cards.answer: No, not on its own. 41 trades is far too few to pin down an average whose per-trade spread is huge. The outcomes run from a stop at about −34% to a target at +100%, so the per-trade standard deviation is around 0.3 to 0.4. The standard error of the mean is then 0.3/√41 ≈ 4.7 points, up to 6.2. The 95% interval is roughly −15% to +4%, or −18% to +7%, and it contains the +2.7% of the backtest. The t-statistic is about −1. To tell +2.7% from zero at 95% you would need roughly 470 to 840 trades, and about 970 to 1,720 for 80% power. What the 41 trades do show is that nothing positive appeared. And the Stage 2 verdict didn't rest on them anyway. The pre-registered test was on all 1,019 simulated buys before costs, which came out at essentially zero against +2.7% in the backtest. I'd say "no evidence of an edge, consistent with a loss", not "proven loss".

follow_ups.q: Where does σ ≈ 0.3 come from?
follow_ups.a: From the exit buckets of the 4,011 Stage 1 candidates: outcomes between −34.27% and +100% give a mixture standard deviation of about 0.31, a lower bound because it ignores spread within the peak-exit bucket. It's an assumption for the 41 trades, not a measurement.

follow_ups.q: How long would paper trading have to run?
follow_ups.a: At about 8 admitted trades a day (41 in 5 days), roughly 60 to 105 days to reach 1.96 SE on +2.7%, and four months or more for 80% power. That's why the next cycle needs the full gross signal flow as its main test.

follow_ups.q: Would a sign test help?
follow_ups.a: It discards the size of the outcomes, which is where the information is for a strategy with rare large winners. It's a useful robustness check, not a replacement.

follow_ups.q: Why not just widen the cost filter to get more trades?
follow_ups.a: Changing the filter after seeing the result turns a test into a fit. The filter's parameters were sourced and frozen in advance; any change would have to be pre-declared for a new window.

cards.topic: Choosing the threshold by maximising z: significance is not money
cards.question: How did you choose the 0.5 probability threshold, and what is wrong with the criterion you used?
cards.answer: I scanned a grid of thresholds, 0.10, 0.15, up to 0.40, then 0.50, on an internal validation split inside the training data. I kept the one with the highest z-score, among thresholds that selected at least 50 trades. The internal z went 1.84, 2.88, 3.60, 3.64, 3.60, 4.01, 4.45, then jumped to 8.26 at 0.50, so 0.50 won. There are three problems. First, z measures how surprising the precision is, not how much money the rule makes: it grows with the square root of the number of trades, while profit grows with the number of trades and depends on payoffs and costs. A rule with a lower z can make more money. Second, taking the maximum of eight noisy, correlated estimates biases the winner upward. A jump from 4.45 to 8.26 between two adjacent points looks more like noise than a smooth optimum. Third, the winner sits on the edge of the grid, and there is no 0.45 point, so I don't know the shape of the curve around it. I documented this and deliberately didn't widen the grid after seeing the test. Next time I'd pick the threshold on expected net return after costs and prefer a stable plateau to a spike.

follow_ups.q: Why not maximise precision instead?
follow_ups.a: Precision alone pushes the threshold to the top few trades, where it is noisiest and the volume too small to matter; it ignores how many trades you get and their payoff. You need an objective that combines count, payoff and cost.

follow_ups.q: Is the floor n ≥ 50 enough?
follow_ups.a: It avoids the absurd cases but 50 trades still give a precision standard error of several points; a stability rule (choose a plateau, require neighbours to agree) does more.

follow_ups.q: How big is the winner's curse here?
follow_ups.a: It can't be computed exactly from one split. A way to measure it is to repeat the selection over several walk-forward folds and compare the chosen threshold's validation score with its score on the next fold.

follow_ups.q: Why didn't you widen the grid after the result?
follow_ups.a: Because the test had been seen: any change after that is chosen with knowledge of the test outcome. It was documented as a known limitation for the next iteration instead.

cards.topic: Moving a threshold between models: 20-day, 25-day and 30-day models share one 0.5
cards.question: Your 0.5 threshold was chosen on a model trained on 20 days, then applied to a model trained on 25 days, and in paper trading to a model trained on 30 days. Why is that a problem, and what does 0.5 even mean with class weighting?
cards.answer: A threshold is not a property of the problem, it's a cut on one model's score distribution. I chose 0.5 with an internal model trained on 20 days and scored on the last 5 days of training. Then I applied the same 0.5 to the model retrained on all 25 days, which was the one tested, and in Stage 2 to a deployment model retrained on 30 days. Each retrain changes the scores, so the same 0.5 can select a different share of trades and a different quality. On top of that, the model used class weighting: positives weighted by negatives over positives, 19.88 for the 30-day model. With that weighting, a score of 0.5 doesn't mean a 50% chance of winning. For a well-calibrated weighted model, it means a true probability of about 1/(1 + 19.88), roughly 4.8%, which is the base rate. And since the weight is recomputed for every training window, the meaning of 0.5 shifts slightly each time. Better options are to transfer a selection rate, like the top 23% of scores, rather than a raw cutoff, or to calibrate each model's scores into real probabilities before applying a threshold chosen on them.

follow_ups.q: Why use class weighting at all?
follow_ups.a: With about 5% positives, an unweighted model can minimise loss by predicting low scores everywhere; weighting forces it to separate the rare winners. It's fine for ranking, but it distorts the scores as probabilities.

follow_ups.q: How would you calibrate the scores?
follow_ups.a: Hold out data the model didn't train on, then fit a monotone map from score to observed win rate: isotonic regression (step function) or Platt scaling (logistic). Check with a reliability plot: predicted versus observed by score bucket.

follow_ups.q: Did the selection rate change in Stage 2?
follow_ups.a: I don't have a clean like-for-like number to quote, so I wouldn't claim one. It's exactly what I'd log next time, the share of candidates above the threshold for each deployed model.

follow_ups.q: Is ranking more robust than thresholding?
follow_ups.a: Usually: retraining tends to keep the order of trades more stable than the raw score level. But a top-k rule takes a fixed share even on a bad day, so it should be combined with a cost-based floor.

cards.topic: Two definitions of a "win": the win-rate feature (8.03%) vs the label (5.01%)
cards.question: Your main feature is the wallet's historical win rate, and your label is whether the trade wins. Is a "win" defined the same way in both? Does it matter?
cards.answer: No, they're defined differently. For the feature, a past buy counts as a win if its price ever reached 2× within 24 hours, with no time condition. For the label, a trade is a win only if it reaches 2× before the maximum holding time of about 3 hours 11, because that's when the exit policy would actually have sold. On the 4,011 test candidates, 322 reach 2× within 24 hours, 8.03%, but only 201 do so in time, 5.01%. So about 38% of the feature's wins are trades my strategy could not have captured. The feature measures "this wallet picks tokens that pump eventually". The label measures "pumps fast enough for my exit". It still predicts, because the two are correlated, but it's a noisier signal than it should be, and the internal report flagged that the two percentages aren't comparable. A second issue: the win rate is cumulative since the start of the history, not over a rolling window. Old trades weigh as much as recent ones, and a wallet with 10 trades gets the same treatment as one with 600. I'd align the definition with the label and shrink small-sample rates toward the base rate.

follow_ups.q: Why did the model still find the feature useful?
follow_ups.a: Because fast and slow pumps are correlated: a wallet that often picks tokens that double eventually also picks more that double quickly. The mismatch adds noise; it doesn't remove the signal.

follow_ups.q: Wouldn't aligning the definitions create leakage?
follow_ups.a: Not if you only count past trades whose 3 h 11 outcome is resolved at decision time. The definition changes, the point-in-time rule stays.

follow_ups.q: Rolling or decayed window?
follow_ups.a: A decayed window keeps all data but down-weights old trades smoothly; a rolling one drops them abruptly and makes the feature jump. With few trades per wallet, decay plus shrinkage is the safer choice.

follow_ups.q: How would you choose the prior strength m?
follow_ups.a: Empirical Bayes: estimate the spread of true win rates across wallets from the data and set m so the prior matches it; or treat m as a hyperparameter chosen on validation, never on the test.

cards.topic: Cold start: rows with fewer than 10 resolved past buys were dropped
cards.question: Your wallet win-rate feature needs history. What did you do with trades from a wallet that had fewer than 10 resolved past buys, and what does that choice do to your sample, your base rate and your live system?
cards.answer: Those rows were simply excluded from the dataset. The win-rate feature is only computed once a wallet has at least 10 earlier buys whose outcome is known, and the relative-size feature needs at least one earlier buy, so anything before that is dropped from training and from the test. That is the classic cold-start problem: a new entity has no history, so a history-based feature is undefined. Excluding is consistent, because the live rule did the same and simply skipped those trades, so there is no train-serve mismatch on that point. But it has consequences. The model, the 5.01% base rate and the z-score all describe warm wallets only, not every trade the wallets made. A newly added wallet produces no signal at all until it has 10 resolved buys, which in live means at least a day after its tenth buy because labels take 24 hours to resolve. And 10 is itself an untested hyperparameter: at 10 observations the win rate has a standard error of about 8.6 points, larger than the 8% average it estimates. I would keep the rows, give the model the history count, and shrink the win rate towards the population rate instead of dropping data.

follow_ups.q: Why not just fill the missing win rate with zero?
follow_ups.a: Because zero means 'never wins', which is a strong and false statement about a new wallet. Trees would treat those rows like genuinely bad wallets. Missing, or the population rate via shrinkage, is the honest encoding.

follow_ups.q: Did the exclusion create a difference between backtest and live?
