follow_ups.a: Not in the rule itself, which was identical. But the count only includes resolved buys; in the backtest labels were filled in afterwards, so buys looked resolved earlier than they would in live. Some rows that exist in the backtest would not have existed live yet.

follow_ups.q: How would you choose the threshold of 10?
follow_ups.a: I'd stop choosing it: with shrinkage there is no hard threshold. If one is kept, it should be fixed before looking at the test and checked for sensitivity, for example 5, 10 and 20, on the validation split only.

follow_ups.q: Does the base rate of 5.01% include the excluded rows?
follow_ups.a: No. It is computed on the 4,011 test candidates, which already exclude cold-start rows. So the comparison 12.2% against 5.0% is within warm wallets, which is the right comparison for the model but not a statement about all trades.

cards.topic: The co-buyer feature depends on which wallets you track
cards.question: Your 'simultaneous buyers' feature counts other tracked wallets buying the same token within 60 seconds. What happens to that feature when your pool shrinks from 9 wallets to 5?
cards.answer: The feature is not a property of the market, it is a property of my watch list: it counts only other wallets I track and that are still active, excluded wallets being removed from the count. So when the pool went from 9 to 5, the feature changed meaning and distribution even for the very same trades. I recomputed it from the export of the 4,011 test candidates, as an approximation since that export only contains candidate buys. On the trades of the 5 surviving wallets, the share with at least one co-buyer falls from 6.2% when all 9 wallets count to 2.2% when only the 5 count, and the count can never exceed 4. So about two thirds of the 'confirmed' trades lose their confirmation, and the feature becomes almost constant at zero. A model trained on the 9-wallet world and served on the 5-wallet world would see a shifted input, which is covariate shift. The post-audit replay retrained on the 5-wallet data, so it was consistent, but the feature carries much less information there. The fix is to treat it as pool-dependent: retrain whenever the pool changes, or normalise it by the number of other active wallets.

follow_ups.q: Is removing excluded wallets from the count a leak or a fix?
follow_ups.a: A fix. An excluded wallet was removed because its activity was bot-like or contaminated; letting it confirm other trades would carry that noise into the remaining signal. The price is that the feature changes whenever the pool changes.

follow_ups.q: Would a model trained on 9 wallets still work on 5?
follow_ups.a: It would run, but its splits on the co-buyer count were learned on a distribution where confirmation was about three times as common. Predictions on the shifted input are not validated, so I'd retrain rather than trust it.

follow_ups.q: How would you detect this automatically?
follow_ups.a: Log the daily distribution of each feature in live and compare it with training, for example with a population stability index or simply the share of non-zero co-buyer counts. A pool change should also trigger retraining by rule.

follow_ups.q: Why is your recount only approximate?
follow_ups.a: The export contains only the 4,011 test candidates. The real feature counts every buy by active tracked wallets, including rows dropped later for cold start or pending labels, so the true shares can be slightly higher.

cards.topic: The 'favourite tokens' exclusion is not point-in-time
cards.question: For the next cycle you decided to drop smart_money_09's trades on tokens it had traded at least 10 times. How is that list computed, is it point-in-time, and why might that matter?
cards.answer: The rule, decided on 17 September for the next cycle, is: for smart_money_09 only, any token it has traded 10 times or more, buys and sells together, is a 'favourite', and its trades on those tokens are removed from training and test. The list is computed on the whole history in the database at the moment the script runs, not as of each trade. So it is not point-in-time: a token that crosses 10 trades after the test window, or late inside it, is treated as a favourite for the whole period, including the trades where, at the time, it was only the wallet's second or third trade on it. That uses future information to decide which rows exist. It was documented and accepted as data cleaning, not a feature, and on the first cycle's data its effect was tiny: 9 of that wallet's 58 selected signals were on favourite tokens, and removing them moved expectancy from +0.0274 to +0.0278, according to an internal analysis. But it is also a filter you cannot apply live, because live you do not yet know which tokens will become favourites. The point-in-time version counts only trades before each buy, and the honest check is to run both and compare.

follow_ups.q: Why not exclude the whole wallet instead?
follow_ups.a: Because its edge in the first cycle came mostly from isolated picks, not from the favourite regime: removing the wallet entirely lowered expectancy from +0.0274 to +0.0238 in the internal analysis. Excluding only the regime kept the useful part, at the cost of this point-in-time issue.

follow_ups.q: Is this the same issue as for smart_money_03?
follow_ups.a: No. For smart_money_03, the favourite regime carried essentially all of its positive contribution and was concentrated on a single day; that wallet was excluded entirely under the fragile-regime criterion. The token filter was applied only to smart_money_09.

follow_ups.q: Can a row filter leak if the model never sees the filtered column?
follow_ups.a: Yes. The filter decides which outcomes appear in the training and test sets. If it is correlated with outcomes and uses future information, every metric computed on the filtered set is conditioned on the future.

follow_ups.q: Was this hidden?
follow_ups.a: No, it is written in the code's own documentation as a known, accepted limitation, with the condition for revisiting it. What I'd add is the measurement: point-in-time against full-history on the next cycle's window.

cards.topic: No random seed: where the real reproducibility risk was
cards.question: You never set a random seed in your LightGBM training. Isn't your result irreproducible? Where is the real reproducibility risk in your project?
cards.answer: The missing seed is not a problem here, because my configuration used no randomness: no row subsampling, no feature subsampling, no bagging, so the seed has nothing to act on. The training is deterministic, and I confirmed it: rerunning the pipeline reproduced exactly the same 927 selected signals. The real risk is elsewhere, in everything around the model. First, the data is a moving database, not a frozen snapshot: labels were filled in after the fact, a spam reclassification was added, a local copy silently stopped syncing for several days and 5,215 trades were recovered by backfill, and four trades changed status between two snapshots without explanation. Second, the price source changed: a second provider was added and tried first, so relabelling today could give different labels. Third, artefacts: the worst incident of the project was a model-file mix-up, where validation numbers came from the model trained on train plus test, inflating expectancy from +2.7% to +5.39%. Fourth, library versions were not pinned. So reproducibility means versioning data, model files and environment, not choosing a seed.

follow_ups.q: Would adding bagging have helped?
follow_ups.a: Possibly for variance, but it would have introduced seed dependence. Then I'd fix the seed for reproducibility and also run many seeds to measure how much the selected set moves, since a single seed hides that spread.

follow_ups.q: How did you know the model-file mix-up happened?
follow_ups.a: It came out of the re-check in the 24 hours after the PASS: the validation numbers turned out to have been produced, at one point, by the model trained on train plus test, not the genuine out-of-sample one. Rerunning with the genuine out-of-sample model gave +2.7% instead of +5.39%. Recording the model's identity with each result would have caught it at once.

follow_ups.q: Is reproducing exactly the same 927 signals strong evidence?
follow_ups.a: It proves the computation is deterministic on that database state, nothing more. It says nothing about whether the result survives a different window, seed-dependent training or cleaner data, which is what the post-audit replay tested.

follow_ups.q: What is the cheapest single improvement?
follow_ups.a: Freezing an export of the exact rows behind each published number, with a hash written in the report. Most of the project's surprises came from the data underneath changing.

cards.topic: The label definition is a hidden hyperparameter
cards.question: Why a 2x target? If you had labelled wins as 1.5x, 3x or 5x, would you have found the same result, and isn't the label choice itself a parameter you could have overfitted?
cards.answer: Yes, the label is a hyperparameter, and an important one, even though no tuning loop touched it. A win was 'the 15-minute close reaches 2x entry within 3 hours 11 minutes'. Change the multiple and the problem changes: on the 4,011 test candidates the base rate is 6.61% at 1.5x, 5.01% at 2x, 3.91% at 3x and 1.62% at 5x, and 8.03% at 2x with no time limit. So the baseline in the z-test, the class weight and the trees all depend on it. Two things make it sensitive in my project. First, the 2x target came from the exit-policy calibration, which the report itself says was calibrated on a distribution that included the test window, so the label was not chosen blind. Second, I did not test alternatives, so I cannot say whether 2x is a robust choice or a lucky one. If several labels had been tried and the best reported, the 1.96 bar would no longer be honest: with five labels, a Bonferroni correction puts it at about 2.58. The right practice is to fix the label before the test, from economics, and report a sensitivity table across labels as a robustness check, not as a menu.

follow_ups.q: Why not let the model predict the peak ratio directly, as a regression?
follow_ups.a: It avoids choosing a cut-off, but the target is extremely skewed (most tokens never move, a few go 10x), so squared-error regression would be dominated by outliers. A classifier on the traded event is simpler; the cost is the hidden choice of threshold (prj-219 discusses this trade-off).

follow_ups.q: Would 1.5x have been better because there are more positives?
follow_ups.a: More positives give more power, but a 1.5x label with a 2x take-profit teaches the model an event you don't trade. You would have to change the exit rule too, which changes costs and expectancy. The right comparison is label and exit together.

follow_ups.q: How would you present a sensitivity table without it becoming a menu?
follow_ups.a: Pre-register the primary label and the list of alternatives, report all of them with the same metrics, and base the verdict only on the primary one. The alternatives answer 'is it robust?', not 'which is best?'.

follow_ups.q: Isn't 2x just a round number?
follow_ups.a: It is round, and it sits inside the 75th to 90th percentile band of observed peaks. But the band itself came from a calibration that included the test window, so 'round number' does not fully make it data-independent.

cards.topic: Candle timestamps: open time or close time?
cards.question: Your labels use 15-minute candle closes. Does a candle's timestamp mark the start or the end of the period, and what happens if your two price providers use different conventions?
cards.answer: A candle summarises a period, here 15 minutes, with open, high, low and close prices, and its timestamp can mark either the start or the end of that period. It sounds pedantic, but it decides when the close price actually happened. My original provider gives the close time, and I paired that time with the close price, which is consistent. The second provider, added on 22 September and tried first, returns a list whose first field is, by that API's convention, the start of the period, and the code pairs it with the close price. If that convention is confirmed, that price is stamped 15 minutes earlier than it really happened. Since the entry is the nearest close within 30 minutes of the buy, the true entry moves from a random point within 7.5 minutes of the buy to between 7.5 and 22.5 minutes after it, 15 minutes later on average. For a memecoin that moves in minutes, that is a different trade. It has no effect on the published numbers, which predate that change, but the next cycle would mix two conventions over time, which could look like a regime change. The fix is a one-line test against the API and a single timestamp convention.

follow_ups.q: Is using the close the right choice at all?
follow_ups.a: The close is the only price known at the end of the bar, so it is a safe, non-anticipating choice for entries. For the peak, using closes rather than highs underestimates the true maximum and can miss take-profits touched inside a bar (prj-101).

follow_ups.q: Why didn't this affect the published results?
follow_ups.a: All published Stage 1 and Stage 2 labels were computed with the original provider, which uses close-time stamps consistently. The second provider was added on 22 September, after those results.

follow_ups.q: Could this offset be a look-ahead bias?
follow_ups.a: Yes, mildly. An open-time stamp paired with a close makes the price appear earlier than it was, so a 'nearest close' entry can use a price formed up to 22.5 minutes after the buy while looking contemporaneous. That is information from after the decision, inside the label.

follow_ups.q: How would you store timestamps to avoid this in general?
follow_ups.a: Store one convention everywhere, preferably the time the price became known (bar close), in UTC, with the source and bar length recorded next to each value. Convert at the boundary where data enters, never downstream.

cards.topic: Two price sources: how to check they agree
cards.question: After your first price provider ran out of quota, you added a second one and query it first. How would you check that the two sources give consistent prices and labels before mixing them in one dataset?
cards.answer: I would treat it as a measurement problem: two instruments measuring the same thing, and I need to know whether they agree before I average their readings. Concretely, take the tokens both providers cover and compare at three levels. First, the raw series: align the 15-minute closes and measure the gap, at lag zero and at a lag of one bar, which also settles the timestamp convention. Second, the label inputs: entry price, peak ratio and time to peak for the same trades. Third, the labels themselves: the share of trades where both say win or both say no-win, and Cohen's kappa, because with a 5% win rate raw agreement is misleading. Then I'd check the structural differences: which pool each provider picks for a token, whether the token is the base or the quote of that pool, and which tokens only one provider covers. Finally, store the source with every label and test whether the base rate differs by source. As far as the repository documents, only coverage and the base-or-quote trap were checked on examples; a systematic agreement test was not done, so that would be the first step of the next cycle.

follow_ups.q: Why is querying the second provider first a choice with consequences?
follow_ups.a: Because it decides which source labels most new trades. The reason was operational: the first provider's quota error would otherwise stop each labelling pass. But it means the label source changes from 22 September, correlated with time.

follow_ups.q: What is the difference between kappa and accuracy here?
follow_ups.a: Accuracy, or raw agreement, counts all matches, and with 95% no-wins two sources agree most of the time by chance. Kappa subtracts that chance agreement, so it measures how much they agree beyond what their base rates alone imply.

follow_ups.q: What if the two providers pick different pools for the same token?
follow_ups.a: Then they may be measuring different markets, and the right price is the pool where you would actually trade. I'd record the pool, prefer the deepest one consistently, and treat large cross-pool gaps as a liquidity signal, not noise.

follow_ups.q: Would averaging the two sources fix it?
follow_ups.a: No. Averaging mixes conventions and pools and hides disagreement. Better to pick one rule per token, flag fallback labels, and measure whether results change when they are removed.

cards.topic: Paper trading scored with the backtest's labels: it can't test your reaction delay
cards.question: Your strategy copies wallets with a delay of seconds. Did paper trading test whether you could actually get in at a good price after that delay?
cards.answer: No. Paper trading made its decisions live, which protects against hindsight in the decision. But its outcomes were scored with exactly the same machinery as the backtest. Each simulated buy was evaluated with the wallet's own trade: its entry price, its peak over 24 hours from 15-minute candle closes, and the time to that peak, all measured from the wallet's buy, not from when my system would have bought. The paper trader polled the trade database every 30 seconds, so my real entry would have been later and probably higher, and that cost is invisible in the result. Because both stages share the same labels, any bias in them is common to both and Stage 2 cannot detect it. For example, if the price is already 10% up when I'd buy, a 2× target from my entry is 2.2× from the wallet's price. On the 4,011 candidates, the hit rate for 2× is 5.01% and for 3× it's 3.91%, so 2.2× sits somewhere in between. To test the delay you need your own decision timestamp and a live executable quote, for example a swap quote at that moment, then outcomes measured from that price.

follow_ups.q: Why does a shared bias make the comparison useless?
follow_ups.a: Because the comparison only shows differences; an error present equally in both disappears from the difference. You need an independent measurement, here a real executable quote, to see it.

follow_ups.q: How would you estimate the delay cost without trading?
follow_ups.a: Request a swap quote at your decision time for your size and compare it with the wallet's fill price. The ratio is your entry slippage; its distribution by wallet and delay tells you how much edge the delay consumes.

follow_ups.q: Could the delay ever help?
follow_ups.a: Sometimes: waiting can filter out instant dumps. But that's a hypothesis to test with the same timestamped quotes, not something to assume.

follow_ups.q: Is 30-second polling the main delay?
follow_ups.a: It adds up to 30 seconds on top of detection and confirmation time. A push design (react to the stream directly) would cut it; that's an engineering fix, but only measured entry prices show whether it matters.

cards.topic: Optimal trade size with a fixed fee and price impact: S* = √(FR/2)
cards.question: Your cost scenarios use a fixed percentage of slippage per leg, whatever the trade size, plus a fixed priority fee. If price impact actually grows with size, how would you choose the trade size, and does the +2.74% edge survive?
cards.answer: I'd model the round-trip cost as a function of the trade size S in SOL. There are three parts. The fixed fees F are spread over the trade, so they cost F/S. The pool fee a is paid on each leg, so 2a. And the price impact is about S/R per leg in a constant-product pool holding R SOL, so 2S/R. That gives c(S) = F/S + 2a + 2S/R. It's U-shaped: small trades are eaten by the fixed fee, large ones by impact. Setting the derivative to zero gives S* = √(FR/2) and a minimum cost of c* = 2a + 2√(2F/R). With the report's low scenario (priority fee 0.0002 SOL, so F = 2 × 0.000205 = 0.00041 SOL for two transactions, and a pool fee of 0.25% per leg), and assuming a pool of 50 SOL, S* ≈ 0.10 SOL and the cost is 1.31%. At 1 SOL the same formula gives 4.54%, and at the 1.17 SOL behind the cost chart, 5.22%, which is above the +2.74% gross edge. In a 200 SOL pool it's 0.20 SOL and 0.90%. In the moderate scenario the cost is 3.53% at best in a 50 SOL pool, so no size is profitable, and 2.27% in a 200 SOL pool, profitable only between about 0.27 and 1.47 SOL. The pool sizes are my assumption, because the report records no reserves. The point is that size is a decision variable, and the edge has a tiny capacity.

follow_ups.q: Where does the impact S/R come from?
follow_ups.a: In a constant-product pool with R SOL, buying with S SOL gives Y·S/(R+S) tokens, so the average price is (1 + S/R) times spot. For small S that's an impact of S/R per leg, and the sell leg is similar.

follow_ups.q: Why is the optimum where the two costs are equal?
follow_ups.a: The fixed-fee share falls like 1/S and the impact rises like S. The sum of a term in 1/S and a term in S is minimal where they're equal, which gives √(2F/R) each.

follow_ups.q: How realistic are pools of 50 and 200 SOL?
follow_ups.a: I don't know for these tokens: the report and the data don't record reserves. That's why I give two depths and treat them as assumptions. Logging reserves at signal time is the first fix.

follow_ups.q: Would a bigger account make more money?
follow_ups.a: Not proportionally. Beyond S* every extra SOL per trade costs more in impact, and above the band's upper end the trade loses. Capacity is limited by pool depth, not by capital.

cards.topic: The no-price convention: how −34.27% on 40% of candidates flips the sign
cards.question: Scoring all 4,011 test candidates with the exit rule gives about −7.96% per candidate before costs. 40% of them have no price history and are scored at the stop level, −34.27%. How much does that convention drive the result?
cards.answer: Almost entirely. The 1,618 candidates with no price history are 40.3% of the 4,011, and at −34.27% each they contribute −13.82 points, more than the whole −7.96%. Score them at 0 instead and the average becomes +5.86%. Score them at −100%, a total loss, and it becomes −34.48%. The rule of thumb is 4.03 points of average per 10 points of assumed loss, because 40.3% of candidates carry the assumption. The loss that would make the average exactly zero is about 14.5%. On the 2,393 candidates that do have prices, the average is +9.82%. So the sign of the 'buy everything' benchmark is set by a convention, not by prices. The right value depends on what happened: if the buy could never execute because there was no real pool, the honest score is 0, no trade; if it executed and the token was drained, it's close to −100%; the stop level assumes the stop could be filled, which needs a pool. So I'd report a range, from −34.5% to +5.9%, and compare the model with the benchmark only under the same convention, since the +2.74% versus −7.96% gap of about 10.7 points is only meaningful that way.

follow_ups.q: Why not just drop the no-price candidates?
follow_ups.a: Because they're missing for a reason linked to the outcome: tokens that never got a pool or died at once. Dropping them gives +9.82% on the survivors, a survivorship-biased number.

follow_ups.q: How would you pick the right convention?
follow_ups.a: Take a random sample of no-price tokens and check on-chain whether a pool existed and whether a swap at the wallet's time would have filled. That estimates the mix of 'no trade' and 'total loss'.

follow_ups.q: Does this affect the model's +2.74%?
follow_ups.a: It may, through how many no-price tokens the model selects. The +2.74% was computed with the same stop-level convention, so I'd recompute the selected trades under each convention before using the 10.7-point gap.

follow_ups.q: Why is the sensitivity exactly 0.403?
follow_ups.a: The average is linear in the assumed score, with a slope equal to the share of candidates carrying it: 1,618 out of 4,011.

cards.topic: Expectancy by exit bucket: how much of the −7.96% is measured, how much assumed?
cards.question: You decompose the −7.96% average over the 4,011 test candidates into exit buckets: target, approximate peak exit, breakeven, stop and no price. Which part of that number comes from observed prices, and which from approximations?
cards.answer: Only a small part is measured. The outcome is fixed by the price data for just two buckets: the 201 targets at +100% and the 133 confirmed stops at −34.27%. That's 334 candidates, 8.3% of the total, and they contribute +5.01 − 1.14 = +3.87 points. The other 91.7% contribute −11.84 points, and all of it rests on a rule I chose. The 1,526 approximate peak exits are scored at their peak, about +5.2% on average, which is an upper bound since nobody sells exactly at the top. Of these, 922 have a peak ratio of exactly 1.0, meaning the price never rose above entry; they're scored at 0, but their real exit lies somewhere between the stop and 0. The 533 whose peak came after the maximum hold are scored at 0, with the exit price unknown. And the 1,618 with no prices are scored at the stop by convention. So apart from the no-price convention and the late peaks, whose direction is unknown, the approximations lean optimistic. To give one stress: if those 922 had all gone to the stop, the average would fall from −7.96% to about −15.8%. Even the 'confirmed' targets are an upper bound, because the stop could have been hit before the rally. I'd report bounds rather than one number, and store the price path to close the gap.

follow_ups.q: Why is the peak exit an upper bound?
follow_ups.a: It sells at the highest price in the window, which no real exit rule achieves. A time exit sells at whatever the price is at the max hold, at or below the peak.

follow_ups.q: What is the best case for the 922 with a peak ratio of 1.0?
follow_ups.a: Zero: the price never rose above entry, so the best exit is flat. The worst is the stop. That's why scoring them 0 is a bound, not an estimate.

follow_ups.q: Could the measured part alone tell you anything?
follow_ups.a: Yes, as a floor on information: 201 targets and 133 stops are real. But they're 8.3% of candidates chosen by outcome, so their average says nothing about the whole population.

follow_ups.q: What would you store to remove the approximations?
follow_ups.a: The minimum price before the peak, to settle stop-versus-target order, and prices at a few fixed times, including the max hold, to get the time-exit price directly.

cards.topic: Why not bet against the wallets? Shorting, selection value and the −7.96% average
cards.question: If the average candidate trade loses money and your model's rejected trades are worse still, why not do the opposite: bet against the wallets, or short the tokens your model rejects?
cards.answer: Because the negative average is not something you can trade. Across the 4,011 test candidates, if I score each one with the exit rule, the average is about −7.96% per candidate before costs, but almost all of that comes from the 40% of candidates with no price history at all, which I score at −34.27%, the stop level, by convention. Those tokens often never reached a real pool, so there is nothing to short and the 'loss' is an assumption, not a price. On the 60% that do have prices, the average long return is about +9.8% before costs, so shorting them would lose money. On top of that, you can't short a token launched minutes ago: there is no borrow market and no perpetual future, and a short on a token that doubles loses 100% or more. So the only way to 'bet against' a wallet here is not to copy it. That is exactly what the model does: its value is selection, roughly +2.74% per selected trade before costs against −7.96% for buying everything, about 10.7 points. Both numbers come from the same exit evaluation, so they share the stop-level convention for no-price tokens, but the gap inherits that convention (prj-344) and is not significant, so I treat it as indicative.

follow_ups.q: Is the 10.7-point selection value statistically solid?
follow_ups.a: It's a difference of two averages computed differently, and the +2.74% itself was never significant once clustering is counted (prj-230). I'd quote it as a rough order of magnitude, not as an edge.

follow_ups.q: Could you short via a perpetual future on bigger tokens?
follow_ups.a: On large, established tokens yes, but that's a different universe and a different signal. The wallets trade new tokens, where no perpetual exists in the first hours, so the signal and the instrument don't overlap.

follow_ups.q: Then is a wallet with a very low win rate useful as a contrarian signal?
follow_ups.a: Only as a 'don't buy' signal. The wallet with a 0.9% base rate (1 win in 109) tells you to stay out, which saves money, but you can't monetise it by shorting.

follow_ups.q: What would change your mind?
follow_ups.a: Tradable downside: tokens with a borrow market, and a model trained on falls, evaluated after borrow and trading costs. None of that exists in this data.

cards.topic: Copying the wallet's exit instead of a triple barrier
cards.question: You copy the wallets' entries but use your own triple-barrier exit. Why not simply sell when the wallet sells? Could you have tested that with your data?
cards.answer: It's a natural variant, and I didn't test it, for three reasons. First, data: the system records each wallet's sells, with the time and the token quantity, but my prices are 15-minute candle closes and only two price points are kept per trade, entry and peak, so I can't price a sell that happens at a precise second. Second, mechanics: if I sell 5 to 60 seconds after the leader on a thin pool, his sale has already pushed the price down, and other followers are selling too, so I exit after him, at a worse price, which is the exit-liquidity problem. On a constant-product pool, a sale of 2% of the token reserve already moves the price about 3.9%. Third, coverage: wallets sell partially, sell in many pieces, move tokens to other wallets or never sell, so I'd still need a fallback time stop. A track I've considered, but not tested yet, is to start simpler: copy a single wallet's round trips as they are, matching its sells to its buys first-in first-out on token quantity and pricing both legs with market prices, as a first rough check of whether its own exits carry an edge. That would be a possible next step. A clean test would match each buy to the wallet's later sells, first-in first-out on token quantity, price the follower's exit at the sell time plus a lag with trade-level prices, and pre-register it as one extra variant against the barrier rule. My guess is that copying the exit inherits the leader's timing skill but pays his impact, and the net sign is an empirical question.

follow_ups.q: Which exit would you expect to win?
follow_ups.a: I don't know, and that's the honest answer. Copy-exit keeps the leader's timing skill but pays his impact and my delay; the barrier ignores his skill but has a known, bounded loss. It depends on how big his sales are relative to the pool and how fast prices move after them.

follow_ups.q: Doesn't the barrier rule have its own leak?
follow_ups.a: Yes, its parameters were calibrated on a distribution that included the test window, documented and deliberately left frozen (prj-026). A copy-exit rule has no parameters to calibrate, which is one advantage.

follow_ups.q: How would you detect that a wallet dumps on its followers?
follow_ups.a: Look at whether its sells cluster right after bursts of buying by other tracked wallets in the same token, and whether its sell sizes grow with follower inflows (prj-118).

follow_ups.q: What if the wallet sells in ten small pieces?
follow_ups.a: Exit proportionally to each piece, or on the first piece with the remainder on the time stop. That choice must be fixed in advance.

cards.topic: Threats to validity: internal, construct, external and statistical conclusion
cards.question: Organise the weaknesses of your study. Using the four classic threats to validity (internal, construct, external, statistical conclusion), where does your Stage 1 result stand?
cards.answer: I find this framework useful because it separates four different questions. Statistical conclusion validity asks whether the numbers support an effect at all: my z of 10.02 assumed independent signals, and re-clustering by wallet or wallet-and-token brought it to 2.5 to 4.1, with only 9 wallets, so even that is fragile. Internal validity asks whether the selection really causes the higher win rate, or whether something else does: there were leaks, a model trained on part of the test, an exit policy calibrated on a distribution including the test window, label-timing problems in the win-rate feature, no purge, and about half of the lift is simply which wallets the model picks. Construct validity asks whether I measured the right thing: my label is a 2× move on 15-minute closes from the leader's buy time, which is not the follower's profit, and 40% of candidates have no price and get a conventional −34.27%. External validity asks whether it generalises: 9 wallets, 5 days, one hot day carrying almost half the wins, then a pool cut to 5 and a live test that failed. The weakest link for me is construct validity: even a perfectly significant, leak-free result on that label wouldn't prove money for a follower.

follow_ups.q: Which single change would improve validity the most?
follow_ups.a: Labels computed from the follower's realistic entry time with trade-level prices. It fixes the main construct problem, and once the label is right, the other checks become meaningful.

follow_ups.q: Isn't paper trading enough to settle external validity?
follow_ups.a: It settles more than a backtest, because prices were unknown at decision time. But it was 5 days, about 41 admitted trades after costs, and it still used 15-minute candles for labels, so it doesn't test reaction delay or fills (prj-342).

follow_ups.q: Where would a placebo test fit?
follow_ups.a: It checks internal validity of the pipeline: shuffle labels or use random entries, rerun everything, and verify z comes out near zero. If it doesn't, the pipeline itself leaks (prj-228).

follow_ups.q: What's 'conclusion validity' versus 'power'?
follow_ups.a: Power is part of it: a non-significant result with low power is not evidence of no effect. My next cycle, at about 435 signals with clustering, has roughly a one-in-three chance of detecting a lift like the post-audit one (prj-354).

cards.topic: Losing streaks, drawdown and a risk budget for a 12% hit-rate strategy
cards.question: Your strategy wins about one trade in eight. Even taking your initial +2.74% per trade at face value, what losing streaks and drawdowns should you expect, and how would you size positions?
cards.answer: With a 12.2% hit rate, long losing streaks are normal, not a warning sign. The expected longest run of non-wins in 927 trades is about $\ln(np)/\ln(1/q)$, which gives about 36 in a row. The report's numbers imply an average non-win of about −10.8% if a win pays +100%, so that streak costs about 3.9 stakes before costs. Using a drift-and-volatility approximation, +2.74% per trade with a standard deviation around 37%, the probability of ever falling 11.5 stakes below a given level is about 1%, if trades were independent. But they're not: if I apply the same win and loss sizes to the daily table, the first three test days lose about 19 stakes in a row before the hot fifth day makes it all back. So the real drawdown is driven by bad days, not by single unlucky trades. I'd size from a loss budget: decide the drawdown I can accept, divide by a stressed drawdown in stakes, and get a stake of roughly 1% of capital, more than ten times smaller than what Kelly would suggest. And the kill-switch, three negative days in a row, would plausibly have fired before day five.

follow_ups.q: Would the kill-switch have stopped the Stage 1 strategy?
follow_ups.a: In this illustration the first three days are negative before costs, so a three-negative-days rule would have fired before day five, the day carrying most of the profit. That's the trade-off: it stops bad strategies, and sometimes good ones (prj-121).

follow_ups.q: Why not just use the Sharpe ratio for sizing?
follow_ups.a: With a skewed payoff and clustered trades the Sharpe hides the tail; drawdown in stakes, stressed by bad days, is closer to what actually stops you (prj-124).

follow_ups.q: Is −10.8% the real average loss?
follow_ups.a: It's implied by the report's +2.74% and 12.19% if every win pays exactly +100%. Real wins can exceed 2× before exit and costs aren't included, so it's an order of magnitude.

follow_ups.q: How would you set the risk budget in practice?
follow_ups.a: Fix it before trading, in money and in days: for example stop at 20% of capital lost or three negative days, and resume only after a fresh review, never automatically.

cards.topic: Is a 2× peak just volatility? The maximum of a random walk and the reflection principle
cards.question: Your label is 'the price reaches 2× within about 3 hours'. On tokens this volatile, couldn't that happen by pure chance? How likely is a 2× under a random walk, and what does that mean for your 12.2% precision?
cards.answer: Yes, and it's an important check. Under a driftless random walk on the log price, the reflection principle says the probability that the maximum over a horizon $T$ exceeds a level $b$ is twice the probability of ending above it: $2\,(1-\Phi(b/(\sigma\sqrt T)))$. With $b=\ln 2$, a horizon of 11,458 seconds, about 12.7 fifteen-minute periods, and an illustrative volatility of 10% per 15 minutes, that's about 5.2%, almost exactly my 5.0% base rate. So the base rate is consistent with pure noise. Worse, the probability is very sensitive to volatility: a volatility of about 12.6% instead of 9.9% is enough to go from 5.0% to 12.2%. So a model could reach my precision just by picking more volatile tokens, with no directional edge at all. What volatility can't do is create expected profit: if the price is a martingale, the probability of hitting 2× before the stop at 0.6573× is exactly 25.5%, the breakeven hit rate, and the expected return is zero before costs. That's why the precision test alone can't prove an edge, and why the money test matters.

follow_ups.q: Where does the factor 2 come from, intuitively?
follow_ups.a: Once the path touches the barrier, going up or down from there is equally likely, so for every path that touched and ended below, there's a mirror path that ended above. The paths ending above all touched, so the touching probability is twice the ending-above probability.

follow_ups.q: Is 10% per 15 minutes realistic for these tokens?
follow_ups.a: I didn't measure it; it's illustrative. I chose it because it reproduces the 5% base rate, which is the point: the base rate is what pure noise at that volatility would give. Measuring it from candles before entry is part of the test I'd run.

follow_ups.q: Does the stop change the hit probability of 2× within 3 hours?
follow_ups.a: The label I used is '2× before the time limit', not 'before the stop', so the formula applies to the label. For the trade's payoff, the stop matters, and that's where the 25.5% breakeven comes from.

follow_ups.q: If wins are just volatility, why did paper trading not lose more?
follow_ups.a: With a martingale price the expectation is zero before costs, so you'd expect roughly zero gross and minus costs net: Stage 2's corrected gross of about +0.15% per trade and negative net results are consistent with that, though not proof.

cards.topic: Why not use the wallets' realised P&L as the label?
cards.question: You follow 'profitable' wallets, yet your label is a price move after their buy. Why not label each trade with what the wallet actually made on it? Did you ever check that the wallets themselves were profitable?
cards.answer: I couldn't, and that's a real gap. The system stores each buy and sell as a change in the wallet's token balance, in token units; the SOL side of the swap was only read to check that a buy had a counterpart, the spam filter, and was never stored. Without the SOL paid and received, I can't compute any wallet's realised P&L. So the premise that these wallets are profitable rests on the leaderboard, and my data measures something else: what the price did after they bought. A cheap first check I've considered, but not tested yet, would match each wallet's sells to its buys first-in first-out on token quantity and price both legs with candle prices (prj-347): only an approximation, but a possible next step. The data is recoverable, because the spam reclassification already re-fetched about 20,000 historical buys from the node provider, so I'd store the SOL legs and fees. But even with it, the wallet's P&L wouldn't be my label. It includes their speed and their exit timing, which a follower can't copy; it needs matching sells to buys, with partial sales, transfers out and positions never closed; and it's heavy-tailed and noisy. I'd use it for two things: to verify the wallets' profitability independently of the leaderboard, and as a feature or a sanity check, while keeping the label tied to what a follower could have done.

follow_ups.q: Isn't 'profitable on the leaderboard' good enough?
follow_ups.a: It's a selection on past success, so regression to the mean is expected, and the leaderboard's own computation is a black box. For a decision that risks money I'd want an internal, point-in-time measure.

follow_ups.q: Could you approximate the SOL amount from prices?
follow_ups.a: Roughly: token quantity times the 15-minute close. But the close can be far from the execution price on these tokens, and the error would be largest exactly on the big moves, so it's not a substitute for the swap's own numbers. It's still a cheap first check I've considered as a possible next step, not something I've tested.

follow_ups.q: Why did the system skip the SOL leg?
follow_ups.a: The parser was built to detect buys and sells from token balance changes; the SOL side was only used to filter spam. Storing it would have cost nothing; it's a design gap I'd own.

follow_ups.q: Would the model's label change at all?
follow_ups.a: The binary label could stay, but defined from the follower's entry time with trade-level prices. The wallet's P&L would come in as a feature and as a check of the premise.

cards.topic: Train-serve skew: an inventory of where live features differ from backtest features
cards.question: Your paper trading ran the same decision code as the backtest. Does that guarantee the model saw the same inputs live as in training? List the places where training and serving could differ in your system.
cards.answer: No. Same code doesn't mean same inputs, because the inputs depend on what's in the database at decision time. I see at least six differences. One, the wallet win-rate feature: in the backtest, earlier buys already carry their 24-hour outcome, while live, buys less than 24 hours old are still pending and excluded, so the feature is computed on different histories. The same thing changes how many trades pass the 'at least 10 earlier buys with a known outcome' rule. Two, co-buyers: in the backtest the ±60 second window sees buyers after the trade too; live, polling every 30 seconds only sees buys already stored. Three, the wallet pool changed from 9 to 5, which shifts the co-buyer distribution. Four, data cleanliness: the history behind the features wasn't reprocessed for spam, while new trades are parsed with the fixed parser. Five, the model served isn't the one evaluated: the threshold was chosen on a 20-day model, tested on a 25-day model, and deployed on a 30-day retrain. Six, the next cycle may mix two candle-time conventions. The good news is that every live decision stores its feature values, so I'd recompute the same features offline for the same trades at the same timestamps and compare them row by row.

follow_ups.q: Which skew would you expect to matter most?
follow_ups.a: The win-rate maturity, because the win rate is the most informative feature and the effect is systematic: training always sees more resolved history than live. I'd measure it first.

follow_ups.q: Is train-serve skew a leak?
follow_ups.a: Not the same thing, but they're linked here: the symmetric co-buyer window and the matured labels are information from the future in the backtest, so they're leaks, and they show up as skew in production.

follow_ups.q: How does this relate to Stage 2 failing?
follow_ups.a: It's one plausible contributor, among others like the dominant wallet's regime and costs. Paper trading measures the combined effect; the row-by-row comparison would isolate the skew part.

follow_ups.q: What is a PSI and why the 0.25 rule?
follow_ups.a: It's a symmetric, KL-like divergence between two binned distributions. The 0.1 / 0.25 cut-offs are an industry convention from credit scoring, not a statistical test, so I'd use it as a flag, not a verdict.

cards.topic: Is the model just a wallet selector? Decomposing the lift with the real base rates (76.7 vs 113 wins)
cards.question: Your selected signals are concentrated in a few wallets that also have high base rates. With your actual numbers, how much of the jump from 5.0% to 12.2% precision is just 'pick the good wallets', and how much is the model choosing well within each wallet?
cards.answer: I computed it from the export of the 4,011 test candidates, using only columns that don't depend on the model. Each wallet has its own base rate: from 13.2% for the most active one down to 0.9%. If, within each wallet, I picked exactly as many trades as the model did but at random, I'd expect 76.7 wins out of 927, an 8.3% precision. The model got 113, 12.2%. So of the 7.2-point lift over 5.0%, about 3.3 points, roughly 45%, is composition, which wallets the model favours, and about 3.9 points, 55%, is selection within wallets. A stratified test that compares, wallet by wallet, the model's wins with what random picks would give, a Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel-type test, gives a z of about 6.3, but it still treats trades within a wallet as independent, so tokens and days would bring it down. The within-wallet part is real but uneven: strong for one wallet, from 4.2% to 17.2%, absent or negative for others. And part of it may be timing rather than skill: picking a wallet's hot days is still a kind of wallet-period selection.

follow_ups.q: So is the model 'mostly a wallet selector'?
follow_ups.a: About half. Composition explains roughly 45% of the lift and the rest is within-wallet, but concentrated in one wallet that was later excluded, so I wouldn't claim strong within-wallet skill either.

follow_ups.q: Why not just train one model per wallet?
follow_ups.a: With 109 to 795 candidates per wallet and 1 to 83 wins, per-wallet models would be hopelessly noisy. A pooled model with wallet as a stratum in the evaluation is the better compromise.

follow_ups.q: What's the simplest benchmark this suggests?
follow_ups.a: 'Copy every trade of the wallets with the best past base rate.' If the model can't beat that rule on fresh data, it adds nothing (prj-208).

follow_ups.q: Would leave-one-wallet-out help here?
follow_ups.a: Yes, it tests whether the mapping from features to outcomes transfers to an unseen wallet, which is the strongest form of 'not just a lookup table' (prj-215, prj-226).

cards.topic: Next cycle: the minimum detectable effect with about 435 clustered signals
cards.question: Suppose the next cycle produces about as many signals as the post-audit replay, roughly 435, with a base win rate around 5.9%. What is the smallest improvement in win rate you could reliably detect, and is that enough?
cards.answer: Treating the 435 signals as independent, the standard error of the win rate under the base rate is √(0.059 × 0.941 / 435) ≈ 1.13 points. But signals cluster by wallet. In Stage 1 the wallet bootstrap gave a standard error of 1.76 points against 0.716 for independent trades, a design effect of (1.76/0.716)² ≈ 6.0. If that carries over, which is an assumption, the standard error becomes 1.13 × √6.04 ≈ 2.77 points. The minimum detectable effect at 5% two-sided and 80% power is (1.96 + 0.84) × SE: about 3.2 points if independent, 7.75 points with clustering. At 50% power it's about 5.4 points. The post-audit replay showed 10.3% against 5.9%, an excess of 4.4 points. The chance of detecting an excess that size would be about 97% if signals were independent, but only about 36% with clustering. To reach 80% power on 4.4 points you'd need about 225 independent signals, or about 1,350 with a design effect of 6. With the wallet-and-token design effect of about 16, the detectable effect rises to about 12.6 points. So 435 clustered signals is underpowered for an effect of the size seen, and I'd plan the window from the power calculation, not from the calendar.

follow_ups.q: Why use the base-rate variance and not the alternative's?
follow_ups.a: It's the usual simplification. Under the alternative the variance is a bit larger, p(1−p) at 10.3% instead of 5.9%, so the true MDE is slightly bigger. It doesn't change the conclusion.

follow_ups.q: Would a one-sided test help?
follow_ups.a: It lowers 1.96 to 1.645, so the clustered MDE falls from about 7.75 to about 6.9 points. Still above 4.4, and a one-sided test has to be declared in advance.

follow_ups.q: Could you reduce the design effect instead of adding signals?
follow_ups.a: Partly: stratify by wallet and test within wallets, or cap the signals per wallet per day. But that also reduces the sample, so it's a trade-off, not a free gain.

follow_ups.q: Where does the 4.4-point excess come from?
follow_ups.a: From the post-audit replay: about 45 wins out of 435, 10.3%, against a base rate of 5.9%. The 45 is reconstructed from the reported rate.

cards.topic: Combining Stage 1 and Stage 2: inverse-variance pooling, and the gross-versus-net trap
cards.question: Stage 1 gave +2.74% per trade on 927 backtest signals, and Stage 2 about +0.15% on 1,019 simulated live buys, both before costs. Can you combine them into one estimate of the edge? And what about the −5.44% on the 41 trades admitted after costs?
cards.answer: Yes, but carefully. The standard way is inverse-variance weighting: each estimate is weighted by one over its squared standard error. I need a per-trade spread; I assume σ ≈ 0.38, which is an assumption. That gives standard errors of 0.38/√927 ≈ 1.25 points and 0.38/√1,019 ≈ 1.19 points. The pooled estimate is about +1.38% ± 0.86, so z ≈ 1.6: not significant. But first I'd check that the two agree. Their difference is 2.59 points with a standard error of 1.72, z ≈ 1.5. Cochran's Q is 2.25 and I² is about 56%, so there's moderate heterogeneity. A random-effects pool gives +1.42% ± 1.29. More importantly, pooling assumes both stages estimate the same thing without bias. Stage 1 is a backtest that had a leak, while Stage 2 is clean, so I'd trust Stage 2 and use Stage 1 as a prior at most. The trap is the −5.44%. It's net of costs, on an ENR-filtered subset of 41 trades that is itself part of the 1,019. Pooling it with the gross +2.74% gives about +2.39% ± 1.22, which looks precise but averages two different quantities, so it's meaningless.

follow_ups.q: Why weight by the inverse variance?
follow_ups.a: Among weighted averages of unbiased estimates of the same quantity, it's the one with the smallest variance. More precise estimates get more weight.

follow_ups.q: What does I² of 56% mean?
follow_ups.a: About half of the spread between the two stages is more than chance would produce. With only two estimates it's very imprecise, but it's a warning not to read the pooled number as one common effect.

follow_ups.q: How would you combine them in a Bayesian way?
follow_ups.a: Use Stage 1 as a prior, widened to reflect its possible bias, and update with Stage 2. The wider the prior, the closer the posterior is to the live +0.15%.

follow_ups.q: Could you ever compare the −5.44% with something?
follow_ups.a: Yes, with a backtest number built the same way: net of the same costs, ENR-filtered, under the same caps. Gross against net is never a valid comparison.

cards.topic: Walk me through your CV
cards.question: Walk me through your CV.
cards.answer:
*Open question (mock interview): no single right answer. Below is how to build yours, using only facts you've confirmed.*

**Structure: a spine, grouped proofs, the most relevant proof, a character proof, why here (90-120 seconds).**
1. **Who you are** (1 sentence): Diplôme d'ingénieur at Centrale Nantes (applied maths), after CPGE at Collège Stanislas (PCSI then PC). Say early that the finance on the CV is self-taught.
2. **What you've done, grouped not listed**:
   - *Commercial*: CNE (team of 9, 45k EUR of client contracts signed); BNP Paribas (2 partnerships signed, agreements drafted, 500k+ EUR of student loan applications analysed); Polifeb (co-founded, 3 clients signed, including a public-sector body); Sell For You.
   - *Analytical*: the Wavestone academic project (AI architectures and their risks, 50-page report co-authored, later presented in a podcast).
3. **Most relevant proof**: the Solana project: 15 wallets tested, two leaks and signal clustering found myself, the backtest z cut from 10.0 to 2.5–4.1 and a +7.5% simulated return turned into −5.2%, reported honestly in a technical report with zero capital at risk.
4. **Character**: modern pentathlon, two-time French champion, 11th at the Junior World Championships in laser-run (running and shooting), with the French team.
5. **Why here, why now**: the 6-month Global Markets internship from February 2027.

follow_ups.q: Which of these experiences are you proudest of?
follow_ups.a: Pick one and say why (see fit-036); keep it consistent across interviews.

follow_ups.q: Your CV is very dense for 2025-2026. How did you fit it all in?

cards.topic: Why Sales & Trading
cards.question: Why Sales & Trading, and why Global Markets rather than M&A or pure quant?

cards.topic: Why markets after Wavestone and entrepreneurship

**Structure: each experience pointed towards markets, plus a clear commitment signal (45-60 seconds).**

2. **One line per experience** (confirmed facts):

cards.question: Your dates overlap a lot: Wavestone, BNP, CNE, two companies, three projects and your engineering degree, all in 2025-2026. How did you actually manage that?

2. **Shared or delegated work**: CNE ran across the academic year with a team of 9; Polifeb has a CTO co-founder (Léo Lucidor) who owns technical delivery.
3. **The real load of each other role**: give an honest weekly figure or description for BNP (06-08/2026), CNE, Sell For You, Polifeb and the three projects (the trading-signal research, the company database, the interview app: evenings and weekends).
4. **How you managed**: your actual prioritisation method.
5. **The honest cost**: what suffered, if anything (ties to the weakness answer).

**Yours to provide**: the real hours/status of each role. A believable breakdown beats "I managed".
