follow_ups.a: Split paths across threads, each with its own generator stream (e.g. std::mt19937_64 seeded from a seed sequence, or a counter-based generator), accumulate per-thread statistics and combine at the end; avoid shared mutable state.

cards.topic: C++ performance: memory layout, cache misses, stack vs heap, reserve and move semantics
cards.question: You list C++. You sum an 8000 x 8000 matrix of doubles stored in one std::vector, once row by row and once column by column. Same number of additions: why is one version up to 15-20 times slower? Then: stack vs heap, why call reserve() on a vector, and what does std::move actually do?
cards.answer: The two loops do the same arithmetic but not the same memory traffic. The matrix is stored row-major in one contiguous block, so walking along a row reads consecutive addresses: every cache line brought from memory (64 bytes on most CPUs, 128 on the M1) gives eight or sixteen doubles, and the hardware prefetcher sees the pattern and loads the next lines in advance. Walking down a column jumps 8000 doubles, 64 KB, at each step, so every access touches a new cache line and uses only one of the doubles it brings; with a 512 MB matrix nothing stays in cache and the loop is limited by memory latency. On my M1 laptop the row loop took about 0.02 s and the column loop about 0.30 s with -O3 -ffast-math; the gap is smaller at -O2 (0.11 vs 0.26 s) because without fast-math the compiler cannot reorder the floating-point additions to vectorise the row sum. Stack memory is automatic, very cheap to allocate and freed at scope exit, but small; heap memory is for large or dynamically sized data and costs an allocator call. A vector that grows by push_back reallocates and moves its contents each time its capacity is exceeded, so if I know the size I call reserve() first: 50 million push_backs took about 0.42 s without it and 0.13-0.21 s with it. std::move performs no movement by itself: it is a cast to an rvalue reference that allows the move constructor to steal the buffer instead of copying it.

follow_ups.q: How would you make the column-wise traversal fast if you really need column sums?
follow_ups.a: Keep row-order traversal and accumulate into a vector of n column sums (each row updates all n accumulators contiguously), or transpose once / store the matrix column-major. For big matrices, block the loops so a tile fits in cache.

follow_ups.q: Why is a virtual call in a hot loop sometimes a performance issue?
follow_ups.a: The indirect call itself costs a few cycles, but mainly it prevents inlining and therefore vectorisation of the loop body. Dispatching once per batch of paths instead of once per path removes most of the cost.

follow_ups.q: What is the difference between unique_ptr and shared_ptr in cost?
follow_ups.a: unique_ptr is a plain pointer with a destructor, zero overhead. shared_ptr adds a control block with an atomic reference count, so copies cost atomic increments; use it only for genuinely shared ownership.

follow_ups.q: How would you measure performance properly?
follow_ups.a: Compile with optimisation, warm the data, repeat and take the median, make the result observable so the compiler cannot delete the work, and use a profiler (perf, Instruments) to find where time is spent before optimising.

cards.topic: Floating-point arithmetic in pricing code: machine epsilon, cancellation, bump size for Greeks, Kahan summation and log-sum-exp
cards.question: You compute delta by bumping spot and repricing. Someone suggests a bump of 1e-10 'to be as accurate as possible'. Why is that a bad idea, what is the optimal bump for a forward and a central difference, and what other floating-point traps do you know from numerical analysis (0.1 + 0.2, summing ten million numbers, log of a sum of exponentials)?
cards.answer: A double has a 53-bit mantissa, so the relative spacing between representable numbers is machine epsilon, about 2.2e-16, and every operation is exact only up to that relative error. A finite-difference Greek has two errors that move in opposite directions: the truncation error of the formula, of order $h$ for a forward difference and $h^2$ for a central one, and the rounding error, about $\varepsilon V/h$, because we subtract two nearly equal prices and divide by a small number. Balancing them gives an optimal bump of order $\sqrt{\varepsilon}\approx1.5\times10^{-8}$ times the scale of the problem for a forward difference, about 1e-6 for a spot of 100, and of order $\varepsilon^{1/3}\approx6\times10^{-6}$ times the scale for a central difference, a few 1e-4 for a spot of 100. On a Black-Scholes call with spot 100 I measured a central-difference delta error of 5e-9 with a bump of 0.01, 2e-11 with 1e-4, but 5e-7 with 1e-8 and 4e-5 with 1e-10. So the bump of 1e-10 is worse by six orders of magnitude. Gamma, a second difference, is even more sensitive: the error is smallest around a bump of 0.01 and reaches 2e-2 at a bump of 1e-6. Other traps: 0.1 + 0.2 is not equal to 0.3 in binary, so compare with a tolerance; adding 0.1 ten million times gives 999999.99984 instead of a million, while Kahan summation or math.fsum gives the exact million; and to compute a log of a sum of exponentials I subtract the maximum first, otherwise exp(1000) overflows.

follow_ups.q: Why does -ffast-math change results?
follow_ups.a: It lets the compiler treat floating-point addition as associative, reorder sums, use fused multiply-add and ignore NaN/infinity rules. Results change in the last bits, and code that relies on exact IEEE behaviour (Kahan summation, NaN checks) can break.

follow_ups.q: How do you compute Greeks of a Monte Carlo price without noise?
follow_ups.a: Use common random numbers for the bumped revaluations, or pathwise derivatives (differentiate the payoff along each path, fine for Lipschitz payoffs), or the likelihood-ratio method (differentiates the density, works for digitals), or adjoint algorithmic differentiation for many Greeks at once.

follow_ups.q: What is the relative error of the sum of n numbers added naively?
follow_ups.a: The worst-case bound grows like n times epsilon (in practice closer to sqrt(n) times epsilon for random rounding). Pairwise summation, used by NumPy, grows like log n times epsilon; Kahan summation keeps it at order epsilon independent of n.

follow_ups.q: What happens with a digital option and a small bump?
follow_ups.a: The payoff is discontinuous, so in MC the finite difference is zero on almost all paths and huge on a few: variance explodes like 1/h. Smooth the payoff (call spread), or use the likelihood-ratio method.

cards.topic: NumPy vectorisation: from a Python loop to broadcasting, memory and views, with a Monte Carlo example
cards.question: You say you use Python for numerical work. I have a Monte Carlo pricer written as a Python for-loop over one million paths. Why is it slow, how do you vectorise it, how would you price a whole strip of strikes and a path-dependent Asian option without loops, and what are the memory and view/copy traps?
cards.answer: A Python loop is slow because each iteration goes through the interpreter: every number is a boxed object, every operation is a dynamic dispatch, and nothing is vectorised by the CPU. NumPy moves the loop into compiled C code over contiguous arrays of raw doubles. For one million paths of a European call, drawing all normals at once and writing `ST = S0*np.exp((r-0.5*s*s)*T + s*np.sqrt(T)*z)`, then `np.maximum(ST-K, 0).mean()`, gave exactly the same price as the loop, 8.919 against a Black-Scholes value of 8.916 with a standard error of 0.014, but took 0.017 s instead of 0.76 s, about 45 times faster. For a strip of strikes I use broadcasting: `ST[:, None] - Ks[None, :]` produces a paths-by-strikes matrix in one expression. For an Asian option I draw a paths-by-dates matrix of normals and use `np.cumsum` along the time axis to build log-price paths, then average along that axis. The price is memory: 100,000 paths times 252 dates is already 200 MB, so for bigger problems I process paths in batches and accumulate the sums. The classic traps are that slicing returns a view, so modifying it modifies the original, while fancy indexing returns a copy, and that in-place operations keep the dtype, so adding 0.5 in place to an integer array raises an error.

follow_ups.q: How would you vectorise a barrier option check?
follow_ups.a: Build the paths matrix, compute the running minimum or maximum along the time axis with np.minimum.accumulate or simply .min(axis=1), and build a boolean mask of knocked-out paths; the payoff is np.where(mask, 0, vanilla payoff). Correct for discrete monitoring if needed.

follow_ups.q: What is the difference between np.random.seed and default_rng?
follow_ups.a: The legacy seed sets one global Mersenne Twister state shared by all code; default_rng returns an independent Generator object (PCG64) you pass around, which is reproducible, faster and safer for parallel streams.

follow_ups.q: When is a Python loop acceptable?
follow_ups.a: When the loop is over a small dimension (time steps, strikes) and the body is vectorised over the large one (paths). The overhead is per iteration, so 252 iterations cost nothing.

follow_ups.q: How do you check the Monte Carlo price is right?
follow_ups.a: Compare to a closed form when one exists (Black-Scholes here), check the error shrinks like 1/sqrt(n), check put-call parity on the same paths, and check the discounted simulated forward equals S0.

cards.topic: Point-in-time data in pandas: merge_asof, shift, publication lags and resampling labels
cards.question: You use pandas for market data. You must attach to each trade the prevailing mid quote, and to each daily date the latest company earnings. How do you do it without leaking future information? What exactly do merge_asof, shift and the label and closed arguments of resample do, and where do they typically leak?
cards.answer: The rule is that every value attached to a timestamp must have been known at that timestamp. For trades and quotes I use `pd.merge_asof(trades, quotes, on="time", by="sym", direction="backward")`: both tables sorted by time, and each trade receives the last quote at or before its time, per symbol. I decide explicitly whether a quote with exactly the same timestamp is allowed, with `allow_exact_matches`, since the quote may be the consequence of the trade, and I set a `tolerance` so that a trade does not pick up a stale quote from minutes earlier. For fundamentals, the key is the publication date, not the period end: December earnings published on 15 February must only appear from 15 February, so I join on the publication timestamp, and ideally on a point-in-time database that keeps the original release and not the restated figure. For signals, a signal computed from the close of day t can only earn the return of day t+1, so I multiply `signal.shift(1)` by the return; in a toy series the version without the shift had a strongly positive P&L and the correct version a negative one. Finally, `resample` labels bins by their left edge by default: the 09:00 bar contains data up to 09:29, so using its label as the time the bar is known is a 30-minute look-ahead. Backward fills and centred rolling windows leak the same way.

follow_ups.q: How would you do an as-of join in SQL?
follow_ups.a: With a correlated subquery taking the maximum quote time not after the trade time, or a LATERAL join ordered by time descending with LIMIT 1; kdb+ has aj for exactly this. An index on (sym, time) makes it fast.

follow_ups.q: How do you handle data revised after publication, such as GDP?
follow_ups.a: Use vintage (real-time) data: for each date, the value as first published or as known at that date (e.g. ALFRED for US macro). A backtest on final revised data uses information nobody had.

follow_ups.q: What is the difference between shift(1) on prices and on signals?
follow_ups.a: Shifting the signal lags the decision so it only uses past data; shifting the return forward (ret.shift(-1)) is equivalent but easier to get wrong. What matters is that the position held over (t, t+1] uses information up to t.

follow_ups.q: Is the tolerance in merge_asof about look-ahead?
follow_ups.a: No, it is about staleness: without it a trade can be matched to a quote from hours ago, for example after a halt. It guards data quality; direction and exact matches guard against look-ahead.

cards.topic: SQL window functions: returns with LAG, rolling averages, running drawdown and top-N per group
cards.question: You list SQL. Table px(sym, d, close). In one query, give me each day's return per symbol, a 3-day moving average, and the drawdown from the running maximum. Then, from a trades table, the two best traders per desk. What is a window function, how does it differ from GROUP BY, and what is the ROWS vs RANGE trap?
cards.answer: A window function computes a value for each row from a set of related rows, the window, without collapsing the rows as GROUP BY does. The syntax is `function() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... frame)`. For returns, `close / LAG(close) OVER (PARTITION BY sym ORDER BY d) - 1` takes the previous close within the same symbol, so the first day of each symbol is NULL rather than a spurious return computed from another stock. The moving average is `AVG(close) OVER (PARTITION BY sym ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`, and the drawdown is `close / MAX(close) OVER (PARTITION BY sym ORDER BY d) - 1`, since with an ORDER BY the default frame runs from the start of the partition to the current row, giving a running maximum. For the top two traders per desk I compute `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY desk ORDER BY pnl DESC)` in a subquery and filter on it outside, because window functions are evaluated after WHERE, so they cannot be filtered in the same query level. If ties matter, RANK gives equal pnl the same rank and skips the next one, DENSE_RANK does not skip. The trap is the default frame: with ORDER BY but no explicit frame, the frame is RANGE, so rows with the same date are all included together; a running sum over a date with two trades gives the same total to both rows. Writing ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW gives a true row-by-row running total.

follow_ups.q: Why not compute returns with a self-join?
follow_ups.a: You can join px to itself on the same symbol and the previous date, but you need to define the previous date (a subquery with MAX(d) < current d), which is slower and error-prone with gaps. LAG does it in one pass over sorted data.

follow_ups.q: How do you compute a cumulative P&L per trader?
follow_ups.a: SUM(pnl) OVER (PARTITION BY trader ORDER BY trade_time, trade_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), with a unique ordering key so the running total is well defined.

follow_ups.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
follow_ups.a: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can use SUM or COUNT. Neither can use window functions, which are computed afterwards.

follow_ups.q: How would you compute the maximum drawdown per symbol?
follow_ups.a: Compute the drawdown column with the running MAX window in a CTE, then SELECT sym, MIN(dd) FROM cte GROUP BY sym.

cards.topic: SQL indexes and transactions: B-trees, composite and covering indexes, ACID and isolation levels
cards.question: A query that sums the quantity traded in one symbol over a time interval takes a full table scan on 2 million trades. Which index do you create, why does column order matter in a composite index, what is a covering index, and what do indexes cost? Then: what does ACID mean, and which anomaly do isolation levels prevent when two processes update the same position?
cards.answer: Without an index the database must read every row and test the condition: a full scan, linear in the table size. An index is a sorted B-tree on one or more columns that lets the engine descend to the first matching key in logarithmic time and read only the matching range. For `WHERE sym = 'S042' AND ts BETWEEN a AND b`, the right index is composite on (sym, ts): equality column first, range column second, so all matching rows are contiguous in the index. On a 2-million-row SQLite table I measured 0.106 s with a full scan, 3.2 ms with an index on sym only, 1.2 ms with (sym, ts), and 0.09 ms with a covering index on (sym, ts, qty), which contains every column the query needs so the table itself is never read. Column order matters because the B-tree is sorted lexicographically, like a phone book sorted by surname then first name: the (sym, ts) index is useless for a query on ts alone, which still scanned. Indexes cost disk space and slow down writes, because every insert updates every index: inserting 200,000 rows took 2.3 s with three indexes and 0.4 s with none. ACID means atomicity, all or nothing; consistency, constraints hold; isolation, concurrent transactions do not see each other's intermediate states; and durability, a committed transaction survives a crash. The typical problem with positions is the lost update: two processes read a position of 100, each adds its trade and writes back, and one trade disappears. The fix is an atomic `UPDATE ... SET qty = qty + x`, a row lock with SELECT FOR UPDATE, or a serializable isolation level.

follow_ups.q: What is a clustered index?
follow_ups.a: An index where the table rows themselves are stored in index order (the primary key in InnoDB/MySQL or SQL Server; SQLite rowid tables). Range scans on that key read contiguous pages; other indexes then point to the key.

follow_ups.q: Why might the optimiser ignore your index?
follow_ups.a: If the condition is not selective (it returns a large fraction of rows, a scan is cheaper than many random lookups), if statistics are stale, if the column is wrapped in a function or implicitly cast, or if the index columns do not start with the filtered column.

follow_ups.q: What is a deadlock and how do databases handle it?
follow_ups.a: Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs. The database detects the cycle and aborts one of them, which must retry. Acquiring locks in a consistent order (e.g. sorted by account id) prevents it.

follow_ups.q: What is the complexity of a B-tree lookup, and why not a binary tree?
follow_ups.a: O(log N) node visits; with a fan-out of a few hundred, depth stays at 3-4 for billions of keys, and each node is one disk or memory page. A binary tree would have depth around 30 and one random access per level.

cards.topic: SQL traps: NULL and three-valued logic, NOT IN, LEFT JOIN filters, join fan-out and integer division
cards.question: Tables clients(id, name) and trades(id, client_id, notional, status). One trade has a NULL client_id. Which clients have never traded? Your colleague writes WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT client_id FROM trades) and gets zero rows. Why? Then explain what goes wrong with a LEFT JOIN filtered in the WHERE clause, a join that doubles your notional, and COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column).
cards.answer: SQL uses three-valued logic: any comparison with NULL is neither true nor false but unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true. `id NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` means `id <> 1 AND id <> 2 AND id <> NULL`; the last term is unknown, so the whole condition is never true, and the query returns nothing, even for Gamma who never traded. I tested it: zero rows with NOT IN, and Gamma once the subquery filters `client_id IS NOT NULL`, or with `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM trades t WHERE t.client_id = c.id)`, which is the robust way to write an anti-join. Second trap: in `clients LEFT JOIN trades ... WHERE t.status = 'done'`, the clients without trades get NULL in t.status, the WHERE removes them, and the left join silently becomes an inner join; the condition belongs in the ON clause if I want to keep all clients. Third, joining trades to a table with several rows per client, such as two limit records, multiplies each trade: client 1's notional of 150 became 300. I check row counts before and after a join and aggregate the many side first. Fourth, COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values, and SUM and AVG ignore NULLs, so the average notional is over non-missing values only, and SUM over no rows is NULL, not 0, hence COALESCE. Also `status <> 'cancelled'` drops trades whose status is NULL. Finally, `5/2` is 2 in SQLite and PostgreSQL: integer division.

follow_ups.q: How do NULLs behave in GROUP BY and ORDER BY?
follow_ups.a: GROUP BY puts all NULLs into one group (the exception to 'NULL is not equal to NULL'). ORDER BY places them first or last depending on the engine (PostgreSQL: last in ascending order), controllable with NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST.

follow_ups.q: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
follow_ups.a: UNION removes duplicate rows (a sort or hash step, slower); UNION ALL keeps all rows. For stacking two trade tables use UNION ALL, otherwise two genuine identical trades would merge.

follow_ups.q: How would you find duplicate trades?
follow_ups.a: GROUP BY the business key (trade date, instrument, quantity, price, counterparty) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1, or ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY business key ORDER BY insertion time) > 1 to list the extra copies.

follow_ups.q: Which is faster, NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL?
follow_ups.a: Modern optimisers usually turn both into the same anti-join plan. NOT EXISTS is preferred for clarity and because it has no NULL trap; NOT IN can prevent the anti-join optimisation when the column is nullable.

cards.topic: Building an option pricer in Excel: Black-Scholes, Greeks, Goal Seek for implied vol, Data Tables, a binomial tree and Monte Carlo
cards.question: You list Excel. Build me, out loud, a Black-Scholes pricer in a spreadsheet: which cells, which formulas, how do you get delta and vega, how do you back out implied volatility, how do you show the price as a function of spot and vol, and how would you add a binomial tree for an American put and a Monte Carlo? What are the spreadsheet risks?
cards.answer: I would put the inputs in one clearly formatted block and name the cells S, K, r, sigma and T, so the formulas read like the maths and survive copying. With spot 100, strike 100, rate 5%, vol 20% and one year: d1 is `=(LN(S/K)+(r+sigma^2/2)*T)/(sigma*SQRT(T))`, which gives 0.35, d2 is `=d1-sigma*SQRT(T)`, 0.15, and the call is `=S*NORM.S.DIST(d1,TRUE)-K*EXP(-r*T)*NORM.S.DIST(d2,TRUE)`, 10.4506; the put is 5.5735, and a check cell verifies put-call parity, C minus P equal to S minus K e^{-rT}, 4.877. Delta is `NORM.S.DIST(d1,TRUE)`, 0.637, and vega uses the density, `S*NORM.S.DIST(d1,FALSE)*SQRT(T)`, 37.5 per unit of vol, so 0.375 per vol point. For implied vol I use Goal Seek: set the price cell to the market price, say 12, by changing sigma, which gives 24.11%; for many options I would write a small Newton or bisection function instead. A two-variable Data Table shows the price over a grid of spots and vols. The binomial tree is a triangular block where each node is `=EXP(-r*dt)*(p*up+(1-p)*down)` with relative references copied across, and the American put takes `MAX` of that and the exercise value; three steps give 11.04 for the call, converging to 10.45. Monte Carlo uses `NORM.S.INV(RAND())` down a column, with the caveat that RAND recalculates on every edit. The risks are hard-coded numbers inside formulas, broken references, volatile functions and no version control, so I add checks and keep inputs, calculations and outputs separate.

follow_ups.q: How would you compute gamma and theta in the sheet?
follow_ups.a: Gamma = NORM.S.DIST(d1,FALSE)/(S*sigma*SQRT(T)). Theta for a call = -S*NORM.S.DIST(d1,FALSE)*sigma/(2*SQRT(T)) - r*K*EXP(-r*T)*NORM.S.DIST(d2,TRUE), per year; divide by 365 (or 252) for a daily figure. Or bump the input cells and reprice as a check.

follow_ups.q: What is the difference between Goal Seek and Solver?
follow_ups.a: Goal Seek changes one input to hit one target value. Solver optimises an objective over several inputs with constraints, e.g. calibrating a volatility smile parameterisation to several market quotes by least squares.

follow_ups.q: How do you make a Monte Carlo reproducible in Excel?
follow_ups.a: RAND has no seed, so either paste the uniforms as values once, or generate them in VBA with Rnd after Randomize with a fixed seed, or with a formula-based generator. Otherwise every recalculation changes the price.

follow_ups.q: Why use continuous compounding with EXP(-r*T)?
follow_ups.a: Black-Scholes is derived with a continuously compounded rate. If the market rate is quoted annually compounded, convert it first: r_cont = LN(1 + r_annual).

cards.topic: Cost versus accuracy of pricing methods: closed form, trees, PDEs, Monte Carlo, quasi-Monte Carlo and FFT
cards.question: You studied numerical methods. A structurer asks: to get a price accurate to 1 cent, how does the computing cost grow for a binomial tree, a finite-difference PDE and Monte Carlo? Which one would you use for a vanilla, an American put, a 5-asset basket and a whole volatility smile, and why does dimension decide?
cards.answer: The right way to compare methods is the cost needed to reach a given error $\varepsilon$. A closed form costs a constant amount: a Black-Scholes price is about a microsecond, so for vanillas nothing else makes sense. A binomial tree with N steps costs of order $N^2$ operations and its error decreases like $1/N$, so the cost grows like $\varepsilon^{-2}$; for an at-the-money call I measured errors of 2 cents at 100 steps and 0.1 cent at 1600 steps, halving each time N doubles. A Crank-Nicolson PDE in one dimension with M space points and N time steps is second order in both, so the error falls like $1/N^2$ and the cost, of order $MN$, grows only like $\varepsilon^{-1}$: this is the best method for one- or two-factor problems with early exercise, such as the American put. Monte Carlo has an error of $\sigma/\sqrt n$ whatever the dimension, so its cost grows like $\varepsilon^{-2}$; with a payoff standard deviation of 14.7, one cent needs about 2.2 million paths, and time discretisation adds a bias that pushes the cost to $\varepsilon^{-3}$ unless one uses multilevel Monte Carlo. The reason dimension decides is that a PDE grid with 100 points per asset has $100^d$ points: a million for three assets, $10^{10}$ for five, while Monte Carlo is unaffected, so a 5-asset basket is priced by Monte Carlo, ideally with Sobol quasi-random numbers, whose error on my one-dimensional test fell almost like $1/n$ rather than $1/\sqrt n$. For a whole smile under a model with a known characteristic function, the FFT prices all strikes at once in $N\log N$.

follow_ups.q: Why is Monte Carlo's convergence rate independent of dimension?
follow_ups.a: The central limit theorem gives an error sigma/sqrt(n) for any integrand with finite variance; dimension enters only through the variance of the payoff and the cost of simulating one path, not through the rate.

follow_ups.q: What does Richardson extrapolation do to the tree cost?
follow_ups.a: If the error is c/N, then 2V(2N) - V(N) cancels the leading term; with a smooth error (e.g. Leisen-Reimer trees or BBS smoothing of the last step) the order increases and the cost for a given error falls sharply.

follow_ups.q: Why do PDE and tree prices of barrier options converge badly?
follow_ups.a: The barrier falls between grid nodes and the effective barrier jumps with N, causing oscillating errors. Place the barrier exactly on a node or adjust the grid, and smooth the payoff near the barrier.

follow_ups.q: When would you still use Monte Carlo in one dimension?
follow_ups.a: For strongly path-dependent payoffs where the PDE needs extra state variables (Asian with many fixings, lookbacks), or inside a larger simulation framework (xVA) where consistency across products matters more than speed.

cards.topic: Backtesting VaR: counting exceptions, the Kupiec test, the Basel traffic light and Christoffersen's independence test
cards.question: Risk modelling is on your CV. Your bank's 99% one-day VaR had 8 exceptions over the last 250 days. Is the model wrong? Set up the test, compute the Kupiec likelihood ratio, place the result in the Basel traffic light, and tell me why the number of exceptions alone is not enough.
cards.answer: If the model is right, each day's loss exceeds the 99% VaR with probability 1%, independently of the past, so the number of exceptions over 250 days is binomial with parameters 250 and 0.01: we expect 2.5. Kupiec's proportion-of-failures test compares the likelihood of the observed count under p = 1% with the likelihood under the observed frequency, here 8 over 250, 3.2%. The statistic is minus two times the log-likelihood ratio and is asymptotically chi-squared with one degree of freedom: for 8 exceptions it is 7.73, above the 5% critical value of 3.84, p-value 0.5%, so we reject correct coverage. At 5% the test accepts between 1 and 6 exceptions; zero is also rejected, which says that a VaR that is never breached is too conservative. In the Basel traffic light, 0 to 4 exceptions is green, 5 to 9 yellow and 10 or more red; 8 is yellow, with a plus factor of 0.75 added to the capital multiplier of 3 in the original Basel framework. The limit of counting is twofold. The test has low power with 250 observations: if the true exception probability were 2%, it would reject only about a quarter of the time. And it ignores timing: eight exceptions in four pairs of consecutive days signal a model that reacts too slowly to volatility, which Christoffersen's independence test detects; with my clustered example the independence statistic was 18.9, against 0.5 for the same eight exceptions spread out.

follow_ups.q: Why is zero exceptions in 250 days a problem?
follow_ups.a: The probability is 0.99^250 = 8.1%, and the Kupiec statistic is 5.03 > 3.84: the VaR is probably too high, which ties up capital and misleads limit-setting. The regulator is not bothered, but the business and the model validation team are.

follow_ups.q: Which P&L do you backtest against, and why does it matter?
follow_ups.a: Hypothetical P&L (positions frozen, revalued at the next close) tests the model; actual P&L also contains intraday trading, fees and new trades. Differences between them are informative, and FRTB requires both at desk level.

follow_ups.q: How would you increase the power of the backtest?
follow_ups.a: Use more data (longer window, several VaR levels), test the whole distribution (e.g. the probability integral transform of each day's P&L under the model, tested for uniformity), and use tests that account for magnitude.

follow_ups.q: What is the probability of 8 or more exceptions if the model is correct?
follow_ups.a: Under Binomial(250, 1%) it is about 0.40%, which is why 8 falls in the yellow zone close to the red boundary.

cards.topic: Extreme value theory for tail risk: peaks over threshold, the generalised Pareto distribution and VaR/ES at 99.9%
cards.question: Your risk-modelling background: you need a 99.9% one-day VaR and expected shortfall, and you have 5,000 days of data, so only five observations beyond the quantile. Why is the normal distribution useless here and the empirical quantile noisy? What does extreme value theory say, how do you fit it, and what numbers do you get on fat-tailed data?
cards.answer: At 99.9% the answer is driven by the far tail. A normal fitted to the whole sample gets the centre right and the tail badly wrong for financial returns, and the empirical quantile relies on the handful of largest observations, so it jumps from sample to sample. Extreme value theory says that, for almost any distribution, the excesses over a high threshold u are approximately distributed as a generalised Pareto distribution with a shape parameter xi and a scale beta: this is the Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem. Xi positive means a power-law tail, the case for returns; for a Student t with nu degrees of freedom xi equals one over nu. So I pick u around the 95th percentile of losses, fit the GPD to the excesses by maximum likelihood, and extrapolate: VaR at level q is u plus beta over xi times the quantity ((n/N_u)(1-q)) to the power minus xi, minus one, and ES is (VaR + beta - xi u)/(1 - xi). I simulated 5,000 daily losses from a Student t with 3 degrees of freedom scaled to 1% daily vol, where the true 99.9% VaR is 5.90%. The normal VaR was 3.02%, half the truth; the empirical quantile 6.40%; the GPD 6.04%, with xi estimated at 0.35 against a true 1/3. For ES the truth is 8.90%, the GPD gave 9.45% and the normal 3.29%. Over 200 repeated samples the GPD VaR had a standard deviation about 20% smaller than the empirical quantile. The main judgement call is the threshold: too high and there are too few excesses, too low and the GPD approximation is biased.

follow_ups.q: What is the tail index of a Student t with nu degrees of freedom, and why?
follow_ups.a: Its density decays like |x|^-(nu+1), so the tail probability decays like x^-nu: tail index nu and GPD shape xi = 1/nu. Moments of order nu and above are infinite.

follow_ups.q: Block maxima or peaks over threshold?
follow_ups.a: POT uses all large observations rather than only one maximum per block, so it is more data-efficient; block maxima (GEV) is simpler with seasonal data or when only maxima are recorded. Both rest on the same limit theory.

follow_ups.q: How does EVT relate to the square-root-of-time rule?
follow_ups.a: For i.i.d. power tails, the sum of n losses has the same tail index, and the extreme quantile scales roughly like n^xi rather than n^0.5 (Feller). With xi = 1/3 or so, scaling by sqrt(n) overstates somewhat for i.i.d. data, but volatility clustering works the other way, so neither rule is reliable.

follow_ups.q: Why is ES more sensitive to the tail model than VaR?
follow_ups.a: ES averages the whole tail beyond VaR, so it depends on how fast the tail decays, i.e. on xi, through the factor 1/(1-xi). VaR depends only on one quantile.

cards.topic: Coding a delta-hedging simulation in Python: the P&L of a hedged short call, hedging frequency and volatility mismatch
cards.question: Code in Python, on the whiteboard, a simulation where you sell a one-year at-the-money call at 20% implied vol and delta-hedge it until expiry. What should the P&L distribution look like, how does its standard deviation scale with the number of rebalancings, what happens if realised vol is 25%, and what checks prove your code is right?
cards.answer: I simulate many GBM paths at once with NumPy. At time zero I receive the Black-Scholes premium, buy delta shares and put the rest in a cash account; at each date the cash earns the risk-free rate, I recompute delta with the remaining maturity and pay for the change in the share position; at expiry I sell the shares and pay the call payoff. The P&L is the final cash plus the shares minus the payoff. If realised vol equals the 20% I sold at and I hedge continuously, the P&L is zero on every path; with discrete hedging it is centred on zero with a spread that falls like one over the square root of the number of rebalancings. With spot 100, strike 100, 2% rate and a premium of 8.92, I got standard deviations of 1.92 hedging monthly, 0.94 weekly, 0.44 daily and 0.22 four times a day, matching the Derman-Kamal approximation, square root of pi over 4 times vega times vol over the square root of N, which gives 2.00, 0.96, 0.44 and 0.22. If realised vol is 25%, the mean P&L becomes minus 1.98, which is the difference between the Black-Scholes prices at 25% and 20%, carried to expiry, 1.99: I sold volatility too cheap. Hedging with the 25% delta keeps that mean but reduces the dispersion from 0.99 to 0.55. The checks: zero mean in the matched case, the square-root scaling, and a mean P&L that does not depend on the drift of the stock, which I confirmed with a 30% drift.

follow_ups.q: How would you add transaction costs?
follow_ups.a: Subtract a cost proportional to the traded value at each rebalance, e.g. cash -= k*abs(new_delta - delta)*S. The mean P&L then becomes negative and grows with N, which gives an optimal hedging frequency (Leland's adjusted volatility is the classic analytic treatment).

follow_ups.q: Why does the realised-vol-hedged P&L have lower dispersion?
follow_ups.a: With the delta at realised vol, the hedged portfolio replicates the option at the true vol, so the P&L locks in the price difference at inception; with the implied-vol delta the gain or loss accrues through gamma along the path and depends on where the path goes.

follow_ups.q: How would you speed this up for a big grid of scenarios?
follow_ups.a: Vectorise over scenarios too (arrays of shape paths x scenarios), avoid scipy's overhead with scipy.special.ndtr, or compile the loop with Numba; the time loop of a few hundred steps is fine in Python.

follow_ups.q: What changes for a long option position hedged at a lower implied vol than realised?
follow_ups.a: The long gamma position gains: expected P&L is the difference of Black-Scholes prices at realised and implied vol (future-valued), positive. It is the mirror image of the short case.

cards.topic: CV walkthrough (final CV)
cards.question: Walk me through your CV in 60 seconds.
cards.answer:
Structure (60 s, 5 beats, only confirmed facts):

1. **Education (10 s)**: CPGE PCSI-PC, then Centrale Nantes engineering degree in applied maths; finance is self-taught.
2. **Flagship project (20 s)**: the memecoin wallet-tracking bot: built and audited it myself with AI coding agents, zero capital at risk; the key line is that I found my own inflated results: the z-score fell from 10.0 to 2.5-4.1 once wallet clustering was accounted for, and simulated capital went from +7.5 % to -5.2 % once the leaky model was replaced by a true out-of-sample one.
3. **Data and building (15 s)**: the company database (4.97 M companies, 1.25 M contactable, accuracy tested statistically) and the interview-prep app.
4. **Experience (10 s)**: Polifeb, Sell For You, BNP (student-loan files), Wavestone, CNE.
5. **Close (5 s)**: why Global Markets now: I like problems where numbers are checked against reality.

follow_ups.q: Which line are you proudest of?
follow_ups.a: The audit: I found that my own headline result was inflated and published the corrected, worse number. Then point to cv-302/cv-303 details.

follow_ups.q: Why so many different experiences?
follow_ups.a: Link them by the common skill (building something, then checking it against reality), not by apologising. Keep to what is on the CV.

cards.topic: CV walkthrough (final CV), French version
cards.question: Présentez-moi votre CV en une minute (French version of the walkthrough).
cards.answer:
Same 5 beats as cv-300, in French:

1. **Formation** : prépa PCSI-PC puis Centrale Nantes (maths appliquées) ; la finance, je l'ai apprise seul.
2. **Projet phare** : un bot de suivi de wallets memecoin, construit et audité moi-même avec des agents de code IA, sans capital engagé ; j'ai trouvé que mes propres résultats étaient gonflés : z de 10,0 à 2,5-4,1 une fois le clustering pris en compte, capital simulé de +7,5 % à -5,2 % avec un vrai modèle hors échantillon.
3. **Données et outils** : la base d'entreprises (4,97 M d'entreprises, 1,25 M contactables, exactitude testée statistiquement) et l'app de préparation.
4. **Expériences** : Polifeb, Sell For You, BNP (dossiers de prêts étudiants), Wavestone, CNE.
5. **Conclusion** : pourquoi les marchés : des problèmes où les chiffres sont confrontés au réel.

follow_ups.q: Pourquoi la finance de marché après une école d'ingénieur ?
follow_ups.a: Answer from the motivation cards (fit deck); link to the audit habit: confronting numbers with reality.

follow_ups.q: Qu'est-ce que le clustering a changé exactement ?
follow_ups.a: Signals from the same wallets are not independent, so the effective sample is much smaller; the bootstrap by wallet gives z = 4,08, by wallet×token 2,52 (see cv-302).

cards.topic: Bot audit: z 10.0 to 2.5-4.1
cards.question: Your CV says the z-score fell from 10.0 to 2.5-4.1. What exactly caused that drop, and was it the data leaks?
cards.answer: No, the drop is **clustering**, not the leaks. The first test treated the 927 signals as independent: 113 wins against a base rate of 201/4011 gives z = 10.0. But signals are concentrated: one wallet (smart_money_03) produced 322 of the 927 signals (34.7 %), and two wallets produced 59.7 %. Signals from the same wallet, or on the same token, are correlated, so the real information is much smaller. A bootstrap that resamples whole wallets gives z = 4.08; resampling wallet×token clusters gives 2.52. The verdict was still a PASS at that stage. The leaks were a separate issue that changed the return figures, and a later post-audit replay gave z = 3.91 but FAILED on expectancy (-0.022) and robustness (3/5).

follow_ups.q: Why is wallet×token lower than wallet?
follow_ups.a: It is a finer, different grouping that captures correlation between signals on the same token across wallets as well; the resulting standard error is larger, so z is lower (2.52).

follow_ups.q: If z is still about 3-4, why did you not trade it?
follow_ups.a: Significance of the win rate is not positive expectancy after costs: the post-audit replay had z = 3.91 but negative expectancy (-0.022) and failed 2 of 5 robustness checks.

follow_ups.q: What is the effective sample size?
follow_ups.a: n divided by the variance inflation: about 59 with the wallet×token z, about 154 with the wallet z (illustrative).

cards.topic: Bot audit: +7.5 % to -5.2 %
cards.question: Your CV says +7.5 % became -5.2 %. +7.5 % of what, and what changed?
cards.answer: It is the **change in simulated capital**, not a per-trade return. Full setup (entry filter plus caps), low-cost scenario, 200 € starting capital, 927 signals over 5 days. With the leaky model (an artifact trained on train+test) the capital ended at +7.5 %; with the true out-of-sample model it ended at 189.60 €, i.e. -5.2 %. Under moderate costs it goes from -17.7 % to -30.6 % (138.73 €). In per-trade net expectancy, the long report gives -0.09 % (low costs) and -5.31 % (moderate). One trap: the short report wrongly labels +7.5 % / -17.7 % as 'net expectancy, first reported'; they are capital changes.

follow_ups.q: Why not fix the second leak?
follow_ups.a: It is documented in the report as a remaining bias; since the corrected result was already negative, fixing it would most likely make it worse, not change the conclusion. Say it plainly.

follow_ups.q: Is 5 days and 927 signals enough?
follow_ups.a: No, it is short and clustered (see cv-302); the conclusion is 'no evidence of an edge after costs', not a precise return estimate.

cards.topic: Bot: built myself with AI coding agents
cards.question: Your CV says you built the bot solo and lists AI coding agents among your skills. Who did what, and how do you trust code an agent wrote?
cards.answer:
Who did what: no other person worked on it. AI coding agents wrote most of the implementation code and documentation; I set the research question, the architecture, the statistical protocol and acceptance criteria (the pre-registered four-stage gate), the safety rules and every exclusion decision, and I ran the audit. The findings on the CV are mine: the two data leaks (the model-artifact mix-up and the exit-policy calibration) and the signal clustering. How I trust code an agent wrote, in four habits:
1. **Tests**: 463 test functions for 21,991 lines of Python on 22/09 (the CV's 460+ and ≈22k).
2. **Out-of-sample by construction**: walk-forward split; the model-artifact leak (a model trained on train+test used as if out-of-sample) is exactly the silent error an agent can make, so train and test artefacts must be kept explicitly separate.
3. **Reproduce every headline number from raw data before quoting it**: e.g. $z=(0.1219-0.0501)/\sqrt{0.0501\times0.9499/927}\approx10.02$, then a full post-audit replay (z = 3.91).
4. **Assume the number is too good until proven otherwise**: that question led to the cluster bootstrap (z down to 2.52-4.08) and to the corrected backtest (+7.5 % → −5.2 % of simulated capital), and I published the worse numbers, with zero capital at risk.
If asked to explain a module without the agent, I steer to two I can explain line by line: the cost filter and the cluster bootstrap.

follow_ups.q: What is a bug an AI agent introduced?
follow_ups.a: The model-artifact mix-up (a model trained on train+test used as if out-of-sample) is the kind of silent error to cite, if the journal confirms how it arose.

follow_ups.q: Would you use AI agents on a desk?
follow_ups.a: Yes, with the same rule: nothing goes into a decision without a test and a reproduced number; and within the bank's policies on code and data.

cards.topic: Bot: the numbers in bullets 1-2
cards.question: Unpack the numbers on the bot lines of your CV: wallets, lines of code, tests, signals.
cards.answer:
- **15 'profitable' wallets** imported from the Fomo leaderboard to follow (profitable on history, which is exactly what the audit then questioned; 5 still active after vetting), and **40,000+ on-chain trades** collected in the database.
- **About 22k lines / 460+ tests**: the repo on 22/09 had 21,991 lines of Python and 463 test functions; the older long report says about 21,000 / 430+ because it was written earlier. Both are true at their date.
- **1,000+ signals**: 1,019 live decisions logged; after the cost filter (low-cost scenario) only about 41-42 were admitted as trades. So most signals were rejected because expected gain did not cover costs.
- **927 signals over 5 days** is the backtest sample used for the z-test and the capital simulation.

follow_ups.q: Out of all the wallets on a leaderboard, how many would look profitable by pure luck? (Careful: the CV's 40,000+ are trades, not wallets.)
follow_ups.a: Many: with thousands of wallets, the top 15 on past PnL are heavily selected on noise; it is a multiple-testing problem, hence the out-of-sample check.

follow_ups.q: Why only about 42 trades out of 1,000+ signals?
follow_ups.a: The cost filter rejected signals whose expected gain did not cover fees and slippage in the low-cost scenario.

cards.topic: Bot: zero capital at risk, is the cost model right?
cards.question: Your CV says zero capital was put at risk. Then how do you know your cost model is right, and does the conclusion depend on it?
cards.answer: Without live trading I cannot *prove* the cost model; what I can do is make the conclusion robust to it. I built three execution-cost scenarios (low, moderate, high) from sourced inputs: pool fee tiers, Solana priority-fee percentiles and slippage read from live Jupiter quotes. On the full system, net expectancy per trade was about **-0.09 %** in the low scenario and **-5.31 %** in the moderate one; the high scenario charges more on every leg, so it cannot rescue the result. So even with optimistic costs the strategy does not make money after costs: the conclusion 'no tradable edge' does not hinge on the exact cost number. If the answer had flipped sign between scenarios, I would have needed real fills before concluding anything. The next step, if I wanted precision, would be paper trading against live quotes or a tiny real position to measure actual slippage.

follow_ups.q: What is slippage in copy-trading specifically?
follow_ups.a: You enter after the wallet you copy, often after its own buy has pushed the price up, so your fill is worse than its fill. The delay plus your own market impact make up slippage.

follow_ups.q: What would have made you worried about the cost model?
follow_ups.a: If the sign flipped: positive under low costs, negative under moderate. Then the conclusion would depend entirely on the cost assumption and I would need real fills.

follow_ups.q: Why not just trade a little to find out?
follow_ups.a: That is the right next step if the edge looked positive. Here even optimistic costs gave a negative expectancy, so risking money to measure costs precisely would not change the decision.

cards.topic: Company database: walk me through it
cards.question: Walk me through the company database project on your CV.
cards.answer:
Structure (only what is on your CV, no added details):

1. **One-line goal**: what the database was for and who would use it (B2B prospecting: supplying prospecting data to clients).
2. **Scale**: about **4.97 M** French companies, of which about **1.25 M contactable** (25.2 %): 1.16 M with a phone, 0.79 M with an email.
3. **What you did technically**: built solo from public and open data only, within the GDPR framework for B2B prospecting (as on the CV); then only the concrete steps you can back up (sources, joining, cleaning, contact fields), nothing more.
4. **The key insight**: the statistical accuracy test you designed, which exposed one source wrong about 85 % of the time, and the decision: that source was removed.
5. **Result and lesson**: what the output was, and the transferable point: data quality matters more than data volume.

Keep it to 60-90 seconds and let them pick a thread.

follow_ups.q: What was the hardest part?
follow_ups.a: Pick the true answer from your experience (likely data quality or deduplication), give one concrete example, and what you changed after it.

follow_ups.q: How did you know the data was accurate?
follow_ups.a: Describe the test you actually designed (what was checked, how many records, the error rate and its uncertainty) and the decision it led to: the source found wrong about 85 % of the time was removed (that part is on the CV). Do not add details you cannot back up. See cv-309.

follow_ups.q: Who used it / what came out of it?
follow_ups.a: Only what is true and on your CV. If there was no measurable business outcome, say what the deliverable was and what you learnt.

cards.topic: Company database: the coverage numbers
cards.question: On your database: 4.97 M companies, 1.25 M contactable, 1.16 M with a phone, 0.79 M with an email. What share is contactable, and how many have both a phone and an email?
cards.answer: About **25 %** are contactable: 1.25 / 4.97 = 25.2 %. Phone coverage is 1.16 / 4.97 = 23.3 %, email 0.79 / 4.97 = 15.9 %. If 'contactable' means phone **or** email, inclusion-exclusion gives the overlap: both = 1.16 + 0.79 - 1.25 = **0.70 M**. So 0.46 M have only a phone and 0.09 M only an email: email adds very little on top of phone. The sanity check is that the overlap must be between 0 and the smaller set (0.79 M), which it is.

follow_ups.q: If the phone field is 90 % accurate, how many correct phone numbers do you have?
follow_ups.a: About 0.9 × 1.16 = 1.04 M, assuming errors are spread uniformly; in practice you would estimate accuracy by source on a sample.

follow_ups.q: What if contactable was defined differently?
follow_ups.a: Then the inclusion-exclusion decomposition no longer holds; I would recompute the overlap directly from the data rather than infer it.

cards.topic: Checking source accuracy by sampling (Wilson, sample size)
cards.question: You found that one data source was wrong about 85 % of the time. How do you test that statistically, and how big a sample do you need?
cards.answer: You cannot check millions of rows, so you draw a **random sample**, verify each record by hand, and estimate the error rate $\hat p$ with a confidence interval. For illustration (the real sample size is not on the CV), with 85 errors out of 100 checked, the 95 % **Wilson** interval is about **[76.7 %, 90.7 %]**: the source is clearly bad, whatever the exact rate. For sample size, the worst case $p = 0.5$ gives $n = 1.96^2 \times 0.25 / 0.05^2 \approx 385$ records for ±5 points, 1,068 for ±3 points. But to *decide* that a source is bad you need far fewer: when the error rate is that high, even 20 checks (17 wrong, interval about [64 %, 95 %]) settle it. The sample must be random, possibly stratified by source, or the estimate is biased.

follow_ups.q: Why does the population size not matter?
follow_ups.a: The standard error depends on n and p, not on N, as long as the sample is a small fraction of the population. The finite population correction sqrt((N-n)/(N-1)) is about 1 for N in the millions.

follow_ups.q: Why is p = 0.5 the worst case?
follow_ups.a: p(1-p) is maximised at 0.5 (value 0.25), so the variance of the estimate, and thus the required n, is largest there.

follow_ups.q: How would you compare two sources?
follow_ups.a: Sample each, compare error rates with a two-proportion z-test or intervals, and prefer stratified samples so each source gets enough checks.

cards.topic: GDPR and B2B prospecting in France
cards.question: Your database holds contact details of companies. Is that legal under GDPR, and what are the rules for B2B prospecting in France?
cards.answer: Data on a **company** (legal person) is not personal data, but a lot of B2B data is: a sole trader's name, a named manager, a nominative email like firstname.name@company. For those, GDPR applies. The usual lawful basis for B2B prospecting is **legitimate interest**, with duties: inform people, let them **object** easily, keep only what is needed, and honour opt-outs. In France, B2B **email** prospecting to professionals is allowed without prior consent if the message relates to their job and every email has an opt-out; B2C email needs prior consent. **Phone** prospecting to consumers has been **opt-in** since 11 August 2026 (law of 30 June 2025, as of Sept 2026): no call without the consumer's prior consent, except within an ongoing contract; calls between professionals are outside that regime, but GDPR still applies to named individuals. I would not claim a legal opinion: the point is I know where personal data sits and that compliance is designed in, not added afterwards.

follow_ups.q: Is a firstname.name@example.com address personal data?
follow_ups.a: Yes: it identifies a natural person, even if it is a work address. A generic address like contact@ is not.

follow_ups.q: What is legitimate interest?
follow_ups.a: A lawful basis where your interest (e.g. prospecting) is balanced against the person's rights and expectations; it requires informing them and letting them object easily.

follow_ups.q: Why would a bank care about this?
follow_ups.a: Banks handle huge amounts of client data and are heavily supervised; a data breach or unlawful processing means fines and reputational damage, so data discipline is part of the culture.

cards.topic: Deduplication, SIREN/SIRET keys, contact validation
cards.question: How do you deduplicate millions of company records coming from several sources, and how do you validate phone numbers and emails?
cards.answer: First use a **hard key** when there is one: in France the **SIREN** (9 digits, one per company) and **SIRET** (14 digits = SIREN + establishment number). Normalise it, check it with the **Luhn** checksum, then join sources on it: exact deduplication is cheap and reliable. For records without a key, do **fuzzy matching** on normalised name + postcode, with *blocking* (only compare records in the same postcode) so you do not compare every pair. Then merge with rules: keep the most reliable source per field. Validation: phones normalised to international format (+33 plus 9 digits), with type checks (mobile vs landline); emails checked for syntax, then domain (does it have a mail server, MX record). Syntax checks tell you a value is *possible*, not *right*: accuracy still needs sampling.

follow_ups.q: What is the equivalent problem in a bank?
follow_ups.a: Reference data: matching securities by ISIN/CUSIP, counterparties by LEI, and reconciling trades between front office, risk and back office systems.

follow_ups.q: How do you measure dedup quality?
follow_ups.a: Hand-check a random sample of merged pairs (precision) and of candidate pairs not merged (recall), then tune the threshold.

prerequisites: Company database: walk me through it

cards.topic: Why a B2B database on a Global Markets CV?
cards.question: Why is a B2B company database on a CV for a Global Markets role? What does it have to do with markets?
cards.answer:
Structure:

1. **Accept the premise calmly**: it is not a markets project, and you do not pretend it is.
2. **Name the transferable skill in one line**: handling millions of messy records, and above all *not trusting a source until it is measured* (the sampling test that showed one source was wrong about 85 % of the time).
3. **Bridge to the desk**: desks live on data (prices, reference data, client data) and on scepticism about numbers; the same reflex made you audit your own bot and publish worse results.
4. **Bring it back to markets**: your markets evidence is elsewhere (bot, self-taught finance, this preparation); the database shows execution and rigour.

Keep it to 30-45 seconds; do not over-justify.

follow_ups.q: So why not a data engineering job?
follow_ups.a: Answer with your real reason for markets (what attracts you in markets specifically), and say data is a tool you enjoy, not the end goal. Use the fit deck, no invented facts.

follow_ups.q: What did this project teach you that applies to trading?
follow_ups.a: Pick one true lesson: measure before trusting, coverage is not accuracy, or scale forces you to automate checks; link it to backtests or market data.

prerequisites: Company database: walk me through it

cards.topic: The interview prep app: walk me through it
cards.question: Tell me about the interview-preparation app on your CV. What did you build, and what did you do yourself?
cards.answer:
Structure (facts as of 30/09/2026):

1. **Problem**: preparing Global Markets interviews from zero in finance jargon; you wanted to *understand*, not memorise.
2. **What it is**: a flashcard app with a **spaced-repetition scheduler (SM-2)**, about **1,700 cards** across markets, corporate finance, brainteasers and fit.
3. **Where the questions come from**: interview questions from the interview guides of major banks (e.g. Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan, Morgan Stanley) and other public sources, deduplicated to about **2,543** unique questions (exact plus fuzzy matching), then answers with long explanations.
4. **Honesty on who did what**: built with AI agents under your direction: you designed it, set the quality rules, decided the content structure and checked the output; say it plainly.
5. **Result**: launch is planned soon; say how often you use it only if true; the real proof is that you can answer the technical questions in this interview.

45-60 seconds, then offer detail (scheduler, dedup).

follow_ups.q: How does the scheduler decide when to show a card?
follow_ups.a: Each card has an interval and an ease factor (starting at 2.5); a 'good' answer multiplies the interval by the ease, a failure resets it to 10 minutes and lowers the ease. See cv-314 for the numbers.

follow_ups.q: How do you know the AI-written answers are correct?
follow_ups.a: Quality rules (numbers recomputed in code, sources for market facts), cross-checking against textbooks and multiple sources, and my own review when studying; be honest that errors are possible and give a real example only if you have one.

follow_ups.q: Isn't preparing so intensively a form of gaming the interview?
follow_ups.a: The goal was to learn the material, not to recite; interviews test understanding with follow-ups, which memorisation cannot pass.

cards.topic: Spaced repetition (SM-2) as implemented in the app
cards.question: How does the spaced-repetition scheduler in your app work? Give numbers.
cards.answer: It is a variant of **SM-2**. Each card has an **interval** (days until the next review) and an **ease** factor, starting at 2.5, floored at 1.3. You grade each answer Again / Hard / Good / Easy. **Again** sends the card back in 10 minutes and cuts ease by 0.2. The first successful review schedules it in 0.5 / 1 / 4 days (Hard / Good / Easy), the second in 2 / 3 / 6 days; after that the interval is multiplied by 1.2 (Hard), by the ease (Good) or by ease × 1.3 (Easy); Hard lowers ease by 0.15, Easy raises it by 0.15. Intervals are capped at 45 days. So a card answered Good every time comes back after 1, 3, 7.5, 18.75 and then 45 days: geometric growth, so a few reviews cover weeks.

follow_ups.q: Why a floor on the ease factor?
follow_ups.a: So intervals never shrink on success: with ease above 1, a Good answer always pushes the card further away. 1.3 is SM-2's original floor.

follow_ups.q: How would you improve it?
follow_ups.a: Fit a model of recall probability on actual review history (as FSRS does) and schedule each card when predicted recall drops to a target, e.g. 90 %.

follow_ups.q: Why cap at 45 days?
follow_ups.a: The goal is a specific interview season, not lifelong memory; a cap guarantees every card is seen again within the preparation window.

prerequisites: The interview prep app: walk me through it

cards.topic: Deduplicating interview questions: normalisation, fuzzy ratio, TF-IDF
cards.question: You scraped thousands of interview questions. How did you remove duplicates when the same question is phrased differently?
cards.answer: In layers. First **normalise** (lower case, remove punctuation, collapse spaces) and drop exact duplicates. Then a **fuzzy string ratio** (edit-distance based, 0-100) with a threshold of 90: 'what is put call parity' vs 'what is put-call parity?' scores 93.6 raw and 100 after normalisation, so it is merged. That catches typos and punctuation but not rewording: 'explain put call parity' scores only 78.3. For paraphrases you need something semantic: **TF-IDF cosine similarity** on words, or sentence embeddings, with manual review near the threshold. The trade-off is precision vs recall: a low threshold merges genuinely different questions, which is worse than keeping a duplicate.

follow_ups.q: Why is the call vs put delta question a problem for fuzzy matching?
follow_ups.a: The two strings differ by a few characters (ratio 92.6, above the 90 threshold), yet they are different questions with opposite answers. Threshold choice and domain-aware checks prevent the wrong merge.

follow_ups.q: What does IDF do intuitively?
follow_ups.a: It down-weights words that appear in almost every document ('what', 'is') and up-weights rare, informative words, so similarity is driven by content words.

prerequisites: The interview prep app: walk me through it

cards.topic: Polifeb: three clients including a public body
cards.question: Your CV mentions Polifeb, with three clients including a public body. Tell me about it.
cards.answer:
Structure (only what is on your CV and in your confirmed facts):

1. **What Polifeb is, in one sentence** (CV: an AI automation company), and your role in it (Co-Founder & CEO since 08/2026: strategy, product, P&L).
2. **The clients**: three, including a public organisation; say what you delivered to them, in plain words.
3. **One concrete moment**: winning a client, a difficult request, or a delivery under a deadline; what you did and what happened.
4. **What it taught you that a desk values**: dealing with clients, a public buyer's requirements (formality, procurement, deadlines), owning a deliverable end to end.

**Facts to stick to**: the final CV says 3 signed clients to date, including a public body. There is no revenue figure on the CV: do not invent one.

follow_ups.q: How did you find your clients?
follow_ups.a: Give the real channel for each (network, outreach, referral). If one came through a personal contact, say so; it is normal for a first activity.

follow_ups.q: What was different about working with a public body?
follow_ups.a: Answer from what you actually experienced (formality, deadlines, payment delays, documentation). Do not describe procurement rules you did not go through.

follow_ups.q: How much did you earn from it?
follow_ups.a: No revenue figure is on the CV: don't improvise one. Say you prefer not to quote a figure and talk about clients, deliverables and lessons; do not give a number.

cards.topic: Sell For You: 10 k€+ generated for clients (attribution)
cards.question: Your CV says you generated 10 k€+ for clients at Sell For You. How do you know that number, and how much of it was really due to you?
cards.answer:
Structure:

1. **Define the number precisely**: 10 k€+ of what (sales, revenue, deals closed?) and for whom: it was generated **for the clients**, not income for you or for Sell For You. The CV says two clients signed, so that is about 5 k€ per client on average.
2. **How it was measured**: where the figure comes from (sales tracked, invoices, the client's own report), only what is true.
3. **Attribution, honestly**: what share is clearly due to your actions (sales you closed directly) vs what might have happened anyway.
4. **What you did**: the concrete actions behind it.
5. **Lesson**: measuring impact honestly, the same logic as separating skill from luck in a backtest.

follow_ups.q: What is the difference between attribution and incrementality?
follow_ups.a: Attribution assigns an observed outcome to causes; incrementality is the extra outcome versus a counterfactual without your action. Incremental impact is usually smaller than attributed impact.

follow_ups.q: How would you measure your true impact properly?
follow_ups.a: Compare to a baseline or a control group (similar clients or periods without the action), controlling for seasonality and other changes.

follow_ups.q: What is the equivalent in a bank?
follow_ups.a: PnL attribution (explaining a trader's PnL by market moves and risk factors) and performance attribution for funds (beta vs alpha).

cards.topic: BNP: analysing 500 k€+ of student loan files (credit analysis)
cards.question: At BNP you analysed over 500 k€ of student loan applications. How do you assess a student loan, and how does the bank think about the risk?
cards.answer: A student usually has no income and no credit history, so the classic **5 Cs** of credit shift: **Capacity** is future capacity (field of study, school, expected income), **Character** is the student's seriousness and banking behaviour, **Capital** is small, and the real mitigant is **Collateral / guarantees**: a parent as guarantor, or in France a **state-guaranteed student loan** managed by Bpifrance: the State guarantees 70 % of the principal (excluding interest), up to 20 k€, for students under 28, with no guarantor or income condition (Service-Public.fr, as of Sept 2026). BNP Paribas is not among the partner banks listed there, so at BNP the mitigant is mostly a personal guarantor. **Conditions** are the loan terms: amount, deferral of repayment until after studies, rate. The bank's risk view is **expected loss = PD × LGD × EAD**: for a 20 k€ loan with a 3 % default probability and 40 % loss given default, EL = 240 € (illustrative). A guarantor or state guarantee mainly cuts LGD. Then say concretely what you did on the files, only what is true.

follow_ups.q: What is the difference between expected and unexpected loss?
follow_ups.a: Expected loss is the average loss, covered by pricing and provisions; unexpected loss is the deviation above it in bad scenarios, covered by capital.

follow_ups.q: How does a credit spread relate to PD and LGD?
follow_ups.a: To first order, annual spread ≈ PD × LGD: investors need compensation for the average loss rate, plus a risk and liquidity premium.

follow_ups.q: What did you personally do on those files?
follow_ups.a: Describe your real tasks only (document checks, eligibility, preparing files, client contact) and who took the credit decision.

cards.topic: Wavestone: co-writing the full report and the podcast
cards.question: At Wavestone you co-wrote the full report, which was later presented in a podcast. What was your contribution, and what did you learn?
cards.answer:
Structure (only facts on your CV and in your confirmed notes):

1. **Context in one sentence**: what the report was about and for whom.
2. **Your part**: co-wrote the **full report**: say which sections or tasks were yours (research, analysis, drafting, charts), and what 'co-' means (with whom).
3. **The podcast**: the CV says the report was later presented in a podcast; say what it covered and your role in it, if you had one (only what is true).
4. **One concrete learning**: synthesising a complex topic for a non-specialist audience, or defending a view in public.
5. **Link to the role**: sales and research live on turning analysis into a clear message for clients; a morning note or a client call is the same skill.

follow_ups.q: Summarise the report in 30 seconds.
follow_ups.a: Conclusion first, then two or three supporting points, then one number. Rehearse it; this is a likely live test.

follow_ups.q: What was your hardest disagreement while co-writing?
follow_ups.a: Give a real example if you have one, focusing on how you resolved it with evidence; otherwise talk about a real difficulty (scope, deadlines).

follow_ups.q: How is this relevant to a markets job?
follow_ups.a: Desks turn analysis into short client messages (notes, calls, pitches); writing the report trained exactly that.

cards.topic: CNE: 45 k€ of contracts, 3 events, a 10 k€+ hackathon
cards.question: Tell me about your role at CNE: 45 k€ of contracts, three events, a hackathon with 10 k€+, 50 participants and 4 partners.
cards.answer:
Structure (facts from your CV only):

1. **What CNE is and your role** (CV: Business Development Manager, leading a team of 9, 09/2025 – 08/2026), one sentence each.
2. **The numbers with their meaning**: **45 k€ of contracts** (say what kind: sponsorship, partnerships, services, and whether it is your share or the team's); **3 events**; the **hackathon**: 10 k€+ of budget or prizes (say which), **50 participants**, **4 premium partners** (named on the CV: BNP Paribas, Orange Business, AWS, Alten). That is about **200 € per participant**; 45 k€ over a year is about **3.75 k€ a month**.
3. **One story**: how you convinced a partner, or a moment where the event nearly failed and what you did.
4. **What it shows**: selling to companies, negotiating, delivering an event on time, working in a team.
5. **Link**: a sales desk also pitches, negotiates and keeps relationships with corporate clients.

follow_ups.q: How did you convince a partner to pay?
follow_ups.a: Describe a real pitch: what the partner wanted (visibility, recruiting access), what you offered, how you closed. Keep it to facts you remember.

follow_ups.q: What went wrong and what did you do?
follow_ups.a: Pick a real incident, your action and the result; show calm and ownership.

follow_ups.q: Is 200 € per participant a lot?
follow_ups.a: It depends on what is included (food, venue, prizes); give the comparison only if you know it. The point is being able to compute and discuss it.

cards.topic: 'Listed by the French Ministry of Sports': what it means
cards.question: Your CV says you were listed by the French Ministry of Sports. What does that mean, and what did sport bring you?
cards.answer:
Structure (your real sport, level and dates only):

1. **Explain the label in one sentence**: in France, the Ministry of Sports publishes official lists of high-level athletes, on proposal of each sports federation; being on a list means the federation recognised your level. Say **which list/category** you were on and when; the sport is on your CV: **modern pentathlon**, with an **11th place at the Junior World Championships in laser-run (running and shooting), with the French team**.
2. **What it required**: training volume, competitions, combining it with studies (CPGE, Centrale Nantes), only what is true.
3. **One concrete moment**: a competition, an injury, a setback and how you came back.
4. **What transfers to a desk**: discipline, performing under pressure, handling losses without tilting, taking feedback from a coach.

follow_ups.q: How did you combine it with prépa?
follow_ups.a: Give your real schedule and trade-offs (training hours, what you gave up); concrete beats heroic.

follow_ups.q: What is your best result?
follow_ups.a: The CV gives it: 11th at the Junior World Championships in laser-run (running and shooting), with the French team; say it plainly, with the year. Other results (e.g. national titles) only if exact.

follow_ups.q: Do you still practise?
follow_ups.a: Answer truthfully; if you stopped, say why and what replaced it.

cards.topic: One-number drill: every figure on the final CV
cards.question: Drill: for each number on your CV, say in one sentence what it measures and where it comes from.
cards.answer:
- **15 'profitable' wallets**: imported from the Fomo leaderboard (5 active after vetting; profitable on history: selection on the outcome); **40,000+** = on-chain trades collected, not wallets.
- **≈22k lines / 460+ tests**: repo on 22/09 (21,991 lines of Python, 463 test functions); the older report says ≈21,000 / 430+.
- **1,000+ signals**: 1,019 live decisions; only ≈41-42 admitted after the cost filter.
- **z 10.0 → 2.5-4.1**: same 927 signals; the drop is **clustering** (bootstrap by wallet 4.08, wallet × token 2.52), not the leaks.
- **+7.5 % → −5.2 %**: simulated capital, 200 € start, low costs, out-of-sample model: 189.60 €. Moderate costs: −30.6 % (138.73 €).
- **Two data leaks**: model-artifact mix-up, exit-policy calibration.
- **Database**: 4.97 M companies, 1.25 M contactable (25.2 %), source wrong ≈85 %.
- **Prep app**: ≈1,700 cards (1,708 on 01/10), ≈2,543 deduplicated questions from interview guides of major banks and other public sources, SM-2; launch planned.
- **BNP 500 k€+** of student-loan applications analysed; **Sell For You 10 k€+** for clients; **CNE 45 k€**, hackathon 10 k€+ / 50 / 4 partners.

follow_ups.q: Why did z fall from 10 to about 2.5-4?
follow_ups.a: Because signals were not independent: few wallets and repeated tokens. Bootstrapping by wallet or by wallet × token accounts for the clustering and widens the standard error.

follow_ups.q: Is −5.2 % a per-trade number?
follow_ups.a: No, it is the change of simulated capital (200 € → 189.60 €) over the test, low-cost scenario. The per-trade net expectancy was −0.09 % in that scenario.

cards.topic: What would you do differently? (final CV lines)
cards.question: Looking back at the projects on your CV (the bot, the database, the prep app), what would you do differently?
cards.answer:
Structure: pick **one or two** real lessons, each as *mistake → consequence → what you now do*.

1. **Bot**: the audit found inflated results after the fact (leaks, clustering). The protocol was already pre-registered (CV) and still gave a PASS. A true lesson you can use: a pre-registered plan is not enough; **audit the pipeline itself** (train/test separation of model artifacts and calibrations, the independence assumption of the test) **before** trusting a pass.
2. **Database**: measure source accuracy on a sample **early**, before investing in a source that turned out to be wrong about 85 % of the time (only if that ordering is true).
3. **Prep app**: start from the question list and the quality rules before generating content with AI agents (only if true).
4. **Close positively**: the fact that you caught and published the worse numbers is itself the lesson in action.

follow_ups.q: Why didn't you fix the exit-policy leak?
follow_ups.a: The true reason is methodological: the exit-policy leak was identified, measured and deliberately frozen, not corrected, because recalibrating the exits on a window you had already looked at would have created a third leak (see cv-119). The proper fix is to calibrate exits on training data only and re-run on fresh data with the criteria frozen; and since the corrected result was already negative, the conclusion 'no edge after costs' is unlikely to improve with it.

follow_ups.q: How do you avoid fooling yourself now?
follow_ups.a: Protocol first: out-of-sample split, robustness checks and success criteria set before looking; and asking what would make the number too good.

cards.topic: Webhook vs polling vs REST API: HTTP methods, status codes, idempotency
cards.question: You run an AI automation company. Basic question then: what is the difference between a webhook, polling and a REST API? Which HTTP methods and status codes do you know, and is a POST idempotent?
cards.answer: A **REST API** is a set of URLs that a server exposes; my code sends HTTP requests to it (GET to read, POST to create, PUT to replace, PATCH to modify, DELETE to remove) and usually gets **JSON** back. **Polling** means I call that API on a schedule to ask "anything new?"; **a webhook** is the reverse: the other system calls my URL as soon as an event happens. Polling every 60 seconds costs 1,440 calls a day per source, and if only 20 events happen, 1,420 of those calls are wasted, with an average delay of 30 seconds; a webhook is near-instant but I must handle duplicates and missed calls. Status codes: 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content), 4xx the client's fault (400 bad request, 401 not authenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 429 too many requests), 5xx the server's fault (500, 502, 503). **Idempotent** means doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by design, POST is not, so a retried POST can create a duplicate invoice unless I send an idempotency key.

follow_ups.q: Is PATCH idempotent?
follow_ups.a: Not necessarily. "Set the email to x" is idempotent, "append an item to the list" is not. The standard only guarantees idempotency for GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE (and OPTIONS).

follow_ups.q: You receive a 429. What do you do?
follow_ups.a: 429 = too many requests: I am over the rate limit. I wait (respecting the Retry-After header if present) and retry with exponential backoff, and I reduce my request rate.

follow_ups.q: How do you secure a webhook endpoint?
follow_ups.a: HTTPS only, and check a signature (an HMAC of the body computed with a shared secret) or a secret token in the header; reject anything else. Also answer fast with a 2xx and do the heavy work afterwards, because many senders time out after a few seconds and retry.

follow_ups.q: What is the market-data equivalent of polling vs webhook?
follow_ups.a: Snapshot requests versus a streaming subscription. Trading systems subscribe to streams because a 30-second average delay is useless for prices.

cards.topic: Anatomy of an n8n workflow: trigger, nodes, credentials, error workflow, retries, idempotency
cards.question: Your company builds automations with tools like n8n. Take one workflow and walk me through its anatomy. What happens when a step fails at 3 a.m., and how do you make sure a retry does not send the same invoice twice?
cards.answer: A workflow starts with a **trigger** (a webhook, a schedule, or an event in an app such as a new email), then a chain of **nodes**, each one doing one step (read, transform, call an API or an LLM, write); data flows between nodes as a list of JSON items. **Credentials** (API keys, OAuth tokens) are stored encrypted, apart from the workflow, and nodes only reference them. For failures, each node can **retry on fail** with a wait between tries, and the workflow can point to an **error workflow** that starts with an Error Trigger and alerts someone with the failed execution. Retries fix random glitches: with a 2% independent failure rate and 3 tries, 1,000 runs a day go from 20 failures to about 0.008, but they do nothing against a real outage, which is correlated. The danger is the step that succeeded but timed out: a retry repeats it, so every write must be **idempotent**, for example by storing the source id (the email's message id) with a unique constraint and skipping anything already processed.
