In a **drop-down**, the company moves valuable assets (IP, a subsidiary) to an **unrestricted subsidiary** outside the lenders' collateral and raises new debt secured on them (J.Crew 2016). A **double-dip** gives new lenders two claims against the same group (a guarantee and an intercompany loan), raising their recovery. Lenders respond with **cooperation agreements**, contracts to act together so no majority can be formed against the rest, and with blockers in new documents. After Serta (Fifth Circuit, December 2024) the courts drew limits, but LMEs remain a large share of defaults.

follow_ups.q: Why would a sponsor-backed company prefer an LME to Chapter 11?
follow_ups.a: It is faster and cheaper, the sponsor keeps its equity (Chapter 11 would likely wipe it out), and it captures discount on the exchanged debt. The cost is litigation and alienating lenders who will price that risk into future loans.

follow_ups.q: What is a non-pro rata vs a pro rata LME?
follow_ups.a: Non-pro rata deals are offered only to a majority group, leaving the minority behind; pro rata deals are offered to all holders of a class on the same terms. After Serta and the spread of co-ops, pro rata deals became more common.

follow_ups.q: How do rating agencies treat LMEs?
follow_ups.a: Most are distressed exchanges and are rated as a default (selective default), even if the company keeps paying. That is why dual-track default rates including LMEs are much higher than payment default rates.

prerequisites: Restructuring, Chapter 11 and liability management exercises
Out-of-court restructuring: amend-and-extend, exchange offers, exit consents and hold-outs

cards.topic: French restructuring: conciliation, sauvegarde, sauvegarde accélérée and cross-class cram-down since the 2021 reform
cards.question: How does a French company restructure its debt? Explain conciliation, sauvegarde and sauvegarde accélérée, and what changed with the 2021 reform: classes of affected parties and cross-class cram-down. Can creditors now take control against the will of the shareholders?
cards.answer: France has **preventive, confidential** procedures (mandat ad hoc and **conciliation**, at most 4 + 1 months), where a court-appointed conciliator helps negotiate a deal but no one can be forced, and **court** procedures: **sauvegarde** for a company in difficulty but not yet in *cessation des paiements* (unable to pay debts due with available assets), **redressement judiciaire** when it is, and liquidation. **Sauvegarde accélérée** is the bridge: a company already in conciliation with a deal supported by enough creditors can convert it into a court plan in **2 months, extendable to 4**, binding the minority. The **2021 reform** (ordonnance of 15 September 2021, in force 1 October 2021, transposing the EU restructuring directive) replaced creditor committees with **classes of affected parties**, mandatory for large companies and always in sauvegarde accélérée, including **shareholders** as a class. Each class votes by a **two-thirds majority of the amounts voting**, with no headcount test. The court can then impose the plan on dissenting classes through **cross-class cram-down**, subject to a best-interest test and an **absolute priority rule** with possible derogations. Yes: since 2021 shareholders can be crammed down if they are out of the money, as in **Orpea** (2023), **Casino** and **Atos** (2024), where creditors took control and old shareholders were massively diluted.

follow_ups.q: How is sauvegarde accélérée like a US prepack?
follow_ups.a: Both convert a deal negotiated out of court into a court plan quickly, binding the dissenting minority. The difference: sauvegarde accélérée requires a prior conciliation, votes are held in court by classes within 2-4 months, and there is no DIP regime identical to section 364.

follow_ups.q: Why did shareholders have so much power before 2021?
follow_ups.a: Any conversion of debt into equity requires a capital increase, which under French company law needs a shareholder vote. Without cram-down, shareholders could block the plan, so creditors had to pay them to agree. The reform lets the court impose it when they are out of the money.

follow_ups.q: What is the EU restructuring directive?
follow_ups.a: Directive (EU) 2019/1023 on preventive restructuring frameworks. It requires member states to offer a preventive procedure with classes, cross-class cram-down and protection for new financing. France (2021), Germany (StaRUG, 2021) and the Netherlands (WHOA, 2021) all implemented versions.

prerequisites: Confirming a Chapter 11 plan: class voting, best interests, feasibility, cram-down and the absolute priority rule
Debt-for-equity swaps: how creditors take control, recovery maths, hold-outs

cards.topic: UK schemes of arrangement vs Part 26A restructuring plans (and Germany's StaRUG)
cards.question: Why do so many European companies restructure through English law? What is the difference between a scheme of arrangement and a Part 26A restructuring plan, and when can a plan cram down a dissenting class? How does this compare with Chapter 11 and Germany's StaRUG?
cards.answer: A **scheme of arrangement** (Part 26 of the Companies Act 2006) lets a company make a compromise with a class of creditors that binds everyone in the class if **75% by value and a majority in number** of those voting approve and the court sanctions it. It is flexible, quick and available to foreign companies with a sufficient connection to England, typically English-law debt, which is why European groups used it for years. But a scheme **cannot** cram down a dissenting class. The **Part 26A restructuring plan**, introduced in June 2020, adds **cross-class cram-down**: each class votes at 75% by value, no headcount, and the court can sanction over a dissenting class if **no member of it is worse off than in the relevant alternative** (usually administration) and the plan was approved by a class with a **genuine economic interest** in that alternative. There is no strict absolute priority rule; instead the court checks that the benefits of the restructuring are **fairly** shared, and since Adler (2024), Thames Water and Petrofac (2025) the Court of Appeal has made clear that out-of-the-money creditors cannot simply be ignored. Germany's **StaRUG** (2021) offers a similar plan with 75% class votes and cram-down, for companies facing impending illiquidity.

follow_ups.q: How can a German or French company use an English scheme?
follow_ups.a: The court needs a sufficient connection to England, which can be satisfied by English-law governed debt; some companies changed the governing law of their loans or moved their centre of interests. Since Brexit, recognition in the EU relies on private international law rather than EU regulations, which pushed some groups to domestic regimes (StaRUG, sauvegarde accélérée, Dutch WHOA).

follow_ups.q: Why is there no numerosity test in Part 26A?
follow_ups.a: It avoids hold-outs splitting claims to create more voters and makes the outcome depend on economic weight only. Schemes keep the headcount test, which protects small creditors against one large holder.

follow_ups.q: What is a relevant alternative in practice?
follow_ups.a: The court's view of the most likely outcome without the plan: often administration with a sale of the business, sometimes a different restructuring. It is decided on evidence (valuation reports), and dissenting creditors often attack it.

prerequisites: French restructuring: conciliation, sauvegarde, sauvegarde accélérée and cross-class cram-down since the 2021 reform
Confirming a Chapter 11 plan: class voting, best interests, feasibility, cram-down and the absolute priority rule

cards.topic: Quick credit maths: leverage and coverage, distressed bond yields and trading flat
cards.question: Quick maths: a company has leverage of 5x and interest coverage of 5x: what is its interest rate? A bond with a 10% annual coupon maturing in one year trades at 80: what is its yield to maturity? Is the yield higher or lower if it matures in two years? What does it mean when a bond trades at 40?
cards.answer: Leverage 5x means debt = 5 x EBITDA; coverage 5x means interest = EBITDA / 5. So the interest rate is (EBITDA / 5) / (5 x EBITDA) = **1/25 = 4%**. For the bond: in one year you receive 110 for 80, so YTM = 110 / 80 - 1 = **37.5%**. With two years to maturity at the same price, the 20-point discount is spread over two years, so the yield is **lower, about 23.7%** (solve 80 = 10/(1+y) + 110/(1+y)^2); the current yield is 10/80 = 12.5% in both cases. A bond at **40** is not really a yield story any more: the market expects default and prices the **recovery**, roughly the present value of what the bond will receive in a restructuring. Such bonds usually trade **flat**, without accrued interest, and are analysed like equity of the future reorganised company.

follow_ups.q: Leverage 6x and coverage 2x: what is the rate?
follow_ups.a: 1 / (6 x 2) = 8.3%. A company paying 8.3% on 6x leverage covers interest only twice, which is typical of a stressed single-B credit in a high-rate environment.

follow_ups.q: Why are all unsecured bonds of the same issuer priced similarly in default regardless of maturity?
follow_ups.a: Because in bankruptcy all claims are accelerated: a 2-year and a 10-year bond of the same rank both have a claim equal to principal plus accrued interest up to the filing and share pro rata. Differences reflect only coupon accrued, legal entity and documentation.

follow_ups.q: What is the difference between price, yield and spread quotes?
follow_ups.a: IG bonds are quoted in spread over a benchmark, high yield usually in price and yield, distressed in price. The quote convention follows what matters most for the risk: rates for IG, default for HY, recovery for distressed.

prerequisites: Credit metrics: leverage, coverage and relative value
Where the debt and equity trade when Chapter 11 is likely

cards.topic: Private credit and direct lending vs syndicated loans: unitranche, first-out/last-out and the 2026 market
cards.question: What is private credit, and why do sponsors choose a direct lender over a broadly syndicated loan? What is a unitranche and how does a first-out/last-out split work: a 500 unitranche at SOFR + 600bp is split into a 150 first-out at SOFR + 350bp; what margin does the last-out earn? What is going on in private credit as of September 2026?
cards.answer: **Private credit** is lending by non-bank funds (direct lenders, BDCs, insurers) that originate and **hold** loans instead of distributing them. **Direct lending** to sponsor-backed mid-sized companies is the core. Versus a **broadly syndicated loan (BSL)** arranged by banks and sold to CLOs and loan funds, a direct lender offers **certainty and speed** (no market flex or syndication risk), **confidentiality**, one or a few lenders to negotiate with in trouble, flexibility (delayed-draw tranches, PIK options), in exchange for a **higher spread** and often maintenance covenants and call protection. A **unitranche** is one loan replacing senior plus junior debt at a **blended margin**. Lenders can split it privately through an agreement among lenders: the **first-out** gets paid first at a lower margin, the **last-out** takes more risk. Margin is conserved: 500 x 600 = 150 x 350 + 350 x m, so **m ≈ 707bp**. As of September 2026 the market is over **USD 2 trillion**, but under stress: Fitch's US private credit default rate hit a record **6.3%** (trailing 12 months to August 2026), PIK usage in BDC loans rose to about 10%, and investors in non-traded BDCs asked for redemptions well above the usual 5% quarterly caps.

follow_ups.q: Why do banks partner with private credit funds instead of just competing?
follow_ups.a: Capital rules make holding leveraged loans expensive for banks, so they originate, provide back leverage (loans to the funds), sell risk through significant risk transfers and earn fees, while funds provide long-term capital. It is a shift from balance-sheet lending to distribution and financing.

follow_ups.q: What is a BDC's non-accrual rate and why watch it?
follow_ups.a: The share of the portfolio where interest is no longer recognised because repayment is doubtful. It is an early indicator of losses and falling distributions, and it rose in 2025-2026.

follow_ups.q: What is the risk in non-traded BDCs?
follow_ups.a: Liquidity mismatch: investors can redeem only a limited amount each quarter while the loans are illiquid. When many investors want out, gates apply, which can damage confidence and fundraising even if the loans perform.

prerequisites: Covenants: maintenance vs incurrence, headroom, cov-lite and equity cures
PIK interest through the three statements, PIK toggles and leverage creep

cards.topic: Term loan B returns: IRR with OID, amortisation, a falling floating benchmark and early prepayment
cards.question: A lender buys a 200m, 7-year term loan B priced at benchmark + 500bp, issued at a 4% original issue discount (OID), with 1% annual amortisation. The benchmark rate falls from 5% to 3% over the first four years and then stays at 3%. What is the lender's IRR, roughly? How do the OID, the amortisation and an early refinancing change it?
cards.answer: The lender pays 96% of face, **192m**, and receives floating interest on the outstanding balance plus 2m of amortisation a year and the 188m balance at maturity. With the benchmark falling 5%, 4.5%, 4%, 3.5% then 3%, the all-in coupon drops from 10% to 8%, and the IRR comes out at about **9.7%**, so roughly 10%. The quick way to see it: coupon of benchmark + 5%, plus the OID spread over the life of the loan, roughly **4 / 7 ≈ 0.6%** a year and in practice closer to 0.8-0.9% because you earn the discount on a smaller price and amortisation is tiny. A flat 5% benchmark would give about **10.9%**, a flat 3% about **8.8%**: a floating-rate lender has almost no duration risk, but its **income** moves with the base rate. **Amortisation** of 1% barely matters (weighted average life 6.8 years). What matters most is **prepayment**: if the borrower refinances at par after three years, the 4-point discount is earned over 3 years instead of 7, and the IRR rises to about **11.2%**, 11.5% with a 101 soft-call premium. That is why the market quotes loan yields on a **3-year** or 4-year life convention, and why lenders ask for OID and call protection.

follow_ups.q: Why is the market convention to quote loan yields to a 3-year life?
follow_ups.a: Leveraged loans are prepayable at par (after a short soft-call period) and are typically refinanced or repaid in an M&A or IPO after 3 to 4 years. Assuming a 3-year life spreads the OID over the realistic horizon: 4 points over 3 years is about 1.3% a year, versus 0.6% over 7.

follow_ups.q: What does a 1% floor do if SOFR falls to 0.5%?
follow_ups.a: The coupon is computed on max(SOFR, 1%) + margin, so the lender still earns 1% + 500bp. The floor is an interest rate option (a floor) sold by the borrower to the lender; it was valuable in the zero-rate years and is far out of the money at today's rates.

follow_ups.q: The loan now trades at 98. What yield would a buyer earn if it is repaid at par in 2 years?
follow_ups.a: Roughly the coupon plus 2 points over 2 years, so about 1% a year extra on top of benchmark + 500bp (slightly more because you invest only 98). The same logic as OID: the discount is earned through repayment at par.

follow_ups.q: How would a lender hedge the benchmark falling?
follow_ups.a: Receive fixed on an interest rate swap (or buy floors) against its floating assets, which locks in the base-rate component of the income. Many funds do not hedge and let returns float; CLOs match floating assets with floating liabilities.

prerequisites: Private credit and direct lending vs syndicated loans: unitranche, first-out/last-out and the 2026 market
IRR vs money multiple and the LBO value creation bridge

cards.topic: Fixed charge coverage (FCCR) and DSCR vs free cash flow: can the company service its debt?
cards.question: A company has EBITDA of 100, D&A and capex of 20 each, a 5m yearly increase in working capital and a 25% tax rate. It borrows 500 (5x EBITDA) at 10% with 1% annual amortisation. Compute its free cash flow and its fixed charge coverage ratio (FCCR). What changes if leverage goes to 7x? How do FCCR and DSCR differ from free cash flow, and why are FCCRs hard to compare across companies?
cards.answer: **Free cash flow** is what is left in absolute terms: 100 of EBITDA minus 50 interest, 7.5 cash taxes, 20 capex and 5 of working capital = **17.5**, or 12.5 after the 5 of mandatory amortisation. The **FCCR** is a **ratio**: cash available for fixed charges divided by the fixed charges, here (EBITDA − capex − cash taxes) / (interest + scheduled principal) = 72.5 / 55 ≈ **1.32x**. It answers "how many times can the company pay what it contractually must pay?" At **7x** leverage, interest is 70, taxes fall to 2.5, FCF drops to **2.5** (negative 4.5 after amortisation) and the FCCR falls to about **1.0x**: the company only just covers its obligations, with no margin for a bad year. So more leverage can raise the sponsor's equity returns, but a lender sees the cushion disappear. **DSCR** (debt service coverage ratio) is the same idea used in project finance and real estate: cash flow available for debt service over interest plus principal, often tested every period with a lock-up below about 1.1-1.2x. FCCRs are hard to compare because the **definition is negotiated** in each credit agreement: which EBITDA add-backs, whether rent and leases are fixed charges, whether capex is maintenance only, whether dividends and taxes are deducted.

follow_ups.q: What is a typical minimum FCCR covenant?
follow_ups.a: Often 1.0x to 1.25x. In asset-based loans it is typically a springing 1.0x FCCR tested only when availability under the borrowing base falls below a threshold (for example 10% of the commitment).

follow_ups.q: Why might a lender prefer FCF / debt to EBITDA / debt?
follow_ups.a: Two companies with the same EBITDA can have very different capex, taxes and working capital needs. FCF / debt shows how many years of cash it takes to repay the debt; EBITDA / debt overstates capacity for capital-intensive firms.

follow_ups.q: What is debt sculpting in project finance?
follow_ups.a: Setting each period's principal repayment so that the DSCR stays at a target (e.g. 1.3x): principal = CFADS / target DSCR − interest. Repayments are larger in strong years and smaller in weak ones.

follow_ups.q: Interest rates rise by 200bp on a floating loan. What happens to the 5x case?
follow_ups.a: Interest goes from 50 to 60, taxes fall by 2.5 to 5, FCF falls from 17.5 to 10 and the FCCR from 1.32x to (100 − 20 − 5) / 65 = 1.15x. Floating-rate leveraged borrowers were hit exactly this way in 2022-2023.

prerequisites: Covenants: maintenance vs incurrence, headroom, cov-lite and equity cures
Term loan B returns: IRR with OID, amortisation, a falling floating benchmark and early prepayment

cards.topic: Asset-based lending (ABL) vs cash-flow lending: the borrowing base, availability and springing covenants
cards.question: What is the difference between an asset-based loan (ABL) and a cash-flow loan? Compute the borrowing base: receivables of 100 of which 20 are ineligible, advanced at 85%; inventory of 120 at cost with a net orderly liquidation value (NOLV) of 60%, advanced at 85% of NOLV but capped at 50% of cost; 10 of reserves; a 150 commitment and 70 drawn. What is availability, and why do distressed companies and their advisers watch it so closely?
cards.answer: A **cash-flow loan** (term loan, cash-flow revolver) is sized on **EBITDA**, e.g. 4-6x, and protected by covenants on leverage or coverage; the lender relies on the company staying a going concern. An **ABL** is a revolver sized on the **liquidation value of current assets**: receivables and inventory, sometimes equipment. It lends a percentage (the **advance rate**) of **eligible** collateral, recomputed every month or week in a **borrowing base certificate**. Here: receivables 80 eligible × 85% = **68**; inventory 85% × NOLV of 72 = 61.2, capped at 50% of cost = **60**; total 128, less 10 of reserves = **118**. The line is the lower of commitment and borrowing base, so 118, and with 70 drawn **availability is 48**. ABLs are cheaper and usually cov-lite, with only a **springing FCCR** (say 1.0x) that bites if availability falls below a threshold (about 10% of the line), plus **cash dominion**. In distress the danger is that the borrowing base **shrinks exactly when the company needs cash**: sales fall, receivables and inventory fall, the lender adds reserves, and availability collapses. That is why restructuring advisers track availability in the 13-week cash flow, and why ABL lenders often provide the DIP.

follow_ups.q: Why would an ABL lender accept a lower spread than a term loan lender to the same company?
follow_ups.a: Its collateral is liquid, over-collateralised and monitored weekly, and it has a first lien on it, so its expected loss is much lower. Historical recoveries on ABL revolvers are close to full.

follow_ups.q: What is dilution in receivables?
follow_ups.a: The share of invoiced receivables never collected in cash because of credit notes, returns, discounts or disputes. Lenders reduce the advance rate or add a dilution reserve when it exceeds a few percent.

follow_ups.q: What happens to an ABL in Chapter 11?
follow_ups.a: It is often refinanced or rolled up into a DIP ABL with the same lenders, who keep lending against a new borrowing base and get paid from collections. The cash collateral of an ABL cannot be used without the lender's consent or a court order with adequate protection.

prerequisites: Liquidity runway and the 13-week cash flow forecast
DIP financing: superpriority, priming, adequate protection and roll-ups

cards.topic: How a rating agency builds a corporate rating: business risk, financial risk and the anchor matrix
cards.question: How does a rating agency like S&P arrive at a corporate credit rating? A company with a satisfactory business risk profile has EBITDA of 500, debt of 1,600, interest of 80 and cash taxes of 60. Where does it sit in S&P's financial risk categories and anchor matrix, and what happens to its rating if it deleverages to 1,200 of debt or is bought in an LBO with 3,000 of debt?
cards.answer: S&P combines two assessments. The **business risk profile** (1 excellent to 6 vulnerable) comes from **industry and country risk** (the CICRA) and the company's **competitive position** (scale, diversification, margins and their volatility). The **financial risk profile** (1 minimal to 6 highly leveraged) comes mainly from two core ratios, **FFO/debt** and **debt/EBITDA**, on S&P-adjusted figures (leases, pensions, surplus cash netted) and weighted towards forecast years. The **anchor matrix** crosses the two to give an anchor, which is then adjusted by **modifiers** (diversification, capital structure, financial policy, liquidity, management and governance, comparable rating analysis) to get the stand-alone credit profile, and finally for group or government support. Here FFO = 500 − 80 − 60 = 360, **FFO/debt 22.5%** and **debt/EBITDA 3.2x**: both in the **significant** category (20-30%, 3-4x). Satisfactory × significant gives an anchor of **bbb-/bb+**, right on the investment-grade boundary. Deleveraging to 1,200 (2.4x, FFO/debt about 31%) moves it to **intermediate**: anchor **bbb/bbb-**. An LBO with 3,000 of debt (6x, FFO/debt about 8%) makes it **highly leveraged**: anchor **b+**, a drop of about four notches, which is why sponsors' targets are rated single B. Moody's uses published sector **scorecards** with weighted factors instead of a matrix, but the logic is the same: business strength sets how much leverage a rating can bear.

follow_ups.q: Why is FFO/debt preferred to FCF/debt as a core ratio?
follow_ups.a: FFO excludes working capital swings and discretionary capex, so it is more stable and reflects the recurring cash-generating ability. Agencies still look at free operating cash flow/debt and discretionary cash flow/debt as supplementary ratios.

follow_ups.q: What is a fallen angel and why does the market care?
follow_ups.a: An issuer downgraded from investment grade (BBB-) to high yield (BB+ or below). Many funds and mandates can only hold investment grade, so the downgrade forces selling and spreads jump; the bonds also move from IG to HY indices.

follow_ups.q: How does liquidity affect a rating?
follow_ups.a: S&P assesses liquidity from exceptional to weak using sources over uses over 12-24 months. There are five levels (exceptional, strong, adequate, less than adequate, weak): 'less than adequate' caps the stand-alone profile at bb+ and 'weak' at b-, whatever the anchor and the other modifiers.

follow_ups.q: Why do sponsor-owned companies get a financial policy penalty?
follow_ups.a: Agencies assume a financial sponsor will keep leverage high and may re-lever through dividend recaps or acquisitions, so they do not give credit for deleveraging forecasts and often rate them at the lower end of the anchor range.

prerequisites: Credit ratings from the issuer's side: why get rated, managing the rating in M&A, hybrids
Fixed charge coverage (FCCR) and DSCR vs free cash flow: can the company service its debt?

cards.topic: Distressed investing: loan-to-own, blocking positions and the option value of out-of-the-money junior claims
cards.question: A company has an enterprise value of about 300, senior debt of 300 and junior notes of 150. On today's value the juniors recover nothing, yet they trade around 20-25 cents and fight the restructuring plan. Why? And how does a distressed fund run a loan-to-own strategy: it buys the senior debt at 70, the plan gives seniors a 120 take-back loan plus 95% of the new equity. What is its return?
cards.answer: Because a junior claim is an **option on enterprise value**. The juniors are paid only if the value ends up above 300, up to 450: their payoff is a **call spread** on EV. If value is uncertain and the process takes time, that option is worth something today, even though it is out of the money: with 40% EV volatility and two years, a simple Merton-style valuation gives the juniors about **39**, i.e. **26 cents**, and even the equity about 28. So juniors want **time and volatility** (they are long vega): they argue for a higher valuation, delay, litigate, and seniors often pay them a **gift** (a few percent of the new equity or warrants) to get a consensual plan fast. Seniors want **speed** and a low valuation, because they own the business at the end. **Loan-to-own**: the fund buys the **fulcrum** security (the most senior class not covered in full, here the seniors) at a discount, ideally more than **one third** of the class so it can **block** any plan (a class accepts with two thirds in amount and more than half in number of those voting), drives the process, and converts debt into control. With seniors bought at 70 (cost 210 for 300 face), a recovery of 120 plus 95% × 180 = **291**, i.e. 97 cents, gives **1.39x**, about **24% IRR** over 18 months; if EV then grows to 400, the stake is worth **386**, 1.84x.

follow_ups.q: Why can old equity keep trading at a few cents in Chapter 11?
follow_ups.a: Option value (the chance a higher valuation or a turnaround leaves something for equity), retail speculation, and sometimes hold-up value if the plan needs its consent or it can litigate. Once the plan is confirmed and the shares cancelled, the value goes to zero.

follow_ups.q: What is the difference between a restricted and an unrestricted creditor?
follow_ups.a: A restricted creditor has signed an NDA and received material non-public information, so it cannot trade the securities until the information is cleansed (made public). Many funds stay unrestricted until they need to negotiate, then go restricted for a limited period.

follow_ups.q: How does a warrant help settle a valuation fight?
follow_ups.a: Juniors receive warrants struck at an EV above the plan value. If the business is worth more than seniors claim, the warrants pay off; if not, they expire worthless. It lets both sides keep their valuation view: a direct use of option value.

follow_ups.q: Using the model, what is the senior worth in cents at 40% vol over 2 years?
follow_ups.a: About 233 for 300 face, or 78 cents, below the 97 cents it gets in a quick plan at 300: the senior is short volatility, which is why it wants a fast, certain deal.

prerequisites: Recovery waterfall and the fulcrum security
Confirming a Chapter 11 plan: class voting, best interests, feasibility, cram-down and the absolute priority rule
363 sales, stalking horse bids and credit bidding

cards.topic: Who is at the restructuring table: debtor vs creditor advisers, committees, the CRO, KEIP/KERP and critical vendors
cards.question: In a restructuring, what is the difference between debtor-side and creditor-side advisory? Who sits at the table (company, sponsor, ad hoc groups, the official creditors' committee, the CRO), who pays the advisers, and what are KEIPs, KERPs and critical vendor payments? A supplier owed 12 before the filing threatens to stop deliveries: should the company pay it?
cards.answer: **Debtor side**: the bank advises the **company** on its options (liquidity, amend-and-extend, exchange, Chapter 11 or a court process abroad, a sale), builds the business plan, valuation and debt capacity, runs any M&A or new-money raise and negotiates with creditors. **Creditor side**: the bank advises a **group of creditors** (an ad hoc group of bondholders or lenders, or the **official committee of unsecured creditors**, UCC) on what they can recover, how to organise, what to demand, and whether to provide new money or take the equity. Creditor mandates are often more numerous (one per class), debtor mandates bigger and more strategic. Around the table: the company and board (often with independent directors), the **sponsor** or shareholders, secured lenders (often the DIP providers), ad hoc groups, the UCC, sometimes landlords, unions and pension bodies, and the court and US Trustee in Chapter 11. A **CRO** (chief restructuring officer), usually from a turnaround firm, runs cash and the process day to day. In Chapter 11 the **estate pays** the debtor's and the UCC's advisers, and ad hoc groups' fees are usually paid by the company under their agreements. **KERPs** (retention bonuses) for insiders are heavily restricted since 2005, so companies use **KEIPs**, bonuses tied to performance or process milestones. On the supplier: an unsecured claim of 12 might recover about 30%, so paying it in full costs the estate about 8.4 more; if losing the supplier for 6 weeks costs 18 of margin, a **critical vendor** payment, conditioned on continued normal trade terms, is worth it and the court can approve it.

follow_ups.q: Why might a sponsor stay involved in a restructuring where its equity is out of the money?
follow_ups.a: It may inject new money to keep a stake, fear litigation over past dividends or LMEs, want to protect its reputation with lenders for future deals, or negotiate releases from claims in exchange for a contribution.

follow_ups.q: What does the UCC investigate?
follow_ups.a: Whether secured lenders' liens are valid and perfected, whether pre-filing transactions (dividends, asset transfers, LMEs) can be challenged as fraudulent transfers or preferences, and whether the plan valuation is too low. These claims give it leverage to obtain more for unsecured creditors.

follow_ups.q: What is a restructuring support agreement?
follow_ups.a: A contract in which the company and a critical mass of creditors commit to support a specific restructuring (terms, milestones, voting). It is the backbone of prepackaged and prearranged Chapter 11 cases.

prerequisites: Chapter 11 process: prepack vs prearranged vs free-fall, RSAs, the plan and rights offerings
DIP financing: superpriority, priming, adequate protection and roll-ups
Liquidity runway and the 13-week cash flow forecast

cards.topic: Intercreditor agreements: payment vs lien subordination, payment blockage, standstill and turnover
cards.question: What does an intercreditor agreement do? Explain payment subordination vs lien subordination, payment blockage, standstill and turnover. Example: collateral worth 150, a first lien of 200, a second lien of 100, 60 of unencumbered assets and 90 of unsecured claims. What does each class recover if the second lien is only lien-subordinated, and if it is also payment-subordinated?
cards.answer: An **intercreditor agreement (ICA)** is a contract between creditor groups (and the company) that sets **who gets paid first and who can act when**, beyond what the law gives them. **Lien subordination**: the junior secured creditor ranks behind the senior only on the **proceeds of the shared collateral**; for everything else it is a normal creditor. **Payment subordination**: the junior agrees that the senior is repaid **in full from any source** before it receives anything, with a **turnover** clause forcing it to hand over what it receives. **Payment blockage**: after a senior default, payments to the junior are frozen for a period (for US senior subordinated notes, typically up to 179 days in any 360-day period for non-payment defaults; permanently for a senior payment default). **Standstill**: the junior cannot accelerate or enforce for a period after its own default (often 90 to 180 days) so the senior controls the enforcement. In the example, the first lien takes the 150 of collateral and has a 50 **deficiency claim**; the unencumbered 60 is shared by 50 + 100 + 90 = 240 of unsecured claims, 25 cents each. **Lien subordination only**: first lien 150 + 12.5 = **162.5**, second lien **25**, unsecured **22.5**. **Payment subordination**: the second lien's 25 is turned over to the first lien: **187.5 / 0 / 22.5**. Unsecured creditors get the same in both cases: subordination only moves value between the parties to the contract.

follow_ups.q: Why would a junior lender accept a standstill?
follow_ups.a: Because without it the senior would not lend, or would lend on worse terms, and because a coordinated enforcement led by the senior usually preserves more value than a race to enforce. In exchange the junior gets higher pricing, a purchase option and limits on how much senior debt can be added.

follow_ups.q: What is a senior debt cap in an intercreditor?
follow_ups.a: A maximum amount of senior debt (principal plus a cushion, often 10-15%) that ranks ahead of the junior. Senior debt above the cap loses its priority, which protects the junior from being primed by extra borrowing.

follow_ups.q: In a unitranche, where is the intercreditor?
follow_ups.a: In the agreement among lenders between the first-out and last-out lenders. The borrower is not always a party, so it may not even know the split; it matters in enforcement and voting.

prerequisites: Recovery waterfall and the fulcrum security
Liability management exercises in numbers: uptier, drop-down, double-dip and cooperation agreements

cards.topic: The restructuring and distressed credit market today (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: What is going on in the restructuring and distressed credit market right now? Are defaults high or low, and why do different default rates tell different stories?
cards.answer: As of September 2026, the picture is **low headline defaults but lots of quiet restructuring**. On the classic measure, US leveraged loan **payment defaults** are low: PitchBook LCD had them at **0.87% by amount and 1.17% by issuer count in August 2026**. But once you add **liability management exercises** (LMEs: distressed exchanges, uptiers, drop-downs, amend-and-extends at a loss), the **dual-track default rate is about 2.9%**, and LMEs make up well over half of all loan defaults (59% of the trailing-12-month count in August). Formal bankruptcies are also high: S&P Global Market Intelligence counted **372 large US corporate bankruptcies in the first half of 2026**, the most for a first half since 2010, led by industrials, consumer discretionary and healthcare. Big cases this year include **Saks Global** (January, with about USD 1.75bn of DIP and exit financing) and **QVC Group** (a prepack filed in April, cutting debt from about USD 6.6bn to 1.3bn, confirmed in July). The stress has moved to **private credit**: Fitch's US private credit default rate hit a record **6.3%** in the 12 months to August 2026, with rising PIK use and non-accruals, while syndicated markets stay open and high-yield spreads are moderate (CDX HY about 300bp at the end of June). The drivers: rates higher than when the 2020-2021 LBO debt was written, floating-rate interest burdens, tariffs and sector disruption (retail, media, chemicals, healthcare services), and a 2027-2028 maturity wall. In Europe, UK restructuring plans and French accelerated safeguards with cross-class cram-down are the main tools, and US groups increasingly use English Part 26A plans too.

follow_ups.q: Why do so many LMEs end in bankruptcy anyway?
follow_ups.a: An LME often extends maturities or adds priming debt without cutting total debt much, so leverage stays too high and interest keeps rising. Studies by agencies and data providers show a large share of distressed exchanges re-default within a few years; the LME buys time rather than fixing the balance sheet.

follow_ups.q: Which indicator would you watch to anticipate defaults?
follow_ups.a: The distress ratio (share of loans trading below 80), CCC spreads, the share of issuers with interest coverage below 1.5x, maturity schedules for the next 18-24 months, and in private credit the non-accrual and PIK shares. PitchBook LCD also publishes a six-month forward Default Predictor.

follow_ups.q: Why is Texas the main US bankruptcy venue?
follow_ups.a: The Southern District of Texas complex-case panel offers fast, predictable handling of large cases and debtor-friendly procedures, so large companies with a Texas affiliate file there. It lost some appeal after a judge's conflict scandal in 2023 but remained the leading venue with Delaware and New Jersey.

prerequisites: Liability management exercises in numbers: uptier, drop-down, double-dip and cooperation agreements
Private credit and direct lending vs syndicated loans: unitranche, first-out/last-out and the 2026 market
UK schemes of arrangement vs Part 26A restructuring plans (and Germany's StaRUG)
Chapter 11 process: prepack vs prearranged vs free-fall, RSAs, the plan and rights offerings

cards.topic: Multi-year walkthrough: a debt-financed factory that later breaks down, and inventory bought on credit
cards.question: A company buys a factory for 100, financed with a 10% bond; the factory is depreciated straight-line over 10 years and the tax rate is 25%. Walk me through the three statements (a) on day one, (b) at the end of year 1, (c) when the factory breaks down at the start of year 3 and is written off, and the bond becomes due. Then: it orders 10 of inventory on debt and sells it for 20. Walk me through that too.
cards.answer: **Day one**: nothing on the income statement. Investing cash flow is -100 (capex) and financing cash flow +100 (new debt), so cash is unchanged; on the balance sheet PP&E is +100 and debt +100. **End of year 1**: depreciation 10 and interest 10 cut pre-tax income by 20, so net income falls by **15** after tax. On the cash flow statement I start from -15, add back the 10 of depreciation: cash is **-5**, which is just the after-tax interest. Balance sheet: cash -5, PP&E -10, so assets -15; equity -15; it balances. **Start of year 3**: net PP&E is 80, the write-off is an 80 pre-tax loss, net income **-60**; add back the non-cash 80 and cash is **+20** (the tax saving, if the loss is deductible). Assets: cash +20, PP&E -80, so -60; equity -60. The bond coming due only reclassifies it to current liabilities; if it is actually repaid, cash and debt both fall by 100. **Inventory**: buying 10 on debt is inventory +10, debt +10, no P&L. Selling it for 20: revenue 20, COGS 10, net income **+7.5**; cash from operations is 7.5 plus the 10 inventory decrease, so **+17.5**; cash +17.5, inventory -10, equity +7.5.

follow_ups.q: What if the factory is only impaired to 50 instead of written off?
follow_ups.a: Loss 30, net income -22.5, cash +7.5 from the tax saving (if deductible), PP&E -30, equity -22.5. Future depreciation falls to 50 over the remaining 8 years, i.e. 6.25 a year.

follow_ups.q: Where does the factory appear in a DCF?
follow_ups.a: Only through capex (the 100 outflow in the year it is bought) and through the tax shield of its depreciation. The write-off itself is non-cash, so it matters only for taxes and for what it says about future cash flows.

follow_ups.q: If the company pays interest, why is cash only -5 and not -10?
follow_ups.a: Interest is tax-deductible (saves 2.5) and depreciation, although non-cash, also saves 2.5 of tax. So the cash cost is 10 - 2.5 - 2.5 = 5.

sources: Breaking Into Wall Street / Mergers & Inquisitions, 400 Investment Banking Interview Questions guide (paid guide, not linked)

cards.topic: Walkthrough traps: a 100 bailout and a 100 write-down of debt (gain on debt extinguishment)
cards.question: Walk me through a 100 bailout of a company. Then walk me through a 100 write-down of the company's debt (the liability it owes). Tax rate 25%. Why is the second one counter-intuitive?
cards.answer: For a bailout I first ask **what form it takes**. If it is equity, the income statement doesn't move; cash from financing is +100; on the balance sheet cash +100 and equity +100. If it is a loan, it is the same except debt +100 instead of equity, and interest will hit future income statements. A **write-down of debt** is counter-intuitive because it is a **gain**: the company owes less. Pre-tax income +100, net income **+75**. On the cash flow statement I start from +75 and subtract the non-cash gain of 100, so cash is **-25**: that's the tax on the gain. Balance sheet: cash -25; debt -100 and equity +75, so liabilities and equity -25. It balances. In practice, many tax systems let a distressed company avoid paying tax on cancelled debt, reducing its tax losses instead, so the cash cost may be zero. The broader point: a debt forgiveness makes equity holders richer, and debt bought back below face value creates an accounting gain.

follow_ups.q: Who benefits from the debt write-down economically?
follow_ups.a: Shareholders, at the expense of creditors: equity rises by the after-tax gain. That is why write-downs usually come with creditors taking equity (a debt-for-equity swap), so that they get the upside.

follow_ups.q: Does a debt write-down change enterprise value?
follow_ups.a: Not directly: EV reflects operating assets. Equity value goes up and net debt goes down, roughly offsetting, apart from the tax. Indirectly it can raise EV by removing distress costs.

follow_ups.q: What happens if the gain is not taxed but reduces NOLs?
follow_ups.a: No cash effect today: cash 0, debt -100, equity +100 on the income statement gain (with a deferred tax asset reduction if the NOLs had been recognised). The cost is higher cash taxes in the future.

prerequisites: Debt-for-equity swaps: how creditors take control, recovery maths, hold-outs
Tax losses (NOLs), deferred tax assets and effective vs statutory tax rate

cards.topic: Negative working capital: good or bad, and what it does to a DCF and an LBO
cards.question: A company has negative working capital. Is that a bad sign? A retailer has revenue of 1,000, COGS of 750, collects in 5 days, holds inventory 30 days and pays suppliers in 60 days. What is its working capital, and what happens to its cash when it grows 10%?
cards.answer: Negative working capital means current operating liabilities exceed current operating assets: the business is **financed by its customers and suppliers**. It is **not necessarily bad**. For retailers like Amazon, Walmart or McDonald's, customers pay immediately while suppliers are paid later; for subscription or software businesses, customers pay upfront, creating **deferred revenue**. That is a sign of bargaining power. Here receivables are about 13.7, inventory 61.6 and payables 123.3, so working capital is about **-48**, and the cash conversion cycle is 5 + 30 - 60 = **-25 days**. If it grows 10%, working capital becomes about -53, so growth **releases about 5 of cash**: growth pays for itself. It **is** a bad sign when it comes from stretching suppliers or from distress: unpaid bills piling up, supplier finance hiding debt, or a company that would face a cash crunch if its sales fell, because then the mechanism runs in reverse.

follow_ups.q: If the retailer's sales fall 10%, what happens to its cash?
follow_ups.a: With constant days, NWC goes from about -48 to -43: working capital rises by about 5, which is a cash outflow of about 5 on top of the lower profit. Negative-WC businesses burn cash when they shrink.

follow_ups.q: Is supplier finance debt?
follow_ups.a: Legally it is a payable, but economically it is short-term funding provided by a bank. Rating agencies and many analysts add it to debt, especially when payment terms are much longer than the industry norm.

follow_ups.q: How does negative WC affect ROIC?
follow_ups.a: It lowers invested capital, so ROIC is higher. That is why software and retail companies can show very high ROIC; analysts check that it is not just stretched payables.

prerequisites: Reading working capital: DSO, DIO, DPO and what a DSO fall from 58 to 42 days means
sources: Breaking Into Wall Street / Mergers & Inquisitions, 400 Investment Banking Interview Questions guide (paid guide, not linked)

cards.topic: DCF sensitivity mental maths: 1% (or 10%) more revenue vs 1% on the discount rate
cards.question: In a DCF, which has a bigger impact on value: a 1% increase in revenue in every year, or a 1% move in the discount rate? What about 10% more revenue versus one percentage point on the WACC? Give numbers.
cards.answer: It depends on how you read "1%", so I'd say both. If margins are constant, **1% more revenue in every year is roughly 1% more free cash flow, so about 1% more value**. With fixed costs, operating leverage makes it more, perhaps 2-3%. A **one percentage point** change in the WACC is much bigger. In my example, with a 9% WACC, 2.5% terminal growth and about 74% of value in the terminal value, going to 10% cuts value by about **13%**. The quick maths: the terminal multiple is 1/(r - g), and 1/6.5 versus 1/7.5 is about 13% lower. Even a **relative** 1% change, 9% to 9.09%, cuts value by about **1.4%**, a bit more than 1% more revenue, because a DCF has a long **duration**: roughly 1/(r - g), about 15 years. So a 1 point move in WACC outweighs even 10% more revenue: -13% versus +10%. The general answer is "it could go either way, but usually the discount rate matters more", and that's why rates drive valuations so much.

follow_ups.q: Why do growth stocks have a longer duration?
follow_ups.a: Most of their cash flows are far in the future, and r - g is small, so 1/(r - g) is large. A company growing 6% forever with a 9% discount rate has a duration of about 33 years; one growing 1% has about 12.5.

follow_ups.q: And a 1% change in terminal growth?
follow_ups.a: With r = 9%, going from g = 2.5% to 3.5% raises the terminal multiple from 1/6.5 to 1/5.5, +18%. Growth and the discount rate enter symmetrically through r - g, which is why the WACC-vs-g sensitivity table is so wide.

follow_ups.q: Does a 1 pp change in the tax rate matter much?
follow_ups.a: Little: NOPAT scales with (1 - t), so 25% to 26% cuts NOPAT by 1/75, about 1.3%, slightly offset by a lower after-tax cost of debt in the WACC.

prerequisites: DCF sensitivity tables: WACC vs growth and WACC vs exit multiple
sources: Breaking Into Wall Street / Mergers & Inquisitions, 400 Investment Banking Interview Questions guide (paid guide, not linked)

cards.topic: Twin companies, one with debt: cost of equity, WACC, enterprise value and P/E
cards.question: Two companies are identical (EBIT 100 forever, tax 25%, unlevered cost of capital 7.5%) except that B has 400 of permanent debt at 5%. Which has the higher cost of equity, the higher WACC, the higher enterprise value and the higher P/E? B looks cheaper on P/E: is it?
cards.answer: Under Modigliani-Miller with taxes: A is worth 75 / 7.5% = **1,000**. B is worth 1,000 plus the tax shield on its debt, 25% x 400 = 100, so **EV 1,100** and equity 700. **B's cost of equity is higher**: its net income is 60 on 700 of equity, **8.6%** versus 7.5%, because shareholders bear financial risk on top of business risk. **B's WACC is lower**, 6.8% versus 7.5%, only because of the tax shield; without taxes WACCs would be equal. **B's P/E is lower**: 700 / 60 = **11.7x** versus 13.3x for A. That doesn't make B cheaper: its earnings are riskier, so investors demand a higher earnings yield. P/E comparisons across companies with different leverage are misleading, which is why we compare on EV/EBIT or EV/EBITDA. As a rule, more debt raises the cost of equity and, up to the point where distress costs bite, slightly lowers the WACC.

follow_ups.q: What happens if B has 900 of debt instead?
follow_ups.a: In pure MM with taxes, value keeps rising with debt, but in reality spreads widen and distress costs appear, so B's WACC eventually rises and its value falls. The optimum sits where the marginal tax shield equals the marginal expected distress cost.

follow_ups.q: What are B's levered and A's unlevered betas if the market premium is 5% and the risk-free rate 2.5%?
follow_ups.a: A's asset beta = (7.5 - 2.5) / 5 = 1.0. B's equity beta = (8.57 - 2.5) / 5 = 1.21, consistent with beta_E = beta_U + (beta_U - beta_D)(1 - t) D/E = 1 + 0.5 x 0.75 x 400/700, where debt yielding 5% has a beta of 0.5. The simple Hamada formula, which assumes riskless debt, would overstate it at 1.43.

follow_ups.q: Would EV/EBITDA be identical for A and B?
follow_ups.a: Almost: the only difference is the value of the tax shield, 1,100 vs 1,000 here. In practice comps' EV/EBITDA are compared across leverage levels precisely because they are much less sensitive to capital structure than P/E.

sources: Breaking Into Wall Street / Mergers & Inquisitions, 400 Investment Banking Interview Questions guide (paid guide, not linked)

cards.topic: Convertible bonds in the EV bridge, the diluted share count and the WACC: debt or equity?
cards.question: A company has 1 million shares at 100 and 10 million of convertible bonds (par 1,000, conversion price 50). How do you treat the convertibles in the diluted share count and in enterprise value? What changes if the share price is 40, or if the bonds are net-share settled? And how do you put a convertible in the WACC?
cards.answer: The rule: **in the money, treat it as equity; out of the money, treat it as debt**, never both. At 100 the conversion price of 50 is in the money. Each bond converts into 1,000 / 50 = 20 shares, and there are 10,000 bonds, so **200,000 new shares**: 1.2 million diluted shares, equity value **120 million**, and the convertibles are not added again as debt. At 40 it is out of the money, so I keep 1 million shares and add the **10 million face value to debt** in the EV bridge. With **net share settlement**, the company repays the par in cash and delivers only the excess value in shares. That's 200,000 x (100 - 50) / 100 = **100,000 shares**, and the 10 million par stays in debt. For the **WACC**, the coupon understates the true cost, because investors accept a low coupon in exchange for the embedded option. So I either split the convert into a straight bond, at the yield of the company's straight debt, plus an equity option, or I weight it by the conversion probability.

follow_ups.q: What if the share price is exactly around the conversion price?
follow_ups.a: The choice is a convention: many banks count it as debt until clearly ITM. A cleaner approach is the treasury-stock logic applied to the option value, or presenting both cases in a sensitivity.

follow_ups.q: What does a capped call do to dilution?
follow_ups.a: The issuer buys a call spread on its own shares from banks, which offsets dilution from conversion up to the cap price. Above the cap dilution resumes. It effectively raises the conversion price from the issuer's point of view.

follow_ups.q: Do you remove the convert interest from net income when computing diluted EPS?
follow_ups.a: Yes, under the if-converted method you add back the after-tax interest to net income and add the conversion shares, and use it only if it is dilutive.

prerequisites: Convertible bonds: mechanics and why companies issue them
Diluted shares and the treasury stock method

cards.topic: Combined multiples after a merger: is the new EV/EBITDA or P/E the average of the two?
cards.question: A buyer trades at 10x EBITDA (EV 1,000, EBITDA 100) and buys a target trading at 6x (EV 300, EBITDA 50). What is the combined EV/EBITDA? Is it the simple average of 10x and 6x? What if the buyer pays 8x? And for P/E: a buyer at 25x buys a target for 15x earnings in stock. What will the combined P/E be, and does the share price move?
cards.answer: It is **not the simple average** (8x); it is a **weighted average of the two multiples, weighted by EBITDA**, because you add numerators and denominators: (1,000 + 300) / (100 + 50) = **8.67x**. The buyer is twice as big by EBITDA, so it's (2 x 10 + 6) / 3. If the buyer pays 8x, 400, and markets simply add values, the combined EV is 1,400 and the multiple **9.33x**; synergies would add to both. For P/E it is the same logic, weighted by earnings. The BIWS example: a buyer with 10 shares at 25 and net income 10 (P/E 25) buys a target with net income 10 for 150 in stock, issuing 6 shares. EPS goes from 1.00 to 20 / 16 = **1.25**, 25% accretive. But if the market values the combined company at 250 + 150 = 400, the P/E becomes **20x**, a blend of 25x and 15x, and the **share price stays 25**. Accretion doesn't create value on its own: the multiple falls because the buyer has mixed in lower-multiple earnings.

follow_ups.q: Buyer and target have the same EBITDA: what is the combined multiple?
follow_ups.a: Then the weights are 50/50 and it is the simple average, 8x in this example. The simple average is right only when the denominators are equal.

follow_ups.q: Using EV weights, what would you compute?
follow_ups.a: The harmonic mean: 1 / (w1/m1 + w2/m2) with EV weights 1000/1300 and 300/1300, which again gives 8.67x. Both routes agree when done correctly; weighting the multiples by EV arithmetically would give 9.08x, which is wrong.

follow_ups.q: Why might the market not blend the multiples?
follow_ups.a: If investors believe the buyer will improve the target (synergies, better management) or the deal changes growth expectations, the combined company can re-rate up; if they fear overpayment or integration risk, it can trade below the blend.

sources: Breaking Into Wall Street / Mergers & Inquisitions, 400 Investment Banking Interview Questions guide (paid guide, not linked)

cards.topic: Accretion/dilution in 30 seconds: comparing the target's earnings yield with the weighted cost of acquisition
cards.question: Without building a merger model, how can you tell quickly whether a deal is accretive? A buyer trades at 20x earnings, its cash earns 4% pre-tax, it can borrow at 6%, the tax rate is 25%. It buys a target with net income 20 for 300 (15x). Is it accretive if paid in stock? In cash? With 50% stock, 25% cash, 25% new debt? And if the buyer traded at 12x?
cards.answer: Compare the **target's earnings yield at the purchase price** with the **after-tax cost of each funding source**. The target yields 1 / 15 = **6.67%**. The costs are: **stock** costs the buyer's earnings yield, 1 / 20 = **5%**; **cash** costs the forgone interest after tax, 4% x 0.75 = **3%**; **new debt** costs 6% x 0.75 = **4.5%**. All three are below 6.67%, so every structure is **accretive**. The mix costs 0.5 x 5 + 0.25 x 3 + 0.25 x 4.5 = **4.4%**. A quick model confirms it: the buyer has net income 100 and 100 shares at 20, so EPS of 1.00 becomes **1.043 in stock (+4.3%)**, 1.11 in cash (+11%) and 1.064 with the mix (+6.4%). If the buyer traded at **12x**, its stock would cost 8.3%, above 6.67%, so the all-stock deal is **4% dilutive**. Caveats: this ignores fees, write-up amortisation and synergies. And accretion is not value creation.

follow_ups.q: Why do deals financed with cash look so accretive when rates are low?
follow_ups.a: The after-tax cost of cash is tiny (e.g. 1% x 0.75 = 0.75%), so almost any target earnings yield beats it. With policy rates of 3.75-4.00% in the US and 2.50% in the euro area (as of Sept 2026), this advantage is much smaller than in 2020-2021.

follow_ups.q: At what purchase P/E does the all-stock deal become dilutive?
follow_ups.a: Above the buyer's own P/E, 20x here: paying 20x gives exactly zero accretion (target yield 5% equals the cost of stock).

follow_ups.q: Why would a buyer do a dilutive deal?
follow_ups.a: If the target grows much faster, dilution in year 1 can turn into accretion in year 2-3, and the deal can still create value. Management usually quotes 'accretive by year 2' in that case.

prerequisites: Breakeven synergies: why an accretive deal can still destroy value

cards.topic: Exchange ratio and contribution analysis in a merger of equals: who should own what?
cards.question: A has 100m shares at 30 and B has 50m shares at 40. A offers a 25% premium to B's shareholders, paid in A shares. What is the exchange ratio and the pro forma ownership? A contributes EBITDA 400, net income 200 and revenue 3,000; B contributes EBITDA 300, net income 100 and revenue 1,500. A has net debt of 1,000, B of 200. What does a contribution analysis say about the fair split?
cards.answer: The offer is 40 x 1.25 = 50 per B share, so the **exchange ratio** is 50 / 30 = **1.667 A shares per B share**. A issues 83.3m shares, so **B's holders own 83.3 / 183.3 = 45.5%** of the combined company. A **contribution analysis** compares that with what each side brings. B contributes 33% of revenue and 33% of net income, but **43% of EBITDA**. EBITDA is an enterprise-level metric, though, so it must be **adjusted for debt**: A carries 1,000 of net debt and B only 200. At the combined multiple of 8.86x, B's implied equity is about **49%** of the total. So on a leverage-adjusted basis, 45.5% looks fair to generous for A, while on net income it looks generous for B. That's why the analysis is done on several metrics, and why the answer depends on growth, margins and synergies, not on one line.

follow_ups.q: Why would a buyer use a fixed exchange ratio rather than a fixed price?
follow_ups.a: It fixes the ownership split and avoids issuing a lot more shares if its own price falls. The cost is that target holders bear the price risk, so they may demand a collar.

follow_ups.q: How can parties rebalance an ownership split without changing the ER?
follow_ups.a: With a special dividend or cash component paid to one side's shareholders before closing, as in PSA-FCA, or with a cash-and-stock mix.

follow_ups.q: What does the arbitrage spread look like in a fixed-ER stock deal?
follow_ups.a: Arbitrageurs buy the target and short ER acquirer shares; the spread is ER x P_A - P_B, reflecting deal risk and time to close.

prerequisites: Cash vs stock deals: risk sharing, exchange ratios and collars
sources: Breaking Into Wall Street / Mergers & Inquisitions, 400 Investment Banking Interview Questions guide (paid guide, not linked)

cards.topic: Stock deal vs asset deal: deferred tax liabilities on write-ups, tax-deductible goodwill and the 338(h)(10) election
cards.question: A buyer pays 1,000 for a target with book equity of 400 (tax basis equal to book) and writes up its PP&E by 200. Tax rate 25%. Compute goodwill in a stock deal and in an asset deal. Why does a DTL appear in one and not the other? What is a 338(h)(10) election, and why would you write down a seller's deferred tax asset?
cards.answer: In a **stock deal** the buyer purchases the shares, so the target's **tax basis doesn't change**; the 200 write-up is higher book value that will never be deductible. That creates a **deferred tax liability** of 25% x 200 = **50**. Goodwill is 1,000 minus the net assets of 400 + 200 - 50, so **450**, and it is **not tax-deductible**. In an **asset deal** the buyer purchases the assets, so the tax basis is **stepped up** to fair value: no DTL, goodwill **400**. In the US, both the write-up and the goodwill (over 15 years) become **deductible**, worth about **90** in PV at 8% here. A **338(h)(10) election** lets you do a legal stock purchase but be treated as an asset purchase for tax: you keep the contracts and legal simplicity and get the step-up. It works when the target is an S-corp or a subsidiary of a group, and the seller usually asks to be compensated for its extra tax. Finally, a seller's **DTA from tax losses is written down** when the change of ownership limits how much of those NOLs can be used (Section 382).

follow_ups.q: Where does the DTL go in the EV bridge?
follow_ups.a: Usually nowhere: it is a non-cash accounting item unwinding with depreciation. Some analysts treat large DTLs that will reverse soon as debt-like, but the standard bridge ignores them.

follow_ups.q: Does the DTL affect the purchase price?
follow_ups.a: No, the price is 1,000 either way. It only changes how the price is allocated: more goodwill in the stock deal. What changes value is the tax step-up in the asset deal, worth about 90 here.

follow_ups.q: Why can't a C-corp standalone target use 338(h)(10)?
follow_ups.a: Because the deemed asset sale would trigger corporate-level tax on top of the shareholders' tax, destroying the benefit. The election is allowed only where that double layer does not arise, i.e. S-corps and members of a consolidated group.

prerequisites: Deferred taxes and IFRS vs US GAAP
Tax losses (NOLs), deferred tax assets and effective vs statutory tax rate

cards.topic: Buying a company with tax losses: the Section 382 limit and what the NOLs are really worth
cards.question: A US target has 300m of NOLs and expects about 100m of taxable income a year. A buyer acquires its equity for 1bn. How much of the NOLs can the buyer use each year, and what are they worth? Why can't you simply add 21% x 300m to the price?
cards.answer: In the US, after an **ownership change**, Section 382 caps how much of the old losses can be used each year. The cap is the **equity value of the target times the long-term tax-exempt rate** published monthly by the IRS: **3.88% for September 2026** (as of Sept 2026). So the cap here is 1bn x 3.88% = **38.8m a year**, and 300m of NOLs take almost **8 years** to use. Each year saves 38.8 x 21% = 8.1m of tax. At an 8% discount rate the PV is about **46m**, against a face value of 21% x 300 = **63m**, and against 53m if the target could use them freely (post-2017 NOLs can offset only 80% of taxable income). So NOLs are worth their **present value under the limit**, not face value. They're one reason tax-loss companies trade at a premium, and a reason a buyer's model must write down part of the seller's deferred tax asset.

follow_ups.q: Why would a buyer pay less for NOLs when rates are low?
follow_ups.a: The annual cap is equity value times the long-term tax-exempt rate: lower rates mean a lower cap, so slower use of the losses and a lower PV. Higher rates since 2022 have actually increased the usable amount.

follow_ups.q: Does the 382 limit apply to an IPO or a large share issue?
follow_ups.a: It can: any shift of more than 50 points among 5% holders within three years triggers it, including through primary issues. Companies with valuable NOLs sometimes adopt 'NOL poison pills' to stop investors crossing 5%.

follow_ups.q: Can a built-in gain increase the limit?
follow_ups.a: Yes: if the loss company has net unrealised built-in gains, recognising them within five years can increase the limitation. It is a technical adjustment, not needed in a first-round answer.

cards.topic: Earn-outs and CVRs: bridging a valuation gap, valuing the contingent payment and the accounting trap
cards.question: What is an earn-out and why would a buyer offer one? A buyer pays 100 upfront plus 30 in three years if revenue reaches a target, which it judges 50% likely; discount rate 10%. What is the earn-out worth, and how is it accounted for? What happens to the buyer's P&L if the target does well?
cards.answer: An **earn-out** is a deferred, **contingent** part of the price: the seller gets more only if the business hits targets, usually revenue or EBITDA over 1-3 years. It **bridges a valuation gap**: the seller believes in the plan, the buyer doesn't fully. It shifts risk to the seller and keeps founders motivated. It's mostly used for private and early-stage targets; for listed targets the equivalent is a **CVR**, a contingent value right, common in pharma. Here the expected payment is 50% x 30 = 15, worth 15 / 1.1^3 = **11.3** today, so the total consideration is about **111.3**. Under IFRS 3 and ASC 805 it is booked at that **fair value** on day one, which feeds into goodwill. If it's a liability it is then **remeasured through the P&L**. The trap: if the target does very well and payment becomes certain at the end of year 2, the liability rises to 30 / 1.1 = 27.3, which is a **loss of about 16** for the buyer. Good news for the business shows up as a charge.

follow_ups.q: Why would the seller accept an earn-out?
follow_ups.a: Because it can get a higher headline price if it really believes in its plan. It is a signal: a seller refusing any earn-out suggests it doubts its own forecasts.

follow_ups.q: How would a merger-arb desk value a listed CVR?
follow_ups.a: Probability of the milestone (often based on clinical or regulatory odds) times the payment, discounted at a rate reflecting the time and the counterparty, then adjusted for liquidity. CVRs often trade at a big discount because they are illiquid and hard to hedge.

follow_ups.q: Is the earn-out part of the EV bridge?
follow_ups.a: Yes: an expected earn-out payable by the company is a debt-like item at its fair value. Analysts add it to net debt when valuing the buyer after the deal.

sources: Breaking Into Wall Street / Mergers & Inquisitions, 400 Investment Banking Interview Questions guide (paid guide, not linked)

cards.topic: Transaction fees vs financing fees: where they go in the accounts, the sources and uses and the IRR
cards.question: In an acquisition, how do you treat advisory and legal fees versus debt financing fees? A sponsor buys a company for 1,000 with 500 of new debt, pays 20 of M&A fees and 2.5% financing fees on the debt, amortised over 5 years. What happens to the equity cheque, the accounts and the IRR if exit equity is 1,300 in year 5?
cards.answer: **Transaction fees** (M&A advisory, legal, due diligence) are **expensed at closing** under both IFRS 3 and US GAAP: they reduce retained earnings and are **not part of goodwill**. **Financing fees** are part of the cost of borrowing: they are **capitalised and amortised over the life of the debt**, presented as a **reduction of the debt's carrying amount** (US GAAP since ASU 2015-03; IFRS via the effective interest rate). Here, financing fees are 2.5% x 500 = **12.5**, amortised at **2.5 a year** as extra non-cash interest expense. Sources and uses: uses are 1,000 + 20 + 12.5 = **1,032.5**, sources are 500 of debt plus **532.5 of equity** instead of 500. With exit equity of 1,300, the money multiple falls from 2.60x to **2.44x** and the IRR from **21.1% to 19.5%**: fees cost the sponsor about 1.5 points. That's why sponsors negotiate fees hard, and why buyers keep paying for advice anyway.

follow_ups.q: What is OID and why do lenders ask for it?
follow_ups.a: Original issue discount: the loan is funded at, say, 98 for 100 of face value. It raises the lender's yield without raising the coupon, and it is a way to adjust pricing in syndication (flex). For the borrower it is a financing cost amortised like a fee.

follow_ups.q: Are the M&A fees in the target's purchase price for goodwill?
follow_ups.a: No: goodwill = consideration paid for the equity minus fair value of net identifiable assets. Fees are a separate expense of the acquirer.

follow_ups.q: Who pays the sponsor's own transaction fees in an LBO?
follow_ups.a: Economically the fund's investors, because they are funded from the equity; some sponsors also charge 'monitoring' or 'transaction' fees to portfolio companies, which LPs increasingly require to be offset against management fees.

cards.topic: Paper LBO in 60 seconds: IRR mental maths, the MoM-to-IRR table and back-solving the exit EBITDA
cards.question: A sponsor buys a company with EBITDA of 100 at 10x with 60% debt. In year 5 EBITDA is 150, it exits at 9x and it has repaid 250 of debt. What is the IRR, in your head? Now back-solve: what exit EBITDA gives exactly 20%? And can the IRR be positive if the exit EV is below the entry EV?
cards.answer: Entry EV 1,000, debt **600**, equity **400**. Exit EV = 150 x 9 = 1,350; remaining debt 600 - 250 = 350; exit equity **1,000**. Money multiple 1,000 / 400 = **2.5x** over 5 years. The benchmarks I know: 2x in 5 years is about 15%, 3x about 25%, so **2.5x is about 20%** (exactly 20.1%). **Back-solve**: 20% over 5 years is a 2.49x multiple, so exit equity must be about 995; add the 350 of debt to get an exit EV of 1,345; divide by 9x and **exit EBITDA must be about 150**. And **yes**, the IRR can be positive with a lower exit EV. If EBITDA stays at 100 and the exit is at 9x, EV falls to 900, but debt paydown leaves equity at 550: 1.375x, about **6.6%**. Deleveraging alone creates equity value.

follow_ups.q: Same deal, but the sponsor exits in year 3 at 2x. Better or worse?
follow_ups.a: IRR 26%, higher than 20%, but the MoM is lower. Funds care about both: LPs want IRR, but also 'cash on cash'; a quick 2x is great for IRR but deploys less capital for less time.

follow_ups.q: What EBITDA growth gives 25% (3x) with the same assumptions?
follow_ups.a: Exit equity 1,200, exit EV 1,550, EBITDA 1,550 / 9 = 172, about 11.5% annual growth.

follow_ups.q: Why do sponsors assume exit multiple = entry multiple or lower?
follow_ups.a: To avoid relying on multiple expansion, which is outside their control; lenders and investment committees want returns driven by EBITDA growth and deleveraging.

prerequisites: LBO: mechanics, returns and the private equity model
IRR vs money multiple and the LBO value creation bridge
Paper LBO: worked example in 10 minutes

cards.topic: IPO exit vs full sale: why a staged sell-down lowers the sponsor's IRR
cards.question: A sponsor bought a company for 8x EBITDA of 200 with 50% debt. In year 5 the equity is worth 2,600. What is the IRR if it sells everything to a buyer in year 5? What if instead it IPOs, sells one third at the IPO with a 15% discount and the rest in equal blocks in years 6 and 7 with the value flat? When does an IPO still make sense?
cards.answer: Entry EV is 1,600, so equity is **800**. A full sale in year 5 for 2,600 is **3.25x** and an IRR of **26.6%**. In an IPO the sponsor can't sell everything at once: the market can't absorb it, there's a **lock-up**, usually 180 days, and the IPO is priced at a **discount**. Selling a third in year 5 at a 15% discount (737), then 867 in years 6 and 7, gives about **3.1x and an IRR of about 20.7%**: roughly **6 points lower**. Even without the discount it is **22%**, because part of the money comes back later. An IPO still makes sense when public markets value the company much more than private buyers do, when no trade buyer or sponsor can pay enough, for very large companies, or when the sponsor expects the shares to keep rising. With 10% growth in the value in years 6 and 7, the IRR recovers to about 22.6% and the multiple reaches 3.4x. That's why sponsors often run a **dual track** and take the better of the IPO and the sale.

follow_ups.q: How does a sponsor sell its remaining stake after the lock-up?
follow_ups.a: Usually through accelerated bookbuilds or overnight block trades at a discount of a few percent to the last price, sometimes a marketed follow-on. Banks may also buy the block at risk (a bought deal).

follow_ups.q: Why would the stock underperform after lock-up expiry?
follow_ups.a: The market anticipates a large supply of shares (the overhang) and the sponsor's signal when it sells. Stocks often drift down into lock-up expiry and fall on block announcements.

follow_ups.q: What is the IRR if the sponsor IPOs at a higher multiple, 10% above the private value, without discount on later sales?
follow_ups.a: Year 5: 2,860 / 3 x 0.85 = 810, then 953 in years 6 and 7: about 22.7%. Still below the full sale at 2,600 (26.6%), which shows how costly the delay is.

prerequisites: IPO pricing: bookbuilding, underpricing and the first-day pop
Follow-ons, accelerated bookbuilds and block trades

cards.topic: Can the lenders earn more than the private equity fund? When leverage lowers returns
cards.question: In an LBO, is it possible for the debt investors to earn a higher return than the private equity fund? A sponsor buys at 10x EBITDA of 100 with 600 of 8% debt and 400 of equity. EBITDA stays flat, 150 of debt is repaid over 5 years and the exit multiple falls to 8x. What are the two returns, and what does it tell you?
cards.answer: **Yes, and it happens more often than people think.** Lenders are contractually owed their coupon and principal, so as long as the company is worth more than the debt at exit they earn their yield, **about 8%** here. The equity takes the residual. Exit EV is 8 x 100 = 800, debt is 450, so equity is **350**: a multiple of **0.875x** and an IRR of about **-2.6%**. At 7x it would be 250, **-9%**. The general rule: leverage **amplifies** returns in both directions. Equity return is roughly r_A + (r_A - r_D) x D/E. It exceeds the cost of debt only if the return on the assets exceeds the cost of debt. When EBITDA stagnates or multiples contract, and in 2026 debt is expensive, the lenders do better than the fund. It tells you the deal relied on **growth or multiple expansion that didn't happen**, and that the equity effectively behaves like a call on the company that has ended up out of the money.

follow_ups.q: At what exit EV does the sponsor exactly get its money back?
follow_ups.a: When exit equity equals 400: EV = 400 + 450 = 850, i.e. 8.5x flat EBITDA. Below that the sponsor loses money.

follow_ups.q: What do sponsors do when a deal is underwater but not distressed?
follow_ups.a: Hold longer, extend the debt maturities (amend and extend), move the asset to a continuation vehicle, or inject equity to cure covenants and buy time for EBITDA to recover.

follow_ups.q: Why has private credit grown so much?
follow_ups.a: Banks pulled back after regulation, and floating-rate senior loans at 8-11% with covenants and seniority looked attractive against equity returns, especially once rates rose from 2022. Speed and certainty also appeal to sponsors.

prerequisites: LBO: mechanics, returns and the private equity model
Shareholders can like volatility (equity as a call option, Merton)

cards.topic: PIK debt in an LBO: why use it, how it compounds and what it does to IRR in good and bad cases
cards.question: What is PIK debt and why would a sponsor use it? In an LBO at 1,000 EV with 500 of senior debt, the sponsor replaces 150 of its equity with a 12% PIK note. Exit is in year 5 with 300 of senior debt left. Compare equity IRRs with and without the PIK if exit EV is 1,500, and if it is 900.
cards.answer: **PIK (payment-in-kind)** debt pays no cash interest: interest **accrues to the principal**, and everything is repaid at maturity or at exit. A **PIK toggle** lets the borrower choose cash or PIK each period. Sponsors use it to **stretch leverage without using cash flow**, so the senior debt can still be repaid. It is usually issued at a holding company, deeply subordinated, at a high rate. At 12% for 5 years, 150 grows to 150 x 1.12^5 = **264**. With exit EV **1,500**: without PIK, equity of 500 becomes 1,200, **2.4x, 19.1%**. With PIK, equity of 350 becomes 1,500 - 300 - 264 = 936, **2.67x, 21.7%**. With exit EV **900**: without PIK, 1.2x and **3.7%**; with PIK, 0.96x and **-0.8%**. PIK is cheap leverage when the deal works and costly when it doesn't, because it compounds silently at 12%.

follow_ups.q: Why does PIK debt carry a higher rate than senior debt?
follow_ups.a: It is subordinated (often structurally, at HoldCo), receives no cash until exit, and its claim grows, so recovery in default is low. Lenders want 10-15% or equity kickers.

follow_ups.q: What happens to leverage over time with PIK?
follow_ups.a: Total debt grows at the PIK rate; if EBITDA grows more slowly, leverage rises even without new borrowing. 4x total leverage with a 12% PIK tranche and flat EBITDA drifts up every year.

follow_ups.q: Can a company switch existing cash-pay debt to PIK?
follow_ups.a: Only with lenders' consent in an amendment, usually in exchange for a higher rate or fees. It is common in private credit when borrowers struggle and is seen as a soft default signal.
