That gap is not "euro companies are cheaper": it mostly reflects lower expected inflation in euros, so the euro cash flows must be projected with euro inflation too.

follow_ups.q: Why not use the current capital structure for the weights?
follow_ups.a: Because the WACC is applied to cash flows for decades, so it should reflect the structure the company will have on average, usually the target or the peer median at market values. The current structure can be temporarily off, for example just after an acquisition.

follow_ups.q: Is a 4% equity risk premium low or high?
follow_ups.a: Implied ERPs have mostly moved between about 3% and 6% over the last decades, so around 4% is in the lower-middle part of the range. With the 10-year at 5.2%, it means equities are priced to earn only about 9% a year, not much above bonds.

follow_ups.q: How does a 1-point rise in the 10-year yield change this WACC?
follow_ups.a: If spreads and the ERP stay put, both the cost of equity and the pre-tax cost of debt rise 1 point, so the WACC rises by 0.7 + 0.3 x 0.75 = about 0.93 points. In the five-year DCF example, going from 9% to 10% WACC cuts the value per share by about 16%.

cards.topic: The full EV-to-equity bridge: minorities, associates, pensions, leases, preferred, trapped cash
cards.question: A company has a diluted market cap of 2,000, gross debt of 900, lease liabilities of 150, an unfunded pension deficit of 100, preferred shares of 50, minority interests of 120, a stake in an associate worth 80, cash of 300 and non-operating investments of 40. What is its enterprise value? Why do you add minority interests but subtract associates?
cards.answer: EV is the value of the **operating business** to all capital providers, so I add every claim that is not common equity and subtract every asset that is not part of the operations. Here: $2{,}000 + 900 + 150 + 100 + 50 + 120 - 80 - 300 - 40 =$ **2,900**. Leases and the pension deficit are debt-like: fixed obligations to non-shareholders. **Minority interests** are added because the company consolidates 100% of subsidiaries it controls, so its EBITDA includes the share of profit that belongs to outside shareholders of those subsidiaries; the EV must include their claim to be consistent with that EBITDA. **Associates**, stakes of about 20-50% without control, are the mirror image: they are not consolidated, only a share of their net income appears below EBITDA, so their value is not captured by EV/EBITDA and is subtracted. The rule behind everything is **consistency**: whatever is in the denominator of the multiple must be in the numerator, and nothing else. I would also check whether part of the cash is trapped or needed to run the business; if 50 is operating cash, EV becomes 2,950.

follow_ups.q: Should the pension deficit be taken before or after tax?
follow_ups.a: Often after tax, because contributions to fill the deficit are tax-deductible, so the true cost is the deficit times one minus the tax rate. Practice varies; what matters is being consistent with how pension costs are treated in EBITDA.

follow_ups.q: Are convertible bonds debt or equity in the bridge?
follow_ups.a: It depends on moneyness: if the conversion price is below the share price, treat them as converted and add the new shares to the diluted count; if they are out of the money, treat them as debt at face or market value. Never both.

follow_ups.q: What about a big litigation provision?
follow_ups.a: If it is a probable cash outflow not reflected in the cash flows, treat the expected after-tax amount as a debt-like item and add it to EV (or subtract it from equity value).

prerequisites: Diluted shares and the treasury stock method

cards.topic: Valuing a loss-making company: which multiple when EBITDA is negative
cards.question: How do you value a company with negative EBITDA and negative earnings, for example a fast-growing software company? Why can such companies be worth billions?
cards.answer: A negative multiple means nothing, so I move **up the income statement** or **forward in time**. First, **EV/Revenue**, usually on next-twelve-months revenue, adjusted for growth and gross margin: with forward revenue of 280 and peers at 8x, the EV is about **2,240**. For software, **EV/ARR** (annual recurring revenue) or EV/gross profit are finer, because a sale at 80% gross margin is worth far more than one at 30%. Second, a **forward multiple discounted back**: if the plan shows EBITDA of 90 in three years and mature peers trade at 15x, the EV in three years is 1,350, about **960 today** at a 12% cost of capital. Third, a **DCF with a long explicit horizon**, ten years or more, since all the value is in the later years when margins mature. Such companies are worth billions because investors pay for **future** cash flows: losses today are often investment, like customer acquisition, expensed rather than capitalised. The danger is that these valuations are mostly terminal value and very sensitive to rates, so I would cross-check with operating metrics like the rule of 40 and unit economics.

follow_ups.q: Why did unprofitable tech fall more than the market when rates rose in 2022?
follow_ups.a: All their value is in distant cash flows, so they have a very long equity duration: a higher discount rate hits distant flows much harder, exactly like a long zero-coupon bond.

follow_ups.q: What would you use for a pre-revenue biotech?
follow_ups.a: A risk-adjusted NPV: model the cash flows of each drug if approved, multiply by the probability of success at each trial phase, discount, and subtract the R&D costs; sum across the pipeline and add net cash.

follow_ups.q: Is EV/Revenue ever used for profitable companies?
follow_ups.a: Yes, as a cross-check or in sectors where margins are temporarily depressed, like a cyclical at the bottom of the cycle, but you must adjust for margin differences between peers.

cards.topic: Trading comps vs precedent transactions: control premium, synergies and timing
cards.question: What is the difference between trading comparables and precedent transactions? A target has EBITDA of 150; peers trade at 9x forward EBITDA and past takeovers in the sector were done at 11x LTM EBITDA. What range would you give, and why do precedents usually give a higher value?
cards.answer: **Trading comps** value the company at the multiples of similar listed companies today: they give the price of a **minority stake** that changes hands on the stock market. **Precedent transactions** use the multiples paid in past acquisitions of similar companies: they give the price of **control**. Here, comps give $9 \times 150 =$ **1,350** of EV and precedents $11 \times 150 =$ **1,650**, 22% more. Precedents are higher for three reasons. First, the **control premium**: an acquirer must pay shareholders more than the market price, typically 20-40%, to convince them to sell. Second, **synergies**: a strategic buyer can cut costs or grow revenue in a way a stand-alone company cannot, and competitive auctions give part of that to the seller. Third, **timing and data**: deals cluster at market peaks and are quoted on LTM numbers, which are lower than forward ones, so the multiple looks higher. For a minority investment I anchor on comps; for a takeover I anchor on precedents, adjusted for today's market level.

follow_ups.q: Why do cash deals often carry higher premia than stock deals?
follow_ups.a: In a stock deal target shareholders keep exposure to the combined firm, including synergies, so they accept a lower headline premium; in cash they are bought out and demand to be paid up front. Cash is also a signal that the buyer believes its own shares are not overvalued.

follow_ups.q: Can the market price already include a premium?
follow_ups.a: Yes, if takeover rumours or a known strategic review have pushed the price up. That is why premia are measured against the undisturbed price, before any leak.

follow_ups.q: Who usually pays more, a strategic buyer or a private equity fund?
follow_ups.a: Usually the strategic, because it can pay for synergies; the fund is capped by the price that still gives it its target IRR. In periods of cheap debt, sponsors have sometimes outbid strategics.

prerequisites: Comparable company analysis and sum-of-the-parts valuation (conglomerate discount)

cards.topic: Why buyers use EV/EBITDA, not P/E, for LBO and M&A targets
cards.question: Why do private equity funds and acquirers price targets on EV/EBITDA rather than on P/E? Two targets have identical operations, EBITDA 100 and D&A 20, but one has no debt and the other has 400 of debt at 5%; both have an EV of 800. Compare their multiples.
cards.answer: Because the buyer purchases the **whole business and replaces its financing**. The P/E depends on the target's current capital structure, which the buyer will throw away: in an LBO the old debt is refinanced and new debt is sized as a multiple of EBITDA. EV/EBITDA prices the operations independently of how they are financed. In the example, both have an EV/EBITDA of **8x**. But the debt-free one earns $80 \times 0.75 = 60$ and trades at a P/E of $800/60 =$ **13.3x**, while the levered one earns $(80 - 20) \times 0.75 = 45$ on an equity value of 400, a P/E of **8.9x**. Same business, two very different P/Es: only leverage differs. There are three more reasons: EBITDA is a proxy for the cash that can service the new debt, banks lend in turns of EBITDA, typically 4 to 6 turns, and EBITDA is before tax and depreciation, which will change anyway with the new structure and the purchase price allocation. The caveat: EBITDA ignores capex, so for capital-intensive targets I would also look at EV/(EBITDA − capex).

follow_ups.q: Then why do listed acquirers still care about P/E?
follow_ups.a: Because the market watches the acquirer's EPS: buying a company at a lower P/E than your own, financed with stock, is EPS-accretive. It says nothing about value creation, but it affects how the deal is received.

follow_ups.q: What leverage is typical in an LBO?
follow_ups.a: It depends on the credit cycle and the sector; roughly 4 to 7 turns of EBITDA for large buyouts, with stable, cash-generative businesses at the top of the range.

prerequisites: LBO: mechanics, returns and the private equity model

cards.topic: Justified multiples: what EV/EBITDA and P/E should a company trade at?
cards.question: Where does a multiple come from? A company will make EBITDA of 100 next year, with D&A of 20, a 25% tax rate, 3% perpetual growth and a 12% return on new invested capital; its WACC is 8%. What EV/EBITDA is it worth? What happens if growth rises to 4%, or if the return on capital falls to the WACC? And how is EV/Sales linked to EV/EBITDA?
cards.answer: A multiple is a **compressed DCF**: for a company in steady state, $EV = FCFF_1/(WACC-g)$, so dividing by EBITDA gives a **justified multiple** driven by four things: tax, capital intensity, growth and the return on capital. Here EBIT is 80, NOPAT 60. To grow 3% with a 12% return on new capital, it must reinvest $g/ROIC = 25\%$ of NOPAT, so **FCFF is 45**, and $EV = 45/(8\%-3\%) = 900$, i.e. **9.0x EBITDA** (11.25x EBIT). At **4% growth** it must reinvest a third of NOPAT, FCFF falls to 40, but the denominator falls to 4%: **10.0x**. If the return on capital falls to **8%, the WACC**, the multiple is **7.5x whatever the growth rate**: growth then creates no value. Finally, $EV/Sales = EV/EBITDA \times$ EBITDA margin: with a 25% margin, 9x EBITDA is 2.25x sales. So a high multiple is justified only by high growth **combined with** high returns on capital, or by a low cost of capital.

follow_ups.q: What is the equivalent formula for the P/E?
follow_ups.a: Same logic on the equity side: $P/E_1 = (1 - g/ROE)/(K_e - g)$, where $g/ROE$ is the retention ratio needed to grow. With $K_e$ 9%, ROE 15% and g 3%, P/E is 13.3x.

follow_ups.q: Why can a company with negative growth still trade at a decent multiple?
follow_ups.a: If it stops reinvesting, it can pay out more than its NOPAT (it releases capital as it shrinks), so FCFF can exceed NOPAT; with g negative the denominator WACC - g is larger, but the cash yield is high. Tobacco and legacy telecoms are examples.

follow_ups.q: Is 7.5x a floor for the stock?
follow_ups.a: Only for this WACC, tax and D&A profile and if management invests at ROIC = WACC. A management that destroys value (ROIC below WACC while growing) pushes the value below NOPAT/WACC, which is why capital allocation matters for low-return businesses.

prerequisites: ROIC vs WACC and value creation

cards.topic: Is a P/E of 15 high? Justified P/E, PEG and the market multiple (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: A stock trades at 15 times earnings. Is that expensive? How would you decide, and what is the PEG ratio?
cards.answer: On its own, 15x means nothing: it has to be compared with **what the company deserves and what the alternatives pay**. First, the market: the S&P 500 trades at about **19.2x forward earnings as of 25 Sept 2026** (FactSet), so 15x is below the market, but Energy trades around 13x and Financials around 14.5x, so for a bank 15x is full. Second, fundamentals: the justified forward P/E is $(1 - g/ROE)/(K_e - g)$; with a 9% cost of equity and a 15% ROE, 3% growth justifies **13.3x** and 5% growth **16.7x**, so 15x prices growth of about 4%. Third, growth-adjusted: the **PEG** is the P/E divided by expected EPS growth in percent; 15x with 10% growth is a PEG of 1.5, with 20% growth 0.75, which looks cheap. Finally I check the quality of the "E": one-offs, cyclicality (a cyclical at peak earnings looks cheap on P/E just before profits fall) and trailing vs forward. So: 15x is expensive for a no-growth, low-return business and cheap for a high-ROE compounder.

follow_ups.q: Why is the trailing S&P 500 P/E so much higher than the forward?
follow_ups.a: Because analysts expect strong earnings growth: at the same price, higher next-year EPS gives a lower multiple. As of late Sept 2026 FactSet shows about 25.8x trailing vs 19.2x forward, so the market is pricing that growth being delivered.

follow_ups.q: What is the P/E of a company with negative earnings?
follow_ups.a: Not meaningful: you move to EV/Sales, EV/gross profit or a DCF, or you use P/E on a future year when earnings turn positive, discounted back.

follow_ups.q: Does a buyback change the P/E?
follow_ups.a: If the stock is bought at a P/E above the inverse of the after-tax yield on cash, EPS falls; below, EPS rises. The P/E itself only changes if the market re-rates; value per share only rises if the shares were bought below intrinsic value.

cards.topic: Terminal value consistency: the value driver formula, RONIC and the implied exit multiple
cards.question: Your DCF uses a Gordon terminal value: NOPAT next year 100, WACC 8%, perpetual growth 2%. A colleague computes the terminal value as 100 divided by 6%. What is wrong, what should it be if new investments earn 10%, and how do you check that a terminal value is reasonable?
cards.answer: The colleague treats **NOPAT as free cash flow**, i.e. assumes the company grows 2% a year forever **without investing**. That is growth for free, and it overstates the value: $100/6\% = 1{,}667$. Growth must be paid for: with a 10% return on new capital, growing 2% requires reinvesting $g/RONIC = 20\%$ of NOPAT, so the free cash flow is 80 and the terminal value **1,333**, 20% less. This is the **value driver formula**: $TV = NOPAT_{T+1}(1 - g/RONIC)/(WACC - g)$. The key special case: if new investments earn exactly the WACC, $TV = NOPAT/WACC = 1{,}250$ **whatever the growth rate**, which is what McKinsey recommends as a conservative default for mature firms, since competition pushes returns towards the cost of capital. To sanity-check a terminal value I look at three things: the **implied exit multiple** versus peers, the **share of EV** coming from the terminal value, and whether the final-year reinvestment is consistent with the growth assumed.

follow_ups.q: Why would competition push RONIC towards WACC?
follow_ups.a: Excess returns attract entrants and imitators, so without a durable moat (brand, network effects, patents, scale) returns on new projects converge to the cost of capital. Existing capital can keep earning its high return; the assumption only concerns new investment.

follow_ups.q: Gordon gives 1,333 but the exit multiple gives 1,800. Which do you trust?
follow_ups.a: Neither blindly: the gap means the market multiple embeds more growth, higher returns or a lower discount rate than my perpetuity. I back out the growth implied by 1,800 and ask whether it is plausible; if peers trade on a cyclical high, I trust the Gordon more.

follow_ups.q: Can g be negative in the terminal value?
follow_ups.a: Yes, for a declining business (legacy media, coal). Then the company releases capital as it shrinks, so free cash flow can exceed NOPAT, and TV = FCF/(WACC - g) with g below zero.

prerequisites: ROIC vs WACC and value creation
DCF with numbers: a five-year build from revenue to price per share

cards.topic: DCF sensitivity tables: WACC vs growth and WACC vs exit multiple
cards.question: Your DCF gives 21.1 per share with a 9% WACC and 2.5% terminal growth. How do you build and read a sensitivity table, what does it look like here, and why is it not symmetric?
cards.answer: A sensitivity table recomputes the value per share for a grid of the two assumptions that matter most, typically **WACC on one axis and terminal growth on the other** (or WACC vs exit multiple when the TV comes from a multiple). On the base case of the DCF card, the grid from 8% to 10% WACC and 1.5% to 3.5% growth goes from about **15.7 per share** (10%, 1.5%) to **31.4** (8%, 3.5%), around the base of **21.1**. Reading it: one point more WACC takes the value down about **16%** to 17.7, one point more growth takes it up about **18%** to 24.8. It is **not symmetric** because the terminal value is $FCF/(WACC - g)$, a convex function of the spread: as WACC approaches g the value explodes, so the upside corner is much further away than the downside corner. And it is amplified at the equity level because net debt is fixed. The table turns one fake-precise number into a **range**, and you present the central box, not the corners.

follow_ups.q: Why is the equity value more sensitive than the EV?
follow_ups.a: Net debt is fixed, so a given percentage change in EV is a larger percentage change in the residual equity: here equity is 82% of EV, so a 10% move in EV is about a 12% move in equity. That is operating leverage's cousin, financial leverage.

follow_ups.q: What is a tornado chart?
follow_ups.a: A bar chart ranking inputs by how much the output moves when each is flexed alone between a low and a high value. It shows which assumption deserves the most diligence.

follow_ups.q: Is a Monte Carlo DCF better?
follow_ups.a: It gives a distribution rather than a grid, but it needs joint distributions of inputs that are hard to estimate, and it can give false comfort. Most desks use scenarios plus a grid.

prerequisites: DCF with numbers: a five-year build from revenue to price per share

cards.topic: Reverse DCF: what growth is the market pricing?
cards.question: A high-growth stock trades at 40 times earnings. The cost of equity is 9% and a mature company in its sector trades at 18 times earnings. What earnings growth over the next 10 years does the current price imply? How would you use this with a client?
cards.answer: A **reverse DCF** takes the price as given and solves for the assumption, usually growth, that makes the DCF equal to it. Simple version: assume the company reinvests everything for 10 years and is then a mature 18x company. Today's price is 40 times today's earnings, and it must equal the year-10 value, $18 \times E_0(1+g)^{10}$, discounted at 9%. So $(1+g)^{10} = (40/18) \times 1.09^{10}$, which gives **g ≈ 18% a year for ten years**, i.e. earnings multiplied by about 5.3. Another angle: in a single-stage Gordon model with a 20% ROE, a 40x forward P/E implies about **7.4% growth forever**. With a client, the question becomes concrete: "to justify today's price, earnings must grow 18% a year for a decade: has any company of this size done that, and do you believe this one will?". It avoids arguing about a target price and focuses the debate on one testable number.

follow_ups.q: What if the exit P/E is 25 instead of 18?
follow_ups.a: Then $1+g = 1.09 \times (40/25)^{0.1} = 1.09 \times 1.0481$, so g is about 14.2%: the implied growth is very sensitive to where you assume the multiple ends up, so state it explicitly.

follow_ups.q: How does Damodaran compute the implied equity risk premium?
follow_ups.a: He takes the index level, expected cash returned to shareholders (dividends plus buybacks) and consensus earnings growth, solves for the discount rate that equates them to the index, and subtracts the Treasury yield. It is a reverse DCF on the whole market; he estimated about 4.1% on 1 Sept 2026.

follow_ups.q: Is a reverse DCF a valuation?
follow_ups.a: No, it is a diagnostic: it tells you what is priced in. You still need your own view of the drivers to conclude cheap or expensive.

cards.topic: Cost of debt in practice: marginal yield, default risk, and what the tax shield is really worth
cards.question: A company issued a 3% bond in 2021 that now trades at 86.6 with five years left, a yield of 6.2%. It has 500 of debt and pays 25% tax. What cost of debt do you put in the WACC, what is the tax shield worth, and when does the tax shield disappear?
cards.answer: The cost of debt in a WACC is the **marginal** rate at which the company could borrow **today**, not the historical coupon: the bond trades at 86.6, so the market yield is **6.2%**, not 3%. After tax that is $6.2\% \times 0.75 = 4.65\%$. For investment-grade issuers the yield is close to the expected cost; for high yield it overstates it, because the yield is a **promised** return: a B-rated issuer yielding 8.5% with a 4% annual default probability and 40% recovery has an expected cost of about 6%. The **tax shield** is the tax saved because interest is deductible: on 500 of debt at a market rate of about 6%, $500 \times 6\% \times 25\% = 7.5$ a year (less today, since the old bond only pays a 3% coupon). If the debt is permanent and as risky as the debt itself, its value is $t \times D = 125$; if debt moves with firm value, it is discounted at the unlevered cost of capital and is worth less, about 83 at 9%. It shrinks or disappears when the company has **no taxable profit**, or when interest exceeds the deductibility cap: **30% of EBITDA** in the EU (ATAD) and again in the US since 2025.

follow_ups.q: Should you use the yield on short-term or long-term debt?
follow_ups.a: Long-term, to match the horizon of the cash flows and the risk-free rate you use in the cost of equity. If the company only has floating bank debt, use the swap rate to the relevant maturity plus its margin.

follow_ups.q: Why is the after-tax cost of debt below the risk-free rate sometimes?
follow_ups.a: Because the tax shield can bring it there: 6.2% x 0.75 = 4.65%, below the 5.2% Treasury. It is not a free lunch: equity holders bear more risk as leverage rises, so the cost of equity rises.

follow_ups.q: How do you get a cost of debt for a private company?
follow_ups.a: Estimate a synthetic rating from its interest coverage and leverage, compare with rated peers, and add the corresponding spread to the risk-free rate; or use the margin on its bank facilities.

prerequisites: Cost of equity and cost of debt
Credit metrics: leverage, coverage and relative value

cards.topic: The WACC curve: how leverage changes the cost of capital, with numbers
cards.question: Debt is cheaper than equity, so why doesn't a company lower its WACC by borrowing more and more? Show how the WACC moves with leverage for a company with an unlevered beta of 0.9 (risk-free 5.2%, ERP 4.1%, tax 25%): where is the minimum, and what does the calculation leave out?
cards.answer: Because every extra unit of debt makes **both** sources of capital more expensive. As leverage rises, the equity becomes riskier, so the **levered beta and the cost of equity rise**; and lenders demand a **higher spread** as the rating falls. At first the tax shield wins: with an unlevered beta of 0.9, the WACC falls from **8.9%** with no debt (cost of equity = unlevered cost) to about **8.5% at 30% debt-to-capital**, where the company is roughly BBB. Beyond that, the spread jumps as the company drops to high yield and the cost of equity climbs steeply: the WACC is back to **8.9% at 50%** and **9.6% at 60%**. So the WACC curve is a **flat U**: the optimum is where the marginal tax benefit equals the marginal cost of distress risk. In value terms the move from 0% to 30% debt is worth about 6.5% of EV for a company growing 2%, useful but not huge, which is why most investment-grade companies target BBB/A rather than maximum leverage. Without taxes and distress costs, Modigliani-Miller says the WACC would be **flat**. The calculation leaves out direct **distress costs** hitting the cash flows, the value of **flexibility**, limits on interest deductibility, and signalling and agency effects.

follow_ups.q: Why do tech companies often carry little or no debt?
follow_ups.a: Their value is in intangibles and growth options that do not support borrowing, cash flows can be volatile, distress would destroy the franchise, and many have little taxable income early on. The tax shield is worth little relative to the flexibility they lose.

follow_ups.q: Why can a leveraged buyout work if the optimum is around BBB?
follow_ups.a: Sponsors accept higher distress risk in exchange for the tax shield, the discipline of debt on management, and equity returns amplified by leverage; they also pick stable, cash-generative businesses where distress costs are lower.

follow_ups.q: What does MM say about the WACC without taxes?
follow_ups.a: It is constant: the cost of equity rises linearly with D/E exactly enough to offset the cheaper debt, so the value of the firm does not depend on how it is financed.

follow_ups.q: Is the WACC minimum the same as the value maximum?
follow_ups.a: Yes when the free cash flows do not depend on leverage, since value is FCF discounted at the WACC. If distress hurts operations (lost customers, underinvestment), cash flows fall at high leverage and the value maximum sits at even lower debt.

follow_ups.q: How would higher risk-free rates change the optimal leverage?
follow_ups.a: Each unit of debt then carries more interest, so the tax shield per unit is larger, but coverage ratios fall and rating thresholds bite at lower debt levels. In practice companies de-lever when rates rise, because coverage-based rating metrics tighten.

cards.topic: Multiple consistency: numerator and denominator must match (IFRS 16, minorities, associates)
cards.question: A retailer has a market cap of 3,000, net debt of 1,000 and EBITDA of 500 before IFRS 16. It pays 100 a year of rent for 5 years (lease discount rate 5%). Under IFRS 16 its EBITDA becomes 600. A screen shows it at 6.7x EV/EBITDA against peers at 8x. Is it cheap? What is the general rule?
cards.answer: The rule: **the numerator and the denominator of a multiple must cover the same claims and the same perimeter**. Under IFRS 16, rent is no longer an operating expense: it becomes depreciation plus interest, so EBITDA rises to 600, but a **lease liability** of about **433** (100 a year for five years at 5%) appears in net debt. The screen divides the old EV of 4,000 by the new EBITDA of 600, hence **6.7x: it mixes a pre-IFRS 16 EV with a post-IFRS 16 EBITDA**. Consistently, either 4,000 / 500 = **8.0x** (pre-IFRS 16, rent inside EBITDA) or 4,433 / 600 = **7.4x** (post, leases as debt). And the peers must be on the same basis: US companies under ASC 842 keep operating lease expense in EBITDA, so compare them on the pre-IFRS 16 basis. So it is not cheaper than peers at 8x until I know which basis they are on. The same logic applies elsewhere: EV includes minorities, so EBITDA must include 100% of subsidiaries; associates are not in EBITDA, so their value is taken out of EV; P/E uses net income **after** minorities.

follow_ups.q: Does IFRS 16 change the value of the company?
follow_ups.a: No: cash flows are unchanged, only their labels move. A DCF on post-IFRS 16 FCFF must subtract the lease liability in the bridge (and account for lease renewals); a pre-IFRS 16 DCF keeps rent in the cash flows and ignores the liability. Done consistently, both give the same equity value.

follow_ups.q: Why do retailers' net debt/EBITDA ratios change with IFRS 16?
follow_ups.a: Both terms rise, but the lease debt is several times the rent while EBITDA rises only by the rent, so leverage ratios usually go up. That is why covenants are often defined on a frozen-GAAP or pre-IFRS 16 basis.

follow_ups.q: Which multiple avoids the lease issue for comparisons?
follow_ups.a: EV/EBITDAaL or EV/EBIT with leases treated consistently, or equity multiples like P/E, which are almost unaffected by IFRS 16 over the life of the lease.

prerequisites: The full EV-to-equity bridge: minorities, associates, pensions, leases, preferred, trapped cash

cards.topic: LTM, NTM and calendarisation: putting multiples on the same period
cards.question: What do LTM and NTM mean? A company's EBITDA was 400 in FY2025 (December year-end), 190 in H1 2025 and 220 in H1 2026: what is its LTM EBITDA? A peer has a March year-end: how do you compare them? And which multiple do you use for a fast-growing company?
cards.answer: **LTM** (last twelve months, also TTM) is the most recent four quarters of actual results; **NTM** (next twelve months) is the forecast for the coming four quarters. LTM = last full fiscal year + year-to-date current − same period last year: $400 + 220 - 190 =$ **430** for the twelve months to June 2026. For a peer with a **March year-end**, I **calendarise**: calendar 2026 = 3 months of fiscal year to March 2026 + 9 months of fiscal year to March 2027. With 300 and 360, that is $0.25 \times 300 + 0.75 \times 360 =$ **345**. NTM works the same way: at the end of September 2026, NTM = one quarter of FY2026 plus three quarters of FY2027. **LTM** is factual and is the standard for **precedent transactions** and credit metrics; **NTM or forward** multiples are the standard in **equity research and trading comps**, because prices look forward, and for fast growers LTM multiples look absurdly high. The key is that every company in a table is on the **same period** and the same definition.

follow_ups.q: Why is the NTM multiple of a growing company lower than its LTM multiple?
follow_ups.a: Same EV, bigger denominator: forecast EBITDA is higher than trailing EBITDA. The difference is roughly the expected growth rate.

follow_ups.q: What is a 'blended forward' multiple?
follow_ups.a: Another name for the NTM approach: the time-weighted average of FY1 and FY2 so that the forward window always covers the next 12 months, which avoids jumps when the fiscal year rolls over.

follow_ups.q: What does 'LTM adjusted EBITDA with run-rate synergies' mean in a leveraged loan?
follow_ups.a: The sponsor adds back one-offs and expected cost savings to reported EBITDA, which lowers the reported leverage ratio. Credit investors scrutinise these add-backs because aggressive adjustments hide true leverage.

prerequisites: Trading comps vs precedent transactions: control premium, synergies and timing

cards.topic: Auditing a DCF: the ten most common mistakes
cards.question: I give you a colleague's DCF. What would you check first, and what are the most common mistakes you would look for?
cards.answer: I check it in the order value is created. **Cash flows**: FCFF must be unlevered, so no interest deducted; tax on EBIT, not on pre-tax profit; the change in working capital, not its level; capex consistent with growth. **Terminal value**: it is often 70% of the value, so I check the final year is steady state, growth below nominal GDP, reinvestment consistent with growth (the RONIC check) and the implied exit multiple versus peers. **Discounting**: WACC with market-value target weights, a marginal cost of debt, a relevered beta, the TV discounted by the right number of years, and the mid-year convention applied consistently. **Consistency**: nominal cash flows with a nominal rate, same currency and inflation in both, FCFF with WACC, FCFE with cost of equity. **Bridge**: all debt-like items subtracted (leases, pensions, minorities, preferred), non-operating assets added, diluted shares with the treasury stock method. Then I compare the result with multiples and the share price: if it is 50% away, I find out which assumption explains it.

follow_ups.q: Which single check gives you the most information in 30 seconds?
follow_ups.a: The implied exit multiple of the terminal value and its share of EV: if the TV is 90% of value at 15x EBITDA for a mature business, the problem is almost certainly there.

follow_ups.q: Is it wrong to deduct stock-based compensation from cash flows?
follow_ups.a: No, it is the conservative and arguably correct treatment: SBC is a real cost paid in shares. The error is to add it back as non-cash and ignore the future dilution.

follow_ups.q: Should the cost of equity be used with FCFF if the company has almost no debt?
follow_ups.a: With no debt the WACC equals the cost of equity, so it makes no difference. The mismatch matters when leverage is material.

prerequisites: DCF with numbers: a five-year build from revenue to price per share
Terminal value consistency: the value driver formula, RONIC and the implied exit multiple

cards.topic: Sector multiples today: orders of magnitude and why they differ (as of 2026)
cards.question: Roughly what EV/EBITDA and P/E do different sectors trade at today? Why does software trade at 20-25x EBITDA and a telecom operator at 6-7x?
cards.answer: Orders of magnitude for the US market: Damodaran's January 2026 data give EV/EBITDA of about **24.5x for software**, **35x for semiconductors**, **15x for pharma**, **13-14x for utilities and household products**, **8-9x for integrated oil and basic chemicals** and **6.5x for telecom services**, with the whole market around **17x excluding financials**. On P/E, the S&P 500 trades at about **19.2x forward** (FactSet, 25 Sept 2026), from **13.3x for Energy** and **14.5x for Financials** to about **23x for Consumer Discretionary and Industrials**. The differences are the justified-multiple formula at work: **growth, return on capital, capital intensity and risk**. Software grows fast with high margins and very little capex, so almost all EBITDA converts into free cash flow. A telecom operator grows about as fast as inflation, spends a large share of EBITDA on networks and spectrum and carries a lot of debt, so each unit of EBITDA is worth much less. Cyclicals like oil and chemicals get low multiples on current earnings because the market expects them to mean-revert.

follow_ups.q: Why do semiconductors trade even higher than software?
follow_ups.a: The market is pricing very strong earnings growth from AI-related demand for the leaders, and the aggregate is dominated by a few very large companies with exceptional growth; on forward earnings the gap is smaller than on trailing EBITDA.

follow_ups.q: Why is a utility's multiple sensitive to bond yields?
follow_ups.a: Its cash flows are stable and long-dated, like a bond, and its investors often buy it for yield. When government yields rise, its dividend yield must rise too, so its price and multiple fall.

follow_ups.q: What multiple would you use for an oil company?
follow_ups.a: EV/EBITDA or EV/DACF on mid-cycle prices, plus reserve-based metrics (EV per barrel of reserves) and NAV of the assets; P/E is too sensitive to the oil price and impairments.

prerequisites: Justified multiples: what EV/EBITDA and P/E should a company trade at?

cards.topic: LBO analysis as a valuation floor: what can a sponsor pay?
cards.question: Why do bankers include an LBO analysis in a valuation football field? A target has EBITDA of 100, expected to reach 130 in five years. Lenders will give 5x EBITDA of debt, the sponsor expects to exit at 9x with 250 of debt left, and needs a 20% IRR. What is the maximum price it can pay?
cards.answer: Because it answers a different question from a DCF: **what price can a financial buyer pay and still earn its target return?** It gives a practical **floor** for a sale process: if a sponsor can pay 8.7x, a strategic buyer who bids less will be outbid. The calculation runs backwards. At exit, EV is $9 \times 130 = 1{,}170$; minus 250 of remaining debt, the **equity is worth 920**. To earn 20% a year for five years, the sponsor can put in at most $920/1.2^5 \approx$ **370** of equity today. Add the **500 of debt** the lenders provide and the **maximum enterprise value is about 870, 8.7x EBITDA**. At a 25% target IRR it falls to about 800 (8.0x), at 15% it rises to about 960 (9.6x). So the LBO price is driven by **debt capacity, target IRR and exit multiple**, not by the WACC. It is usually below strategic values because sponsors have no synergies and a high required return, which is why it works as the floor of the range.

follow_ups.q: What happens to the LBO value if the sponsor can borrow 6x instead of 5x?
follow_ups.a: More debt at entry directly increases the price at the same equity cheque, but also more interest and less deleveraging, so exit debt is higher. Net, the price usually rises, at the cost of higher risk and a lower margin of safety.

follow_ups.q: Why do sponsors target IRR and also a money multiple?
follow_ups.a: IRR rewards speed (a quick flip can show a high IRR on a small gain), while limited partners are paid in cash multiples. Funds therefore look at both: for example 20% IRR and at least 2.5x in five years.

follow_ups.q: How would you present the LBO range on the football field?
follow_ups.a: As a bar from the EV at a 25% IRR to the EV at a 15-20% IRR, for a range of leverage, e.g. 8.0x to 9.6x here, next to the comps, precedents and DCF ranges.

prerequisites: LBO: mechanics, returns and the private equity model
Paper LBO: worked example in 10 minutes

cards.topic: WACC circularity: why the weights depend on the answer, and how to solve it
cards.question: You value a private company that will keep a fixed 600 of debt. Its FCFF next year is 100, growing 2% a year; unlevered beta 0.9, risk-free 5.2%, ERP 4.1%, pre-tax cost of debt 6.2%, tax 25%. Why is the WACC circular here, and how do you solve it?
cards.answer: The WACC needs the **market value weights** $D/V$ and $E/V$, and the relevered beta needs $D/E$; but for a private company the equity value $E$ is exactly what we are trying to find. So the input depends on the output: a **circular reference**. I solve it by **iteration**: guess a weight, compute the WACC and the value, recompute the weight, and repeat until it stops moving. Starting from 30% debt, the WACC is 8.45% and EV 1,551, so equity 951 and $D/V$ is actually 38.7%; with that, beta rises, the WACC falls to 8.32% and EV to 1,582; after three or four rounds it converges to **D/V ≈ 38%, WACC ≈ 8.33%, EV ≈ 1,580, equity ≈ 980**. Using the guessed 30% would have understated value by about 2% on EV and 3% on equity. Alternatives: a **target** capital structure from peers (no circularity, the usual choice), Excel's iterative calculation, or the **APV** method, which values the tax shield separately and needs no weights at all.

follow_ups.q: Why does the iteration converge so quickly here?
follow_ups.a: The WACC is not very sensitive to leverage in this range (the curve is flat near the optimum), so a change in D/V produces a much smaller change in value and then in D/V: the map is a strong contraction.

follow_ups.q: Is the circularity a problem for a listed company?
follow_ups.a: Much less: you observe the market value of equity, so you can use current market weights, or better a target structure. The circularity is mainly for private companies, targets in M&A and LBO models.

follow_ups.q: How do you avoid circularity in an LBO model interest calculation?
follow_ups.a: Compute interest on the opening debt balance of each period, or turn on iterative calculation with an on/off switch cell so the model can be reset if it breaks.

prerequisites: The WACC curve: how leverage changes the cost of capital, with numbers

cards.topic: APV (adjusted present value): valuing the tax shield separately
cards.question: What is the adjusted present value method and when do you prefer it to a WACC-based DCF? A company has FCFF of 100 next year growing 2%, an unlevered cost of capital of 9%, 600 of permanent debt and a 25% tax rate. What is it worth? What changes for an LBO whose debt is repaid over five years?
cards.answer: APV splits the value into **the business as if all-equity financed, plus the value of financing side effects**: $APV = V_U + PV(\text{tax shields}) - PV(\text{expected distress costs})$, plus any subsidised financing or issue costs. Here the unlevered value is $100/(9\% - 2\%) = 1{,}429$. With 600 of **permanent** debt, the tax shield is $t \times K_d \times D$ every year; discounted at the cost of debt, its PV is simply $t \times D =$ **150**. So APV ≈ **1,579**, which corresponds to an implied WACC of about 8.3%. I prefer APV when the **debt is fixed in amount or follows a schedule** rather than a constant share of value: LBOs, project finance, a company changing its capital structure. For an LBO paying down 500 of 8% debt by 100 a year, the tax shields are 10, 8, 6, 4, 2 and worth only about **25**: the WACC approach with a constant leverage ratio would get this badly wrong. The APV also makes the sources of value transparent: operations vs financing.

follow_ups.q: Why discount the tax shield at the cost of debt?
follow_ups.a: If the amount of debt is fixed, the shield is as certain as the interest payments themselves, so it has the risk of the debt. If the company keeps debt at a constant share of firm value, the debt and its shields move with firm value and should be discounted at the unlevered cost of capital.

follow_ups.q: Does APV give the same answer as the WACC method?
follow_ups.a: Yes, if both use the same debt policy and consistent inputs. They differ in practice because the standard WACC DCF assumes a constant D/V while APV usually uses a fixed schedule.

follow_ups.q: What other financing side effects could you add?
follow_ups.a: Subsidised government loans (PV of the interest saved), issue costs (subtract), and hedging benefits. APV lets you value each separately.

prerequisites: Cost of debt in practice: marginal yield, default risk, and what the tax shield is really worth
LBO: mechanics, returns and the private equity model

cards.topic: Valuing a bank with a two-stage dividend discount model and P/TBV
cards.question: Value a bank with book value of 50 per share, a sustainable ROE of 12% and a 10% cost of equity. For five years it grows its balance sheet 8% a year, then 3% forever. What is the share worth, and what price-to-book does that imply? Why not a DCF on free cash flow?
cards.answer: For a bank, debt is raw material, not financing, so I value **the equity directly**, from the dividends it can pay while keeping enough capital. Growth has to be funded by retained earnings: to grow book value 8% with a 12% ROE the bank retains $8/12 = 2/3$ of earnings and pays out one third; in steady state at 3% growth it retains a quarter and pays out **75%**. Earnings per share start at 6.0 (12% of 50) and grow 8% a year, so dividends go 2.00, 2.16, 2.33, 2.52, 2.72, worth **8.8** today. At the end of year 5, book value is 73.5 and the bank is in steady state, so its value is $P/B \times BV$ with $P/B = (ROE - g)/(K_e - g) = 9/7 = 1.29$: **94.5**, or 58.7 today. The total is about **67.4 per share, 1.35x book** and 11.2x forward earnings. The P/B is above 1 because ROE exceeds the cost of equity; a bank earning 8% would trade below book. A free-cash-flow DCF fails because deposits and loans are the business itself, so "unlevered cash flow" and "net debt" have no meaning.

follow_ups.q: Why P/TBV rather than P/E for banks?
follow_ups.a: Book value is marked close to market for much of the balance sheet and is what regulators constrain, so value creation shows up as ROTE vs cost of equity relative to tangible book. P/E is also used, but earnings are volatile through the credit cycle.

follow_ups.q: How do share buybacks fit in the DDM?
follow_ups.a: Treat total distributions (dividends plus buybacks) as the cash returned to shareholders, or equivalently value total equity and divide by the current share count. What matters is the excess capital distributed, not its form.

follow_ups.q: What would you use for an insurer?
follow_ups.a: Also equity-based: P/E, P/B, dividend models, and embedded value (EV) or the Solvency II own funds for life insurers, with the solvency ratio playing the role of CET1.

prerequisites: Bank ROE, ROTE, ROA, DuPont and P/TBV
Bank balance sheet: why banks are different

cards.topic: Stub periods and the mid-year convention for the terminal value
cards.question: You value a company on 30 September 2026. Its December year-end FCFF is forecast at 120 for 2026, then 130, 140, 150 and 160 for 2027-2030; WACC 9%. How do you discount the cash flows, and should the terminal value be discounted with the mid-year convention?
cards.answer: Two adjustments. First, the **stub period**: on 30 September, three quarters of 2026 have already happened and belong to the past, so I only count the **last quarter**, 30 (a quarter of 120), received over the next 0.25 year. Then FY2027 is a full year ending 1.25 years away, FY2028 2.25 years, and so on. With the **mid-year convention**, each flow is discounted to the middle of its own period: the stub at 0.125 year, 2027 at 0.75, 2028 at 1.75, up to 2030 at 3.75. The PV of the flows is about **506**, versus 486 with end-of-period discounting. Second, the **terminal value**, which sits at the end of 2030, 4.25 years away. A **Gordon** TV is a perpetuity of mid-year flows, so it is discounted at **3.75 years** too: $TV = 160 \times 1.025/6.5\% = 2{,}523$, PV about **1,826**. An **exit-multiple** TV is a price paid on a date, at the end of 2030, so it is discounted at the full **4.25 years**: at 9x EBITDA of 250 that is 2,250, PV about **1,560**. Pulling the exit-multiple TV forward half a year overstates EV by about 3%.

follow_ups.q: What if the company is seasonal, like a retailer earning most of its cash in Q4?
follow_ups.a: The mid-year convention then misstates timing; you can use quarterly flows or a weighted cash-flow date. In the stub, the Q4 share may be much more than a quarter of the annual flow.

follow_ups.q: Why does the mid-year convention matter more at high discount rates?
follow_ups.a: Its effect is a factor of about the square root of (1 + WACC): 4.4% of value at 9%, about 7% at 15%, so it matters for emerging-market or venture-style valuations.

follow_ups.q: Which net debt do you use with a 30 September valuation date?
follow_ups.a: The balance sheet at the valuation date, e.g. the September quarter-end, since the cash generated in the first three quarters of 2026 is already in it.

prerequisites: DCF practicalities: horizon, mid-year convention, when not to use it
DCF with numbers: a five-year build from revenue to price per share

cards.topic: Emerging-market valuation: country risk premium and currency consistency (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: How do you estimate the cost of equity for a Brazilian company? Do you do the DCF in dollars or in reais, and how do you make sure the two give the same answer?
cards.answer: I add a **country risk premium** to the equity risk premium. Damodaran's January 2026 data give Brazil (Ba1) a sovereign **default spread of 2.13%**, scaled up by the relative volatility of equities to bonds (about 1.5x) into a **CRP of 3.24%**, so a total ERP of **7.47%** versus 4.23% for a mature market. In **dollars**, with the US 10-year at about 5.2% as of 30 Sept 2026 and a beta of 1.0, the cost of equity is about **12.7%**. For a DCF in **reais**, the key rule is that **cash flows and discount rate must carry the same inflation**. One way: convert the dollar rate with the inflation differential, $(1 + K_{USD}) \times (1 + \pi_{BRL})/(1 + \pi_{USD}) - 1$: with 4.5% vs 2.5% expected inflation, about **14.9%**. The other way starts from local yields: the Brazilian 10-year yields about **14.4%** (early Sept 2026, with the Selic at 13.75%), which minus the default spread gives a local risk-free of 12.3% and a cost of equity near **19.7%**. The gap tells you the market expects far more than 2% of annual BRL depreciation: you must project reais cash flows with inflation consistent with the rate you choose, or discount dollar cash flows converted at **forward FX rates**. Done consistently, both routes give the same value.

follow_ups.q: Should the CRP depend on where the company is listed or where it operates?
follow_ups.a: Where it operates, i.e. where its revenues and assets are exposed. Damodaran's lambda approach scales the CRP by that exposure, so a Brazilian-listed exporter gets less than a domestic Brazilian bank, and a US multinational with big Brazilian sales gets some.

follow_ups.q: Why is the CRP larger than the sovereign default spread?
follow_ups.a: Because equity markets are more volatile than government bonds: Damodaran multiplies the default spread by the ratio of equity to bond volatility, about 1.5 in his January 2026 data.

follow_ups.q: How would you convert a BRL DCF into USD?
follow_ups.a: Convert each year's BRL cash flow at the forward FX rate for that year (from interest rate parity) and discount at the USD rate, or discount in BRL and convert the result at spot. Both give the same USD value if the rates are consistent.

prerequisites: WACC with today's market inputs (USD vs EUR, as of Sept 2026)

cards.topic: Strategic vs financial buyers: who can pay more
cards.question: What is the difference between a strategic buyer and a financial buyer? In an auction, who can usually pay more for the same company, and why?
cards.answer: A **strategic buyer** is a company in the same or a related industry: it buys to combine the target with its own business. A **financial buyer** is a private equity fund: it buys the company as a standalone investment, finances it largely with debt and plans to sell it in 3-7 years. Strategics can **usually pay more** because they can count **synergies** in their price: cost savings and extra revenue that only exist once the two businesses are combined. A sponsor's maximum price is instead set by the **return it must earn**: it works backwards from a target IRR of around 20%, a debt capacity and an exit multiple. In my example, a company earning 100 of EBITDA and worth 9x is worth about **1,020 to a strategic** with 15 of synergies, but a sponsor needing 20% cannot pay much more than **about 8.5x, 855**. Sponsors win when there are few strategic buyers, when credit is cheap and plentiful, when the business is a carve-out that strategics don't want, or when they already own a platform and can add their own synergies in a **buy-and-build**.

follow_ups.q: Why might a seller prefer a sponsor even at a slightly lower price?
follow_ups.a: Certainty and speed: fewer antitrust issues, no shareholder vote on the buyer side, committed financing, and sometimes management wants the equity incentive package a sponsor offers. Sellers compare risk-adjusted value, not headline price.

follow_ups.q: What is a secondary buyout?
follow_ups.a: A sale from one private equity fund to another. It is a common exit when IPO markets are shut. Critics argue the second sponsor has less left to improve, so returns rely more on leverage and multiples.

follow_ups.q: How do rising rates affect this competition?
follow_ups.a: They hit sponsors more: the interest bill eats cash that would have repaid debt, lenders allow less leverage, and the exit multiple may fall. Strategics paying partly in stock or from balance sheet cash are less affected.

prerequisites: LBO: mechanics, returns and the private equity model

cards.topic: Paper LBO: worked example in 10 minutes
cards.question: Do a paper LBO: a sponsor buys a company with EBITDA of 100 at 10x, pays 20 of fees, and funds it with 5x debt at 8%. EBITDA grows 10% a year, D&A equals capex at 20, tax is 25% and it exits after 5 years at 10x. What are the MoM and IRR, and where does the return come from?
cards.answer: **Sources and uses**: the price is 1,000 plus 20 of fees, so 1,020 of uses, funded by **500 of debt** and **520 of equity**. EBITDA grows from 100 to about **161** in year 5. Free cash flow is net income plus D&A minus capex, so here just net income, $(EBITDA - D\&A - interest)(1-t)$: 37.5 in year 1 rising to about 89 in year 5, and it all repays debt, which falls from 500 to about **192**. At exit, EV is 10 × 161 = **1,611**, so equity is 1,611 − 192 = **1,418**. That is **2.7x the money** and an IRR of about **22%**, since 2.7x over five years is between 2.5x (20%) and 3x (25%). Of the 898 gain, about **611 comes from EBITDA growth** at a constant multiple, **308 from debt paydown**, and the 20 of fees is a drag. There is no multiple expansion. If the exit multiple falls to 8x, the IRR drops to about 16%, so the exit multiple is the key risk.

follow_ups.q: What happens to the IRR if the sponsor adds a dividend recap in year 2?
follow_ups.a: The IRR rises because cash comes back earlier, even if the total MoM barely changes or falls slightly (more interest). Funds judged on IRR like recaps; lenders dislike them because leverage goes back up.

follow_ups.q: How would you raise the IRR without changing the business plan?
follow_ups.a: More leverage at entry (smaller equity cheque), cheaper debt, a lower entry price, an earlier exit, or a recap. Each raises risk or depends on the market, which is why investors look at the returns bridge.

follow_ups.q: Why is the interest bill falling over time?
follow_ups.a: Because the cash sweep repays debt each year, so interest is charged on a smaller balance. That leaves more cash to repay debt the following year, which accelerates deleveraging.

prerequisites: LBO: mechanics, returns and the private equity model

cards.topic: Debt or equity? Pecking order, signalling and market timing
cards.question: When should a company issue debt rather than equity? And why does a company's share price usually fall when it announces a new share issue?
cards.answer: A company should prefer **debt** when it has **stable, predictable cash flows**, taxable profits to use the **interest tax shield**, **low existing leverage** and headroom under its rating, and assets it can pledge. It should prefer **equity** when it is already highly levered, when its cash flows are volatile or it is loss-making (so no tax benefit and high distress risk), when it is investing in risky growth, or when its **shares look expensive**. Beyond this trade-off, the **pecking order** theory says firms finance first with **retained cash**, then **debt**, and **equity last**, because of **asymmetric information**: managers know more than investors. If management issues shares, investors infer the shares are probably **overvalued**, since managers would not sell underpriced stock. So the price falls on the announcement, historically by a few percent in US studies, while debt issues barely move the price. That is also why firms issue equity after strong share price rises (**market timing**), and why convertibles, which are part-debt, are popular for firms whose stock investors struggle to value.

follow_ups.q: Why do some very profitable companies have almost no debt?
follow_ups.a: Pecking order: they fund everything with internal cash. They may also value flexibility for acquisitions, fear rating downgrades, or operate in volatile industries such as tech, where distress costs of debt are high.

follow_ups.q: Why might a stock rise when a company announces a debt-financed buyback?
follow_ups.a: It signals management thinks the shares are cheap, commits cash that could have been wasted (free cash flow problem), and adds a tax shield. The effect is the mirror image of an equity issue.

follow_ups.q: Is a rights issue better than a placement for signalling?
follow_ups.a: A rights issue lets existing shareholders buy the new shares pro rata, so no value is transferred to outsiders even at a discount. It limits the dilution problem, but it is slower and signals a need for capital, often in distress.

cards.topic: Cash vs stock deals: risk sharing, exchange ratios and collars
cards.question: An acquirer can pay for a target in cash or in its own shares. How does the choice change who bears the risk of the deal? Explain fixed exchange ratios, fixed-value offers and collars.
cards.answer: In a **cash deal**, target shareholders receive a fixed amount and walk away: the acquirer's shareholders keep **all the upside and all the risk** of the synergies. In a **stock deal**, target shareholders become shareholders of the combined company, so the two groups **share the risk**: if synergies disappoint, the target's holders lose part of the premium too. Example: the acquirer is worth 50 a share with 100m shares; it pays 25 for 40m target shares trading at 20, a premium of 200. If synergies are worth 300, a cash deal gives acquirer shareholders +100, a stock deal gives them only +83. With no synergies at all, the cash deal costs them 200, the stock deal only 167. With a **fixed exchange ratio**, say 0.5 acquirer share per target share, the number of shares is fixed and the value received moves with the acquirer's price. With a **fixed value**, the price per target share is fixed and the number of shares issued floats. A **collar** mixes both: fixed value inside a price band, fixed ratio outside it. Choice also sends a signal: paying in stock suggests the acquirer thinks its own shares are expensive or is unsure about the synergies.

follow_ups.q: In a fixed-ratio stock deal, how does a merger arbitrageur hedge?
follow_ups.a: Buy one target share and short the exchange ratio in acquirer shares (0.5 here). The position earns the spread between the target's price and 0.5 times the acquirer's price if the deal closes, and is roughly neutral to general market moves.

follow_ups.q: Why do acquirer shares often fall on the announcement of a stock deal?
follow_ups.a: Signalling (management thinks its stock is expensive), the risk of overpaying, arbitrage short selling, and the dilution overhang from new shares arriving.

follow_ups.q: What is a walk-away right in a collar?
follow_ups.a: If the acquirer's price falls far below the collar, the target can terminate (or the acquirer can if it rises far above). It caps the risk of a deal whose value has moved a long way from what the boards agreed.

cards.topic: Valuing synergies and the maximum premium
cards.question: An acquirer expects 60 a year of run-rate cost synergies, phased in over three years, with one-off integration costs of 60. Tax is 25% and the discount rate is 8%. How much are the synergies worth, and what is the maximum premium it should pay?
cards.answer: I value synergies like a project: after-tax cash flows, phased in, minus the one-off costs to achieve them, discounted. Phasing one third, two thirds, then 100% of 60, with the 60 of costs split over years 1 and 2, gives after-tax flows of **−7.5, +7.5 and +45**, then 45 a year forever. The perpetuity from year 4 is 45 / 8% = 562.5 at the end of year 3, about **447 today**, and the whole package is worth about **482**. Ignoring phasing and costs, 45 / 8% = 562.5 would overstate it by 17%. So the **maximum premium** is about 480: paying more destroys value for the acquirer's shareholders, however accretive the deal looks. In practice the acquirer should pay much less, since **revenue synergies** are less reliable, costs overrun, and paying away all the synergies leaves no reward for the integration risk. A target market cap of 1,000 with a 30% premium, 300, leaves the acquirer with an NPV of about 180 if everything is delivered.

follow_ups.q: How can you back out what the market thinks of the synergies?
follow_ups.a: Compare the change in combined market value (acquirer plus target) around the announcement with the premium. If the combined value rises by 200 while the premium is 300, the market values the net synergies at about 200 and thinks the acquirer overpaid by about 100.

follow_ups.q: Why are revenue synergies discounted more heavily?
follow_ups.a: They depend on customers' behaviour, on competitors' responses and on integrating sales forces, which often fails. Cost synergies are largely under management's control, such as closing an office.

cards.topic: Analysing an announced acquisition like an investor
cards.question: You cover a USD 1bn-revenue US listed company with 15% operating margins. It announces the acquisition of a USD 500m-revenue private company in Canada. Once you know roughly what it paid, what else does your investor want to know?
cards.answer: First, **what multiple** it paid versus its own multiple and the sector: at 1.5x sales, USD 750m, that is 15x EBIT if the target earns a 10% margin, which I would compare with the acquirer's own trading multiple. Then **how it pays**: cash on hand, new debt or shares. If fully debt-funded, pro forma leverage goes to about **3x EBITDA** from zero, so the investor asks about the **rating**, covenants and the dividend or buyback. Third, **accretion**: at a 6% cost of debt the deal adds about 3% to EPS before synergies, but accretion is not value creation, so I would compare the target's return on the price, about 5% after tax, with the acquirer's cost of capital. Fourth, the **synergies**: cost or revenue, timeline, integration costs. Then the **strategic logic** and the business: growth, margins, customer concentration, why a private company sold. Finally the **cross-border risks**: CAD currency exposure and hedging, tax, **Investment Canada Act** and antitrust approvals, management retention, earn-outs, and the timeline to closing.

follow_ups.q: Why might the acquirer's share price rise even though the deal is dilutive?
follow_ups.a: Dilution in year 1 can be outweighed by long-term value: strong growth, strategic position, or synergies that come later. The market prices NPV, not year-1 EPS.

follow_ups.q: What is a deal-contingent FX hedge?
follow_ups.a: A forward that only settles if the acquisition closes. It lets the acquirer lock in the exchange rate for the purchase price without being left with a naked FX position if regulators block the deal; the bank charges a premium for that contingency.

prerequisites: Credit metrics: leverage, coverage and relative value
ROIC vs WACC and value creation

cards.topic: Breakeven synergies: why an accretive deal can still destroy value
cards.question: An acquirer earns 500 of net income, has 100m shares at 75 (P/E 15). It buys a target earning 100 that is worth 1,200, paying a 30% premium. What are the breakeven synergies for an all-stock deal? The same deal financed with debt at 5% is accretive with no synergies: does that mean it creates value?
cards.answer: The offer is **1,560**, so the acquirer pays **15.6x** the target's earnings with shares valued at **15x**: in an all-stock deal it must issue 20.8m shares and EPS falls from 5.00 to about **4.97, 0.7% dilutive**. The **breakeven synergies** are the extra earnings that bring EPS back to 5.00: pro forma net income must reach 5 x 120.8m = 604, so **4 after tax, about 5.3 pre-tax** at a 25% tax rate. With debt at 5%, the after-tax cost is 3.75% while the target yields 1/15.6 = 6.4% on the price paid, so EPS rises **8.3%** with no synergies. But **accretion is not value creation**. The acquirer paid a **premium of 360** over fair value; the deal creates value only if the present value of synergies exceeds 360. At an 8% discount rate that means about **29 a year after tax, 38 pre-tax, forever**, seven times the EPS breakeven. Debt looks cheap in EPS terms only because it ignores the extra risk it puts on shareholders: leverage raises the cost of equity, so the P/E should fall.

follow_ups.q: Why do boards still care about accretion if it is not value?
follow_ups.a: Management pay and market communication are often tied to EPS, and analysts screen on it. A dilutive deal is harder to sell to shareholders even if NPV is positive, so bankers show both: accretion by year and ROIC vs WACC by year 3.

follow_ups.q: When is an all-stock deal accretive?
follow_ups.a: When the P/E paid for the target (offer price / target earnings, including synergies) is lower than the acquirer's own P/E. A high-P/E acquirer can buy lower-P/E targets accretively, which is the 'bootstrapping' trap of 1960s conglomerates.

follow_ups.q: The acquirer's shares fall 5% on announcement. What does it tell you?
follow_ups.a: The market thinks the premium exceeds the value of synergies. Here 5% of 7,500 is 375, close to the 360 premium: the market is pricing roughly zero net synergies.

prerequisites: Valuing synergies and the maximum premium

cards.topic: Higher rates and the cost of capital: what it does to valuations and deals (as of Sept 2026)
cards.question: How does the current interest rate environment affect companies' cost of capital, valuations and deal activity?
cards.answer: As of **Sept 2026** rates are going **up again**: the Fed hiked 25bp on 16 Sept to **3.75-4.00%**, its first hike since 2023, the ECB hiked on 10 Sept to a **2.50%** deposit rate, and the US 10-year yield is around **5.2%**, the highest in about 19 years. A higher risk-free rate raises **both** the cost of debt and the cost of equity, so WACC goes up almost one for one if spreads and the equity risk premium stay put. Valuations fall, and long-duration growth companies fall most: with 2.5% growth, a WACC going from 8% to 9% cuts a perpetuity value by **15%**. For **LBOs**, floating-rate debt becomes expensive: at 10x EBITDA with 5x debt, interest coverage falls from **4.0x at 5% to 2.7x at 7.5%**, sponsors pay down less debt and must put in more equity or pay lower prices. For **M&A**, the valuation gap between buyers and sellers widens and sponsor exits slow. Strategic buyers with strong balance sheets and stock to use gain the edge. Companies also face refinancing debt issued cheaply in 2020-21, and the EUR versus USD rate gap makes euro funding relatively cheap for global issuers.

follow_ups.q: Why can a 10-year yield rise while the Fed only hiked 25bp?
follow_ups.a: The 10-year reflects expected future short rates plus a term premium. Higher inflation expectations, heavy government and corporate bond supply and uncertainty about policy raise the term premium, so long yields can rise more than the policy rate.

follow_ups.q: Which sectors are most hurt by higher rates?
follow_ups.a: Long-duration equities (unprofitable tech, biotech), highly levered sectors (real estate, utilities, LBO-owned companies with floating debt) and bond proxies with stable dividends. Banks can benefit through higher net interest margins, as long as credit losses stay contained.

follow_ups.q: Would you advise a client to issue fixed or floating debt now?
follow_ups.a: It depends on its view and risk tolerance: fixing locks in today's high long rates; floating is cheaper if cuts come but exposes it to further hikes. Many issue fixed and swap part to floating, or issue floating with caps.

prerequisites: LBO: mechanics, returns and the private equity model

cards.topic: IRR vs money multiple and the LBO value creation bridge
cards.question: A sponsor buys a company at 10x EBITDA of 100 with 600 of debt and 400 of equity. After five years EBITDA is 140, the exit multiple is 11x and net debt is 300. What are the money multiple and the IRR, and where did the gain come from? Why would a fund care about both measures?
cards.answer: Exit enterprise value is 140 x 11 = 1,540; minus 300 of net debt, equity is worth **1,240**, so the **money multiple (MoM or MOIC) is 3.1x** and the **IRR is 3.1^(1/5) - 1, about 25%**. The gain of 840 splits into three sources: **EBITDA growth** 40 x 10 = 400, **multiple expansion** 1 x 140 = 140, and **debt paydown** 600 - 300 = 300. The MoM says **how much** money you made; the IRR says **how fast**. The same 2.5x is 36% a year over three years but only 14% over seven, so IRR rewards quick exits and early distributions. For example a **dividend recap** of 200 in year 2 lifts the IRR to about 29% even if the total cash back falls to 3.0x. That is why LPs look at both: a high IRR on a small, short deal returns little money, while a high MoM over ten years may barely beat the stock market.

follow_ups.q: Which lever do LPs value most?
follow_ups.a: EBITDA growth driven by operations, because it is repeatable skill. Multiple expansion is market luck and deleveraging mostly rewards leverage risk. Funds that can show value creation beyond leverage and multiples raise money more easily.

follow_ups.q: Can the IRR be high while the fund loses money overall?
follow_ups.a: Deal by deal yes: a small quick deal at 60% IRR adds little money while a large deal at 0.8x loses a lot. Pooled at fund level, the IRR weights by timing, so LPs also look at the fund's TVPI and DPI.

follow_ups.q: What is a quick way to compute IRR for 2x over 4 years?
follow_ups.a: The fourth root of 2: 2^0.25 is about 1.19, so about 19%. Or rule of 72: 72/4 = 18%.

prerequisites: LBO: mechanics, returns and the private equity model

cards.topic: LBO sources and uses and the debt tranches
cards.question: Build the sources and uses table for an LBO: target EBITDA 200, bought at 10x EV with 500 of existing net debt to refinance, 2% transaction fees, 30 of financing fees and 30 of cash left on balance sheet, 5x total leverage. Which debt instruments would you use, in what order of seniority?
cards.answer: **Uses** are what the money pays for: equity to the sellers **1,500** (EV 2,000 minus 500 of net debt), **refinancing** the existing debt 500, **transaction fees** 40, **financing fees** 30 and 30 of **cash** to the balance sheet: total **2,100**. **Sources** must match: debt of 5 x 200 = **1,000**, say a **Term Loan B** of 700 (3.5x) and **senior notes** of 300 (1.5x), plus an undrawn **revolver**; the rest, **1,100**, is equity, 1,050 from the sponsor and 50 **rolled over** by management, so equity is about **52%** of the total. The capital structure goes from most senior and cheapest to most junior and most expensive: **revolver and term loan A** (banks, secured, amortising), **Term Loan B** (institutional investors like CLOs, secured, floating, 1% amortisation, covenant-lite), **second lien**, **high yield bonds** (fixed coupon, incurrence covenants, non-call period), then **mezzanine or holdco PIK notes**, then equity. Today a **private credit unitranche** often replaces the whole debt stack in one loan at a higher spread.

follow_ups.q: Why do sponsors like covenant-lite TLBs?
follow_ups.a: There are no maintenance tests, so a bad quarter cannot trigger a default; lenders only have incurrence covenants that bite when the company takes an action, like more debt or a dividend. It gives the sponsor time and flexibility, at the cost of lower recoveries for lenders.

follow_ups.q: Why capitalise financing fees but expense transaction fees?
follow_ups.a: Financing fees are a cost of obtaining the debt, so they are spread over its life like extra interest; advisory fees are a cost of the acquisition and are expensed (or, historically, capitalised into goodwill). For the cash equity cheque both must be funded at closing.

follow_ups.q: What happens to the TLB if the Fed hikes 100bp?
follow_ups.a: Interest rises by 1% of 700, i.e. 7, cutting coverage from 2.6x to about 2.4x; that is why sponsors often buy interest rate caps or swaps on part of the floating debt.

prerequisites: LBO: mechanics, returns and the private equity model
Recovery waterfall and the fulcrum security

cards.topic: What makes a good LBO target and how much debt it can carry
cards.question: What makes a company a good LBO candidate? For a target with EBITDA 200, capex 40 and working capital needs of 10 a year, how would you estimate the maximum debt it can carry if lenders want interest coverage of at least 2x at an 8% interest rate and the market allows at most 5.5x leverage?
cards.answer: A good LBO target can **service a lot of debt safely**: stable, predictable **free cash flow** (recurring revenue, non-cyclical demand), **low capex** and working capital needs, a strong market position with pricing power, a clean balance sheet, a good management team, room to **cut costs** or grow by add-ons, and a clear **exit route** to a strategic or another sponsor, all at a reasonable entry price. For **debt capacity**, I compute each lender constraint and take the tightest. Coverage: EBITDA of 200 at 2x allows 100 of interest, so 100 / 8% = **1,250** of debt. A coverage test on EBITDA minus capex at 1.5x would allow about **1,330**. The market cap of **5.5x EBITDA gives 1,100**, so that binds: the company can raise about **1,100**. I then check it can repay: interest 88, tax 18, capex 40 and working capital 10 leave about **44 of free cash flow**, 4% of the debt a year. That is thin, so a prudent structure would be nearer 5x.

follow_ups.q: Would a fast-growing software company be a good LBO target?
follow_ups.a: Historically no because it burns cash, but mature software with recurring revenue became a favourite target: high margins, low capex, sticky customers. Lenders then lend on annual recurring revenue (ARR loans) rather than EBITDA.

follow_ups.q: Why does the leverage multiple allowed by the market change over time?
follow_ups.a: It depends on investor demand (CLO formation, private credit fundraising, HY fund flows), base rates and default expectations. In 2021 good credits got 6-7x; after the 2022 rate shock it fell to about 5x.

follow_ups.q: How does a revolver help?
follow_ups.a: It covers seasonal working capital swings so the company does not breach liquidity; it is senior and usually has the only maintenance covenant.

prerequisites: LBO: mechanics, returns and the private equity model
Credit metrics: leverage, coverage and relative value

cards.topic: The sell-side M&A process: auction, rounds, locked box
cards.question: Walk me through a sell-side M&A process. Why would a seller run an auction rather than negotiate with one buyer, and what is a locked-box mechanism?
cards.answer: A sell-side process usually takes **4 to 9 months**. In **preparation** the bank builds the equity story, the model, a **teaser** (anonymous one-pager) and an **information memorandum**, often with vendor due diligence. In the **first round** it contacts a list of strategics and sponsors, who sign an NDA and submit **non-binding indicative offers**. A shortlist of maybe **3 to 6** goes to the **second round**: data room access, management presentations, confirmatory due diligence, and **binding offers** with a mark-up of the sale agreement (**SPA**) and financing commitments. The seller then negotiates with the preferred bidder, **signs**, and **closes** after regulatory approvals such as antitrust. An **auction** creates competition, so it maximises price and terms, while a **bilateral** negotiation is faster, more confidential and suits a single natural buyer. In a **locked-box** deal, common in Europe, the price is fixed on a past balance sheet date and the seller promises no value **leaks** out afterwards. Price adjustments after closing are avoided, and the buyer usually pays a small daily **ticker** for the cash the business generates meanwhile.

follow_ups.q: Why would a buyer pay a break fee or accept a 'hell or high water' clause?
follow_ups.a: To make its bid more attractive to the seller by taking regulatory risk: it commits to accept remedies (divestments) or to pay the seller if antitrust blocks the deal. Sellers value certainty of closing, not just price.

follow_ups.q: Why do sell-side banks offer stapled financing?
follow_ups.a: It gives every sponsor a financing floor, speeding the process and supporting price. The bank also earns financing fees, which creates a conflict of interest that must be managed.

follow_ups.q: What is exclusivity and why does the seller resist it?
follow_ups.a: A period where the seller negotiates only with one bidder. It removes competitive pressure, so sellers grant it late and for short periods.

cards.topic: The IPO process and its alternatives: direct listing, SPAC, dual track
cards.question: Walk me through the IPO process. What are the alternatives, direct listing, SPAC merger, dual track, and why would a company choose one over another?
cards.answer: A traditional IPO takes about **4 to 6 months**. The company picks **bookrunners**, does due diligence and drafts the **prospectus** (an S-1 filed with the SEC in the US, approved by the regulator in Europe). Analysts from the syndicate publish research before the deal, and the banks **test investor demand** early. They announce the deal, set a **price range**, run a one- or two-week **roadshow** and **bookbuild**, then **price** and **allocate** the shares. After listing there is a **greenshoe** for stabilisation and a **lock-up** of about 180 days for existing holders. The fees are roughly **4-7%** of the proceeds in the US and **1.5-3%** in Europe. A **direct listing** just lists existing shares with no underwriting and no lock-up: it is cheaper, but it raises no (or little) new money and offers no price support, so it suits well-known companies that don't need cash, like Spotify in 2018. A **SPAC** is a listed cash shell that merges with a private company: it is faster and allows forecasts, but it is expensive because of the sponsor's **20% promote**, and if many shareholders redeem, little cash is left. **Dual track** means preparing an IPO and a sale at the same time to maximise the value and certainty of the exit.

follow_ups.q: Why are European IPO fees lower than US ones?
follow_ups.a: European deals are more competitive among banks, often larger per bank and sold mainly to institutions; the US 7% gross spread for mid-size IPOs is a long-standing convention. Very large US IPOs also pay much less than 7%.

follow_ups.q: What happens at lock-up expiry?
follow_ups.a: Insiders can sell, so supply increases; stocks often underperform around the expiry date, and banks may run a follow-on or block trade to sell insiders' shares in an orderly way.

follow_ups.q: What is a cornerstone investor?
follow_ups.a: An investor who commits before launch to buy a fixed amount at the IPO price, giving a signal of quality; common in Europe and Asia.

prerequisites: IPO pricing: bookbuilding, underpricing and the first-day pop

cards.topic: The M&A and private equity market today (as of 1 Oct 2026)
cards.question: What is going on in the M&A and private equity market right now, and what is driving it?
cards.answer: As of **end-September 2026** the story is **a record first half followed by a sharp Q3 slowdown**. In 1H26, global M&A reached about **USD 3.2tn, up 44%** year on year according to Mergermarket, the best first half on record. It was driven by **megadeals**: 48 deals of USD 10bn or more made up 42% of the value, and **strategic buyers** accounted for about 76% of it, while sponsor investment actually fell 6%. The recovery was **narrow**: BCG notes that deals below USD 1bn are still lagging.
